questions.stem: Regarding the minimum welding width in a batten (of a built-up compression member), which statement is correct?
options: The length of weld connecting each end of the batten should be less than one fourth the depth of the plate
The length of weld and the depth of the batten shall be measured perpendicular to the longitudinal axis of the member
The weld shall be returned only along the other two edges for a length less than the minimum lap
The length of weld connecting each end of the batten should be such that at least one third of its length is placed on each end
questions.solution:
**At least one third of the weld length should be placed on each end of the batten.**

**What a batten (batten plate or tie plate) does:**

> **A BUILT-UP compression member — two channels, two angles, four angles — is not a single section until its components are TIED TOGETHER.**

> **Battens (or lacing) connect the components so that the member buckles as ONE unit about the built-up axis, rather than each component buckling separately.**

> **If the connection fails, the member's capacity collapses to that of its individual components buckling alone**, which may be a small fraction of the built-up capacity. **So the batten connection is not a detail — it is what makes the built-up section exist.**

**Why the weld must be distributed to the ENDS:**

> **A batten transfers SHEAR between the components, and it does so as a rigid frame element — so it carries both shear and MOMENT at its connections.**

> **A moment is resisted by a couple, which needs the weld to be as far apart as possible.** Concentrating the weld at the middle of the batten's end gives almost no lever arm and the connection rotates.

> **Distributing at least one third of the weld length to each END of the batten gives the couple its lever arm.** That is the requirement, and it is why the code specifies a distribution rather than merely a total length.

**The IS 800 requirements for battens, which is the wider content:**

| Requirement | Value |
|---|---|
| **Effective DEPTH of end battens** | **Not less than the distance between centroids of the components, nor less than twice the width of the smaller component** |
| **Effective depth of intermediate battens** | **Not less than THREE QUARTERS of the above, and never less than twice the smaller component's width** |
| **THICKNESS of the batten** | **Not less than 1/50 of the distance between the innermost lines of welds or bolts** |
| **Number of battens** | **At least THREE — one at each end and one at mid-length** |
| **Design shear (transverse)** | **2.5 % of the axial force in the member, divided among the batten planes** |
| **Slenderness of components between battens** | **Not more than 50, nor more than 0.7 times the member's slenderness** |

> **The 2.5 per cent transverse shear is the one to remember**, and its logic is worth stating: **a real compression member is never perfectly straight, so a notional lateral force must be resisted.** Codes make that notional force explicit rather than leave it to judgement.

> **The requirement that the component slenderness between battens be at most 0.7 of the whole member's slenderness is the other key rule** — it guarantees the components cannot buckle locally before the member buckles overall. **That is the whole purpose of spacing the battens.**

**Why the distractors are wrong:**

| Option | Note |
|---|---|
| **Weld length LESS than one fourth the plate depth** | **Backwards — the code sets MINIMUMS, not maximums, on connection length. A shorter weld is weaker, not compliant** |
| **Measured perpendicular to the longitudinal axis** | **The depth of a batten IS measured perpendicular to the member axis — but the WELD length runs along the connected edges, so the statement conflates two dimensions** |
| **Returned only along the other two edges for a length less than the minimum lap** | **A garbled version of the end-return rule. Welds ARE returned round corners, for a length of TWICE the weld size, and "less than the minimum lap" is meaningless** |
| **At least one third on each end** | ✓ |

> **Option (a) is worth flagging because it inverts the direction of a code requirement**, and that is a general reading skill: **a clause that permits a connection to be SMALLER than a stated fraction is almost always a misreading of a minimum.**

**Battens versus lacing, since they are the two alternatives and are examined together:**

| | **BATTENS (tie plates)** | **LACING** |
|---|---|---|
| **Form** | **Solid plates at intervals** | **Diagonal bars or angles, single or double** |
| **Structural action** | **Acts as a rigid FRAME — carries shear AND moment** | **Acts as a TRUSS — members in axial force only** |
| **Analysis** | Frame analysis, moments at connections | Truss analysis, simpler |
| **Efficiency** | **Less efficient — moments are resisted in bending** | **MORE efficient — axial action only** |
| **Use** | Where lacing is impractical or the member is short | The usual choice for long columns |

> **Lacing is the more efficient system for the same reason a truss beats a beam: axial action uses the whole cross-section, while bending does not.** Battens are used where lacing cannot be fitted, and they are correspondingly heavier for the same duty.

> **And one rule that catches candidates: battens and lacing must NOT be mixed in the same plane of the same member**, because the two systems have different stiffnesses and would not share the shear as either analysis assumes.

examTip.trick: **A batten carries SHEAR AND MOMENT, and a moment needs a lever arm** — so the weld must be distributed to the ENDS of the batten, at least a third at each, not concentrated in the middle.
examTip.trap: **Option (a) inverts a code requirement.** Codes set MINIMUM connection lengths; a clause permitting something SMALLER than a stated fraction is almost always a misread minimum.
examTip.mnemonic: **Design battens for 2.5 % of the axial force as transverse shear** — the notional force from unavoidable out-of-straightness. And keep component slenderness between battens under **0.7 × the member's**, so components cannot buckle first.

questions.stem: The section modulus of a circle is:
questions.solution:
**Z = πd³/32.**

**The derivation, which is one division:**

> **SECTION MODULUS Z = I / y_max**

| Quantity | For a solid circle of diameter d |
|---|---|
| **I about the centroidal axis** | **πd⁴/64** |
| **y_max (centroid to extreme fibre)** | **d/2** |

> **Z = (πd⁴/64) ÷ (d/2) = (πd⁴/64) × (2/d) = πd³/32** ✓

**The DIMENSIONAL check settles this question in five seconds:**

> **I has dimensions of LENGTH⁴. Z has dimensions of LENGTH³**, because Z = I/y divides a fourth power by a first power.

| Option | Power of d | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| πd⁴/64 | **d⁴** | **Fails — that is I, not Z** ← |
| πd³/128 | d³ | Correct dimensions, wrong constant |
| **πd³/32** | **d³** | **Correct** ✓ |
| πd⁴/128 | **d⁴** | **Fails on dimensions** |

> **Two of the four options can be struck out on dimensions alone**, leaving a choice between the constants 32 and 128. **And the constant follows from 64 ÷ 2 = 32, since y_max is d/2 — the halving turns 64 into 32, not into 128.**

> **Option (a) is the designed trap: πd⁴/64 is the MOMENT OF INERTIA of a circle**, the formula a candidate is far more likely to have memorised. **The question asks for the section modulus, and the two differ by exactly one factor of d/2.**

**Why the section modulus matters — it is the property that carries the design:**

> **The bending stress formula is σ = M/Z.**

> **So Z is the single geometric number that converts a bending moment into a stress**, and comparing Z values compares sections directly for bending.

> **Which is why steel section tables list Z (and the plastic modulus Z_p) rather than only I** — a designer needs the stress, not the curvature.

**The section properties worth having memorised:**

| Section | I about centroid | y_max | Z |
|---|---|---|---|
| **RECTANGLE b × d** | **bd³/12** | **d/2** | **bd²/6** |
| **CIRCLE, diameter d** | **πd⁴/64** | **d/2** | **πd³/32** ← |
| **HOLLOW circle, D and d** | **π(D⁴−d⁴)/64** | **D/2** | **π(D⁴−d⁴)/32D** |
| **TRIANGLE, base b height h** | **bh³/36** | **2h/3** | **bh³/36 ÷ 2h/3 = bh²/24** |
| **SEMICIRCLE about its diameter** | **πd⁴/128** | — | — |

> **The triangle is the one to be careful with: its centroid is at h/3 from the base, so y_max is the LARGER distance 2h/3**, and Z = bh²/24 rather than bh²/12.

> **Note also that option (d) πd⁴/128 is the moment of inertia of a SEMICIRCLE about its diameter** — half of a full circle's πd⁴/64. **So three of the four options in this question are real formulae for other things, which is what makes it a good question rather than a guess.**

**And the plastic modulus, since limit-state design uses it:**

| Section | Elastic Z | PLASTIC Z_p | Shape factor Z_p/Z |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Rectangle** | **bd²/6** | **bd²/4** | **1.5** |
| **Circle** | **πd³/32** | **d³/6** | **1.70** |
| **Triangle** | bh²/24 | — | **2.34** |
| I-section | — | — | **~1.10-1.15** |

> **The SHAPE FACTOR measures how much reserve there is between first yield and full plastification**, and the pattern is instructive: **a rectangle and a circle have a great deal of material near the neutral axis doing little, so their shape factors are high; an I-section has almost none, so its shape factor is barely above 1.**

> **Which is the whole reason I-sections are used: they put the material where the stress is.** The low shape factor is not a defect — it is the sign of an already-efficient section.

examTip.trick: **Z = I/y_max = (πd⁴/64) ÷ (d/2) = πd³/32.** The halving turns 64 into 32 — not into 128.
examTip.trap: **Option (a) πd⁴/64 is the MOMENT OF INERTIA**, the formula more often memorised. **I is length⁴, Z is length³** — that dimensional check kills two options instantly. And πd⁴/128 in (d) is a SEMICIRCLE's I.
examTip.mnemonic: **σ = M/Z**, so Z is what converts a moment into a stress. Have the set: rectangle bd²/6, circle πd³/32, triangle bh²/24 (y_max = 2h/3, not h/3).

questions.stem: The moment of inertia of a rectangle of width b and depth d, about the centroidal axis parallel to the width, is:
questions.solution:
**bd³/12.**

**The rule that generates all four options:**

> **I = (dimension PARALLEL to the axis) × (dimension PERPENDICULAR to the axis)³ / 12**

> **The CUBED dimension is always the one measured PERPENDICULAR to the axis of bending** — because the further a fibre is from the axis, the more it contributes, and the contribution goes as the square of the distance integrated over the area.

> **Here the axis is parallel to the width b, so the depth d is the perpendicular dimension.** Hence **I = bd³/12.**

**How to read the four options — each is a real formula:**

| Option | What it is |
|---|---|
| **bd³/12** | ✓ **Rectangle, about the axis parallel to b (the usual bending axis)** |
| **bd³/36** | **The /36 denominator belongs to a TRIANGLE about its centroidal axis (bh³/36), not to a rectangle at all** ← |
| **db³/12** | **The SAME rectangle about the PERPENDICULAR centroidal axis — the weak axis, if d > b** |
| **db³/36** | Neither |

> **Option (c) db³/12 is the designed trap and it is a genuinely useful confusion to resolve**: it is the correct moment of inertia of the same rectangle about the *other* centroidal axis. **So the question is entirely about identifying which axis is meant.**

> **The two are the SAME formula with b and d exchanged**, and for a rectangle with d > b, db³/12 is the SMALLER — the weak axis, about which the section will buckle or deflect most.

**The related values for a rectangle, which must be kept apart:**

| Axis | I |
|---|---|
| **Centroidal, parallel to b** | **bd³/12** ← |
| **Centroidal, parallel to d** | **db³/12** |
| **Along the BASE (parallel axis theorem)** | **bd³/12 + bd(d/2)² = bd³/3** |
| Polar, about the centroid | **bd(b²+d²)/12** |

> **The bd³/3 for the base is worth having**, and it demonstrates the parallel axis theorem in its simplest form: **shifting the axis from the centroid to the base multiplies I by four.** That factor of four is why the centroid matters so much in compound sections.

**The general parallel axis theorem, since everything above follows from it:**

> **I_axis = I_centroid + A·d²**

> **Note that I is ALWAYS LEAST about the centroidal axis**, because A·d² is never negative. **So a computed I smaller than the centroidal value is an arithmetic error, and that check is free.**

**And why this particular formula is the most-used in structural engineering:**

> **Every beam of rectangular section — timber joists, RCC beams treated as gross sections, plate elements — uses bd³/12.**

> **The CUBE on the depth is the most consequential fact in beam design:**

| Change | Effect on I (and therefore on stiffness) |
|---|---|
| **Double the WIDTH** | **I × 2** |
| **Double the DEPTH** | **I × 8** |
| **Increase depth by 26 % (one size)** | **I × 2** |

> **Depth is eight times more effective than width, per unit of extra material in that direction.** Which is why beams are deep and narrow rather than wide and shallow, why an I-section puts its flanges as far apart as it can, and why the practical limit on beam depth is architectural (headroom) rather than structural.

> **And the corollary for section modulus: Z = bd²/6 goes as the SQUARE of the depth**, so doubling the depth quadruples the moment capacity while only doubling the material. **Stiffness gains by d³, strength by d² — both favour depth, and stiffness favours it more.**

verification.notes: The source stem read "Moment of inertia of a rectangle with respect to width is", which is loose - "with respect to width" does not name an axis unambiguously. The stem has been made explicit as the centroidal axis PARALLEL to the width, which is the reading under which the source's keyed answer (a) bd^3/12 is correct. The alternative reading gives db^3/12, which is option (c); the solution sets out both so the distinction is visible rather than hidden.

examTip.trick: **The CUBED dimension is always the one PERPENDICULAR to the axis.** Axis parallel to b, so d is cubed: bd³/12.
examTip.trap: **Option (c) db³/12 is the same rectangle about the OTHER centroidal axis** — the weak axis if d > b. The question is entirely about identifying which axis is meant. And /36 belongs to a TRIANGLE.
examTip.mnemonic: **Double the width, I × 2; double the DEPTH, I × 8.** Depth is eight times more effective. And **I is always LEAST about the centroidal axis**, since A·d² is never negative — a free check.

questions.stem: The vane shear test is done in:
questions.solution:
**Soft clays.**

**Why only soft cohesive soil:**

> **The vane must be PUSHED INTO the ground without excessive disturbance, and must then shear the soil on a clean cylindrical surface.**

> **Neither is possible in coarse-grained soil.** The vane cannot penetrate sand, shingle or gravel at all — and even if it could, **shearing them would be DRAINED, so there is no undrained shear strength to measure.**

> **That single observation disposes of three of the four options at once**, and it is the reasoning to reach for: **undrained shear strength is a concept for FINE-GRAINED soil.**

**The formula, since it is examined:**

> **c_u = T / [π D² (H/2 + D/6)]**  for a vane shearing on its sides and both ends

| Symbol | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **T** | **Torque at failure** |
| **D** | Vane diameter |
| **H** | **Vane height, usually H = 2D** |

> **The H/2 term accounts for the cylindrical SIDE surface and the D/6 for the two circular ENDS**, so the bracket is simply the sum of the three surfaces' resisting moments divided by πD².

> **Standard rotation rate: about 0.1° per second** — deliberately slow, so that the test is genuinely undrained and not merely fast.

**Why the test is valuable, and the argument is specific to soft clay:**

> **A soft clay is the soil most damaged by SAMPLING.** Pushed into a tube, transported, extruded and trimmed, it has already lost part of the strength it had in the ground.

> **The vane test measures the strength IN SITU, on soil nothing has been done to.**

> **So for a soft clay the vane may be MORE reliable than a laboratory test on a nominally good sample** — which is an unusual position for a field test to be in, and it is why the vane remains the reference method for soft-clay strength profiles.

> **It is also fast: a full strength-depth profile through a soft deposit in a day.**

**The correction that must be applied, and it is not small:**

> **c_u(design) = μ × c_u(vane)**, with Bjerrum's factor μ depending on plasticity index:

| Plasticity index | μ |
|---|---|
| **20** | **~1.0** |
| **40** | **~0.85** |
| **60** | **~0.75** |
| **100** | **~0.6** |

> **Two effects combine to make the vane overestimate: the shearing RATE is still far faster than a real embankment loads the ground, and the vane shears mostly on a VERTICAL surface while a foundation failure is largely horizontal (ANISOTROPY).**

> **A highly plastic clay needs up to a 40 per cent reduction.** The correction was established by back-analysing embankment failures that uncorrected vane strengths had declared stable — **so it is empirical in the strongest sense: it exists because structures fell down.**

**The bonus measurement, which no laboratory test gives as directly:**

> **After the peak, keep rotating rapidly through several revolutions to REMOULD the soil in place, then retest.**

> **The ratio (undisturbed ÷ remoulded) is the SENSITIVITY, measured in situ:**

| Sensitivity | Classification |
|---|---|
| **1 - 4** | Normal |
| **4 - 8** | Sensitive |
| **8 - 16** | Extra sensitive |
| **> 16** | **QUICK CLAY — loses nearly all strength on remoulding** |

> **A quick clay above 16 is almost a liquid once remoulded**, which is the mechanism of the Scandinavian and Canadian flow slides. **The engineering consequence is that any disturbance during sampling or construction destroys strength that cannot be recovered.**

**And which test suits which soil, as a pair worth holding:**

> **SPT for sand, VANE for soft clay.** They are complementary, and **neither works in the other's ground** — an SPT in soft clay gives N values of 0 to 2, which carry almost no information, and a vane in sand cannot be inserted.

examTip.trick: **Coarse sand, shingle and gravel fail for the SAME two reasons** — the vane cannot be inserted, and shearing them would be DRAINED, so they have no undrained strength. One observation kills three options.
examTip.trap: **The vane OVERESTIMATES design strength** — apply Bjerrum's μ, down to about 0.6 at a plasticity index of 100. The correction exists because embankments that uncorrected vane strengths called stable fell down.
examTip.mnemonic: **SPT for sand, VANE for soft clay** — neither works in the other's ground. And the vane's bonus: remould in place by rapid rotation, retest, and the ratio gives **SENSITIVITY** (over 16 = quick clay).

questions.stem: The Nepal Engineers' Association (NEA) is founded under which act?
options: Social Service Act of the Government of Nepal
questions.solution:
**The Social Service Act of the Government of Nepal.**

**Why an ASSOCIATION is registered under a social-service statute:**

> **The Nepal Engineers' Association is a VOLUNTARY PROFESSIONAL ASSOCIATION, not a regulator.** It exists to serve its members and to represent the profession.

> **A body of that kind is registered like any other non-governmental social organisation** — under the Social Service Act (and its successor, the Social Welfare Act 2049) — because it exercises no statutory power over anybody.

> **It does not license, does not discipline, and cannot prevent anyone from practising.** So it needs no Act of its own; it needs only to be lawfully registered.

**The contrast with the NEC, which is the whole point of the question:**

| | **NEC — Nepal Engineering Council** | **NEA — Nepal Engineers' Association** |
|---|---|---|
| **Created by** | **Its own statute: NEC Act 2055 (1998)** | **REGISTERED under the Social Service Act** ← |
| **Nature** | **STATUTORY REGULATOR, autonomous body** | **Voluntary association / NGO** |
| **Membership** | **COMPULSORY to practise** | **Voluntary** |
| **Function** | **Registration, licensing, examination, discipline, standards** | **Advocacy, welfare, CPD, technical events, representing members** |
| **Can it stop you practising?** | **YES — by refusing or removing registration** | **NO** |
| **Whose interest?** | **The PUBLIC's** | **The MEMBERS'** |

> **The last row is the deepest distinction: a regulator protects the public from bad engineering; an association advances the interests of engineers.** Both are legitimate, they are not the same job, and where they conflict the regulator must win — **which is precisely why they are separate bodies and why only one of them has its own Act.**

> **A body created BY statute has statutory powers. A body merely REGISTERED under a statute has none.** That is the general principle the question tests.

**Why the distractors are wrong:**

| Option | Note |
|---|---|
| **NEC Act 2055** | **Creates the COUNCIL, not the association.** The two are constantly confused, and this is the confusion in its plainest form ← |
| **NEA Act 1962** | **There is no such Act.** The NEA was founded in 1963 (2020 BS) but not by statute — the option invents an Act to match the association's name |
| **Social Service Act** | ✓ |
| **All of the above** | Cannot stand once the others are excluded |

> **Option (b) is a well-made distractor because it is exactly what a candidate would EXPECT to exist.** A national professional association surely has its own Act? **It does not, and noticing that absence is the insight.**

**The relationship between the two bodies, since they are not simply separate:**

> **The NEA is represented ON the Council.** Under the NEC Act, **members are DIRECTLY ELECTED to the Council from the Nepal Engineers' Association** — five of them, with a tenure of four years.

> **So the profession has a voice in its own regulation without controlling it**, which is the standard arrangement for professional regulation worldwide: **the regulator's board includes practitioners, elected by practitioners, alongside government appointees and lay members.**

> **That balance is deliberate.** A regulator composed entirely of practitioners risks becoming a guild that protects its members; one with no practitioners risks lacking the technical judgement to regulate at all.

**And the practical advice that follows:**

> **Registration with the NEC is a legal requirement to practise; membership of the NEA is not.**

> **A graduate must pass the NEC license examination and register.** Joining the NEA is optional and brings professional benefits — continuing education, technical divisions, publications, a professional network — **but no one is prevented from working by declining to join.**

> **Confusing the two has a real consequence: an engineer who joins the association and assumes they are thereby licensed is practising unlawfully.**

examTip.trick: **A body created BY statute has statutory powers; a body merely REGISTERED under a statute has none.** The NEC has its own Act; the NEA is registered like any social organisation.
examTip.trap: **Option (b) invents an "NEA Act 1962" — exactly the Act a candidate would EXPECT to exist.** It does not. Noticing the absence is the insight.
examTip.mnemonic: **NEC protects the PUBLIC and can stop you practising; NEA advances MEMBERS' interests and cannot.** But the NEA elects FIVE members onto the Council — a voice in regulation without control of it.

questions.stem: The first amendment of the NEC Act was on:
questions.solution:
**2079/05/05.**

**The legislative timeline of engineering regulation in Nepal:**

| Instrument | Year (BS) | Note |
|---|---|---|
| **Nepal Engineering Council ACT** | **2055 (1998 AD)** | **The primary statute — creates the Council** |
| **Nepal Engineering Council REGULATION (Rules)** | **2057** | **Subordinate legislation under the Act** |
| **FIRST AMENDMENT to the NEC Act** | **2079/05/05** | ← |

> **The set to hold is 2055 Act, 2057 Regulation, 2079 first amendment.** Those three dates answer most questions in this area, and this paper asks about two of them separately.

> **Note the gap: the Act stood UNAMENDED for twenty-four years.** That is worth remembering as a fact in itself, because it makes the 2079 date memorable rather than arbitrary — **there is only one amendment to place, not a series.**

**Why the ACT and the REGULATION have different dates, and it is not an accident:**

> **An Act is PRIMARY legislation, passed by the legislature.** It creates the body and states its powers in general terms.

> **A Regulation is SUBORDINATE legislation, framed by the Council and APPROVED by the Government of Nepal.** It supplies the operational detail: registration procedure, examination, fees, categories, disciplinary process.

> **The Regulation necessarily comes AFTER the Act, because the Act must first create the power to make it.** Two years elapsed here — which is normal, since the Council had to be constituted before it could frame rules.

> **So a question asking "when did the Council's regulation start" (2057) has a different answer from one asking "when was the Act passed" (2055)**, and both appear in this same paper. **Reading which is asked is half the mark.**

**Why the distractors are wrong:** **2066/10/07, 2075/11/19 and 2076/09/06 are plausible-looking Nepali dates with no standing in this statute's history.** The question tests a single recalled fact, and the defence is to hold the three-date set rather than to recognise one date among four.

**What the Council's structure looks like, since the Act and its amendment define it:**

| Position | Note |
|---|---|
| **CHAIRMAN** | Appointed by the Government of Nepal |
| **VICE CHAIRMAN** | **Qualification: B.E. plus 10 years of experience** |
| **Members elected from the NEA** | **FIVE, directly elected, tenure 4 years** |
| Members from universities and institutions | Representing engineering education |
| Government representatives | From relevant ministries |
| **Registrar** | The executive officer |

> **The vice-chairman's qualification (B.E. + 10 years) is asked in this very paper as a separate question**, so the two facts travel together.

**And the substantive content of the Act, since dates alone are thin:**

| The Act provides for | Note |
|---|---|
| **Constitution of the Council** | An AUTONOMOUS corporate body |
| **REGISTRATION of engineers** | **The core function** |
| **Recognition of qualifications** | Which degrees and institutions qualify |
| **The LICENSE EXAMINATION** | The gate to registration for graduates |
| **CODE OF ETHICS** | Standards of professional conduct |
| **DISCIPLINARY powers** | **Warning, suspension, removal from the register** |
| **Offences** | **Practising or using the title without registration** |

> **The offence provision is what gives the whole Act force.** Without it, registration would be a courtesy; with it, **signing drawings or certifying work while unregistered is unlawful** — which is why the license examination exists and why a graduate cannot simply begin practising.

> **And the minimum qualification for registration as a general engineer is a BACHELOR'S degree** — a diploma holder registers in a different category, with a correspondingly limited scope of practice. **That graded structure is one of the things the Regulation, rather than the Act, sets out.**

examTip.trick: **Hold the three-date set: Act 2055, Regulation 2057, first amendment 2079/05/05.** This paper asks about two of them separately.
examTip.trap: **The Act stood UNAMENDED for twenty-four years**, so there is only ONE amendment to place, not a series. That makes 2079 memorable rather than arbitrary.
examTip.mnemonic: **A Regulation must come AFTER its Act, because the Act creates the power to make it.** So "when did the regulation start" (2057) is a different question from "when was the Act passed" (2055) — and both appear in this paper.

questions.stem: The kinematic indeterminacy for a propped cantilever beam, with axial deformation considered, is:
questions.solution:
**2.**

**What kinematic indeterminacy is:**

> **KINEMATIC INDETERMINACY (the degree of freedom) is the number of INDEPENDENT DISPLACEMENTS AND ROTATIONS needed to define the deformed shape of the structure completely.**

> **It is the count the STIFFNESS (displacement) method works with**, just as static indeterminacy is the count the flexibility (force) method works with. **The two are different questions about the same structure and are often confused.**

**Counting the freedoms of a propped cantilever:**

> **A propped cantilever is FIXED at one end and has a ROLLER (prop) at the other.**

| Support | Restrains | Freedoms left at that joint |
|---|---|---|
| **FIXED end** | **Horizontal, vertical AND rotation — all three** | **0** |
| **ROLLER (propped) end** | **Vertical only** | **2 — horizontal translation and rotation** |

> **Total kinematic indeterminacy = 0 + 2 = 2** ✓

> **That is exactly the source's own reasoning: the fixed support has zero degrees of freedom, and the roller support restrains only vertical movement, so it leaves two.**

**Why axial deformation matters — it is the whole point of the qualifier in the stem:**

> **The roller's HORIZONTAL translation is a freedom only if the beam can change length**, that is, only if AXIAL DEFORMATION is considered.

> **If axial deformation is NEGLECTED — as it usually is in beam analysis, since axial stiffness EA/L is enormous compared with flexural stiffness EI/L³ — the beam is treated as INEXTENSIBLE.**

> **Then the roller cannot move horizontally either, because the fixed end holds it and the beam cannot stretch.**

| Assumption | Kinematic indeterminacy |
|---|---|
| **Axial deformation CONSIDERED** | **2 (rotation + horizontal translation)** ← as asked |
| **Axial deformation NEGLECTED (usual)** | **1 (rotation only)** |

> **So the answer to this question depends entirely on the stem's qualifier**, and a candidate who answers from the usual beam-analysis habit will say 1 and be caught. **Option (b) is that trap, and it is a fair one — the stem says "with axial deformation", which is unusual and therefore significant.**

> **The lesson generalises: when a stem states an assumption explicitly, it is stating it because it changes the answer.**

**The general formula, for structures where counting by inspection is harder:**

> **D_k = 3j − r**  (plane frame, axial deformation considered)

| Symbol | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **j** | **Number of JOINTS, including supports** |
| **r** | **Number of RESTRAINTS provided by the supports** |
| **3** | Freedoms per joint in a plane frame (two translations, one rotation) |

> **For this beam: j = 2, r = 3 (fixed) + 1 (roller) = 4, so D_k = 3(2) − 4 = 2** ✓ — which confirms the count.

> **And if axial deformation is neglected, subtract one freedom per inextensible member: D_k = 3j − r − m = 6 − 4 − 1 = 1** ✓, confirming the other case too.

**The contrast with STATIC indeterminacy, since both are asked about the same beams:**

| Beam | **STATIC** indeterminacy D_s | **KINEMATIC** indeterminacy D_k (axial considered) |
|---|---|---|
| **Simply supported** | **0** | **3** |
| **Cantilever** | **0** | **3** |
| **PROPPED cantilever** | **1** | **2** ← |
| **Fixed both ends** | **3** | **0** |
| Continuous, two equal spans | 2 | — |

> **Notice the pattern: as supports are added, STATIC indeterminacy RISES and KINEMATIC indeterminacy FALLS.** They move in opposite directions, because a restraint removes a freedom and adds an unknown reaction.

> **The fully fixed beam is the extreme: D_s = 3 and D_k = 0.** It has nothing free to move, so the stiffness method has no unknowns to solve for — **and the flexibility method has three.**

> **Which is the practical reason for choosing between the methods: use the one with FEWER unknowns.** For a highly restrained structure that is the stiffness method; for a lightly restrained one, the flexibility method. **And since computers use the stiffness method universally, most real structures are analysed by the method that suits restrained frames — which is what buildings are.**

examTip.trick: **Fixed end restrains all three, so 0 freedoms; a roller restrains only vertical, so 2 (rotation + horizontal).** Total 2. Or D_k = 3j − r = 6 − 4 = 2.
examTip.trap: **Neglect axial deformation — the usual beam assumption — and the answer is 1**, because an inextensible beam cannot let the roller move horizontally. Option (b) is that trap. **When a stem states an assumption explicitly, it does so because it changes the answer.**
examTip.mnemonic: **Adding supports RAISES static indeterminacy and LOWERS kinematic indeterminacy** — they move oppositely. A fully fixed beam is D_s = 3, D_k = 0. Choose the analysis method with fewer unknowns.

questions.stem: The length of an upstream guide bank is generally taken as:
questions.solution:
**1.25 L, where L is the length of the barrage or the waterway between the abutments.**

**The standard proportions:**

| Element | Length |
|---|---|
| **UPSTREAM guide bank** | **1.0 L to 1.5 L, generally taken as 1.25 L** ← |
| **DOWNSTREAM guide bank** | **0.2 L to 0.4 L, generally taken as 0.25 L** |

> **The upstream arm is roughly FIVE TIMES the downstream arm**, and that asymmetry is the thing to understand rather than memorise.

**Why the upstream arm must be so much longer:**

> **A guide bank's job is to GUIDE the river into the barrage opening and to keep it there.**

> **Upstream, the river arrives across a wide, braided flood plain and must be gathered in and steered.** That takes distance — a sharp deflection would cause severe scour and would fail.

> **Downstream, the water is already flowing in the direction the structure gave it.** The downstream arm only has to protect the approach embankment from the expanding, decelerating flow just past the structure, and to keep the exit flow from attacking the bank.

> **So: a long arm to STEER, a short arm to PROTECT.**

**Why guide banks exist at all — the problem they solve:**

> **A barrage or bridge occupies a waterway far narrower than the river's natural flood width.**

> **The river must therefore be CONSTRICTED into the opening, and an unconstrained river in alluvium will simply outflank the structure** — cutting round the abutment through the flood plain, which destroys the approach embankment and leaves the structure standing in dry ground.

> **Guide banks (also called Bell's bunds) prevent outflanking**, and that is their primary function. **Everything else about them follows from it.**

| Function | Note |
|---|---|
| **Prevent OUTFLANKING** | **The primary purpose** |
| **Guide the flow centrally into the waterway** | Reduces oblique attack on the piers |
| **Protect the approach embankments** | From direct attack |
| **Confine the river to a defined width** | Making the scour predictable |

**The other proportions of a guide bank, since they are asked together:**

| Element | Value |
|---|---|
| **RADIUS of the upstream curved head** | **0.4 L to 0.5 L** |
| **Sweep angle of the upstream head** | **120° to 145°** |
| **Radius of the downstream head** | **0.3 to 0.5 of the upstream radius** |
| **Sweep angle of the downstream head** | **45° to 60°** |
| **Side slopes** | **2:1 to 3:1 (H:V)** |
| **Top width** | 6 to 9 m (often carries a road) |
| **Free board above HFL** | 1.5 to 2 m |

> **The CURVED HEAD is the critical part of the whole structure**, and its radius matters because it must turn the flow without separating it. **A head curved too sharply causes the flow to separate and scour violently at the nose.**

> **The deepest scour on the entire work occurs at the upstream curved head**, which is why the launching apron there is the heaviest.

**The launching apron, which is the concept that makes guide banks survive:**

> **Stone is laid on the bed beyond the toe of the pitching, in a quantity sufficient to cover the slope that will form when the bed scours.**

> **As the scour hole develops, the apron stone SLIDES — "launches" — down into it, armouring the new slope automatically.**

| Design rule | Value |
|---|---|
| **Apron thickness** | **1.5 to 2.25 times the pitching thickness** |
| **Launched slope assumed** | **2:1** |
| **Scour depth at the curved head** | **2.0 to 2.5 times Lacey's normal scour depth R** |
| Scour along the straight reach | 1.25 to 1.75 R |

> **The apron is designed to be destroyed in an orderly way**, and that is the point: **a protection without a launching apron simply undermines and collapses.** Providing enough stone to cover the launched slope is the whole of the design.

> **Lacey's normal scour depth R = 0.47(Q/f)^{1/3}** (or **1.35(q²/f)^{1/3}** in terms of discharge intensity), and the multiplier depends on where on the guide bank you are — **deepest at the nose, less along the shank.**

examTip.trick: **Upstream 1.0-1.5 L (take 1.25 L); downstream 0.2-0.4 L (take 0.25 L).** The upstream arm is about FIVE times the downstream one.
examTip.trap: **Option (d) 0.4 L is the DOWNSTREAM value** — the top of its range. Both numbers come from the same table, so read which arm is asked.
examTip.mnemonic: **A long arm to STEER the arriving river, a short arm to PROTECT the exit.** The primary purpose is preventing OUTFLANKING, and the deepest scour is at the upstream curved head — which is why its launching apron is heaviest.

questions.stem: The qualification of the Vice Chairman of the Nepal Engineering Council is:
questions.solution:
**B.E. plus 10 years of experience.**

**The requirement:**

> **Under the Nepal Engineering Council Act, 2055, the Vice Chairman must hold at least a BACHELOR'S degree in engineering and have at least TEN YEARS of professional experience.**

> **B.E. + 10 years.** The two numbers to fix are the degree level (bachelor, not master) and the years (ten).

**Why the requirement is set as it is — and the reasoning makes the numbers stick:**

> **A BACHELOR'S degree is specified because that is the minimum qualification for REGISTRATION as a general engineer.** The Council's officers must be drawn from the body of registrable engineers, not from a narrower academic elite.

> **Requiring a master's degree would exclude the great majority of practising Nepali engineers from ever holding the office**, which would be an odd result for a body whose legitimacy rests on representing the profession.

> **Ten years of experience is specified because the office involves judgement about professional competence and conduct** — deciding who may practise, and who should stop. **That is not a judgement a newly qualified engineer can make, whatever their academic attainment.**

> **So the requirement trades academic level for practical seniority, deliberately.** Option (b), M.E. + 7 years, is the exact opposite trade and is the designed near-miss.

**Why each distractor is wrong:**

| Option | Note |
|---|---|
| **B.E. + 15 years** | **Right degree, too many years** — 15 would narrow the field further without adding to the judgement required |
| **M.E. + 7 years** | **The INVERTED trade: higher degree, less experience.** Plausible-looking and wrong ← the near-miss |
| **B.E. + 7 years** | **Right degree, too few years** |
| **B.E. + 10 years** | ✓ |

> **Note that three of the four options name B.E.**, so the degree is not really where the question lives — **the discrimination is the number of years, and only one option pairs the right degree with it.**

**The Council's composition, since this question is one of a family:**

| Position | Note |
|---|---|
| **CHAIRMAN** | **Appointed by the Government of Nepal** |
| **VICE CHAIRMAN** | **B.E. + 10 years of experience** ← |
| **Members ELECTED from the NEA** | **FIVE, directly elected, tenure 4 years** |
| Members from engineering institutions | Representing education |
| Government nominees | From relevant ministries |
| **REGISTRAR** | **The executive officer, who maintains the register** |

> **This paper asks about the vice chairman's qualification, the number of NEA-elected members, the Act's amendment date, the Regulation's start year, and what kind of body the Council is — five questions from the same corner of the syllabus.**

> **That concentration is worth noticing when preparing: the regulatory-body material is a small, closed body of facts that recurs heavily**, and it is among the cheapest marks in the paper to secure. **Ten facts learned properly will answer most of what is asked.**

**The ten facts, gathered:**

| Fact | Value |
|---|---|
| **NEC Act** | **2055 BS (1998 AD)** |
| **NEC Regulation** | **2057 BS** |
| **First amendment to the Act** | **2079/05/05** |
| **Nature of the Council** | **AUTONOMOUS body** |
| **Who approves its rules** | **Government of Nepal** |
| **Vice chairman** | **B.E. + 10 years** ← |
| **NEA-elected members** | **5, tenure 4 years** |
| **Minimum qualification to register (general engineer)** | **Bachelor's degree** |
| **Inspection of institutions, bachelor permanent approval** | **Every 2 years** |
| **NEA's own legal basis** | **Registered under the Social Service Act** |

> **Every one of those has appeared in this series of papers**, several of them in this single paper — which is the practical argument for learning the set rather than meeting each fact separately.

examTip.trick: **B.E. + 10 years.** Three of the four options say B.E., so the question really turns on the number of years — and only one option pairs the right degree with the right count.
examTip.trap: **Option (b) M.E. + 7 years is the INVERTED trade** — higher degree, less experience. The Act deliberately trades academic level for practical seniority, not the reverse.
examTip.mnemonic: **This corner of the syllabus is a small closed set of about ten facts and it recurs heavily** — this one paper asks five of them. Learn the set: Act 2055, Regulation 2057, amendment 2079, autonomous, GoN approves, B.E.+10, five NEA members.

questions.stem: The NEC is:
questions.solution:
**An autonomous body.**

**The statutory position:**

> **The Nepal Engineering Council was constituted under the NEC Act, 2055 as an AUTONOMOUS and corporate body** — with perpetual succession, its own seal, and the capacity to sue and be sued in its own name.

> **AUTONOMOUS means created BY statute and governing itself UNDER that statute**, rather than operating as a department of a ministry within the civil service chain of command.

> **It is a statutory regulator, which is the standard model for a professional council worldwide.**

**Why autonomy is necessary rather than merely convenient:**

> **The Council's central function is to decide who may practise engineering, and to remove those who practise it badly.**

> **Both decisions must be made on PROFESSIONAL grounds and must be seen to be free of political direction.**

> **A regulator that could be instructed whom to license, or whom not to discipline, would produce a register carrying no information at all.** The register's value is exactly its independence.

> **So autonomy is not a privilege granted to the profession — it is the condition on which the register means anything.**

**Why each distractor is wrong:**

| Option | Why not |
|---|---|
| **Government Body** | **The Council is not a ministry department.** Its members are not civil servants and it raises its own fees rather than living on a budget line ← |
| **Autonomous Body** | ✓ |
| **Independent Body** | **Loose and unofficial.** "Independent" is not the statutory category, and it overstates the position — the Government appoints the chairman and approves the Council's rules ← the interesting one |
| **All of the above** | Cannot hold, since the first is false |

> **Option (c) deserves a careful answer because it sounds like a synonym for (b) and is not.**

| | **AUTONOMOUS** | **INDEPENDENT (as loosely used)** |
|---|---|---|
| **Created by** | **Statute** | — |
| **Government role** | **Appoints the chairman; APPROVES the rules** | Implies none |
| **Day-to-day decisions** | **Free of direction** | Free of direction |
| **Accountability** | **To the statute and, through the rules, to government** | Implies none |

> **The Council is autonomous, not unaccountable.** Its general rules require government approval precisely because they bind every engineer in the country — **and rules that bind the public need someone accountable to the public to sanction them.**

> **So the correct description has to capture both halves: self-governing in individual decisions, accountable in general rule-making.** "Autonomous" is the term that does; "independent" claims more than is true.

**The division of authority, which resolves the apparent contradiction in this paper:**

| Layer | Who decides |
|---|---|
| **The ACT itself** | **PARLIAMENT** |
| **RULES and REGULATIONS under the Act** | **Council FRAMES, GOVERNMENT approves** |
| **Individual decisions under the rules** | **The COUNCIL alone — registration, examination results, discipline** |

> **This paper asks separately what kind of body the Council is (autonomous) and who approves its rules (the Government).** The two answers look inconsistent and are not — **and a candidate who reads them as contradictory will get one of the two wrong.**

> **The resolution is the table above: autonomy where it matters, in decisions about individuals; shared authority where accountability requires it, in general rules.**

**And the consequence that makes the whole arrangement matter:**

> **An unregistered person may not practise as an engineer or use the title**, and signing drawings or certifying work without registration is an offence under the Act.

> **The Council's real power is therefore the power to strike a name off the register** — everything else it does leads to or from that. **Recognising a degree matters because it leads to registration; the code of ethics matters because breaching it can end registration.**

> **Which is also why the license examination exists, and why it is not a formality.**

examTip.trick: **AUTONOMOUS — created by statute and self-governing under it.** Not a ministry department: members are not civil servants and the Council raises its own fees.
examTip.trap: **Option (c) "independent" sounds like a synonym and claims too much.** The Government appoints the chairman and approves the rules. The Council is autonomous, not unaccountable.
examTip.mnemonic: **This paper also asks who approves the rules (the Government).** No contradiction: **autonomy in decisions about INDIVIDUALS, government approval for GENERAL RULES** — because rules binding the public need public accountability.

questions.stem: Blue baby syndrome is due to:
questions.solution:
**Nitrate.**

**The mechanism, which is worth understanding rather than memorising:**

> **Nitrate (NO₃⁻) in drinking water is reduced to NITRITE (NO₂⁻) in an infant's gut**, whose low acidity permits the bacteria that do it.

> **Nitrite oxidises the iron in HAEMOGLOBIN from Fe²⁺ to Fe³⁺, converting it to METHAEMOGLOBIN.**

> **Methaemoglobin CANNOT CARRY OXYGEN.**

> **The infant becomes oxygen-starved and the skin takes on a blue tinge — hence "blue baby".** The clinical name is **METHAEMOGLOBINAEMIA.**

**Why INFANTS specifically, which is the key epidemiological fact:**

| Factor | Why it matters |
|---|---|
| **Low stomach acidity in infants** | **Permits nitrate-reducing bacteria to survive and convert nitrate to nitrite** |
| **FOETAL haemoglobin** | **More easily oxidised than adult haemoglobin** |
| **Immature enzyme systems** | **The enzyme that reconverts methaemoglobin is not yet fully active** |
| **High water intake per unit body weight** | Bottle-fed infants take a large dose relative to their size |

> **All four factors point the same way, and they explain the disease's specificity: adults drinking the same water are unaffected.** So a water supply can be safe for a whole community and dangerous to its infants — **which is why the nitrate standard is set for the most vulnerable consumer, not the average one.**

**The standards:**

| Standard | Nitrate limit |
|---|---|
| **WHO guideline** | **50 mg/l as NO₃ (equivalently 11.3 mg/l as N)** |
| **Nepal (NDWQS) and IS 10500** | **50 mg/l as NO₃, no relaxation** |

> **Note the two ways of expressing it — as NO₃ or as N — differing by a factor of 4.43.** **50 mg/l as NO₃ is the same as 11.3 mg/l as nitrate-nitrogen**, and confusing the two makes a compliant water look grossly contaminated or the reverse. **Always read which basis a figure uses.**

> **"No relaxation" is unusual and significant**: many parameters have a permissible limit above the desirable one where no alternative source exists. **Nitrate does not, because the harm is acute rather than cumulative.**

**Where the nitrate comes from — and this is why the problem is growing:**

| Source | Note |
|---|---|
| **Agricultural FERTILISER leaching to groundwater** | **The dominant source worldwide** |
| **Animal waste and manure** | Concentrated near sheds and pens |
| **Septic tanks and pit latrines** | **The dominant source in unsewered settlements — and often close to the well** |
| **Decaying organic matter** | Natural background |
| Industrial discharge | Local |

> **Nitrate is a GROUNDWATER problem far more than a surface-water one**, because it is highly soluble, is not adsorbed by soil, and is not removed by the natural filtration that removes bacteria.

> **That last point is the important one: a shallow well may deliver bacteriologically clean water that is high in nitrate**, because the soil filtered out the pathogens and passed the nitrate through. **A clean bacteriological test is not evidence of nitrate safety.**

**Why nitrate is hard to treat, which shapes the practical response:**

| Method | Note |
|---|---|
| **Conventional treatment (coagulation, filtration, chlorination)** | **DOES NOT REMOVE NITRATE AT ALL** ← |
| **Ion exchange** | Effective; produces a brine to dispose of |
| **Reverse osmosis** | Effective; expensive, wastes water |
| **Biological denitrification** | Effective; complex to operate |
| **BLENDING with a low-nitrate source** | **Often the cheapest practical answer** |
| **Protecting the source** | **The real solution — setback distances, latrine siting, fertiliser management** |

> **The first row is the fact with the greatest practical weight.** A community that builds a conventional treatment plant to fix a nitrate problem has spent its money on nothing.

> **Which is why SOURCE PROTECTION is the answer in practice**, and why well siting — distance from latrines and animal pens, and the depth of the aquifer tapped — is a design decision rather than a matter of convenience.

**Why the distractors are wrong:**

| Option | What it actually causes |
|---|---|
| **Nitrate** | ✓ **Methaemoglobinaemia (blue baby)** |
| **Carbon dioxide** | **Corrosive, lowers pH — but not a health hazard at water concentrations** |
| **IRON** | **Taste, staining of laundry and fixtures, turbidity — an AESTHETIC problem, not a toxic one** ← |
| **Carbon monoxide** | **An AIR pollutant that binds haemoglobin — which is why it feels plausible here** ← the interesting trap |

> **Option (d) is the well-made distractor**, because carbon monoxide genuinely does block haemoglobin — forming carboxyhaemoglobin. **But it is an inhaled gas, not a waterborne contaminant.** The mechanism is analogous and the route of exposure is wrong.

> **And option (c) iron is the other worth naming**, because iron IS the element oxidised in this disease — **but the iron involved is the iron already in the haemoglobin, not iron in the water.** The question rewards knowing which substance does the oxidising.

examTip.trick: **Nitrate → nitrite in the infant gut → oxidises haemoglobin's iron to methaemoglobin, which cannot carry oxygen.** Limit 50 mg/l as NO₃, with NO relaxation, because the harm is acute.
examTip.trap: **Carbon monoxide (d) genuinely blocks haemoglobin** — but by inhalation, not through water. And **iron (c) is the element OXIDISED in the disease** — the iron in the haemoglobin, not iron in the water.
examTip.mnemonic: **Conventional treatment removes NO nitrate at all**, so a plant built to fix it wastes the money. And **50 mg/l as NO₃ = 11.3 mg/l as N** — a factor of 4.43 between the two bases.

questions.stem: The modulus of elasticity of M25 concrete is:
questions.solution:
**25000 N/mm².**

**The code formula:**

> **E_c = 5000 √f_ck**  (IS 456:2000, clause 6.2.3.1), with both in N/mm².

> **For M25: E_c = 5000 √25 = 5000 × 5 = 25,000 N/mm² = 25 GPa** ✓

> **M25 is the grade to be quickest with, because √25 = 5 exactly** — the arithmetic is a single multiplication.

**The values for the common grades:**

| Grade | √f_ck | E_c = 5000√f_ck (N/mm²) |
|---|---|---|
| **M20** | **4.47** | **22,360** |
| **M25** | **5.00** | **25,000** ← |
| **M30** | 5.48 | **27,390** |
| **M35** | 5.92 | 29,580 |
| **M40** | **6.32** | **31,620** |
| M50 | 7.07 | 35,360 |

> **Notice that option (c) 28,500 sits between M30 and M35, and option (a) 33,500 between M40 and M50** — the distractors are plausible concrete moduli for other grades, which is what makes the question worth doing properly rather than eyeballing.

**Why the SQUARE ROOT — and this is the conceptual content:**

> **E rises much more slowly than strength.** Quadrupling the strength only doubles the modulus.

| Grade change | Strength ratio | Modulus ratio |
|---|---|---|
| **M25 → M100** | **× 4** | **× 2** |

> **So a high-strength concrete is much stronger but only modestly stiffer**, and that has a real design consequence: **going to a higher grade to control DEFLECTION is an inefficient move.** The right answer to a deflection problem is more depth, not more strength.

> **Conversely, going to a higher grade to control a stress or reduce a column size works well.** Strength and stiffness respond differently to the same change, and knowing which one governs decides whether a grade increase helps at all.

**The important qualification — what E_c actually is:**

> **Concrete has no straight portion to its stress-strain curve worth speaking of.** So E_c is not a measured slope in the way steel's E is.

> **The code's 5000√f_ck is a defined SHORT-TERM STATIC modulus** — a convention that gives consistent answers, not a physical constant.

> **And the LONG-TERM modulus is far lower, because of CREEP:**

> **E_ce = E_c / (1 + θ)**, with θ the creep coefficient.

| Age at loading | Creep coefficient θ | Long-term E as a fraction of E_c |
|---|---|---|
| **7 days** | **2.2** | **0.31** |
| **28 days** | **1.6** | **0.38** |
| **1 year** | **1.1** | **0.48** |

> **So sustained loading reduces the effective modulus by a factor of two to three.** That is not a refinement — **it is the dominant term in long-term deflection**, and it is why a slab that passes an elastic deflection check can still sag visibly after a year.

> **The 28-day figure θ = 1.6 is the one to remember**, giving a long-term modulus of about 0.38 E_c — for M25, roughly 9,600 N/mm² rather than 25,000.

**Comparison with steel, which puts the number in perspective:**

| Material | E (GPa) |
|---|---|
| **Structural steel** | **200-210** |
| **M25 concrete (short term)** | **25** |
| **M25 concrete (long term)** | **~10** |
| Aluminium | 70 |
| Timber, along grain | 8-15 |

> **Steel is about EIGHT TIMES stiffer than concrete in the short term and TWENTY TIMES in the long term.**

> **That ratio is the whole basis of reinforced concrete design.** The modular ratio m = E_s/E_c ≈ 8 to 10 is what the old working-stress method used to transform the steel area into an equivalent concrete area — **and it is why a small area of steel can carry the whole of the tension: it is far stiffer, so it attracts far more stress at the same strain.**

> **IS 456's working stress annexure takes m = 280/(3σ_cbc)**, which gives about 9.3 for M25 and folds a creep allowance into the figure.

examTip.trick: **E_c = 5000√f_ck.** For M25, √25 = 5 exactly, so E_c = 25,000 N/mm² in one multiplication.
examTip.trap: **The distractors are plausible moduli for OTHER grades** — 28,500 sits near M30-M35 and 33,500 near M40-M50. Compute rather than recognise.
examTip.mnemonic: **Quadrupling strength only DOUBLES the modulus**, so raising the grade is a poor cure for DEFLECTION (use depth) and a good one for stress. And **creep cuts the long-term modulus to about 0.38 E_c** at θ = 1.6.

questions.stem: What is the standard temperature for the Marshall Stability test?
questions.solution:
**60 °C.**

**Why 60 °C and not room temperature:**

> **The Marshall test measures the stability of a BITUMINOUS MIX, and bitumen is a temperature-sensitive material.**

> **60 °C represents the HOTTEST PAVEMENT SURFACE TEMPERATURE a road is likely to reach in service** — which is far above air temperature, because dark bitumen absorbs solar radiation.

> **A mix must be stable at its WORST condition, and its worst condition is hot.** At 60 °C the bitumen is softest, the mix is weakest, and rutting is most likely.

> **Testing at 25 or 27 °C would show a mix that passes comfortably and then ruts in the first summer.**

> **So the test temperature is chosen to represent the critical service condition, not the laboratory's convenience.**

**The test parameters:**

| Parameter | Value |
|---|---|
| **Test TEMPERATURE** | **60 °C** ← |
| **Water bath immersion before testing** | **30 to 40 minutes at 60 °C** |
| **Rate of loading** | **50 mm per minute** |
| **Specimen size** | **101.6 mm diameter × 63.5 mm high** |
| **Compaction** | **75 blows per face (heavy traffic), 50 (medium), 35 (light)** |
| **Rammer** | **4.54 kg falling 457 mm** |

> **The two numbers to fix are 60 °C and 50 mm/min**, and both appear in almost every question on the test.

> **The 75 blows per FACE — both faces — is the other detail commonly got wrong**, and the blow count is chosen for the traffic the road will carry.

**What the test outputs, and both matter:**

| Output | Meaning | Typical requirement |
|---|---|---|
| **MARSHALL STABILITY** | **The maximum load the specimen carries, in kg or kN** | **Minimum 9 kN (heavy traffic)** |
| **FLOW value** | **The deformation, in units of 0.25 mm, at maximum load** | **2 to 4 mm (8 to 16 units)** |

> **The FLOW value is the one candidates forget, and it is a two-sided limit — a maximum AND a minimum:**

| Flow | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Too LOW** | **The mix is too brittle** — it will crack under repeated loading |
| **Too HIGH** | **The mix is too plastic** — it will rut and shove |

> **So a mix can fail the Marshall test by being too stiff as well as by being too soft**, which is a genuinely useful idea: **the requirement is a window, not a floor.**

**What the test is used for — the design procedure:**

> **The Marshall method determines the OPTIMUM BINDER CONTENT (OBC).**

| Step | Action |
|---|---|
| **1** | **Make specimens at several binder contents (e.g. 4.0, 4.5, 5.0, 5.5, 6.0 %)** |
| **2** | **Plot stability, flow, unit weight, air voids (Vv) and voids filled with bitumen (VFB) against binder content** |
| **3** | **Read the binder content at maximum stability, at maximum unit weight, and at 4 % air voids** |
| **4** | **AVERAGE those three to get the OBC** |
| **5** | **Check that all the other criteria are satisfied at that OBC** |

> **The averaging of three separately-read optima is the characteristic feature of the method**, and the reason is that the three peaks do not coincide: **maximum stability, maximum density and the target void content occur at slightly different binder contents.**

> **The 4 per cent air voids target is the most important single criterion.** Too few voids and the mix bleeds and ruts in hot weather as the bitumen expands with nowhere to go; **too many and it is permeable, and water gets in and strips the binder from the aggregate.**

**The other mix criteria, since the OBC must satisfy all of them:**

| Criterion | Requirement |
|---|---|
| **Air voids, Vv** | **3 to 5 %** |
| **Voids in mineral aggregate, VMA** | **Minimum by aggregate size, typically 13-16 %** |
| **Voids filled with bitumen, VFB** | **65 to 75 %** |
| **Stability** | **9 kN minimum** |
| **Flow** | **2 to 4 mm** |

> **A mix meeting stability alone is not a designed mix.** Every one of these must be satisfied at the same binder content, and it is common for a first trial to fail on VMA — **which usually means the aggregate GRADING must change, not the binder content.**

> **That distinction is the practical skill the method teaches: read which criterion has failed, and it tells you whether to adjust the binder or the aggregate.**

examTip.trick: **60 °C represents the hottest pavement SURFACE temperature in service**, where the bitumen is softest and the mix weakest. Testing at room temperature would pass a mix that ruts in its first summer.
examTip.trap: **The FLOW value is a two-sided limit (2-4 mm), not a floor** — too low means brittle and crack-prone, too high means plastic and rut-prone. A mix can fail by being too STIFF.
examTip.mnemonic: **OBC is the AVERAGE of three separately-read optima** — maximum stability, maximum unit weight, and 4 % air voids — because the three peaks do not coincide. Failing on VMA means change the GRADING, not the binder.

questions.stem: The main difference between a weir and a dam is:
options: A dam stops the flow of water, a weir allows water to flow over the crest
A dam has more storage capacity as compared to a weir
The height of a dam is more than that of a weir
questions.solution:
**All of the above — all three statements are correct.**

**Why each statement holds:**

> **(a) FLOW OVER THE CREST is the defining hydraulic difference.** A weir is designed for water to pass OVER its crest as a matter of routine; **a dam retains water and passes surplus through a separate SPILLWAY.** In normal operation a dam's crest stays dry and a weir's does not.

> **(b) STORAGE.** A dam creates a reservoir and stores water for months; **a weir raises the level only enough to divert flow into a canal, ponding a small volume.** A weir is a diversion structure, not a storage one.

> **(c) HEIGHT.** A dam is tall; a weir is low. This follows directly from (b) — **storage requires head, and head requires height.**

> **Since all three are true, the answer is (d).**

**The comparison in full, which is the substance:**

| Feature | **DAM** | **WEIR** | **BARRAGE** |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Size** | **Large** | **Small** | Medium |
| **Height** | **Tall** | **Low** | Medium |
| **Purpose** | **Irrigation, HYDROPOWER, flood control, water STORAGE** | **Irrigation, water supply, fish passage** | **Irrigation, navigation, flood control** |
| **Water passes** | **Through a separate SPILLWAY** | **OVER the crest** | **Through GATED openings** |
| **GATES** | **No (spillway may have them)** | **NO** | **YES — the defining feature** |
| **Level control** | By reservoir operation | **By the fixed crest — none** | **By the gates — precise** |
| Material | Concrete, earth, rock | Concrete, stone, timber | Concrete, steel |

> **The GATES row is the discrimination that matters most, and it separates a weir from a BARRAGE — which this question does not ask about but which is the neighbouring confusion:**

> **A WEIR has a fixed crest and no gates, so the upstream level is whatever the discharge makes it.**

> **A BARRAGE has a low crest with GATES on top, so the upstream level is set by the operator regardless of the discharge.**

> **That is the engineering advantage of a barrage: LEVEL CONTROL.** And it comes with a corresponding disadvantage — **gates must be maintained, operated, and are vulnerable to sediment and debris.**

> **A weir needs no operator and cannot be mis-operated; a barrage can do more and can be got wrong.**

**Why answering "all of the above" is defensible here, when it usually is not:**

> **An "all of the above" fails if ANY member is false**, which is why it is normally treated with suspicion.

> **Here each option states a different TRUE attribute of the same distinction** — hydraulic behaviour, function, and dimension. **None contradicts the others; they are three views of one thing.**

> **The test to apply is therefore mechanical: check each statement independently, and only then decide.** A candidate who reasons "one of these must be the *main* difference, so the others are wrong" has imported an assumption the question does not make.

> **And the word "main" in the stem is what tempts that reasoning.** It suggests a single answer is wanted — **but all three statements are true, so the honest response is (d).**

**The examples worth knowing:**

| Structure | Examples |
|---|---|
| **Dams** | **Hoover, Jinping-I; in Nepal, KULEKHANI (the only storage dam)** |
| **Weirs** | Dobbs weir, Proston weir, Yanco weir |
| **Barrages** | **KOSHI BARRAGE, Delta barrage, Assiut barrage; in Nepal also the Gandak and Laxmanpur/Rasiyawal works** |

> **The Koshi Barrage is the one with local significance**, and it illustrates the barrage's purpose exactly: **it controls the level of a river carrying an enormous sediment load, and its gates are used both to divert flow and to sluice sediment past the structure.**

> **Which also illustrates the barrage's cost: the Koshi's gates and its embankments have required continuous attention for decades**, because the river's bed has risen inside the embanked reach. **A fixed weir would have needed less operation and would have offered no control at all.**

examTip.trick: **All three statements are true and are three views of one distinction** — hydraulic behaviour (over the crest vs through a spillway), function (divert vs store) and dimension (low vs tall).
examTip.trap: **The word "main" tempts you to pick a single answer.** Check each statement INDEPENDENTLY; an all-of-the-above fails only if a member is false, and here none is.
examTip.mnemonic: **GATES are the real discriminator, and they separate a WEIR from a BARRAGE**: a weir's fixed crest gives no level control; a barrage's gates give precise control — and must be maintained and can be mis-operated.

questions.stem: A disease spread worldwide is called:
questions.solution:
**Pandemic.**

**The three terms, which differ only in SCALE:**

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **ENDEMIC** | **The amount of a disease USUALLY PRESENT in a community — the baseline. Constant, expected, not an outbreak** |
| **EPIDEMIC** | **An INCREASE — often sudden — in cases ABOVE what is normally expected, in a specific area** |
| **PANDEMIC** | **An epidemic that has SPREAD OVER SEVERAL COUNTRIES OR CONTINENTS, affecting many people** ← |

> **The progression is baseline → local excess → international spread.** Endemic is the normal level; epidemic is above it locally; pandemic is above it across continents.

> **The stem's phrase "spread worldwide" names the third precisely.**

**Why ENDEMIC is the most instructive of the three:**

> **Endemic does NOT mean rare or harmless.** A disease can be endemic at a very high level.

> **Malaria in parts of the Terai, or diarrhoeal disease in a community with contaminated water, is ENDEMIC — constantly present, causing continuous illness and death, and never called an outbreak precisely because it is expected.**

> **That is the trap in the word, and it has a practical consequence: an endemic burden attracts far less attention and funding than an epidemic of the same size, because nothing has "happened".**

> **For a water supply engineer this is the central point of the whole topic.** The disease burden a clean water supply prevents is mostly ENDEMIC diarrhoeal disease — continuous, unremarkable, and larger in total than the epidemics that make the news.

**A fourth term worth adding, since it completes the set:**

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **OUTBREAK** | **An epidemic limited to a very localised area — a village, a school, a single water supply** |
| **SPORADIC** | **Cases occurring irregularly and infrequently, with no pattern** |

> **An outbreak is what a contaminated well produces**, and it is the scale at which a water engineer usually meets the problem: **a cluster of cases traceable to one source.**

**The waterborne diseases, since this is why the vocabulary is in the syllabus:**

| Disease | Agent | Note |
|---|---|---|
| **CHOLERA** | Bacterium (*Vibrio cholerae*) | **Classically epidemic and pandemic; kills by dehydration in hours** |
| **TYPHOID** | Bacterium (*Salmonella typhi*) | Endemic in much of South Asia |
| **Bacillary dysentery** | Bacterium (*Shigella*) | — |
| **HEPATITIS A and E** | **Virus** | **Chlorine-resistant relative to bacteria** |
| **Polio** | Virus | Faecal-oral |
| **Amoebic dysentery, giardiasis** | **Protozoa (cysts)** | **CYSTS RESIST CHLORINE — filtration is essential** |
| **Cryptosporidiosis** | **Protozoan (oocysts)** | **Highly chlorine-resistant** |
| Guinea worm, roundworm | Helminths | Removed by filtration |

> **The chlorine-resistance column is the engineering content.** Chlorination handles bacteria well and **protozoan cysts badly** — *Cryptosporidium* survives normal chlorine doses almost entirely.

> **So a plant relying on chlorination alone is protected against cholera and typhoid and NOT against cryptosporidiosis.** Removing cysts requires **filtration** (or UV, or ozone), which is why the multiple-barrier principle exists:

| Barrier | Removes |
|---|---|
| **Source protection** | Reduces the load reaching the works |
| **Coagulation and sedimentation** | Turbidity, some pathogens |
| **FILTRATION** | **Cysts, oocysts, remaining turbidity** |
| **DISINFECTION** | **Bacteria and viruses** |
| **Residual chlorine in the network** | Recontamination after treatment |

> **No single barrier is sufficient, and that is the design principle rather than a slogan** — each barrier fails against something, and the barriers are chosen so that no pathogen passes them all.

**Why the distractors are wrong:** **endemic is the baseline (wrong scale), epidemic is local excess (wrong scale), and "all of the above" cannot hold when the three terms are mutually exclusive by definition.** **The question is a pure scale discrimination, and the phrase to attach to each is: endemic = always here; epidemic = more than usual, here; pandemic = everywhere.**

examTip.trick: **Endemic = always here (baseline). Epidemic = more than usual, here. Pandemic = everywhere.** The three differ only in SCALE, and "spread worldwide" names the third.
examTip.trap: **Endemic does NOT mean rare or mild** — a disease can be endemic at a devastating level. Which is exactly the burden a clean water supply prevents, and why it attracts less attention than an epidemic of the same size.
examTip.mnemonic: **Chlorine handles bacteria and viruses; protozoan CYSTS resist it** — Cryptosporidium almost entirely. Hence the MULTIPLE BARRIER principle: filtration for cysts, disinfection for bacteria, no single barrier sufficient.

questions.stem: The influence line diagram (ILD) for the shear force at the support of a cantilever beam is a:
questions.solution:
**A rectangle.**

**Why — reason from what the influence line means:**

> **An INFLUENCE LINE for a quantity shows how that quantity VARIES as a UNIT LOAD moves across the structure.**

> **Consider the shear force at the fixed support of a cantilever, and place a unit load anywhere along the span.**

> **The support must carry the whole of that load — there is nowhere else for it to go.** So the shear at the support is **1, wherever the load sits.**

> **A quantity that is constant at 1 over the whole span plots as a RECTANGLE of unit height.** ✓

> **That is the entire argument, and it needs no formula.**

**The Müller-Breslau route, which the source uses:**

> **Müller-Breslau's principle: the influence line for a force quantity is the DEFLECTED SHAPE the structure takes when the corresponding restraint is RELEASED and a unit displacement is applied in the direction of that force.**

> **For shear at a section: cut the beam there and impose a unit RELATIVE VERTICAL displacement across the cut, keeping the two faces parallel.**

> **At the fixed support of a cantilever, releasing the vertical restraint and lifting the member bodily by one unit leaves the whole beam translated by one unit — a rectangle.** ✓

> **The source states it exactly this way: "neglect the support at the given point, lift the member providing it unit displacement upward, and let the rest of the beam follow suit."**

**The influence lines for a cantilever, as a set:**

| Quantity, at the fixed end | Influence line |
|---|---|
| **SHEAR force** | **RECTANGLE of height 1 over the whole span** ← |
| **BENDING moment** | **TRIANGLE, zero at the free end, maximum L at the support** |
| Vertical reaction | Rectangle of height 1 |
| Fixing moment | Triangle |

> **Note that the shear and the reaction have the SAME influence line for a cantilever**, which is obvious once stated: at the fixed end of a cantilever, the shear force IS the reaction.

**And for a simply supported beam, for contrast — because the two are constantly confused:**

| Quantity | Influence line |
|---|---|
| **Reaction at A** | **Triangle: 1 at A, 0 at B** |
| **Shear at a section C** | **TWO triangles of opposite sign, with a UNIT JUMP at C** |
| **Bending moment at C** | **TRIANGLE, peak ab/L at C** |

> **The unit jump in the shear influence line at the section is its characteristic feature**, and it is why a shear influence line for a simply supported beam is never a single triangle.

> **Option (a) triangle is the designed trap here, because it is the correct answer for the BENDING MOMENT influence line of the same cantilever** — and "triangle" is the shape most associated with cantilever diagrams generally.

**Why options (c) and (d) can be struck out immediately:**

> **A parabola of any order requires the quantity to vary NON-LINEARLY with the load position.**

> **But influence lines for FORCE quantities in a statically determinate structure are made of STRAIGHT LINES, always.** The reason is that reactions and internal forces depend LINEARLY on the load position when equilibrium alone determines them.

> **Curved influence lines appear only for INDETERMINATE structures** (where the deflected shape of Müller-Breslau is itself a bending curve) **or for DEFLECTION influence lines.**

> **So for a determinate cantilever, no parabola of any degree can be correct** — which removes half the options on a structural principle rather than by recall.

**What influence lines are used for, since they look abstract:**

| Use | Note |
|---|---|
| **Position a MOVING load for maximum effect** | **The reason they exist — bridges, cranes, trains** |
| **Compute the effect of a set of loads** | **Multiply each load by the ordinate under it and add** |
| **Compute the effect of a udl over part of the span** | **Load × AREA of the influence line under the loaded length** |
| Identify which spans to load in a continuous beam | Load the spans where the ordinate has the desired sign |

> **The udl rule — effect = intensity × area under the influence line — is the most useful single result**, and it explains the standard bridge-loading question: **to maximise a quantity, load exactly the length over which the influence line has the sign you want, and no more.**

> **That is also why a continuous beam is loaded in alternate spans (a chequerboard pattern) for maximum sagging moment**: the influence line changes sign from span to span, so loading every span would let the negative parts cancel the positive.

examTip.trick: **Place a unit load anywhere on a cantilever: the support carries all of it, so the shear is 1 everywhere — a RECTANGLE of unit height.** No formula needed.
examTip.trap: **Option (a) triangle is the correct answer for the BENDING MOMENT influence line of the same cantilever.** And note that at a cantilever's fixed end, the shear force IS the reaction, so they share one influence line.
examTip.mnemonic: **Influence lines for FORCE quantities in a DETERMINATE structure are always straight lines** — which strikes out both parabola options on principle. And **effect of a udl = intensity × AREA under the influence line.**

questions.stem: A hydraulic structure is constructed when the Full Supply Level (FSL) of a canal is much higher than the High Flood Level (HFL) of the stream, which in turn is lower than the bottom of the canal trough. Such a structure is called:
questions.solution:
**An aqueduct.**

**Read the level relations in the stem, because they name the structure exactly:**

> **The canal's FSL is much HIGHER than the stream's HFL** → the canal is above the drain.

> **The stream's HFL is LOWER than the bottom of the canal trough** → there is CLEAR HEADROOM beneath the trough, so the drain flows freely under gravity.

> **Canal on top + drain flowing free underneath = AQUEDUCT.** ✓

> **The source's own explanation states it: "when the HFL of the drain is sufficiently below the bottom of the canal such that the drainage water flows freely under gravity, the structure is known as an aqueduct."**

**The rule that resolves the whole family:**

> **Name the structure after WHAT IS CARRIED ON TOP; add "siphon" when the lower channel is forced to run under PRESSURE.**

| Structure | On top | Underneath | Lower channel flows |
|---|---|---|---|
| **AQUEDUCT** | **CANAL** | **Drain, in a barrel** | **FREE (gravity)** ← |
| **SIPHON AQUEDUCT** | **CANAL** | **Drain** | **UNDER PRESSURE** |
| **SUPER PASSAGE** | **DRAIN** | **Canal** | **FREE** |
| **CANAL SIPHON** | **DRAIN** | **Canal** | **Canal PRESSURISED** |
| **LEVEL CROSSING** | — | — | **The two MIX, then separate again** |

> **The mnemonic: an aqueDUCT carries the canal, as a Roman aqueduct carries water over a valley. A SUPER passage has the drain SUPERior — on top.**

**The critical distinction the stem is testing — aqueduct versus SIPHON aqueduct:**

| | **AQUEDUCT** | **SIPHON AQUEDUCT** |
|---|---|---|
| **Drain's HFL vs the canal trough bottom** | **BELOW it — clear headroom** ← as in this stem | **ABOVE it — the drain must be pressurised to pass** |
| **Barrel flows** | **Part full, at atmospheric pressure** | **FULL, under pressure** |
| **Requires** | A simple barrel | **Impervious floor, upstream and downstream CUT-OFFS, energy dissipation** |
| **Silting risk** | Low | **HIGH — velocity varies and silt deposits in the barrel** |
| Cost | Lower | Higher |

> **The stem's clause "which in turn is lower than the bottom of the canal trough" is doing precise work: it is what makes this an aqueduct and not a siphon aqueduct.** Remove that clause and the answer changes.

> **A siphon aqueduct's barrel runs under pressure, so it needs the same uplift and exit-gradient analysis as a weir floor** — and its silt must be flushed, or capacity is progressively lost.

**Why each distractor is wrong:**

| Option | What it actually is |
|---|---|
| **Super passage** | **The EXACT REVERSE — drain carried over the canal, which the stem's levels forbid** ← the mirror trap |
| **Aqueduct** | ✓ |
| **INLETS** | **Used where the drain is VERY SMALL: it is simply admitted INTO the canal at an inlet and taken out at an outlet downstream** |
| **Level crossing** | **Canal and drain allowed to MIX in a common pool, then separated by regulators — used where the drain is LARGE and the canal small** |
