> **Option (c) inlets is worth knowing because it is the cheapest option of all and is often the right one.** For a small drain, building a barrel is disproportionate — **letting the drain water into the canal and drawing an equal quantity out downstream costs almost nothing.**

> **Its limitation is that the drain's water and its silt enter the canal**, so it suits only small, clean drains.

**How the choice is actually made — the whole selection is a matter of comparing FOUR levels:**

| Situation | Structure |
|---|---|
| **Canal bed well above the drain bed; drain HFL low** | **AQUEDUCT** |
| **Canal bed above the drain bed, but drain HFL is high** | **SIPHON AQUEDUCT** |
| **Drain bed well above the canal FSL** | **SUPER PASSAGE** |
| **Drain bed above the canal, but canal FSL is higher** | **CANAL SIPHON** |
| **Drain LARGE, canal small, levels similar** | **LEVEL CROSSING** |
| **Drain very small** | **INLET and OUTLET** |

> **Canal bed, canal FSL, drain bed, drain HFL — those four levels determine the answer completely, with no judgement required once they are surveyed.**

> **Which is why accurate levelling at every drainage crossing is the first task in canal alignment**, and why an error there is expensive to discover after the alignment is fixed.

> **And the economic preference that shapes routes: an aqueduct is the cheapest of the barrel structures and a canal siphon the most troublesome** (a pressurised canal barrel silts and cannot easily be inspected). **So where the ground allows, a canal is aligned to stay ABOVE the drains it crosses.**

examTip.trick: **Name the structure after WHAT IS ON TOP.** Canal above + drain flowing FREE underneath = aqueduct. The stem's clause about the trough bottom is what rules out a SIPHON aqueduct.
examTip.trap: **Option (a) super passage is the exact mirror image**, and the words give no help without the naming rule. Learn one rule, not four definitions.
examTip.mnemonic: **Four surveyed levels decide it completely** — canal bed, canal FSL, drain bed, drain HFL. Which is why accurate levelling at every crossing is the first task in canal alignment.

questions.stem: The number of machine-made bricks required for 1 m³ of brickwork is:
questions.solution:
**550 numbers.**

**Where the figure comes from — the arithmetic is worth doing once:**

> **A modular brick is 190 × 90 × 90 mm; with a 10 mm mortar joint on each face its NOMINAL size becomes 200 × 100 × 100 mm.**

> **Nominal volume of one brick = 0.20 × 0.10 × 0.10 = 0.002 m³**

> **Bricks per cubic metre = 1 ÷ 0.002 = 500**

> **That gives 500 for a perfectly modular brick — and 500 is option (b), the designed trap.**

**Why the accepted figure is higher than the theoretical 500:**

| Reason | Effect |
|---|---|
| **Traditional (non-modular) brick sizes are SMALLER** | **A common Nepali/Indian brick is 230 × 110 × 70 mm or 240 × 115 × 57 mm, giving more bricks per cubic metre** |
| **WASTAGE and breakage** | **Typically allowed at 5-10 % — bricks break in handling and in cutting to fit** |
| **Closers and bats at corners and openings** | Cut bricks are counted as whole ones |
| Joint thickness in practice | Often thinner than the nominal 10 mm |

> **The standard estimating allowance is therefore about 500 bricks plus wastage, taken as 550 per cubic metre** — which is what the source keys and what a bill of quantities uses.

> **So the theoretical figure and the estimating figure are different numbers, and the question asks for the second.** Recognising that is the whole content: **an estimate is not a calculation, it is a calculation plus an allowance.**

**The brick sizes to know, since the arithmetic depends on which is meant:**

| Brick | Actual size (mm) | Nominal with joints |
|---|---|---|
| **Modular (IS 1077)** | **190 × 90 × 90** | **200 × 100 × 100** |
| **Traditional / conventional** | **230 × 110 × 70** | 240 × 120 × 80 |
| Nepali common brick | ~240 × 115 × 57 | — |

> **The modular brick's virtue is exactly that its nominal dimensions are round numbers**, so wall lengths, openings and courses all work out in multiples of 100 mm without cutting. **That is what "modular" means, and it saves the labour of cutting far more than it costs in brick.**

**The companion estimating quantities, since they are asked together:**

| Item | Quantity per m³ of brickwork |
|---|---|
| **BRICKS** | **~500-550 nos.** ← |
| **MORTAR** | **~0.20-0.25 m³ (about 20-25 % of the volume)** |
| **Cement, 1:6 mortar** | ~1.2 bags (60 kg) |
| **Sand, 1:6 mortar** | ~0.25 m³ |
| Water | As required for workability |

> **The mortar figure of 20-25 per cent of the wall volume is the one most often underestimated**, and it follows directly from the geometry: **a 10 mm joint around a 90 mm brick is a substantial fraction of the whole.**

**The wider set of estimating allowances, which is the real content of this corner of the syllabus:**

| Item | Allowance |
|---|---|
| **Binding wire** | **~1 kg per quintal of steel** |
| **Steel wastage (cutting)** | **3-5 %** |
| **Cement wastage** | **2-3 %** |
| **Brick wastage** | **5-10 %** |
| **Bulking of damp sand** | **20-30 % — affects VOLUME batching** |
| **Cement bag** | **50 kg = 0.035 m³** |
| **Dry volume of mortar/concrete** | **1.52-1.54 × wet volume** |

> **The 1.54 dry-volume factor and the 0.035 m³ cement bag are the two most-used numbers in estimating**, and the bulking allowance is the one whose omission causes real trouble: **volume-batching damp sand without allowing for bulking delivers LESS sand than intended, and therefore a richer and more shrinkage-prone mix.**

> **Why the allowances matter at all: a tender is won or lost on a few per cent.** Omitting one allowance changes little; omitting the habit of including them changes the outcome. **Which is why an estimator works from a checklist rather than from memory.**

examTip.trick: **A modular brick's nominal size with joints is 200 × 100 × 100 = 0.002 m³, giving 500 theoretically.** The estimating figure is 550, the difference being wastage and non-modular sizes.
examTip.trap: **Option (b) 500 is the THEORETICAL figure** — the designed trap. The question asks for the estimating quantity, and **an estimate is a calculation PLUS an allowance.**
examTip.mnemonic: **Mortar is 20-25 % of the wall volume** — a 10 mm joint round a 90 mm brick is a large fraction. And learn the allowance family: **cement bag 0.035 m³, dry volume 1.54 × wet, sand bulking 20-30 %.**

questions.stem: NBC 102 talks about:
options: Seismic design of Buildings in Nepal
questions.solution:
**Unit weight of materials.**

**The NBC loading series, which is what this question is drawn from:**

| Code | Subject |
|---|---|
| **NBC 102** | **UNIT WEIGHT of materials** ← |
| **NBC 103** | **OCCUPANCY (IMPOSED / live) load** |
| **NBC 104** | **WIND load** |
| **NBC 105** | **SEISMIC design of buildings in Nepal** |
| **NBC 106** | **SNOW load** |

> **102 unit weight, 103 imposed, 104 wind, 105 seismic, 106 snow.** Every one of the four options in this question is a member of that series, so **the question is a pure five-way match and the whole series must be known.**

> **The mnemonic that helps: the series runs in the order the loads are applied to a building.** First its own weight (102), then what is put in it (103), then what the weather does (104 wind, 106 snow), with the earthquake case (105) sitting between them because seismic force is derived from the dead and imposed loads already established.

**Why unit weight comes FIRST — it is not an arbitrary ordering:**

> **The DEAD LOAD must be established before anything else, because every other load depends on it.**

> **Seismic force is proportional to the SEISMIC WEIGHT, which is the dead load plus a fraction of the imposed load.** So NBC 105 cannot be applied until NBC 102 has been.

> **And dead load is usually the LARGEST load on a building** — for a typical RC frame, the self-weight of slabs, beams, columns and walls exceeds the imposed load by a factor of two or three.

> **Which makes the unit-weight code, the least glamorous of the five, the one whose errors propagate furthest.**

**The unit weights that matter most:**

| Material | Unit weight (kN/m³) |
|---|---|
| **REINFORCED concrete** | **25** |
| **Plain concrete** | **24** |
| **STEEL** | **78.5** |
| **Brick masonry** | **19-20** |
| **Stone masonry** | 24-27 |
| **Cement mortar / plaster** | 20-21 |
| **Water** | **9.81** |
| Timber | 6-10 |
| Soil (bulk) | 16-20 |

> **25 for RCC and 78.5 for steel are the two to have instantly**, since they appear in almost every dead-load calculation.

> **And note that these are UNIT WEIGHTS (force per volume), not densities (mass per volume).** RCC's density is 2500 kg/m³ and its unit weight 25 kN/m³ — **the factor between them is g, and omitting it is a real and expensive error.**

**The imposed loads of NBC 103, for contrast, since the two are used together:**

| Occupancy | Imposed load (kN/m²) |
|---|---|
| **Residential rooms** | **2.0** |
| **Office floors** | **2.5-4.0** |
| **Classrooms** | 3.0 |
| **Assembly, shops, corridors** | **4.0-5.0** |
| **Staircases and balconies** | **3.0-5.0** |
| **Inaccessible roof** | **0.75** |
| Accessible flat roof | 1.5 |

> **2 kN/m² for residential is the anchor**, and it is worth appreciating how modest it is: **2 kN/m² is about 200 kg spread over every square metre of floor** — far more than a room normally holds, which is the margin the code builds in.

**And the relationship to the Indian codes, since both are examined:**

| Nepali | Indian equivalent |
|---|---|
| **NBC 102 (unit weights)** | **IS 875 Part 1 (dead loads)** |
| **NBC 103 (imposed)** | **IS 875 Part 2 (imposed loads)** |
| **NBC 104 (wind)** | **IS 875 Part 3 (wind loads)** |
| **NBC 106 (snow)** | **IS 875 Part 4 (snow loads)** |
| **NBC 105 (seismic)** | **IS 1893 Part 1** |

> **The parallel is almost exact for the loading codes, and it breaks for seismic** — where Nepal has its own code because its seismic hazard, soil conditions and building stock differ from India's.

> **NBC 105 (2020) is the revision to know**, replacing the 1994 edition with a modern response-spectrum approach, four soil classes and two hazard levels. **A question may be asked in either the Nepali or the Indian frame, so both mappings are worth holding.**

examTip.trick: **102 unit weight, 103 imposed, 104 wind, 105 seismic, 106 snow.** All four options are members of that series, so the whole set must be known — this is a five-way match.
examTip.trap: **These are UNIT WEIGHTS (kN/m³), not densities (kg/m³)** — RCC is 2500 kg/m³ and 25 kN/m³, differing by g. Omitting that factor is a real and expensive error.
examTip.mnemonic: **The series runs in the order loads reach a building**: its own weight, then what is put in it, then the weather — with seismic between, because seismic force is DERIVED from the dead and imposed loads already established.

questions.stem: Cyclopean aggregate has a size more than:
questions.solution:
**75 mm.**

**The aggregate size classification:**

| Class | Size |
|---|---|
| **FINE aggregate** | **Passing 4.75 mm (and retained on 0.15 mm)** |
| **COARSE aggregate** | **4.75 mm to 75 mm** |
| **CYCLOPEAN aggregate** | **75 mm to 150 mm** ← |

> **4.75 mm and 75 mm are the two dividing lines**, and both are worth fixing: **4.75 separates fine from coarse, and 75 separates coarse from cyclopean.**

> **The 4.75 mm sieve is the single most important sieve size in concrete technology**, because it defines the fine/coarse boundary on which every mix design rests.

**What cyclopean concrete is and where it is used:**

> **CYCLOPEAN (or plum) concrete is ordinary concrete into which large stones — "plums" — are embedded**, typically making up 20 to 40 per cent of the volume.

| Application | Why cyclopean concrete suits it |
|---|---|
| **MASS CONCRETE — gravity dams, massive retaining walls, thick foundations** | **The stones displace cement paste, which is the expensive and heat-generating component** ← |
| **Heavy blinding and filling** | Cheap bulk |
| Bridge abutments and piers of older construction | Historic practice |

> **The two reasons for using it are ECONOMY and HEAT, and the second is the engineering one:**

> **Cement hydration is EXOTHERMIC.** In a thick pour the heat cannot escape, the core reaches a high temperature, and as it later cools it CONTRACTS while the already-cooled surface does not — **producing THERMAL CRACKING.**

> **Displacing 30 per cent of the concrete with inert stone removes 30 per cent of the cement and therefore 30 per cent of the heat.** That is a substantial and cheap mitigation.

> **The other measures against the same problem are worth knowing alongside:**

| Measure | Note |
|---|---|
| **LOW HEAT cement** | **Reduced C₃A and C₃S — the two high-heat compounds** |
| **Pozzolana replacement (fly ash, PPC)** | Slower, cooler hydration |
| **Cyclopean aggregate / plums** | **Less cement per unit volume** ← |
| **Pre-cooling the aggregate and mixing water; ICE in the mix** | Lowers the placing temperature |
| **Post-cooling by embedded pipes** | Used on large dams |
| **Placing in LIFTS with time between** | Lets each lift lose its heat before the next |

> **The lift-and-wait method is the most basic and is why dam concrete is placed in horizontal layers of limited thickness with a stated interval between them** — a construction sequence dictated entirely by heat.

**The rules for using plums, since they are not simply thrown in:**

| Requirement | Note |
|---|---|
| **Stones must be clean, sound and free of dust** | Otherwise no bond |
| **Well distributed, not touching each other** | **Each plum must be fully surrounded by concrete** |
| **Not within about 150 mm of any face** | **A plum at the surface is a weak point and a leakage path** |
| **Placed by hand into fresh concrete, not dropped** | So they are properly bedded |
| **Limited to about 20-40 % by volume** | Beyond that the concrete cannot be placed round them |

> **The "not touching" rule is the one that governs on site**, and its reason is simple: **two stones in contact have no concrete between them, so there is a plane of zero tensile and shear strength through the pour.**

**Why the distractors are wrong — and two of them are real boundaries:**

| Option | What it actually is |
|---|---|
| **4.75 mm** | **The FINE/COARSE aggregate boundary — a real and important limit, wrong one here** ← |
| **25 mm** | **A common maximum aggregate size for RCC**, and near the 20 mm nominal size most used |
| **45 mm** | Not a standard boundary |
| **75 mm** | ✓ |

> **Option (a) is the trap for a candidate who remembers "the aggregate boundary is 4.75 mm" without asking WHICH boundary.** There are two, and the question names the upper one.

**And the practical limit on maximum aggregate size in ordinary concrete, since it is the neighbouring topic:**

> **The nominal maximum size must not exceed the LEAST of:**

| Limit | Value |
|---|---|
| **One quarter of the minimum member thickness** | — |
| **5 mm less than the minimum clear cover** | So the aggregate can pass outside the steel |
| **5 mm less than the minimum clear spacing between bars** | **Otherwise the aggregate arches over the reinforcement and leaves a void** |
| Practical maximum for RCC | **20 mm generally, 40 mm for lightly reinforced work** |

> **The bar-spacing limit is the one that bites in practice**, and its failure mode is visible: **honeycombing beneath a congested reinforcement cage, where the aggregate bridged across the bars and the mortar alone flowed through.**

examTip.trick: **Two dividing lines: 4.75 mm (fine/coarse) and 75 mm (coarse/cyclopean).** Cyclopean runs 75 to 150 mm.
examTip.trap: **Option (a) 4.75 mm is the OTHER aggregate boundary.** A candidate who remembers "4.75 is the aggregate limit" without asking WHICH limit is caught — there are two.
examTip.mnemonic: **Plums are used to cut CEMENT and therefore HEAT** in mass concrete, since hydration is exothermic and a cooling core cracks. Rules: clean, well distributed, **never touching**, and 150 mm clear of any face.

questions.stem: Which of the following is categorized as a deep foundation?
questions.solution:
**Pile foundation.**

**The defining criterion, which is a ratio rather than a depth:**

> **A foundation is DEEP when its DEPTH-TO-WIDTH RATIO (D/B) exceeds about 4 to 5.**

> **It is not a matter of absolute depth.** A 3 m wide raft at 3 m depth is SHALLOW (D/B = 1); a 0.5 m diameter pile 10 m long is DEEP (D/B = 20).

> **That is why a large raft several metres below ground is still classed as a shallow foundation, which surprises candidates.**

**The classification:**

| **SHALLOW foundations** | **DEEP foundations** |
|---|---|
| **Spread / isolated footing** | **PILE foundation** ← |
| **Combined footing** | **WELL (caisson) foundation** |
| **STRAP (cantilever) footing** | **Pier / drilled shaft** |
| **MAT (raft) foundation** | Caisson (open, box, pneumatic) |
| **Strip / continuous footing** | Barrette |
| Stepped and sloped footings | Micropile |

> **The source states it exactly: "Mat foundation, strap footing and spread footing are shallow foundations, whereas well foundation and pile foundation are deep foundations."**

> **So three of the four options are members of the same shallow family, and one is not** — which makes the question a clean elimination.

**Why the distinction matters mechanically — the two behave differently:**

| | **SHALLOW** | **DEEP** |
|---|---|---|
| **Load transfer** | **By BEARING on the soil directly beneath** | **By SKIN FRICTION along the shaft plus END BEARING at the tip** |
| **Overburden term in bearing capacity** | Modest | **Large — the q·N_q term dominates** |
| **Settlement** | **Larger, and mostly immediate + consolidation of the stratum below** | **Smaller, and mostly elastic shortening plus tip settlement** |
| **Suits** | **Competent soil near the surface** | **Weak soil near the surface, competent stratum deeper — or heavy/uplift/lateral loads** |

> **The friction-plus-bearing split is what makes a pile a different structure rather than a deeper footing.** A friction pile may carry almost nothing on its tip; an end-bearing pile may carry almost nothing on its shaft. **Which mechanism dominates is a design decision, not an accident.**

**When a deep foundation becomes necessary:**

| Situation | Note |
|---|---|
| **Weak or compressible soil near the surface** | **The commonest reason — reach a firm stratum below** |
| **Very heavy or concentrated loads** | Bridge piers, tall buildings |
| **UPLIFT or overturning loads** | **A pile can carry TENSION; a footing essentially cannot** ← |
| **Large horizontal loads** | Piles resist by bending along their length |
| **SCOUR-prone sites (bridges in rivers)** | **Must found below the maximum scour depth** |
| Expansive or collapsible soil | Bypass the active zone |

> **The uplift point is the one worth emphasising**, because it is a capability a shallow foundation simply lacks. **A transmission tower, a tall chimney, a structure subject to wind or seismic overturning — these need a foundation that can be pulled on, and that means piles or anchors.**

> **And the scour requirement is why bridge foundations in Himalayan rivers are almost always deep**: the bed can scour several metres in a single flood, and a foundation resting above that level is founded on ground that will not be there.

**Why STRAP FOOTING is the interesting distractor:**

> **A strap (or cantilever) footing joins TWO footings with a rigid beam — the strap — so that the eccentricity on one is transferred to the other.**

> **It is used when a column sits close to a PROPERTY LINE and its footing cannot be centred beneath it.** The strap lets the eccentric footing lean on its neighbour.

> **It is unmistakably shallow — two spread footings and a connecting beam — but its name sounds specialised**, and a candidate who does not know it may guess it is something deeper.

> **The lesson: the shallow family contains several purpose-made variants (combined, strap, trapezoidal, raft) and all of them remain shallow.** The variation is in PLAN geometry, not in depth.

**And when a RAFT is chosen, since it is the other option worth understanding:**

| Choose a raft when | Note |
|---|---|
| **The total footing area would exceed about half the building footprint** | Individual footings would nearly touch anyway |
| **The soil is weak and uniform** | Spreads the load over the whole area |
| **Differential settlement must be controlled** | **The raft's stiffness ties the columns together** |
| **A basement is required** | The raft is the basement floor |
| **A FLOATING (compensated) foundation is wanted** | **The excavated soil weight offsets the building weight — net stress change near zero** |

> **The compensated-raft idea is elegant and worth knowing: excavate a weight of soil equal to the weight of the building, and the soil below sees no net increase in stress at all.** In soft clay that can be the difference between a viable building and an impossible one.

examTip.trick: **The criterion is the RATIO D/B > about 4-5, not an absolute depth.** A wide raft 3 m down is shallow; a 0.5 m pile 10 m long is deep. Three options here are the same shallow family.
examTip.trap: **Strap footing sounds specialised and is unmistakably shallow** — two spread footings joined by a beam, used where a column sits on a property line. The shallow family varies in PLAN geometry, not depth.
examTip.mnemonic: **A pile can carry TENSION; a footing essentially cannot** — which is why towers, chimneys and overturning-critical structures need piles. And bridge foundations must sit BELOW maximum scour depth.

questions.stem: The exact use of the core cutter method is:
questions.solution:
**In-situ dry density of soil, specifically in fine-grained cohesive soils without stones.**

**How the method works:**

> **A steel cylinder of known volume — the CORE CUTTER — is driven into the soil with a dolly and rammer, dug out, trimmed flush at both ends, and weighed.**

| Step | Note |
|---|---|
| **1. Weigh the empty cutter** | Known volume, typically 1000 cc |
| **2. Drive it into the levelled soil surface** | Through a dolly, using a 9 kg rammer |
| **3. Excavate around it and lift it out with the soil inside** | |
| **4. Trim both ends flush** | So the soil volume equals the cutter volume exactly |
| **5. Weigh, then determine the water content** | Oven-dry a sample |

> **Bulk density γ = (mass of soil) / (volume of cutter)**

> **Dry density γ_d = γ / (1 + w)**, with w the water content as a fraction.

> **The method's whole virtue is that the VOLUME is known exactly from the cutter's dimensions** — no measurement of an irregular hole is needed. That is what makes it quick and accurate.

**Why cohesive soil ONLY, which is the substance of the question:**

| Requirement | Why cohesionless soil fails it |
|---|---|
| **The soil must hold together when the cutter is lifted** | **Sand FALLS OUT of the cutter — so the volume is no longer known** ← |
| **The cutter must be drivable without disturbing the soil** | Driving into sand densifies it locally, so the measured density is not the in-situ one |
| **The soil must be free of STONES** | **A stone deflects or jams the cutter, or is pushed ahead of it, and the sample is disturbed or the cutter damaged** |

> **The first row is decisive: the method depends on the soil staying in the tube.** Cohesion is what keeps it there, so **the method requires cohesion by construction.**

> **And the "without stones" clause matters as much as the "cohesive" one.** A gravelly clay defeats the cutter even though it is cohesive.

> **So option (b) is wrong for a definite physical reason, and option (c) — which asserts both — fails with it.**

**The field density methods and which soil each suits:**

| Method | Suits | Volume determined by |
|---|---|---|
| **CORE CUTTER** | **Fine-grained COHESIVE soil, no stones** | **The cutter's own dimensions** ← |
| **SAND REPLACEMENT (sand cone)** | **ANY soil, including gravelly and cohesionless** | **The mass of calibrated sand that fills the hole** |
| **Water displacement** | Cohesive soil that can be coated | Water displaced by the coated lump |
| **Rubber balloon** | Most soils | Water volume pushed into the hole |
| **NUCLEAR density gauge** | **Any soil; fast and non-destructive** | **Backscatter of gamma radiation** |

> **SAND REPLACEMENT is the general method and the fallback whenever the core cutter cannot be used** — which is why the two are always taught as a pair.

> **Sand replacement works precisely because it does not care whether the hole holds its shape**: the hole is dug however it comes out, and its volume is found by filling it with sand of known bulk density. **That is slower and more error-prone (the sand's density must be calibrated, and it must be poured consistently), but it works in gravel.**

> **The nuclear gauge is the modern choice for road earthworks** — a reading in minutes rather than an hour — **but it requires calibration against a conventional method and a radiation license, so it supplements rather than replaces them.**

**What the result is used for:**

> **The measured in-situ dry density is compared with the LABORATORY maximum dry density from the Proctor test:**

> **RELATIVE COMPACTION = (field γ_d / laboratory γ_d,max) × 100 %**

| Requirement | Typical |
|---|---|
| **Embankment fill** | **95 % of laboratory maximum** |
| **Road subgrade** | **97-100 %** |
| **Water content at compaction** | **Within ±2 % of the OMC** |

> **BOTH conditions must be met.** A fill at 98 per cent density but 4 per cent wet of optimum has been compacted on the wrong side of the curve and will behave differently — **lower strength, and shrinkage on drying** — even though the density figure passes.

> **And the specification must state WHICH Proctor test the maximum refers to**, since light and heavy compaction give different maxima for the same soil. **A specification saying "95 % of maximum dry density" without naming the test is incomplete, and that omission is common.**

examTip.trick: **The method depends on the soil STAYING IN THE TUBE**, because that is what makes the volume known. Cohesion is what keeps it there — so the method requires cohesion by construction.
examTip.trap: **The "without stones" clause matters as much as "cohesive"** — a gravelly clay defeats the cutter even though it has cohesion. Sand replacement is the fallback for both cases.
examTip.mnemonic: **Core cutter for cohesive soil, SAND REPLACEMENT for anything** — sand replacement works because it does not care whether the hole holds its shape. And compaction needs BOTH the density AND the ±2 % OMC condition.

questions.stem: The observed N-value of an SPT test is 21. The corrected value after the dilatancy correction is:
questions.solution:
**18.**

**The dilatancy correction formula:**

> **When N₀ (the value after overburden correction) EXCEEDS 15, in saturated fine sand or silt:**

> **N = 15 + ½(N₀ − 15)**

> **N = 15 + ½(21 − 15) = 15 + ½(6) = 15 + 3 = 18** ✓

> **The formula halves only the EXCESS above 15**, not the whole value — which is why the answer is 18 rather than 10.5. **That structure is the point of the formula and the commonest error in applying it.**

> **The correction is from IS 2131:1981, following Terzaghi and Peck.**

**Why the correction exists — the physical reason, which makes it memorable:**

> **In SATURATED FINE SAND or SILT, driving the sampler tends to DILATE the soil — to make it want to expand.**

> **Because the soil is saturated and the loading is rapid, that tendency to expand generates NEGATIVE pore pressure (suction).**

> **Negative pore pressure means HIGHER effective stress, and therefore temporarily HIGHER strength — so the sampler meets more resistance than the soil's true density warrants.**

> **The blow count is therefore INFLATED, and the correction removes the inflation.**

> **Note the direction: the dilatancy correction always REDUCES N (for N₀ > 15).** A correction that increased it would be unsafe and would contradict the mechanism.

**The two corrections and the order they are applied — and the order matters:**

| Order | Correction | For | Effect |
|---|---|---|---|
| **FIRST** | **OVERBURDEN correction** | **The confining pressure at the test depth** | **Can increase or decrease N** |
| **SECOND** | **DILATANCY correction** | **Saturated fine sand and silt, when N₀ > 15** | **Always DECREASES N** |

> **Overburden first, dilatancy second — and the dilatancy correction is applied to the ALREADY-CORRECTED N₀, not to the raw field value.**

> **Applying them in the wrong order gives a different answer**, and the question's phrase "the corrected value after the dilatancy correction" implies the overburden step has already been taken (here N₀ = 21).

> **The overburden correction exists because the SAME sand gives a higher blow count at depth than near the surface, simply from confinement** — so raw N values from different depths are not comparable until they are normalised. **Various formulae exist (Gibbs and Holtz, Peck, Liao and Whitman); the common Liao-Whitman form is C_N = √(100/σ′_v) with σ′_v in kPa.**

**Why the distractors are wrong:**

| Option | Where it comes from |
|---|---|
| **18** | ✓ |
| **21** | **The UNCORRECTED value — the correction not applied at all** ← |
| **19** | Arithmetic slip |
| **15** | **The THRESHOLD value, mistaken for the answer** ← the interesting trap |

> **Option (d) 15 is the well-made distractor**: 15 appears twice in the formula and is the number a candidate remembers. **But 15 is where the correction STARTS, not where it ends.**

> **And option (b) 21 catches anyone who does not notice that a correction is being asked for.**

**What the N-value is used for, since the corrections only matter because the value is used:**

| Correlation | Note |
|---|---|
| **Relative density of sand** | **N < 4 very loose, 4-10 loose, 10-30 medium, 30-50 dense, > 50 very dense** |
| **Angle of internal friction φ** | Empirical charts |
| **Allowable bearing pressure** | Terzaghi-Peck charts for footings on sand |
| **LIQUEFACTION potential** | **The corrected (N₁)₆₀ is the standard input** ← |
| Pile capacity | Meyerhof and other correlations |

> **The liquefaction application is the one with the most weight in Nepal.** Loose saturated sand can lose almost all its strength in an earthquake, **and the corrected N-value is the primary field measure of whether it will.**

> **Which makes the corrections a safety matter rather than bookkeeping: an uncorrected, inflated N-value in saturated fine sand would declare a liquefiable deposit safe.** The dilatancy correction exists precisely to prevent that.

**And a caution on the test itself:**

> **The SPT is notoriously operator- and equipment-dependent** — hammer type, rope-and-drum versus automatic trip, rod length, borehole diameter and cleanliness all affect the result.

> **Which is why the modern practice is to correct to (N₁)₆₀ — normalised to 100 kPa overburden AND to 60 per cent energy transfer** — and why a bare "N = 21" from an unspecified rig means less than it appears to.

examTip.trick: **N = 15 + ½(N₀ − 15) = 15 + 3 = 18.** The formula halves only the EXCESS above 15, not the whole value — which is why it is 18 and not 10.5.
examTip.trap: **Option (d) 15 is where the correction STARTS, not where it ends** — 15 appears twice in the formula and is the number most remembered. And option (b) 21 catches anyone who misses that a correction is asked for.
examTip.mnemonic: **Overburden correction FIRST, dilatancy SECOND** — and dilatancy always REDUCES N, because saturated fine sand dilates, generating suction that temporarily inflates the blow count. Which matters most for LIQUEFACTION assessment.

questions.stem: The formula to get the horizontal reaction in a two-hinged arch is:
questions.solution:
**H = (∫Myds/EI) / (∫y²ds/EI).**

**Where the expression comes from:**

> **A two-hinged arch is statically indeterminate to the FIRST degree, and the redundant is the horizontal thrust H.**

> **The compatibility condition is that the HORIZONTAL DISTANCE BETWEEN THE TWO HINGES DOES NOT CHANGE** — both supports are pinned, so neither can move.

> **Apply Castigliano's second theorem: ∂U/∂H = 0, where U is the strain energy.**

> **With the bending strain energy U = ∫M²ds/(2EI) and the total moment M_total = M − H·y:**

> **∂U/∂H = ∫(M − Hy)(−y)ds/EI = 0**

> **⟹ ∫Myds/EI = H ∫y²ds/EI**

> **⟹ H = (∫Myds/EI) / (∫y²ds/EI)** ✓

**How to read the two integrals — the structure is the same as every unit-load solution:**

| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Numerator ∫Myds/EI** | **The horizontal spreading the LOAD would cause if H were absent** |
| **Denominator ∫y²ds/EI** | **The horizontal spreading caused by a UNIT value of H — the arch's flexibility against H** |

> **So H = (displacement the load wants to cause) ÷ (displacement per unit thrust)** — which is the general form of every force-method redundant: **H = Δ₁₀ / δ₁₁.**

> **Recognising that structure is worth more than memorising the formula, because it generalises to every redundant in every structure.**

**Why the distractors are wrong — a dimensional check disposes of two:**

| Option | Dimensions | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| **(∫Myds/EI)/(∫y²ds/EI)** | **[FL·L·L/EI] ÷ [L²·L/EI] = FL³ ÷ L³ = FORCE** ✓ | **Correct** |
| **wl²/64** | **(F/L)·L² = FORCE** ✓ | Dimensionally OK but not a general formula ← |
| **5wl²/96** | **FORCE** ✓ | Same |
| **None** | — | — |

> **All three candidates are dimensionally forces, so dimensions do not discriminate here** — which is worth knowing rather than discovering.

> **The discrimination is that options (b) and (c) are SPECIFIC RESULTS for particular arches and loadings, while the question asks for the FORMULA — the general expression.**

> **Compare the two kinds of answer:**

| For a two-hinged PARABOLIC arch, rise h, span L | Result |
|---|---|
| **udl w over the whole span** | **H = wL²/(8h)** |
| **udl w over HALF the span** | **H = wL²/(16h)** |
| **Central point load W** | **H = 25WL/(128h)** |

> **Notice that every one of these has h in the denominator, and neither option (b) nor (c) does.** So they cannot be thrust formulae for an arch at all — **a thrust must fall as the rise increases, which is the most basic property of an arch.**

> **That check is the decisive one and it needs no recall: H must be inversely proportional to the rise.** A flat arch pushes harder; a tall arch pushes less. **Any candidate expression without the rise in the denominator is wrong on sight.**

**The refinements to the basic formula, since real arches need them:**

> **The denominator gains terms for every additional flexibility:**

> **H = ∫(Myds/EI + LαT) / ∫(y²ds/EI + L/AE + k)**

| Extra term | Represents |
|---|---|
| **LαT in the numerator** | **TEMPERATURE change — a rise ADDS, so it INCREASES H** |
| **L/AE in the denominator** | **RIB SHORTENING (axial compression) — extra flexibility, so it REDUCES H** |
| **k in the denominator** | **SUPPORT YIELDING — likewise reduces H** |

> **Any mechanism that lets the springings move toward each other reduces the thrust**, and all of them appear in the denominator for that reason. **Any mechanism that pushes them apart appears in the numerator.**

> **That sign logic is easier to hold than the formula, and it answers the harder version of this question directly.**

**And the reason a three-hinged arch is often preferred on poor ground:**

> **A three-hinged arch is DETERMINATE, so H follows from statics alone: H = M_beam/h at the crown hinge.**

> **It therefore develops NO stresses at all from temperature change, rib shortening, shrinkage or support settlement** — every one of the terms above vanishes.

| Arch | Indeterminacy | Sensitive to movement? |
|---|---|---|
| **THREE-hinged** | **0** | **NO — completely insensitive** |
| **TWO-hinged** | **1** | **YES** ← this question |
| **FIXED** | **3** | **MOST sensitive** |

> **The trade-off is clean: more restraint means smaller moments under load and larger stresses from movement.** A fixed arch is the most efficient under its design load and the most vulnerable to a settling abutment — **which is why a three-hinged arch on doubtful foundations is a sound engineering choice rather than a compromise.**

examTip.trick: **H = (∫Myds/EI)/(∫y²ds/EI)** — the general force-method form **Δ₁₀/δ₁₁**: what the load wants to cause, divided by what a unit thrust causes. That structure generalises to every redundant.
examTip.trap: **Options (b) and (c) have NO RISE h in them** — and a thrust must fall as the rise increases. Any candidate arch-thrust expression without h in the denominator is wrong on sight, with no recall needed.
examTip.mnemonic: **Anything that lets the springings move TOGETHER (rib shortening, support yielding) goes in the DENOMINATOR and reduces H; anything pushing them APART (load, temperature rise) goes in the numerator.** Sign logic beats memorising.

questions.stem: The number of directly elected members for the Council from the Nepal Engineering Association is:
questions.solution:
**Five, with a tenure of four years.**

**The provision:**

> **Under the Nepal Engineering Council Act, 2055, FIVE members are DIRECTLY ELECTED to the Council from the Nepal Engineers' Association**, and they serve a term of **four years.**

> **Five members, four years.** Both numbers are worth fixing together, because either may be asked.

**Why elected members exist at all — the design of a professional regulator:**

> **A regulator's board is deliberately MIXED, and each element is there for a reason:**

| Element | Contributes |
|---|---|
| **ELECTED practitioners** | **Technical judgement, and legitimacy with the profession being regulated** ← |
| **Government appointees** | **Public accountability; the chairman is a government appointment** |
| **Academic representatives** | Judgement on qualifications and institutions |
| **Registrar (executive)** | Continuity and administration |

> **A regulator composed ENTIRELY of practitioners risks becoming a GUILD** — protecting its members' interests rather than the public's, and reluctant to discipline its own.

> **A regulator with NO practitioners lacks the technical judgement to regulate at all** — it cannot assess whether a piece of engineering was competent.

> **So the mixture is not a political compromise; it is the only arrangement that can do the job.** And the elected element must be substantial enough to carry weight, which is what five members achieves.

**The relationship between the two bodies, which this question sits on:**

| | **NEC — Nepal Engineering Council** | **NEA — Nepal Engineers' Association** |
|---|---|---|
| **Nature** | **STATUTORY REGULATOR (Act 2055), autonomous** | **Voluntary professional ASSOCIATION** |
| **Legal basis** | **Its own Act** | **Registered under the Social Service Act** |
| **Membership** | **Compulsory to practise** | **Voluntary** |
| **Serves** | **The PUBLIC** | **Its MEMBERS** |
| **Link** | **Receives FIVE directly elected members from the NEA** ← | Elects them |

> **So the profession has a voice in its own regulation without controlling it** — the standard arrangement for professional regulation worldwide.

> **This paper asks about that link twice: here, and in the question about which Act the NEA is founded under.** The two answers together describe the whole relationship.

**The Council's composition, gathered:**

| Position | Detail |
|---|---|
| **CHAIRMAN** | **Appointed by the Government of Nepal** |
| **VICE CHAIRMAN** | **B.E. + 10 years of experience** |
| **Members elected from the NEA** | **FIVE, tenure 4 years** ← |
| Members from engineering institutions | Representing education |
| Government nominees | From relevant ministries |
| **REGISTRAR** | Executive officer; maintains the register |

> **This single paper asks five separate questions from this table and its neighbouring facts** — the vice chairman's qualification, the number of elected members, the Act's amendment date, the Regulation's start year, and what kind of body the Council is.

> **That concentration is the practical point: the regulatory-body material is a small closed set of about ten facts that recurs heavily across the papers**, and it is among the cheapest marks available. **Learning the set as a set answers most of what is asked; meeting each fact separately does not.**

**The ten facts:**

| Fact | Value |
|---|---|
| **NEC Act** | **2055 BS (1998 AD)** |
| **NEC Regulation** | **2057 BS** |
| **First amendment to the Act** | **2079/05/05** |
| **Nature of the Council** | **AUTONOMOUS body** |
| **Who approves its rules** | **Government of Nepal** |
| **Vice chairman** | **B.E. + 10 years** |
| **NEA-elected members** | **5, tenure 4 years** ← |
| **Minimum qualification to register (general engineer)** | **Bachelor's degree** |
| **Institutional inspection, bachelor permanent approval** | **Every 2 years** |
| **NEA's own legal basis** | **Social Service Act** |

> **Why the distractors are wrong:** 2, 3 and 4 are near counts with no standing. **But note that 4 is the TENURE in years, which is the designed confusion** — the two numbers travel together and are easily swapped. **Five members, four years, not four members.**

examTip.trick: **FIVE members, FOUR years' tenure.** Both numbers travel together and either may be asked.
examTip.trap: **Option (c) 4 is the TENURE in years, not the number of members** — the two are easily swapped, which is exactly why 4 is offered.
examTip.mnemonic: **A regulator of only practitioners becomes a GUILD; one with none lacks the technical judgement to regulate.** The mixed board is the only arrangement that works — and the elected element must be substantial enough to carry weight.

questions.stem: The minimum qualification of a general engineer required to register with the Nepal Engineering Council is:
options: Bachelor's Degree along with two years of work experience
questions.solution:
**A Bachelor's degree.**

**The requirement:**

> **Registration as a GENERAL ENGINEER (the graduate engineer category) requires a recognised BACHELOR'S degree in engineering** — and, for a graduate of a Nepali programme, passing the Council's LICENSE EXAMINATION.

> **No work experience is required for initial registration.** That is the point of the category: **it is the entry point to the profession, taken immediately after graduation.**

**Why no experience is required — and why option (d) is the designed trap:**

> **Option (d), "Bachelor's degree along with two years of work experience", is exactly what a candidate would expect a professional register to demand**, because many jurisdictions do require a period of supervised practice before full professional status.

> **Nepal's structure separates the two questions:**

| Question | Requirement |
|---|---|
| **May I practise as an engineer at all?** | **Bachelor's degree + license examination → REGISTRATION** ← |
| **May I hold senior professional roles?** | **Experience, and higher categories of registration** |

> **So registration is the LICENSE to begin practising, not a certificate of seniority.** Requiring experience before registration would create an impossible circle: **you cannot gain engineering experience if you may not lawfully practise engineering.**

> **That circularity is the real argument, and it is why every functioning licensing system admits graduates and then supervises them.**

**The graded categories of registration:**

| Category | Qualification | Scope |
|---|---|---|
| **GENERAL / graduate engineer** | **Bachelor's degree in engineering** | **Full engineering practice within competence** ← |
| **Sub-engineer / technician** | **DIPLOMA (or overseer certificate)** | **RESTRICTED scope — limited size and complexity of work** |
| **Professional / specialist categories** | **Degree plus stated experience** | Senior roles, specialised certification |

> **A diploma holder DOES register — but in a different category with a limited scope of practice.** So option (b) is not simply wrong: **it names a real registration route, at a lower level than the question asks about.**

> **The stem's words "general engineer" are what select the bachelor's degree**, and reading them is half the question.

> **The graded structure exists because Nepal's construction industry needs both** — a diploma-qualified sub-engineer supervising a village water supply is appropriate and lawful; the same person designing a multi-storey frame is not.

**Why option (c) Master's degree is wrong, and the reasoning is worth stating:**

> **Requiring a master's degree for registration would exclude the great majority of practising Nepali engineers from the profession entirely.**

> **A bachelor's degree in engineering is a professional qualification in its own right** — that is what distinguishes engineering from disciplines where the first degree is academic and the professional qualification comes later.

> **A master's is a specialisation, not an entry requirement**, and treating it as one would misdescribe what an engineering bachelor's degree is.

**What registration actually requires in practice, since the degree is only part of it:**

| Step | Note |
|---|---|
| **1. A RECOGNISED degree** | **From a programme the Council has approved — check the list BEFORE enrolling** |
| **2. The LICENSE EXAMINATION** | **100 marks, pass 50; the gate for graduate engineers** |
| **3. Application and fee** | To the Registrar |
| **4. Entry on the REGISTER** | Registration certificate issued |
| **5. Renewal** | Periodic, as the Regulation provides |

> **Step 1 carries a warning worth passing on: a graduate of an UNRECOGNISED programme cannot register, and therefore cannot practise** — and that consequence falls on the student, after four years and considerable expense, not on the institution.

> **University affiliation does NOT imply Council recognition.** They are separate approvals answering different questions: **the university asks whether the institution can award its degree; the Council asks whether that degree qualifies its holder to practise engineering on the public.**

**And the consequence of practising without registration:**

> **It is an OFFENCE under the Act to practise as an engineer, or to use the title, without being registered** — including signing drawings and certifying work.

> **Which is the whole reason the license examination exists and is not a formality.**

examTip.trick: **A bachelor's degree, with no experience required.** Registration is the LICENSE TO BEGIN practising, not a certificate of seniority.
examTip.trap: **Option (d) adds two years' experience — which many jurisdictions do require.** Requiring it here would be circular: you cannot gain engineering experience if you may not lawfully practise. And **option (b) diploma is a REAL route, at a lower category with restricted scope.**
examTip.mnemonic: **University affiliation does NOT imply Council recognition** — two separate approvals answering different questions. A graduate of an unrecognised programme cannot register, and that falls on the student, not the institution.

questions.stem: The relation between total float, free float and interfering float is:
options: Interfering Float = Total Float + Free Float
Interfering Float = Total Float − Free Float
Interfering Float = Total Float − Free Float − Duration
Free Float = Total Float + Interfering Float
questions.solution:
**Interfering Float = Total Float − Free Float.**

**The three floats and what each one means:**

| Float | Definition | Formula |
|---|---|---|
| **TOTAL float** | **Delay possible without delaying the PROJECT** | **LFT − EFT (or LST − EST)** |
| **FREE float** | **Delay possible without delaying the EARLIEST START of any successor** | **min(ES of successors) − EFT** |
| **INTERFERING float** | **The part of the total float whose use DOES delay a successor (though not the project)** | **Total − Free** ← |

> **The names describe the relationship exactly: total float splits into a part that interferes with nothing (FREE) and a part that interferes with successors (INTERFERING).**

> **Total = Free + Interfering**, so **Interfering = Total − Free.** ✓

**Why the split matters — this is the part with real management content:**

> **Suppose an activity has a total float of 5 days and a free float of 0.**

> **It can be delayed up to 5 days without delaying the PROJECT — so a manager looking only at total float sees 5 days of slack.**

> **But its free float is zero, so ANY delay at all pushes its successors' earliest starts.** The successors lose float of their own, and the slack has simply been moved down the chain.

> **The interfering float here is 5 − 0 = 5 days: all of the slack interferes.**

> **So float is a SHARED RESOURCE ALONG A PATH, not a property of a single activity.** The first activity to use it takes it from the others.

| Consequence | Note |
|---|---|
| **Float must be managed at PATH level, not activity level** | **Promising the same five days to three subcontractors along one chain promises fifteen days that do not exist** ← |
| **Free float can be used with impunity** | Nothing downstream is affected |
| **Interfering float should be used consciously** | Successors must be told |

> **That distinction is why the concept exists at all**, and it is the answer to a common site complaint: an activity "had float" and yet delaying it caused trouble.

**A worked example, since the definitions are easier to hold with numbers:**

> **Activity B: ES = 5, duration 4, so EF = 9. Its successors' earliest starts: 9 and 12. Its LF = 14.**

| Float | Calculation | Value |
|---|---|---|
| **Total** | **LF − EF = 14 − 9** | **5** |
| **Free** | **min(ES of successors) − EF = 9 − 9** | **0** |
| **Interfering** | **Total − Free = 5 − 0** | **5** |

> **And if the successors' earliest starts were 11 and 12 instead: free float = 11 − 9 = 2, so interfering float = 3.** Two days can be used freely; the remaining three push a successor.

**Why the distractors are wrong:**

| Option | Note |
|---|---|
| **Total + Free** | **Adds instead of subtracting.** Would make the interfering part LARGER than the total, which is impossible since it is a part of it ← |
| **Total − Free** | ✓ |
| **Total − Free − Duration** | **Duration has no place in a float relation** — the floats are all differences of times, and subtracting a duration is dimensionally sensible but conceptually unrelated |
| **Free = Total + Interfering** | **The relation with the wrong term isolated.** Rearranged it says Interfering = Free − Total, which is negative whenever free < total |

> **Option (a) fails a sanity check that costs nothing: interfering float is a PART of total float, so it can never exceed it.** Any relation that adds the two must be wrong.

> **Option (d) fails the same check from the other side.** Recognising "a part cannot exceed the whole" disposes of both.

**The fourth float, for completeness, since a full question may ask for it:**

> **INDEPENDENT float = max[0, min(ES of successors) − max(LF of predecessors) − Duration]**

> **It is the delay possible in the WORST CASE — when every predecessor finishes as late as it can and every successor must start as early as it can.**

> **It is the only float that can be used with no effect on anything whatever**, and it is frequently ZERO, which is why the max[0, ...] appears: **a negative result means no such margin exists.**

**And the definition that ties it all together:**

> **An activity is CRITICAL when its TOTAL FLOAT is ZERO**, and the critical path is the chain of such activities — which is also the LONGEST path through the network. **Those two descriptions are equivalent, and holding both makes most network questions immediate.**

examTip.trick: **Total float SPLITS into free (interferes with nothing) and interfering (delays a successor but not the project).** So Total = Free + Interfering, hence Interfering = Total − Free.
examTip.trap: **Interfering float is a PART of total float, so it can never exceed it** — which kills options (a) and (d) on a sanity check, with no recall needed.
examTip.mnemonic: **Float is shared along a PATH, not owned by an activity** — the first to use it takes it from the others. Promising the same five days to three subcontractors in one chain promises fifteen days that do not exist.

questions.stem: What is the indication for the upward and downward direction of a cash flow diagram?
options: Upward = positive cash flow, downward = negative cash flow
questions.solution:
**All of the above — the three statements are three ways of saying the same thing.**

**The convention:**

> **In a CASH FLOW DIAGRAM, a horizontal line represents time, marked in periods, and vertical arrows represent cash movements.**

> **UPWARD arrows: money COMING IN** — positive cash flows, inflows, receipts, income, revenues, savings, salvage value.

> **DOWNWARD arrows: money GOING OUT** — negative cash flows, outflows, disbursements, expenses, costs, investments.

> **Each arrow represents the NET cash flow in that period: receipts minus disbursements.** That netting is worth noting — **a period with both income and expense is drawn as ONE arrow, not two.**

**Why all three options are correct:**

| Option | The vocabulary it uses |
|---|---|
| **positive / negative** | **The SIGN convention — mathematical** |
| **inflows / outflows** | **The CASH FLOW vocabulary** |
| **income / expenses** | **The ACCOUNTING vocabulary** |

> **They are three registers describing one convention.** None contradicts the others, and the source's own explanation gives all three in a single sentence.

> **So the answer is (d), and the reasoning is mechanical: check each statement independently, and only then decide.** A candidate who reasons "only one of these can be the answer, so I must choose the best" has imported an assumption the question does not make.

**Where the convention matters — the sign is not decoration:**

> **Every discounting formula depends on getting signs right, because the whole point is that inflows and outflows offset each other.**

> **NPV = Σ (cash flow at period t) / (1+i)^t**

> **If an investment is entered as positive and a return as positive too, the NPV of every project is positive and the calculation is worthless.**

> **The classic pattern of a project's diagram is therefore unmistakable:**

| Period | Arrow |
|---|---|
| **0** | **A large DOWNWARD arrow — the initial investment** |
| **1 to n** | **Small UPWARD arrows — annual net benefits** |
| **n** | **An additional UPWARD arrow — the SALVAGE value** |
| Mid-life | Occasional downward arrows — major overhauls |

> **PERIOD 0 IS "NOW", not "the end of year 1".** That is the other convention worth stating, and it matters: **an amount at period 0 is not discounted at all, and putting the initial investment at period 1 by mistake understates its cost.**

> **And the END-OF-PERIOD convention applies to everything else: a cash flow within year 3 is drawn at the end of year 3** unless the problem says otherwise.

**Why the diagram is drawn at all, since it looks like a formality:**

> **A cash flow diagram is the engineering-economics equivalent of a free-body diagram.**

> **Its purpose is to fix the TIMING and the SIGN of every amount before any arithmetic begins**, and almost every error in the subject is an error of timing or sign rather than of formula.

| Common error the diagram prevents | Note |
|---|---|
| **Discounting an amount by the wrong number of periods** | **Off-by-one on the exponent** |
| **Treating a cost as a benefit** | Sign error |
| **Missing the salvage value** | An inflow at the end, easily forgotten |
| **Missing a mid-life replacement cost** | A downward arrow inside the run |
| **Comparing projects of unequal life without adjustment** | Visible immediately on two diagrams |

> **The last one deserves a note because it is a genuine analytical trap: two projects with different lives cannot be compared on NPV directly.**

> **Either use the LEAST COMMON MULTIPLE of the lives (repeating each project until the horizons match), or compare EQUIVALENT ANNUAL COST (EAC) instead.**

> **A 10-year machine and a 15-year machine compared on raw NPV will favour the longer one for no reason but its length**, and drawing both diagrams side by side makes the mismatch obvious in a way a table of numbers does not.

**The standard interest factors, since the diagram is drawn in order to apply them:**

| Find | Given | Factor |
|---|---|---|
| **F** | **P** | **(1+i)^n — compound amount** |
| **P** | **F** | **1/(1+i)^n — present worth** |
| **P** | **A** | **[(1+i)^n − 1]/[i(1+i)^n] — series present worth** |
| **A** | **P** | **[i(1+i)^n]/[(1+i)^n − 1] — CAPITAL RECOVERY** |
| **F** | **A** | **[(1+i)^n − 1]/i — series compound amount** |
| **A** | **F** | **i/[(1+i)^n − 1] — SINKING FUND** |

> **The capital recovery factor and the sinking fund factor are the two with names worth knowing**, because they are the ones an engineer actually uses: **capital recovery converts a capital cost into an annual charge, and the sinking fund converts a future replacement cost into an annual saving.**

examTip.trick: **All three options are three registers — mathematical (positive/negative), cash-flow (inflow/outflow) and accounting (income/expense) — for one convention.** Check each independently, then decide.
examTip.trap: **PERIOD 0 IS "NOW" and is not discounted at all.** Putting the initial investment at period 1 understates its cost. Everything else follows the END-OF-PERIOD convention.
examTip.mnemonic: **A cash flow diagram is the free-body diagram of engineering economics** — it fixes timing and sign before any arithmetic, and almost every error in the subject is timing or sign, not formula. It also exposes unequal project lives, which cannot be compared on raw NPV.

questions.stem: The Nepal Engineering Council Regulation started from:
questions.solution:
**2057 BS.**

**The three dates, which must be held as a set:**

| Instrument | Year (BS) | Nature |
|---|---|---|
| **Nepal Engineering Council ACT** | **2055 (1998 AD)** | **PRIMARY legislation — creates the Council** |
| **Nepal Engineering Council REGULATION (Rules)** | **2057** | **SUBORDINATE legislation — the operational detail** ← |
| **FIRST AMENDMENT to the Act** | **2079/05/05** | Amendment to the primary Act |

> **2055 Act, 2057 Regulation, 2079 amendment.** Note that **every one of the four options in this question is one of those years or a near-miss between them** — so the question is a pure set-recall, and knowing one date is not enough.

> **This same paper asks separately about the Act's first amendment**, so two of the three dates appear in one sitting.

**Why the Act and the Regulation have different dates — and it is not an accident:**

> **An ACT is passed by the legislature.** It creates the body, states its powers in general terms, and **grants the power to make rules.**

> **A REGULATION is framed by the Council and APPROVED by the Government of Nepal.** It supplies the detail the Act deliberately leaves out: registration procedure, categories, the examination, fees, disciplinary process.

> **The Regulation MUST come after the Act, because the Act must first create the power to make it.**

> **Two years elapsed here, which is normal: the Council had to be constituted, appointed and convened before it could frame anything.**

> **So a question asking when the REGULATION started (2057) has a different answer from one asking when the ACT was passed (2055)** — and option (a) 2055 is the designed trap for anyone who has learned only one date.

**What each instrument contains, since the division explains the dates:**

| The ACT provides for | The REGULATION provides for |
|---|---|
| **Constitution of the Council as an autonomous body** | **The registration PROCEDURE and forms** |
| **The power to register engineers** | **The CATEGORIES of registration and their scopes** |
| **The power to recognise qualifications** | **The LICENSE EXAMINATION — syllabus, marks, pass mark** |
| **The power to make a code of ethics** | **The code of ethics itself** |
| **Disciplinary powers** | **The disciplinary PROCEDURE** |
| **Offences and penalties** | **FEES and renewal periods** |
| The power to make rules | **Inspection intervals for institutions** |

> **The pattern is consistent: the Act grants powers, the Regulation exercises them.**

> **Which means the details a candidate is most often asked about — the pass mark, the inspection intervals, the registration categories — are in the REGULATION, not the Act.** That is a useful orientation: **if the question concerns a number or a procedure, it comes from the Regulation.**

**Why the distinction has practical force:**

> **A Regulation can be amended far more easily than an Act** — the Council frames the change and the Government approves it, with no legislative process.

> **So the operational details move over time while the framework is stable.** The Act stood unamended for twenty-four years; **the Regulation has been revised several times, which is exactly what the arrangement is designed to permit.**

> **And it is why an examination question about a fee or a procedure should be answered from the current Regulation rather than from memory of an older edition** — the framework is durable, the details are not.

**The wider set, for the whole corner of the syllabus:**

| Fact | Value |
|---|---|
| **NEC Act** | **2055 BS (1998 AD)** |
| **NEC Regulation** | **2057 BS** ← |
| **First amendment to the Act** | **2079/05/05** |
| **Nature of the Council** | **AUTONOMOUS body** |
| **Who approves the rules** | **Government of Nepal** |
| **Vice chairman** | **B.E. + 10 years** |
| **NEA-elected members** | **5, tenure 4 years** |
| **Minimum qualification (general engineer)** | **Bachelor's degree** |
| **Institutional inspection, bachelor permanent approval** | **Every 2 years** |
| **NEA's own legal basis** | **Social Service Act** |

> **This paper asks five of those ten.** Which is the practical argument for learning them as a block: **the material is small, closed, and recurs heavily, and it is among the cheapest marks in the examination.**

examTip.trick: **2055 Act, 2057 Regulation, 2079 amendment.** All four options are members or near-misses of that set, so knowing one date is not enough.
examTip.trap: **Option (a) 2055 is the ACT's year** — the designed trap. A Regulation must come AFTER its Act, because the Act creates the power to make it.
examTip.mnemonic: **The Act grants powers; the Regulation exercises them.** So any question about a NUMBER or a PROCEDURE — pass mark, fees, inspection intervals, categories — comes from the Regulation, which is also why those details change while the Act does not.

questions.stem: The design value of the coefficient of lateral friction recommended for horizontal curve design is:
questions.solution:
**0.15.**

**Why 0.15 and not the tyre's actual grip — the criterion is COMFORT:**

> **The lateral friction a tyre can actually develop on dry road is around 0.4 to 0.6.**

> **Designing curves to that value would give radii on which no vehicle would skid — and on which the passengers would be thrown sideways uncomfortably.**

> **So the design value is limited by PASSENGER COMFORT, not by safety: the ratio of lateral to vertical force on the passenger is capped at 0.15.**

> **This is a rare and instructive case in which the governing criterion is human tolerance rather than material strength**, and it is worth recognising as such — most design values are strength limits, and this one is not.

**Where it is used — the superelevation equation:**

> **e + f = V² / (127 R)**

| Symbol | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **e** | **Superelevation (banking), as a ratio** |
| **f** | **Coefficient of LATERAL friction = 0.15** ← |
| **V** | **Design speed in km/h** |
| **R** | **Radius in metres** |
| **127** | **= 3.6² × 9.81 — converts km/h to m/s and includes g** |

> **The centrifugal force is resisted partly by the BANKING and partly by SIDE FRICTION, and the equation says the two together must take all of it.**

> **Hence the minimum radius: R_min = V² / [127(e_max + f)].**

> **With e_max = 7 % and f = 0.15: R = V²/27.94.** For a 60 km/h design speed, **R_min = 3600/27.94 = 129 m** — a useful feel for the scale.

**The maximum superelevation, which is the companion limit:**

| Terrain | e_max |
|---|---|
| **Plain and rolling** | **7 %** |
| **Hilly (no snow)** | **10 %** |
| **Snow-bound** | **7 %** |
| **Urban roads with frequent intersections** | **4 %** |

> **Superelevation has an upper limit for a reason worth stating: on a steeply banked curve a SLOW OR STOPPED vehicle slides DOWN the slope.**

> **A heavily loaded truck creeping round a 10 per cent banked bend is at real risk of exactly that**, which is why urban roads — where vehicles stop on curves — are limited to 4 per cent.

**The design sequence, since the numbers are meaningless without it:**

| Step | Action |
|---|---|
| **1** | **Compute e for 75 % of the design speed, assuming NO friction: e = (0.75V)²/(127R)** |
| **2** | **If e ≤ e_max, adopt it — done** |
| **3** | **If e > e_max, set e = e_max and CHECK f: f = V²/(127R) − e_max** |
| **4** | **If the required f ≤ 0.15, accept** |
| **5** | **If f > 0.15, INCREASE the radius or restrict the speed** |

> **The 75 per cent in step 1 is a deliberate device**: it designs the banking for the *average* vehicle rather than the fastest, so slow vehicles are not over-banked, **and friction then covers the faster ones.**

**The two friction coefficients that must be kept apart — this is the mark-losing confusion:**

| Coefficient | Value | Used in |
|---|---|---|
| **LATERAL friction, f** | **0.15** | **Horizontal curves and superelevation** ← |
| **LONGITUDINAL friction, f** | **0.35 to 0.40** | **STOPPING SIGHT DISTANCE (braking)** |

> **The same letter f is used for both, in adjacent calculations of the same design**, which is exactly why they are confused.

> **A useful anchor: the lateral value is comfort-limited and therefore SMALL; the longitudinal value is grip-limited and therefore LARGE.** The reasoning behind each number tells you which is which.

> **In this very paper, another question uses f = 0.36 in an SSD calculation** — the longitudinal value — while this question wants 0.15. **Both appear in the same sitting, which makes the distinction worth more than a single mark.**

**And the other elements of a horizontal curve, since they follow:**

| Element | Purpose |
|---|---|
| **SUPERELEVATION** | Counteracts centrifugal force |
| **TRANSITION (spiral) curve** | **Introduces the curvature GRADUALLY, so the steering and the superelevation can be applied progressively** |
| **EXTRA WIDENING** | **Mechanical (off-tracking of rear wheels) plus psychological widening** |
| **Set-back distance** | Clearance for sight distance on the inside of the curve |

> **The transition curve is the element whose absence is most felt**: without it, curvature jumps from zero to its full value at a point, and the driver must apply a steering input instantaneously. **The spiral is what makes a curve comfortable rather than merely safe — the same concern that sets f at 0.15.**

verification.notes: Stem wording adjusted. The source printed "The minimum value of coefficient of lateral friction is", while its own explanation reads "Recommended value of the lateral friction coefficient by the Indian Road Congress is 0.15" - that is, a recommended DESIGN value rather than a minimum. The same series prints the same figure as a "maximum" in another paper (source set 16, Q67), so the source is inconsistent about the label while consistent about the number. The stem now says "design value ... recommended", which is what 0.15 is; the keyed answer (b) is unchanged and the solution explains why the value is comfort-limited rather than grip-limited.

examTip.trick: **0.15 is limited by PASSENGER COMFORT, not tyre grip** — real lateral friction is 0.4-0.6. A rare case where human tolerance, not material strength, sets the design value.
examTip.trap: **The LONGITUDINAL (braking) friction is 0.35-0.40 and is used for stopping sight distance** — and this same paper uses 0.36 in an SSD question. Same letter f, adjacent calculations, different numbers.
examTip.mnemonic: **e + f = V²/127R**, the 127 being 3.6² × 9.81. Design e for **75 % of the design speed** so slow vehicles are not over-banked. And e_max is capped (4 % urban) because a STOPPED vehicle slides down a steep bank.

questions.stem: The width of a single lane road is:
questions.solution:
**3.75 m.**

**The carriageway widths, which must be held as a set:**

| Road | Carriageway width |
|---|---|
| **SINGLE lane** | **3.75 m (reduced to 3.0 m in difficult terrain)** ← |
| **INTERMEDIATE lane** | **5.5 m** |
| **TWO lane, without raised kerbs** | **7.0 m** |
| **Two lane, with raised kerbs** | 7.5 m |
| **MULTILANE pavements, per lane** | **3.5 m** |

> **Notice the deliberate oddity: a SINGLE lane is 3.75 m wide but a lane of a MULTILANE road is only 3.5 m.** The single lane is wider.

> **The reason is that a single-lane road must accommodate a vehicle with clearance on BOTH sides**, since there is no adjacent lane to borrow from and vehicles must pass each other by using the shoulders. **A lane within a multilane carriageway has its neighbours' width available for the small lateral wander a driver makes.**

> **That is why option (a) 3.5 m is the designed trap — it is a real and standard width, for a different situation.**

**Why option (d) 5.5 m appears — it is also a real figure:**

> **5.5 m is the INTERMEDIATE lane width**, and it is also the **total treated width recommended for a single-lane road**: the source notes that a single-lane road should have two treated shoulders to make up a total treated surface of 5.5 m.

> **So 5.5 m is right for the total treated width and wrong for the carriageway** — and the distinction between CARRIAGEWAY and TREATED WIDTH is exactly what the question tests.

> **Three of the four options are genuine standard dimensions, which makes this a matching question rather than a recall one.**

**The nested widths of a road cross-section, since they are confused constantly:**

| Element | Meaning | Single-lane example |
|---|---|---|
| **CARRIAGEWAY** | **The part built for vehicles to run on** | **3.75 m** |
| **Treated / sealed width** | **Carriageway plus treated shoulders** | **5.5 m** |
| **FORMATION (roadway) width** | **Carriageway plus full shoulders — the top of the earthwork** | **6.0-8.0 m by class** |
| **RIGHT OF WAY** | **The LAND acquired for the road** | **15-50 m by class** |

> **Four different widths for the same road**, and every question names one specifically. **Reading which is asked is genuinely half the mark**, and it is the commonest way to lose one in this topic.

> **Recall the right-of-way series alongside: National Highway 50 m, Feeder 30 m, District 20 m, Village 15 m** — asked elsewhere in this same series of papers.

**Why shoulders matter, since the treated-width figure depends on them:**

| Function of a shoulder | Note |
|---|---|
| **LATERAL SUPPORT to the pavement** | **A granular pavement gets its strength from confinement; without a shoulder the edge spreads and fails** ← |
| **Emergency stopping and passing** | **On a single-lane road, PASSING happens on the shoulders — which is why they must be treated** |
| Space for services and signs | — |
| Drainage path to the side drain | Camber continues across it |

> **The lateral-support function is the structural one and the most underestimated.** **Edge failure — the pavement crumbling inward from its edge — is the characteristic failure of a road with inadequate shoulders**, and it is why the treated width matters as much as the carriageway.

**And the geometric elements that accompany the width:**

| Element | Typical value |
|---|---|
| **CAMBER, bituminous surface** | **2.0 to 2.5 %** |
| **Camber, gravel or WBM** | **3.0 to 4.0 %** |
| **Camber, earth road** | **4.0 %** |
| **Ruling gradient, plain terrain** | **3.3 % (1 in 30)** |
| **Ruling gradient, hilly** | **5 % (1 in 20)** |
| **Limiting gradient, hilly** | **6 %** |
| **Exceptional gradient** | **7 %, over short lengths only** |

> **The camber sequence is worth reasoning rather than memorising: the LESS waterproof the surface, the STEEPER the camber must be**, because water must be shed before it can soak in. **A bituminous surface can afford 2 %; an earth road needs 4 %.**

> **And the gradient limits matter in Nepal more than almost anywhere**, since a road climbing a Himalayan valley wall is gradient-constrained throughout — **which is why hill roads have so many hairpin bends: the length has to be found somewhere to keep the gradient within 5 to 6 per cent.**

examTip.trick: **3.75 m single lane, 5.5 m intermediate, 7.0 m two-lane, 3.5 m per lane of a multilane road.** A single lane is WIDER than a multilane lane, because it has no neighbour to borrow clearance from.
examTip.trap: **Three of the four options are real standard widths.** 3.5 m is a multilane lane; 5.5 m is the intermediate lane AND the total TREATED width of a single-lane road. Read whether carriageway, treated, formation or right-of-way is asked.
examTip.mnemonic: **The less waterproof the surface, the STEEPER the camber** — bituminous 2-2.5 %, gravel 3-4 %, earth 4 %. And shoulders give the pavement LATERAL SUPPORT, without which it fails from the edge inward.

questions.stem: The formula for superelevation is:
questions.solution:
**e = v²/(127R) − f.**

**Where it comes from:**

> **The centrifugal force on a vehicle rounding a curve is resisted by TWO things: the component of gravity along the banked surface (superelevation) and the SIDE FRICTION between tyre and road.**

> **The two together must take the whole of it:**

> **e + f = v² / (127 R)**

> **Rearranged for e:**

> **e = v²/(127R) − f** ✓

**Two checks that settle this question without recalling the formula:**

> **CHECK 1 — the SIGN of f.** Friction HELPS resist the centrifugal force, so it does part of the job the banking would otherwise have to do.

> **Therefore more friction means LESS banking needed: f must be SUBTRACTED.**

> **Option (b), which ADDS f, says that the more friction is available the MORE banking is required — plainly backwards.** ✓ eliminated

> **CHECK 2 — the presence of g.** The constant 127 ALREADY CONTAINS g.

> **127 = 3.6² × 9.81 = 12.96 × 9.81 = 127.1**, where 3.6² converts km/h to m/s and 9.81 is g itself.

> **So writing 127gR includes gravity TWICE.** Options (a) and (d) both do that, and both are wrong for the same reason. ✓ eliminated

> **Those two checks remove three options in a few seconds and leave only (c)** — which is a better method than recall, because it also tells you what the formula means.

**The units that the constant 127 implies, and this is where errors happen:**

| Symbol | Unit required |
|---|---|
| **v** | **km/h** ← |
| **R** | **metres** |
| **e, f** | Dimensionless ratios |

> **The formula is written for v in KILOMETRES PER HOUR.** If v is given in m/s, the correct form is **e + f = v²/(gR)** with no 127 at all.

> **Mixing the two — putting m/s into the 127 formula — gives an answer wrong by a factor of 12.96**, and it is the standard slip in this topic.

**The design procedure, since the formula alone is not the design:**

| Step | Action |
|---|---|
| **1** | **Compute e for 75 % of the design speed, assuming NO friction: e = (0.75v)²/(127R)** |
| **2** | **If e ≤ e_max, adopt it** |
| **3** | **If e > e_max, set e = e_max and CHECK f: f = v²/(127R) − e_max** |
| **4** | **If the required f ≤ 0.15, accept** |
| **5** | **If f > 0.15, INCREASE R or restrict the speed** |

> **The 75 per cent in step 1 is deliberate: it banks the road for the AVERAGE vehicle rather than the fastest**, so that slow and stopped vehicles are not over-banked. **Friction then covers the faster ones.**

> **Note the logic of the procedure: banking is designed FIRST, without friction, and friction is called on only as a reserve.** That ordering is not arbitrary — **friction is unreliable (it falls on a wet or dusty surface) while the banking is a permanent geometric fact.**

**The two limits the procedure enforces:**

| Limit | Value | Reason |
|---|---|---|
| **e_max** | **7 % plain/rolling, 10 % hilly, 4 % urban** | **A SLOW or STOPPED vehicle slides down a steep bank** |
| **f_max** | **0.15** | **PASSENGER COMFORT — not tyre grip, which is 0.4-0.6** |

> **Both limits are set by something other than skidding**, which is worth noticing: **the superelevation limit protects the slow vehicle and the friction limit protects the passenger.** Neither is about the fast vehicle losing grip.

**And the elements that must accompany a superelevated curve:**

| Element | Purpose |
|---|---|
| **TRANSITION (spiral) curve** | **Introduces curvature GRADUALLY, so steering and superelevation can be applied progressively** |
| **Attainment of superelevation over the transition length** | **By rotating about the centre line or about the inner edge** |
| **EXTRA WIDENING** | **Mechanical (rear wheels off-track) plus psychological** |
| **Set-back (clearance) on the inside** | For sight distance |

> **The superelevation must be ATTAINED somewhere, and that somewhere is the transition curve** — which is a practical reason for providing one beyond passenger comfort. **Without a transition, the full banking would have to appear at a point, which is impossible to build and unpleasant to drive.**

> **The rotation method matters for drainage: rotating about the INNER EDGE raises the whole carriageway and avoids a flat spot, while rotating about the CENTRE LINE keeps the profile smoother but passes through zero cross-slope**, where water stands. **In heavy-rainfall terrain the inner-edge method is preferred for that reason.**

examTip.trick: **Two checks kill three options.** Friction HELPS, so f is SUBTRACTED (kills (b)); and **127 already contains g** (127 = 3.6² × 9.81), so 127gR counts gravity twice (kills (a) and (d)).
examTip.trap: **The 127 form requires v in km/h.** With v in m/s the formula is e + f = v²/(gR) with no 127 at all — and mixing them is wrong by a factor of 12.96.
examTip.mnemonic: **Design the banking FIRST without friction, and call on friction only as a reserve** — because friction falls on a wet surface while the banking is permanent geometry. And **e_max protects the SLOW vehicle; f_max protects the PASSENGER.**

questions.stem: The central raised part of the road is called:
questions.solution:
**The crown.**

**The distinction the question turns on — a PLACE versus a SLOPE:**

| Term | What it is |
|---|---|
| **CROWN** | **The HIGHEST POINT of the cross-section — the raised centre line itself. A LOCATION** ← |
| **CAMBER (cross slope)** | **The SLOPE from the crown down to the edges. A RATE, expressed as a percentage or 1 in n** |
| **SUPERELEVATION** | **The transverse slope on a CURVE, banked toward the inside. Also a rate — but on a curve, and one-way** |
| Apex height | Not a road term |

> **Crown and camber are the pair that must be separated: the crown is WHERE, the camber is HOW STEEP.**

> **Option (b) camber is therefore the designed trap, and it is a good one** — the two words are used together so often that they blur. **The stem says "the central raised PART", which names a location, so it is the crown.**
