> **Wherever INERTIA competes with VISCOSITY, the ratio involves ν rather than μ:**

| Group | Form | Compares |
|---|---|---|
| **REYNOLDS number** | **Re = VD/ν = ρVD/μ** | **Inertia to viscous force** |
| Froude number | **Fr = V/√(gL)** | Inertia to gravity |
| Weber number | We = ρV²L/σ | Inertia to surface tension |
| Mach number | M = V/c | Inertia to compressibility |

> **Re = VD/ν is the form worth using**, because it needs only one fluid property instead of two.

> **And the transition values that follow:**

| Flow | Reynolds number |
|---|---|
| **Pipe flow, laminar** | **Re < 2000** |
| **Pipe flow, turbulent** | **Re > 4000** |
| **Open channel, laminar** | **Re < 500** |
| **Flow past a sphere, laminar** | **Re < 1** |

> **The pipe-flow figures 2000 and 4000 are the ones examined**, with the range between them the transitional zone.

**How viscosity varies with temperature — and the two fluid types behave OPPOSITELY:**

| Fluid | Rising temperature | Mechanism |
|---|---|---|
| **LIQUIDS** | **Viscosity DECREASES** | **Cohesive intermolecular forces weaken** |
| **GASES** | **Viscosity INCREASES** | **Molecular momentum transfer intensifies** |

> **This opposite behaviour is a favourite examination point, and it follows from the different mechanism**: in a liquid viscosity is intermolecular attraction; in a gas it is molecules carrying momentum across the shear layer. **Heat weakens the first and strengthens the second.**

> **The familiar consequences: engine oil thins when hot, and bitumen must be heated to be pumped and sprayed** — which is why the bitumen questions elsewhere in this paper concern temperature at all.

verification.notes: Option (a) corrected. The source printed option (a) as "m/s2", which is an acceleration, and its own explanation repeats the same typographical slip ("Kinematic Viscosity: m/s2, stokes"). Kinematic viscosity is mu/rho and its SI unit is m2/s. The option has been corrected to m2/s, which is what makes the keyed answer (d) "both (a) and (b)" correct - as printed, option (a) was wrong and the key would have had no support.

examTip.trick: **ν = μ/ρ, so the SI unit is m²/s and the CGS unit is the STOKE (1 m²/s = 10⁴ stokes).** Both name the same quantity, so both hold.
examTip.trap: **Option (c) N·s/m² is DYNAMIC viscosity.** Check for mass: **kinematic units contain no mass** (m²/s is length and time only), because dividing by density is exactly what removes it — which is what "kinematic" means.
examTip.mnemonic: **ν = 10⁻⁶ m²/s for water** — the number in every Re = VD/ν. And note that **AIR's kinematic viscosity is ~15× LARGER than water's** despite its dynamic viscosity being 50× smaller, because air is 800× less dense.

questions.stem: A Bourdon gauge measures:
questions.solution:
**Gauge pressure.**

**Why — the reason is in how the instrument is built:**

> **A BOURDON GAUGE consists of a curved, flattened metal tube, sealed at one end and connected to the fluid at the other.**

> **When pressure is applied inside, the tube tends to STRAIGHTEN**, and the movement of its free end is transmitted through a linkage to a pointer.

> **The crucial point: the OUTSIDE of the tube is exposed to the ATMOSPHERE.**

> **So the tube deflects in response to the DIFFERENCE between the internal pressure and atmospheric pressure — which is precisely the definition of GAUGE PRESSURE.**

> **The instrument cannot measure absolute pressure because it has no vacuum reference.** It reads zero when the inside is at atmospheric pressure, not when the inside is at absolute zero.

**The pressure vocabulary, which the four options are drawn from:**

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **ABSOLUTE pressure** | **Measured from a PERFECT VACUUM as zero** |
| **GAUGE pressure** | **Measured from ATMOSPHERIC pressure as zero** ← |
| **ATMOSPHERIC pressure** | **The local pressure of the air, about 101.325 kPa at sea level** |
| **VACUUM (negative gauge) pressure** | **Gauge pressure BELOW zero — i.e. below atmospheric** |

> **The relation that ties them together:**

> **p_absolute = p_gauge + p_atmospheric**

> **And for a vacuum: p_absolute = p_atmospheric − p_vacuum**

**Why each distractor is wrong — and each names a real measurement:**

| Option | The instrument that measures it |
|---|---|
| **Gauge pressure** | ✓ **BOURDON gauge** |
| **ATMOSPHERIC pressure** | **BAROMETER — mercury or aneroid** ← |
| **ABSOLUTE pressure** | **An absolute-pressure gauge, with a SEALED EVACUATED reference chamber** |
| **VACUUM pressure** | **A VACUUM gauge — which is in fact a Bourdon gauge with its scale marked in the negative direction** ← |

> **Option (d) deserves care, because a Bourdon-type element genuinely IS used in vacuum gauges.** The tube uncurls under internal pressure and curls further under external pressure, so the same mechanism reads both ways.

> **But a vacuum gauge is a Bourdon gauge SCALED for negative gauge pressure**, and a plain Bourdon gauge reads gauge pressure. **The question asks what the instrument measures, and the general answer is gauge pressure — of which vacuum is the negative part.**

> **Option (b) is the clean elimination: a barometer measures atmospheric pressure, and it must be an absolute instrument (a sealed vacuum above the mercury column) precisely because there is no atmosphere to reference it to.**

**The key numbers:**

| Quantity | Value |
|---|---|
| **Standard atmospheric pressure** | **101.325 kPa = 1.01325 bar = 760 mm Hg = 10.33 m of water** |
| **1 bar** | **100 kPa** |
| **1 atm in metres of water** | **10.33 m** ← |
| **1 mm Hg (torr)** | 133.3 Pa |

> **The 10.33 m of water figure is the one with the most engineering content**, because it sets an absolute limit that appears repeatedly:

> **A PUMP CANNOT LIFT WATER BY SUCTION MORE THAN 10.33 m, EVEN IN THEORY** — because the best it can do is create a perfect vacuum, and atmospheric pressure can push water up only that far.

> **In practice the limit is 6 to 7 m**, because of friction losses in the suction pipe, the vapour pressure of the water (which must not be reached, or the water boils), and the need for a margin against **CAVITATION.**

> **That is why a deep well needs a submersible or a jet pump rather than a surface suction pump**, and it is a limit set by the atmosphere rather than by the machine.

**Where each type of reading is used, since the distinction is practical:**

| Use | Which pressure |
|---|---|
| **Pipe and vessel design (stress in the wall)** | **GAUGE — the wall feels the difference across it** |
| **Pump suction calculations, NPSH** | **ABSOLUTE — because vapour pressure is an absolute quantity** ← |
| **Gas law calculations (pV = nRT)** | **ABSOLUTE, always** |
| Hydraulic head and energy calculations | Gauge, conventionally |

> **The NPSH row is where the distinction earns its place.** Cavitation occurs when the ABSOLUTE pressure falls to the water's vapour pressure — **so a suction calculation done in gauge pressure will be wrong by one atmosphere, which is the whole of the available margin.**

> **Similarly, using gauge pressure in a gas law gives nonsense**: a gas at zero gauge pressure is not a gas at zero absolute pressure, and pV = nRT knows only about the latter.

examTip.trick: **The OUTSIDE of the Bourdon tube is open to the atmosphere**, so the tube deflects with the DIFFERENCE from atmospheric — which is the definition of gauge pressure. It has no vacuum reference, so it cannot read absolute.
examTip.trap: **Option (d): a vacuum gauge IS a Bourdon gauge, scaled for negative gauge pressure.** Vacuum is the negative part of gauge pressure, not a separate quantity. And a barometer must be an ABSOLUTE instrument, with a sealed vacuum.
examTip.mnemonic: **1 atm = 10.33 m of water, so no suction pump can lift water further than that even in theory** (6-7 m in practice). And use ABSOLUTE pressure for NPSH and gas laws — a gauge-pressure suction calculation is wrong by a whole atmosphere.

questions.stem: The stiffness of a member if the farther end is hinged is:
questions.solution:
**3EI/L.**

**The four values, one for each far-end condition:**

| Far end | Stiffness | Relative stiffness |
|---|---|---|
| **FIXED** | **4EI/L** | **1** |
| **HINGED (pinned)** | **3EI/L** ← | **3/4** |
| **GUIDED ROLLER** | **EI/L** | 1/4 |
| **FREE** | **0** | 0 |

> **STIFFNESS is the moment required at a joint to produce UNIT ROTATION there.**

> **The sequence 4 : 3 : 1 : 0 in units of EI/L is the whole answer**, and every option in this question is a member of it.

**Why the hinged case gives exactly three quarters — the derivation is short:**

> **For a member AB with A rotating by θ and B FIXED, slope-deflection gives:**

> **M_AB = (4EI/L)θ  and  M_BA = (2EI/L)θ**

> **The carry-over factor is 1/2 — half the applied moment appears at the far end.**

> **Now RELEASE the far end (make B a hinge).** B cannot carry moment, so **M_BA must be released to zero — and releasing it carries HALF of it back to A:**

> **carry-back to A = ½ × (2EI/L)θ = (EI/L)θ, OPPOSING the applied moment.**

> **Net moment needed at A = 4EI/L − EI/L = 3EI/L** ✓

> **So the factor 3/4 is not arbitrary: it is 1 minus the product of the two carry-over halves.**

> **And the same release gives the second key fact: for a member hinged at its far end, the CARRY-OVER FACTOR IS ZERO** — there is nowhere for a moment to be carried to.

**How this is used — the moment distribution shortcut:**

> **DF for a member at a joint = (its stiffness) / (sum of stiffnesses of all members at that joint)**, and ΣDF at any joint = 1.

| Approach | Consequence |
|---|---|
| **Use 4EI/L and distribute the far-end moment each cycle** | Correct, but wastes cycles |
| **Use the MODIFIED 3EI/L once, with zero carry-over** | **Correct and finishes the hinge in ONE step — the standard method** ← |

> **That is the practical reason for knowing the modified stiffness at all**: it removes the hinged member from the iteration entirely.

**A caution on distribution factors AT supports, because the circulating notes state this badly:**

| Support at the joint | Distribution factor of the member there |
|---|---|
| **FIXED support** | **0 — the support is infinitely stiff and absorbs everything** |
| **HINGED or ROLLER END support** | **1 — the support takes no moment, so the member takes all of it** |

> **Those two are the standard convention and they are the way round shown here** — and the source's own answer table for this very question states exactly that: **fixed support DF = 0, hinged support DF = 1.**

> **Some circulating solutions assert instead that "the distribution factor of a hinge joint is always zero", which is misleading**: it is true of a member running into a FIXED support and false of a member at a hinged END support.

> **The underlying rule settles it without memorising either case: DF = (member stiffness) / (sum of stiffnesses at the joint).** A fixed support contributes infinite stiffness to that sum, driving the member's fraction to zero; **a hinged end support contributes none, leaving the member as the only term and its fraction equal to one.**

> **So the two facts to keep apart are: STIFFNESS of a member HINGED AT ITS FAR END is 3EI/L, and the DF of a member AT a hinged end support is 1.** Both concern hinges and they answer different questions.

**Why each distractor is a real value, wrongly placed:**

| Option | Whose value it is |
|---|---|
| **0** | **FREE far end** — and separately the DF of a member into a FIXED support |
| **EI/L** | **Guided roller far end** |
| **3EI/L** | ✓ **Hinged far end** |
| **4EI/L** | **FIXED far end — the value everyone learns first** ← the trap |

> **Option (d) is the designed trap** because 4EI/L is met first and remembered best. **The question deliberately asks for the modified value.**

**The related quantities, since they are asked together:**

| Quantity | Value |
|---|---|
| **Stiffness, far end fixed** | **4EI/L** |
| **Stiffness, far end hinged** | **3EI/L** |
| **CARRY-OVER factor, far end fixed** | **+1/2** |
| **Carry-over factor, far end hinged** | **0** |
| **FEM, udl, both ends fixed** | **wL²/12** |
| **FEM, udl, one end hinged** | **wL²/8 at the fixed end** |
| **FEM, central point load, both fixed** | **WL/8** |

> **Notice the pattern in the fixed-end moments: releasing one end RAISES the moment at the other from wL²/12 to wL²/8** — a 50 per cent increase, because the released end's moment has to go somewhere.

> **The same logic that gives 3EI/L gives that too**, which is why the two sets of numbers are worth learning together rather than as separate tables.

examTip.trick: **4 : 3 : 1 : 0 in units of EI/L** for far end fixed, hinged, guided roller, free. And the 3/4 is derivable: releasing the far end carries back half of 2EI/L against the applied moment, so 4 − 1 = 3.
examTip.trap: **Option (d) 4EI/L is the FIXED value, met first and remembered best.** And keep two hinge facts apart: **stiffness with a hinged FAR END is 3EI/L; DF of a member AT a hinged end support is 1** (not 0).
examTip.mnemonic: **Carry-over to a hinged far end is ZERO**, so using 3EI/L finishes the hinge in one step of moment distribution. And releasing one end raises the other's FEM from wL²/12 to wL²/8 — same logic, 50 % increase.

questions.stem: The radial thrust on a three-hinged arch is:
options: H cos θ + V sin θ
H sin θ − V cos θ
V cos θ − H sin θ
questions.solution:
**Radial thrust = V cos θ − H sin θ.**

**The resolution that produces both answers:**

> **At any section of an arch, the internal forces are found by resolving the horizontal thrust H and the vertical shear V along and NORMAL to the arch axis at that point.**

> **θ is the angle the arch axis makes with the horizontal at the section.**

| Direction | Component | Name |
|---|---|---|
| **ALONG the arch axis (tangential)** | **H cos θ + V sin θ** | **NORMAL THRUST (axial compression)** |
| **PERPENDICULAR to the arch axis (radial)** | **V cos θ − H sin θ** | **RADIAL THRUST (the shear force in the arch)** ← |

> **The source's own answer gives both lines together: "Normal thrust: V sin θ + H cos θ; Radial thrust: V cos θ − H sin θ."**

> **So option (a) is not wrong — it is the NORMAL thrust**, and the question's word "radial" is what selects between them. **That single word is the whole discrimination.**

**How to get the signs right without memorising — and this is the reliable method:**

> **Both expressions are just a rotation of axes through the angle θ.**

> **The TANGENTIAL component takes the cos of the horizontal force and the sin of the vertical one, and they ADD** — because at a crown (θ = 0) the whole of H acts along the axis and none of V does.

> **Check it: at θ = 0, normal thrust = H cos0 + V sin0 = H.** ✓ **Correct — at the crown, the axial force IS the thrust.**

> **The RADIAL component takes the cos of the vertical force and the sin of the horizontal one, and they SUBTRACT.**

> **Check it: at θ = 0, radial thrust = V cos0 − H sin0 = V.** ✓ **Correct — at the crown, the shear IS the vertical shear.**

> **Those two checks at θ = 0 verify both formulae in seconds and settle which is which**, and they are worth doing rather than trusting recall.

> **The second check also disposes of option (b), H sin θ − V cos θ**: at θ = 0 it gives **−V**, the right magnitude with the wrong sign. **It is the answer with the subtraction the wrong way round.**

**Why the RADIAL thrust matters — it is the arch's shear force:**

> **The radial thrust is the SHEAR FORCE at the section, resolved into the arch's own frame of reference.**

> **An efficiently shaped arch has a SMALL radial thrust everywhere**, because that means the resultant force at every section is nearly ALONG the axis — pure compression, no shear.

> **A large radial thrust means the arch is being asked to act as a curved beam rather than as an arch.**

| Radial thrust | What it indicates |
|---|---|
| **≈ 0 everywhere** | **The arch axis follows the FUNICULAR (thrust) line of the loading — ideal** |
| **Large** | **The load is not the one the shape was chosen for** |

> **For a three-hinged parabolic arch under a udl over the whole span, the radial thrust is zero at every section** — which is the same result as the bending moment being zero, seen from the other side. **Both statements say the resultant is purely axial.**

**Why three-hinged arches are worth this attention:**

> **A three-hinged arch is STATICALLY DETERMINATE**, so H, V and the internal forces follow from equilibrium alone.

> **The crown hinge supplies the third equation: the bending moment there is ZERO by definition, which gives H = M_beam(crown)/h directly.**

| Arch | Indeterminacy | Sensitive to movement? |
|---|---|---|
| **THREE-HINGED** | **0 — determinate** | **NO — completely insensitive** ← |
| **TWO-hinged** | 1 | YES |
| **FIXED** | 3 | **MOST sensitive** |

> **Being determinate, a three-hinged arch develops NO stresses at all from temperature change, rib shortening, shrinkage or support settlement.** All those effects simply move the hinges slightly, and nothing is restrained.

> **Which makes it the sound choice on doubtful foundations** — not a compromise but a positive engineering decision. **A fixed arch on a settling abutment is a much worse structure than a three-hinged arch on the same ground.**

**The three internal forces at an arch section, gathered:**

| Force | Expression | Note |
|---|---|---|
| **NORMAL thrust** | **H cos θ + V sin θ** | **Axial compression — the arch's purpose** |
| **RADIAL thrust** | **V cos θ − H sin θ** | **Shear — should be small** ← |
| **BENDING MOMENT** | **M = M_beam − H·y** | **Zero for a funicular shape under its design load** |

> **All three come from the same two quantities (H and V) and the same angle θ**, so once the reactions are found the whole internal state of the arch follows by resolution — **which is why an arch problem is really a problem about finding H.**

examTip.trick: **Check both at θ = 0 (the crown).** Normal thrust must reduce to H (so H cos θ + V sin θ) and radial thrust must reduce to V (so V cos θ − H sin θ). Two checks verify both formulae in seconds.
examTip.trap: **Option (a) is the NORMAL thrust** — the word "radial" is the whole discrimination. And option (b) gives −V at the crown: right magnitude, subtraction the wrong way round.
examTip.mnemonic: **Radial thrust IS the arch's shear force**, so a well-shaped arch has it near zero everywhere — meaning the resultant runs along the axis. And a **three-hinged arch is immune to temperature, rib shortening, shrinkage and settlement**, being determinate.

questions.stem: The maximum bending moment in a simply supported beam due to a train of wheel loads:
options: Always occurs at the centre of span
Always occurs under a wheel load
Never occurs under a wheel load
questions.solution:
**Always occurs under a wheel load.**

**Why — the reason is the shape of the bending moment diagram:**

> **Between two point loads there is no distributed load, so the SHEAR FORCE is constant and the bending moment varies LINEARLY.**

> **A linear function has no interior maximum.** Its extreme values occur at its ends.

> **The bending moment diagram for a set of point loads is therefore a POLYGON of straight segments, with vertices AT the loads.**

> **A maximum of a polygon must occur at a VERTEX — that is, under a load.** ✓

> **Equivalently: dM/dx = V, and the maximum moment occurs where the shear changes sign.** For point loads the shear is constant between loads and JUMPS at each load — **so the sign change can only happen AT a load, never between two.**

> **That argument is complete and needs no formula.**

**Why option (a) is wrong, and it is the substantive trap:**

> **For a SINGLE central point load, the maximum moment is at mid-span — so the instinct is understandable.**

> **But for a TRAIN of loads it is generally NOT at mid-span**, and it is not even at the load nearest mid-span in every case.

> **The governing rule is the one the source states: the maximum bending moment occurs under a chosen wheel load when the CENTRE OF THE SPAN LIES MIDWAY between that wheel load and the RESULTANT of the whole load system.**

> **In symbols: place the load system so that the wheel and the resultant are EQUIDISTANT from mid-span, at distance x on either side.**

> **The load is then NOT at mid-span — it is offset by x** — so the maximum moment occurs off-centre.

**The procedure for the ABSOLUTE maximum bending moment:**

| Step | Action |
|---|---|
| **1** | **Find the RESULTANT of all the loads — magnitude and position** |
| **2** | **Choose a wheel load and position the system so that the wheel and the resultant straddle mid-span equally** |
| **3** | **Compute the bending moment under that wheel** |
| **4** | **REPEAT for each wheel in turn** |
| **5** | **The largest of those values is the ABSOLUTE maximum bending moment** |

> **Step 4 is the one candidates omit.** The rule tells you where to put the system for a GIVEN wheel; **it does not tell you which wheel gives the largest moment.** That has to be tested.

> **In practice the answer is usually one of the heavier wheels near the middle of the group**, which is a useful guide for choosing the order to test — but it is a guide, not a rule.

**Why option (c) "never under a wheel load" is wrong:**

> **It is the exact inversion of the correct answer**, and it can be dismissed on the polygon argument alone: **the vertices of the diagram are AT the loads, so the maximum must be there.**

> **It may appeal to a candidate confusing this with the SHEAR force, where the maximum does occur at a support rather than under a load** — and where the shear is discontinuous at each load, so "the value at a load" is ambiguous.

**The companion result for shear, since the two are asked together:**

| Quantity | Where its absolute maximum occurs |
|---|---|
| **Bending moment** | **UNDER A WHEEL LOAD, positioned by the equidistant rule** |
| **SHEAR FORCE** | **AT A SUPPORT, with the leading (or trailing) load AT the support and as many loads as possible on the span** |

> **The shear rule is simpler: crowd the load system as close to one support as possible.** There is no equidistance condition, because the shear influence line is a triangle with its peak at the support.

**How this is actually done in practice — INFLUENCE LINES:**

> **The influence line for bending moment at a section C at distances a and b from the supports is a TRIANGLE with peak ab/L at C.**

> **The effect of a set of loads is then Σ(load × ordinate under it)**, and positioning the loads to maximise that sum is a mechanical exercise.

> **For a udl over part of the span, the effect is intensity × AREA under the influence line** — so the udl should cover exactly the length over which the influence line has the sign you want, and no more.

> **That is why a continuous beam is loaded in ALTERNATE spans (a chequerboard pattern) for maximum sagging moment**: the influence line changes sign span by span, so loading every span would let the negative parts cancel the positive.

**And why any of this matters:**

> **This is BRIDGE loading.** A bridge is not loaded by a fixed set of forces — **it is loaded by whatever crosses it, in whatever position does the most harm.**

> **So a bridge designer must find the worst position of a moving load system, not merely analyse a given one.** Influence lines and the rules above are the tools for doing it, and IRC's standard loadings (Class AA, Class A, 70R) are the load trains they are applied to.

examTip.trick: **Between point loads the moment is LINEAR, so the diagram is a polygon with vertices AT the loads — and a maximum of a polygon is at a vertex.** Equivalently, dM/dx = V and the constant shear can only change sign AT a load.
examTip.trap: **Option (a) is right for a SINGLE central load and wrong for a train.** The rule is that the wheel and the RESULTANT straddle mid-span equally — so the load is OFF-centre by that distance.
examTip.mnemonic: **Test every wheel in turn** — the equidistant rule places the system for a GIVEN wheel but does not say which wheel governs. And for SHEAR the rule is different and simpler: crowd the loads at a support.

questions.stem: The ratio of linear stress to linear strain is called:
questions.solution:
**Modulus of Elasticity (Young's modulus, E).**

**The four elastic constants, each a ratio of a different stress to its own kind of strain:**

| Constant | Definition | Symbol |
|---|---|---|
| **MODULUS OF ELASTICITY (Young's)** | **LINEAR (direct) stress ÷ LINEAR strain** | **E = σ/ε** ← |
| **MODULUS OF RIGIDITY (shear)** | **SHEAR stress ÷ SHEAR strain** | **G = τ/γ** |
| **BULK MODULUS** | **DIRECT stress ÷ VOLUMETRIC strain** | **K = σ/(Δv/v)** |
| **POISSON'S RATIO** | **LATERAL strain ÷ LONGITUDINAL strain** | **μ = −ε_lat/ε_long** |

> **The pattern is systematic: each modulus pairs a stress with the strain it produces**, and the question's phrase "linear stress to linear strain" names the first exactly.

> **Poisson's ratio is the odd one out — it is a ratio of two STRAINS, so it is DIMENSIONLESS**, while the three moduli all have the units of stress.

> **That observation eliminates option (d) instantly on dimensions: a modulus has units of N/mm²; a ratio of two strains has none.**

**The relations between them — three constants determine all four:**

> **E = 2G(1 + μ)**

> **E = 3K(1 − 2μ)**

> **E = 9KG/(3K + G)**

> **So any TWO of E, G, K, μ determine the other two**, for an isotropic material.

> **The consequences of the second relation are worth reading:**

| Poisson's ratio | Bulk modulus | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| **μ = 0** | **K = E/3** | No lateral contraction (cork approximates this) |
| **μ = 0.25** | K = 2E/3 | Typical of many metals |
| **μ = 0.30** | K = 0.83E | **Steel** |
| **μ → 0.5** | **K → ∞** | **INCOMPRESSIBLE — the theoretical upper limit** ← |

> **μ = 0.5 is the theoretical maximum for any material**, and the reason falls straight out of the relation: **at μ = 0.5 the bulk modulus becomes infinite, meaning no volume change is possible under any pressure.**

> **Rubber and saturated undrained clay both approach 0.5**, which is why an undrained clay is analysed as an incompressible material — **and why its immediate settlement occurs at constant volume, by shape change only.**

**Typical values, since the question is really about knowing the family:**

| Material | E (GPa) | μ | G (GPa) |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Structural steel** | **200-210** | **0.30** | **~80** |
| **Concrete (M25)** | **25** | **0.15-0.20** | ~11 |
| **Aluminium** | **70** | 0.33 | 26 |
| Timber (along grain) | 8-15 | — | — |
| **Rubber** | ~0.01-0.1 | **~0.5** | — |

> **For steel: G = E/[2(1+0.3)] = E/2.6 ≈ 0.385E ≈ 80 GPa** — worth checking once, because it shows the relation working.

> **And note that G is always LESS than E for any positive Poisson's ratio**, since E = 2G(1+μ) means G = E/[2(1+μ)] < E/2. **A computed G greater than E is an arithmetic error.**

**Why option (a) modulus of rigidity is the designed near-miss:**

> **Both E and G are ratios of a stress to a strain, and both have the units of stress.** The only difference is WHICH stress and WHICH strain.

> **The stem's word "linear" is the discriminator: linear (direct, axial) stress and strain give E; SHEAR stress and strain give G.**

> **A candidate who reads only "ratio of stress to strain" cannot choose between them** — and that is exactly what the question is testing.

**And where each one is actually used:**

| Constant | Appears in |
|---|---|
| **E** | **Axial deformation δ = PL/AE; beam deflection; Euler buckling P = π²EI/L²** |
| **G** | **TORSION T/J = Gθ/L; shear deflection; shear modulus in plate analysis** |
| **K** | **Water hammer wave speed; compressibility problems** |
| **μ** | **Lateral strain; plane-stress and plane-strain conversions; earth pressure at rest K₀ = μ/(1−μ)** |

> **The K₀ relation is the one that connects this topic to geotechnics: the coefficient of earth pressure at rest is derived from Poisson's ratio** — **K₀ = μ/(1 − μ)**, which for μ = 0.3 gives 0.43, close to the commonly used 0.4 to 0.5 for normally consolidated soil.

> **So the four elastic constants are not confined to strength of materials; they reappear wherever a material's deformation matters.**

examTip.trick: **Each modulus pairs a stress with the strain it produces.** "Linear stress to linear strain" is E. Shear stress to shear strain is G; direct stress to VOLUMETRIC strain is K.
examTip.trap: **Poisson's ratio is a ratio of two STRAINS, so it is DIMENSIONLESS** — that eliminates (d) instantly. And option (a) G is the near-miss: the stem's word "linear" is the only discriminator.
examTip.mnemonic: **E = 2G(1+μ) and E = 3K(1−2μ)**, so any two constants give the other two. Note **K → ∞ as μ → 0.5**, the incompressible limit — which is why undrained clay (μ ≈ 0.5) settles at constant volume.

questions.stem: With a percentage increase of carbon in steel, which property decreases?
questions.solution:
**Ductility.**

**What carbon does to steel — the whole pattern in one table:**

| Property | Effect of INCREASING carbon |
|---|---|
| **STRENGTH (tensile, yield)** | **INCREASES** |
| **HARDNESS** | **INCREASES** |
| **BRITTLENESS** | **INCREASES** |
| **DUCTILITY** | **DECREASES** ← |
| **Weldability** | **DECREASES** |
| **Toughness (impact resistance)** | **DECREASES** |
| Machinability | Decreases above about 0.3 % |
| Hardenability by heat treatment | Increases |

> **Three of the four options INCREASE and only one DECREASES**, so the question is a clean elimination once the pattern is known.

> **And the pattern itself is memorable as a single trade: carbon buys STRENGTH and HARDNESS at the cost of DUCTILITY, TOUGHNESS and WELDABILITY.**

**Why — the metallurgy, briefly, because it makes the trade-off intelligible:**

> **Carbon in steel forms hard, brittle IRON CARBIDE (cementite, Fe₃C), which appears with ferrite as the layered structure PEARLITE.**

> **More carbon means more cementite, and cementite is hard and brittle.** It obstructs the movement of dislocations through the crystal lattice.

> **Obstructing dislocation movement is precisely what makes a metal STRONGER and HARDER — and it is the same thing that makes it LESS ABLE TO DEFORM PLASTICALLY, which is what ductility means.**

> **So strength and ductility are not two independent properties that happen to move oppositely: they are two descriptions of the same mechanism seen from opposite ends.** Whatever impedes plastic flow raises strength and lowers ductility.

> **That is the deepest idea in the topic, and it applies far beyond carbon content** — cold working, alloying and heat treatment all trade the same way.

**Note that BRITTLENESS increases, which is the trap in the option list:**

> **Brittleness and ductility are OPPOSITES**, so exactly one of them must appear in the answer and the other must not.

> **A candidate reading quickly may see "brittleness" and think "that is the bad property, so it must be the one that decreases"** — but the question asks which property DECREASES, and brittleness increases.

> **The question is testing whether the direction of each property is held, not merely which properties are involved.**

**The classification by carbon content, and why structural steel sits where it does:**

| Type | Carbon | Character and use |
|---|---|---|
| **Wrought iron** | **< 0.05 %** | **Very ductile, very weak; obsolete** |
| **LOW carbon (mild) steel** | **0.05-0.25 %** | **DUCTILE and WELDABLE — structural sections, reinforcement, plates** ← |
| **Medium carbon** | **0.25-0.60 %** | Stronger, less ductile — shafts, rails, forgings |
| **HIGH carbon** | **0.60-1.5 %** | **Hard, brittle — springs, cutting tools, high-strength wire** |
| **CAST IRON** | **2-4 %** | **Very hard, very brittle; NOT weldable in the ordinary sense; strong in compression** |

> **Structural steel is deliberately LOW carbon, and the reason is worth stating: a structure must be DUCTILE.**

> **A ductile structure gives WARNING before it fails** — it deflects, it yields, it redistributes load to less-stressed members, and it absorbs energy. **A brittle structure fails suddenly and completely, with no warning and no reserve.**

> **In seismic design that reserve is the whole strategy.** A building is not designed to remain elastic in a major earthquake; **it is designed to yield in a controlled way and absorb the energy through plastic deformation.** A brittle structure cannot do that at any strength.

> **So low-carbon steel is chosen not because it is the strongest available but because it is DUCTILE and WELDABLE** — and paying for higher strength with brittleness would be a bad trade for a structure.

**The weldability point, since it is the practical constraint:**

> **Carbon above about 0.30 per cent makes steel difficult to weld** — the heat-affected zone hardens and cracks.

> **This is why structural steels and reinforcement bars are specified with a maximum carbon content and a CARBON EQUIVALENT limit**, not merely a minimum strength.

> **And it is why WELDABLE reinforcement is a distinct specification: ordinary Fe415 bars can be welded only with care, and Fe500 with more.** **Welding reinforcement without checking its carbon equivalent is a real site error**, and the resulting brittle weld is invisible until it fails.

**And the modern route around the trade-off:**

> **HSD and TMT bars achieve high strength WITHOUT high carbon** — by cold-twisting (HSD) or by controlled quenching of the surface while the core stays hot (TMT).

> **A TMT bar has a hard, strong outer rim and a soft, ductile core**, so it delivers strength and ductility together. **That is why TMT has displaced cold-twisted bars, and it is a genuine improvement rather than a marketing one.**

examTip.trick: **Carbon buys STRENGTH, HARDNESS and BRITTLENESS and costs DUCTILITY, TOUGHNESS and WELDABILITY.** Three options increase, one decreases — a clean elimination once the direction is held.
examTip.trap: **Brittleness and ductility are opposites, so exactly one appears in the answer.** Reading "brittleness" as "the bad property, so it must decrease" is the trap — the question asks which DECREASES, and brittleness rises.
examTip.mnemonic: **Strength and ductility are two views of ONE mechanism** — whatever impedes dislocation movement raises one and lowers the other. Structural steel is low-carbon because a structure must be DUCTILE: it must warn, redistribute and absorb energy.

questions.stem: What is the length of the slender beam portion of the Benkelman beam?
questions.solution:
**3.66 m.**

**The full geometry of the instrument, which must be learned as a set:**

| Dimension | Value |
|---|---|
| **TOTAL beam length** | **3.66 m** ← |
| **Pivot to PROBE tip** | **2.44 m** |
| **Pivot to DIAL GAUGE** | **1.22 m** |
| **Pivot to FRONT leg** | **0.25 m** |
| **Pivot to REAR leg** | **1.66 m** |

> **Note that 2.44 + 1.22 = 3.66** — the two arms about the pivot add to the total length. **That relation is a check on the whole set and makes it easier to hold.**

> **And the ratio 2.44 : 1.22 = 2 : 1 is the most important single fact about the geometry: the probe arm is exactly TWICE the gauge arm, so EVERY DIAL READING IS DOUBLED to give the actual deflection.**

> **Option (b) 2.44 m is the designed trap** — it is the probe arm, the figure most often memorised because it appears in the lever ratio. **The question asks for the whole beam.**

**What the test measures:**

> **A loaded truck's rear dual wheel is placed over the test point, the probe inserted between the tyres, and the pavement's REBOUND as the truck moves away is measured.**

| Parameter | Standard value |
|---|---|
| **Axle load** | **8170 kg (80 kN)** |
| **Tyre pressure** | **5.6 kg/cm²** |
| **Readings taken at** | **Initial (Do), intermediate at 2.7 m (Di), final at 9 m (Df)** |
| **Result** | **Rebound deflection, in mm** |

> **It measures REBOUND — elastic recovery — not the deflection under load.** The truck is driven away and the pavement springs back; the dial records that recovery.

> **The three legs form the reference frame, and they must rest OUTSIDE the deflected area** — which is why the beam has to be 3.66 m long. **A shorter beam would have its legs sitting inside the deflection bowl, and the instrument would measure the difference between two deflections rather than one.**

> **That is the engineering reason for the length**, and it makes the figure something to reason about rather than merely recall.

**The corrections, which are the examinable content:**

> **True deflection D = 2(Do − Df)**, the factor 2 from the lever ratio.

> **If (Di − Df) > 0.025 mm, the legs were themselves on deflected pavement**, and a **LEG CORRECTION** applies: **D = 2[(Do − Df) + 2.91(Di − Df)].**

> **Then two further corrections:**

| Correction | For |
|---|---|
| **TEMPERATURE** | **Standardised to 35 °C — bitumen is stiffer when cold, so a cold-weather deflection UNDERSTATES the true value** |
| **SEASONAL / moisture** | **The subgrade is weakest just after the monsoon; a dry-season test must be factored UP** |

> **Both corrections matter more than they look.** A deflection measured in a cold, dry January and used untreated **makes a weak pavement look adequate — and the overlay designed from it fails in the first monsoon.**

> **The leg correction's 2.91 factor is itself derived from the geometry above**, which is another reason the dimensions are worth knowing rather than looking up.

**What the answer is for:**

> **CHARACTERISTIC DEFLECTION = mean + 2 standard deviations** for a major road (mean + 1 SD for lesser roads), over at least ten points on a homogeneous section.

> **That single figure, entered in the IRC 81 chart with the design traffic, gives the required OVERLAY THICKNESS.**

> **So the whole purpose of the test is STRENGTHENING design of an existing pavement** — it answers "how much overlay?" without excavating anything. **A high deflection means a weak pavement and a thick overlay.**

**Why the statistical treatment is used rather than the mean:**

> **A pavement is not uniform, and an overlay designed for the AVERAGE deflection would be inadequate over the weakest half of the section.**

> **Taking mean + 2SD designs for roughly the worst 2.5 per cent** — a deliberate choice about how much of the road may fail early.

> **And it explains the requirement for at least ten points: a standard deviation computed from three readings is meaningless.**

**And the modern successor:**

> **The FALLING WEIGHT DEFLECTOMETER (FWD)** applies an impulse load and measures a deflection BASIN with several sensors, from which the modulus of EACH LAYER can be back-calculated.

> **The Benkelman beam gives one number; the FWD gives a layer-by-layer diagnosis** — which tells you WHERE the weakness is, not merely that there is one.

> **But the beam needs only a truck and two people, which is why it remains in use** wherever an FWD is not available. **The choice is availability, not principle.**

examTip.trick: **Total 3.66 m = probe arm 2.44 + gauge arm 1.22** — the two arms add to the total, which checks the whole set. And 2.44 : 1.22 is 2 : 1, so every dial reading is DOUBLED.
examTip.trap: **Option (b) 2.44 m is the probe arm**, the figure most often memorised. The length exists so the LEGS rest OUTSIDE the deflection bowl — a shorter beam would measure the difference between two deflections.
examTip.mnemonic: **Correct to 35 °C and for season, then take mean + 2SD over at least ten points** → IRC 81 gives the overlay thickness. An uncorrected cold, dry-season reading makes a weak pavement look adequate.

questions.stem: Based on wind speed, Nepal is divided into how many zones?
questions.solution:
**Two.**

**The two wind zones:**

| Zone | Region | Basic wind velocity |
|---|---|---|
| **1. Lower plains and hills** | **The Terai, the Kathmandu Valley, and generally BELOW 3000 m elevation** | **47 m/s** |
| **2. The mountains** | **All areas ABOVE 3000 m** | **55 m/s** |

> **The dividing line is an ELEVATION of 3000 metres**, and the source's own explanation states it: the first zone covers regions generally below 3000 m and the second all areas above it.

> **The Nepalese plains continuous with the Indian plains take 47 m/s, and the higher hills 55 m/s.**

**Why only two zones — and the contrast with the seismic map is instructive:**

> **Wind speed in Nepal correlates strongly and simply with ALTITUDE.** Higher ground is more exposed, has less shelter and experiences stronger winds.

> **That single variable explains most of the variation, so a two-zone map captures it adequately.**

> **Seismic hazard does NOT correlate with altitude** — it depends on distance from the fault system, local geology and basin effects — **which is why NBC 105's seismic zoning is a continuous factor map rather than two bands.**

| | **WIND** | **SEISMIC** |
|---|---|---|
| **Governing variable** | **ELEVATION — simple and monotonic** | **Fault proximity, geology, basin geometry** |
| **Nepal's treatment** | **TWO zones, split at 3000 m** | **A continuous zoning factor map, plus FOUR soil classes** |
| **Code** | **NBC 104** | **NBC 105** |

> **This paper asks about NBC 102 (unit weights) and about the soil classes elsewhere in the series**, so the loading-code family recurs and is worth knowing whole.

**How the basic wind velocity becomes a design pressure:**

> **Design wind speed:  V_z = V_b × k₁ × k₂ × k₃**

| Factor | Accounts for |
|---|---|
| **V_b** | **BASIC wind velocity — 47 or 55 m/s here** |
| **k₁** | **Risk / return period — importance of the structure and its design life** |
| **k₂** | **TERRAIN, height above ground and structure size** |
| **k₃** | **TOPOGRAPHY — hills, ridges, escarpments** |

> **Then the design wind PRESSURE:**

> **p_z = 0.6 V_z²**  (p in N/m², V in m/s)

> **The coefficient 0.6 is ½ρ for air, with ρ ≈ 1.2 kg/m³** — so the formula is simply the dynamic pressure of the airstream.

> **Check the scale: with all factors equal to 1 and V_b = 55 m/s, p = 0.6 × 3025 = 1815 N/m²** — a figure that appears as a computed answer elsewhere in this same paper.

**Why the SQUARE matters more than the zone:**

> **Pressure varies as the SQUARE of the velocity**, so the difference between the two zones is larger than it looks:

| Zone | V_b | p = 0.6V² |
|---|---|---|
| **Lower** | **47 m/s** | **1325 N/m²** |
| **Mountain** | **55 m/s** | **1815 N/m²** |
| Ratio | **1.17** | **1.37** |

> **A 17 per cent increase in speed gives a 37 per cent increase in pressure.** Which is the general lesson: **in wind engineering, small changes in the speed assumption are large changes in the load.**

> **And it is why the k₃ topography factor matters so much in Nepal.** A structure on a ridge crest can see a factor of 1.36, which on top of the mountain zone's 55 m/s produces a very large pressure — **and ridge tops are exactly where communication towers and viewing structures get built.**

**Which structures wind actually governs:**

| Structure | Wind's role |
|---|---|
| **Low-rise buildings** | **Usually NOT critical — seismic and gravity govern** |
| **ROOFS, especially light ones** | **CRITICAL — wind UPLIFT is the classic failure** ← |
| **Tall or slender structures** | Critical, and dynamic effects appear |
| **Communication towers, chimneys, poles** | **Wind usually GOVERNS** |
| Signboards, hoardings, cladding | Wind governs |

> **The roof-uplift case is the one that causes most actual damage, and it is regularly under-appreciated.** Wind flowing over a roof produces SUCTION on the upper surface, and if the roof is light — CGI sheeting on a light frame — **the net uplift can exceed its self-weight and the roof leaves the building.**

> **The remedy is not a stronger roof but better ANCHORAGE: the sheets to the purlins, the purlins to the trusses, the trusses to the walls, and the walls to the foundation.** A continuous load path in TENSION, which is the opposite of what a gravity-designed structure needs.

> **Which is why roof failures in high winds are almost always CONNECTION failures rather than member failures**, and why the detailing matters more than the member sizes.

examTip.trick: **TWO zones, split at 3000 m elevation: 47 m/s below, 55 m/s above.** Wind correlates simply with altitude, which is why two bands suffice.
examTip.trap: **Do not import the SEISMIC zoning, which is a continuous factor map with FOUR soil classes.** Seismic hazard does not follow altitude, so its treatment is quite different.
examTip.mnemonic: **p = 0.6V² (which is ½ρ for air), so pressure goes as the SQUARE** — a 17 % speed difference between the zones is a 37 % pressure difference. And wind's real victim is **ROOF UPLIFT**, failing at the CONNECTIONS, not the members.

questions.stem: Nappe means:
questions.solution:
**The flowing water above the crest — the sheet of water passing over a weir.**

**The terminology of a weir, which is what the question tests:**

| Term | What it is |
|---|---|
| **CREST or SILL** | **The TOP EDGE of the weir, over which the water passes** |
| **HEAD (H)** | **The height of the upstream water surface ABOVE the crest** |
| **NAPPE (or vein)** | **The SHEET OF WATER itself, flowing over and past the crest** ← |
| Ventilation | Admitting air beneath the nappe |
| Drowned / submerged | When the downstream level rises above the crest |

> **Note that CREST and SILL are two names for the same thing**, and that the question distinguishes the STRUCTURE (crest), the HYDRAULIC CONDITION (head), the STORED WATER (option c) and the FLOWING SHEET (nappe).

> **Only one of those is a sheet of moving water.**

**Why option (c) is the substantive distractor:**

> **"Water stored behind the weir" is a real thing — it is the PONDAGE**, and it is the whole purpose of a diversion weir: to raise the upstream level enough to feed a canal.

> **But it is stored water, not flowing water**, and the nappe is specifically the moving sheet. **The distinction is between what the weir HOLDS and what passes OVER it.**

**Why the nappe matters — the VENTILATION problem:**

> **A free nappe springs clear of the weir and encloses a pocket of air beneath it.**

> **The falling sheet ENTRAINS that air and carries it away downstream.** If air cannot get back in, the pocket is progressively evacuated.

| Consequence of an unventilated nappe | Note |
|---|---|
| **Sub-atmospheric pressure under the nappe** | **The sheet is SUCKED toward the weir face** |
| **The nappe CLINGS to the downstream face** | It no longer springs clear |
| **The effective head changes, so the DISCHARGE COEFFICIENT changes** | **The weir stops being a reliable measuring device** ← |
| **Fluctuation and vibration** | The nappe oscillates between clinging and springing |

> **So a measuring weir MUST BE VENTILATED** — by air vents through the weir wall, or by making the weir NARROWER than the channel so air reaches the underside from the sides.

> **This is a real and frequently overlooked source of field error: a weir built across the full channel width with no air path reads HIGH, and no amount of care in measuring the head corrects it.**

**The three nappe conditions, since each changes the discharge relation:**

| Condition | Description |
|---|---|
| **FREE (aerated)** | **Nappe springs clear, atmospheric pressure underneath — the DESIGN condition** |
| **DEPRESSED / clinging** | **Partial vacuum underneath, nappe drawn in — coefficient increases** |
| **DROWNED (submerged)** | **Downstream level above the crest — discharge REDUCED and dependent on BOTH levels** |

> **The drowned condition destroys a measurement most completely**, because the discharge then depends on the tailwater as well as the head — **so a single upstream reading no longer determines the flow.**

> **Which is why a measuring weir needs a free fall downstream, and why that drop must be provided by design rather than assumed.**

**The weir discharge relations, since they follow:**

| Weir | Discharge |
|---|---|
| **Rectangular sharp-crested** | **Q = (2/3) C_d L √(2g) H^{3/2}** |
| **Triangular (V-notch), angle θ** | **Q = (8/15) C_d √(2g) tan(θ/2) H^{5/2}** |
| **Ogee spillway** | **Q = C L H^{3/2}, C ≈ 2.2 (SI)** |
| **Broad-crested** | Q = 1.71 L H^{3/2} |
| Cipolletti (trapezoidal) | Q = 1.86 L H^{3/2} |

> **Note the exponents: 3/2 for a rectangular weir, 5/2 for a V-notch.**

> **The V-notch's higher exponent is exactly why it suits SMALL flows**: as the head falls, the flow area of a V-notch shrinks in BOTH dimensions, so the head varies far more for a given change in discharge. **A rectangular weir's head becomes too small to read accurately at low flow; a V-notch's does not.**

> **And the corollary: a V-notch is poor at HIGH flow**, since the head then becomes inconveniently large. **Rectangular for large flows, V-notch for small ones** — the practical selection rule.

**One further correction worth carrying:**

> **The effective length of a rectangular weir is reduced by END CONTRACTIONS:**

> **L_effective = L − 0.1 n H**, with n the number of contracted ends.

> **A weir spanning the full channel width has NO end contractions** — which is one of the very few advantages of that arrangement, **and it is not nearly enough to justify losing the ventilation.**

examTip.trick: **The nappe is the SHEET OF WATER itself**, not the structure (crest/sill), not the head, and not the stored water. The options separate structure, condition, storage and flowing sheet.
examTip.trap: **Option (c) names a real thing — the PONDAGE, the weir's whole purpose.** But that is water HELD, and the nappe is water PASSING OVER. The distinction is holds versus passes.
examTip.mnemonic: **An unventilated nappe CLINGS to the weir face, changing the discharge coefficient** — so the weir reads high and no care in measuring the head corrects it. Measuring weirs must be aerated, or made narrower than the channel.

questions.stem: A Kaplan turbine is a:
questions.solution:
**A reaction turbine.**

**The classification, which is the whole content:**

| Class | How energy is transferred | Members |
|---|---|---|
| **IMPULSE** | **The whole head is converted to VELOCITY in a nozzle BEFORE the runner; the runner turns at ATMOSPHERIC pressure** | **PELTON, TURGO, Cross-flow (Banki-Michell)** |
| **REACTION** | **The runner is FULLY SUBMERGED and PRESSURE drops across it as well as velocity; the runner does work by reaction** | **KAPLAN, Propeller, FRANCIS, Bulb, Deriaz** ← |

> **The source's own answer lists them exactly: "Reaction Turbine: Kaplan, Propeller, Francis. Impulse Turbine: Pelton wheel, Turgo, Cross-Flow."**

> **Option (c) Turgo is the designed trap: it is a real turbine and it is an IMPULSE one**, so a candidate who recognises the name but not its class may reach for it.

**The distinguishing test, which is more reliable than a memorised list:**

> **Is the runner FULL OF WATER and under PRESSURE, or is it running in air and struck by a jet?**

| | **IMPULSE** | **REACTION** |
|---|---|---|
| **Runner** | **Runs in AIR; buckets struck by a jet** | **FULLY SUBMERGED, flow fills the passages** |
| **Pressure across the runner** | **CONSTANT (atmospheric)** | **DROPS** |
| **Casing** | **A simple housing, not pressure-bearing** | **A pressure-bearing SPIRAL CASING** |
| **DRAFT TUBE** | **NOT used — and cannot be** | **ESSENTIAL** ← |
| **Flow control** | **Nozzle / spear valve** | **Adjustable GUIDE VANES (wicket gates)** |
| **Head** | **HIGH** | **Medium to LOW** |

> **The DRAFT TUBE is the single most reliable discriminator**, and its purpose is worth knowing:

> **A reaction turbine's runner sits ABOVE the tailwater, and without a draft tube the head between the runner and the tailwater would be LOST.**

> **The draft tube is a gradually expanding passage that recovers that head by converting the exit velocity back into pressure — creating a partial VACUUM at the runner exit and so making the effective head larger than the runner would otherwise see.**

> **An impulse turbine cannot use one, because its runner is already at atmospheric pressure and must stay there** — the buckets have to be free to discharge into air.

> **So: draft tube present → reaction. Draft tube absent → impulse.** One question settles the class.

**Where the Kaplan sits, and why it has adjustable blades:**

| Turbine | Head | Specific speed (metric) | Flow direction |
|---|---|---|---|
| **PELTON** | **High: 250-1800 m** | **8-30** | Tangential |
| **Turgo, cross-flow** | Medium-high | 30-100 | — |
| **FRANCIS** | **Medium: 45-400 m** | **50-250** | **Mixed (radial in, axial out)** |
| **KAPLAN** | **LOW: below ~60 m** | **250-850** | **AXIAL** ← |
| Bulb / tubular | Very low: under 15 m | 800+ | Axial |

> **The Kaplan's defining feature is ADJUSTABLE RUNNER BLADES**, and that is what distinguishes it from the otherwise identical PROPELLER turbine (fixed blades).

> **Why adjustable blades matter: a fixed-blade propeller turbine's efficiency collapses away from its design flow**, because the blade angle no longer matches the flow angle.

> **A Kaplan adjusts BOTH its guide vanes and its runner blades together — "double regulation" — so the flow angle matches the blade angle at every discharge.**

| Turbine | Efficiency at part load |
|---|---|
| **Propeller (fixed blades)** | **Falls sharply** |
| **KAPLAN (adjustable)** | **Stays high over a WIDE range — a flat efficiency curve** ← |
| Francis | Falls moderately |
| **Pelton (multi-jet)** | **Stays high — jets can be shut off individually** |

> **The flat part-load efficiency curve is precisely why the Kaplan suits a LOW-HEAD RIVER installation**, where the discharge varies enormously between seasons and the machine must work well at all of them.

> **A Francis at 40 per cent flow is inefficient; a Kaplan at 40 per cent flow is nearly as good as at full flow.** That is worth a great deal of annual energy.

**Why option (d) "mechanical turbine" can be dismissed on sight:**

> **It is not a category in turbine classification.** Turbines are classified by **action (impulse/reaction), by head, by flow direction (tangential/radial/mixed/axial), and by specific speed** — never as "mechanical".

> **Recognising a non-existent category is a legitimate technique**, and it appears often enough in this examination to be worth naming.

**And the selection logic, since it is what the classification is for:**

> **HIGH head, LOW flow → PELTON (impulse). LOW head, HIGH flow → KAPLAN (reaction). In between → FRANCIS.**

> **Nepal's mountain sites are overwhelmingly high-head and low-flow**, which is why the Pelton dominates the country's small and micro-hydro schemes — **and why Kaplan turbines appear mainly on the larger Terai-edge and canal-drop schemes.**

examTip.trick: **Reaction: Kaplan, Propeller, Francis. Impulse: Pelton, Turgo, Cross-flow.** The reliable test is the DRAFT TUBE — present means reaction, absent means impulse, because an impulse runner must discharge into air.
examTip.trap: **Option (c) Turgo is a real turbine and an IMPULSE one** — recognising the name is not enough. And option (d) "mechanical turbine" is not a category at all; spotting a non-existent class is a legitimate technique.
examTip.mnemonic: **Kaplan = adjustable blades; Propeller = fixed.** Double regulation keeps the efficiency curve FLAT over a wide flow range — which is exactly what a low-head river with big seasonal variation needs.

questions.stem: An enoscope is used to determine:
questions.solution:
**Spot speed.**

**What an enoscope is:**

> **A simple hand-held instrument containing a MIRROR set at 45°**, which lets an observer standing at the roadside see along a line PERPENDICULAR to the road while facing along it.

> **Two enoscopes are set a short measured distance apart** (or one enoscope and a direct line of sight), and the observer times a vehicle passing between them with a stopwatch.

> **Speed = measured distance ÷ measured time.**

> **Because the distance is short — typically 30 to 90 m — the result is the vehicle's speed AT THAT POINT, which is by definition its SPOT SPEED.**

> **The mirror's purpose is to remove PARALLAX ERROR.** An observer looking obliquely at a vehicle cannot judge the instant it crosses a line; **the 45° mirror lets him watch a perpendicular sightline while standing safely at the roadside.**

**Why SHORT distance means SPOT speed — the definitions that the options are drawn from:**

| Speed | Definition | Measured over |
|---|---|---|
| **SPOT speed** | **The instantaneous speed of a vehicle at a specified POINT** | **A very short base — a point in effect** ← |
| **AVERAGE (journey) speed** | **Total distance ÷ total time, INCLUDING stops and delays** | **A long section** |
| **Running speed** | **Distance ÷ time in MOTION only, excluding stops** | A long section |
| **TIME mean speed** | **Arithmetic mean of spot speeds at a POINT over a period** | A point, many vehicles |
| **SPACE mean speed** | **Mean speed of vehicles occupying a LENGTH at an instant** | A length, many vehicles |

> **The enoscope measures one vehicle at one point, so it gives a spot speed** — and averaging many enoscope readings gives the **TIME MEAN SPEED**, since they are all taken at the same point.

> **That distinction is examined in its own right: time mean speed is measured AT A POINT; space mean speed is measured OVER A LENGTH**, and **space mean speed is always LESS than or equal to time mean speed.**

> **The reason is that slow vehicles occupy a length for longer, so they are over-represented in a space-based average.** Only when all vehicles travel at the same speed do the two coincide.

**What spot speed studies are used for:**

| Application | Note |
|---|---|
| **Setting SPEED LIMITS** | **Conventionally the 85TH PERCENTILE speed** ← |
| **Geometric design checks** | Is the actual speed consistent with the design speed? |
| **Accident analysis** | Speed at a black spot |
| **Assessing the effect of a measure** | Before-and-after study of a hump, sign or camera |
| **Traffic signal and sign placement** | Amber time depends on approach speed |

> **The 85th percentile rule deserves explanation because it is counter-intuitive: the speed limit is set at the speed which 85 per cent of drivers do not exceed.**

> **The reasoning is that the great majority of drivers choose a reasonable speed for the conditions, and a limit set below that is widely disobeyed and therefore unenforceable.** A limit that most traffic ignores reduces respect for limits generally.

> **Conversely the 15th percentile speed is used to identify vehicles travelling unusually slowly**, which are themselves a hazard on a fast road.

**The percentile speeds and their uses, since they are a set:**

| Percentile | Use |
|---|---|
| **98th** | **DESIGN SPEED for geometric design** |
| **85th** | **SPEED LIMIT** |
| **50th (median)** | Typical speed; used in some capacity work |
| **15th** | **Lower limit — identifies slow vehicles** |

> **Note that the DESIGN speed (98th) is higher than the SPEED LIMIT (85th)**, which is deliberate: **the geometry must be safe for the fastest realistic vehicle, not merely for the legal maximum.**

**The other spot-speed instruments, for context:**

| Method | Note |
|---|---|
| **ENOSCOPE** | **Simple, cheap, needs two observers; a stopwatch method** ← |
| **Radar / lidar speed meter** | **Direct, instantaneous, one operator — the modern standard** |
| **Pneumatic tube or loop detectors** | Automatic, continuous, records every vehicle |
| **Photographic / video with time stamps** | Gives speed and much else |
| Stopwatch over a marked base | The crudest version; parallax error is the problem the enoscope solves |

> **The enoscope is essentially obsolete in practice** — a radar meter does the job better with one operator — **but it remains on the syllabus because it makes the definition of spot speed concrete, and because its mirror illustrates exactly the measurement error that all such methods must deal with.**

examTip.trick: **A short measured base (30-90 m) means the result is the speed AT A POINT — spot speed.** The 45° mirror exists to remove PARALLAX ERROR, letting the observer watch a perpendicular sightline from the roadside.
examTip.trap: **Average speed and travel time need a LONG section**, not a short base. Averaging many enoscope readings gives TIME mean speed (all at one point), not space mean speed (over a length).
examTip.mnemonic: **Design speed = 98th percentile; SPEED LIMIT = 85th percentile; 15th identifies slow vehicles.** The limit is set at the 85th because a limit most traffic ignores is unenforceable — and design must exceed the limit.

questions.stem: The test intended to study the resistance of aggregates to weathering action is:
questions.solution:
**The soundness test.**

**What the soundness test does:**

> **It subjects the aggregate to ACCELERATED WEATHERING CYCLES** — repeated immersion in a saturated solution of **sodium sulphate or magnesium sulphate**, followed by drying.

> **The salt crystallises in the aggregate's pores as it dries, and the crystallisation exerts pressure that breaks up weak or porous particles** — mimicking, in days, what frost action and salt weathering would do over years.

> **The loss in weight after a stated number of cycles is the measure**, and the limit is typically **12 per cent for sodium sulphate and 18 per cent for magnesium sulphate.**

> **So the test is a durability test, not a strength test** — and that is the distinction the question turns on.

**The aggregate test family, and each measures a DIFFERENT property:**

| Test | Measures | Property class |
|---|---|---|
| **ABRASION (Los Angeles, Deval)** | **Resistance to WEAR by rubbing** | **Hardness** |
| **CRUSHING** | **Resistance to gradually applied COMPRESSIVE load** | **Strength** |
| **IMPACT** | **Resistance to SUDDEN shock or blow** | **Toughness** |
| **SOUNDNESS** | **Resistance to WEATHERING (accelerated cycles)** | **DURABILITY** ← |
| **Water absorption** | Porosity | Durability indicator |
| **Shape (flakiness, elongation)** | Particle geometry | Workability and interlock |
| **Stripping value** | Adhesion to bitumen in water | Durability of the bond |

> **The four options are the four principal mechanical tests, and each names a distinct property: hardness, strength, toughness, durability.**

> **The stem's word "WEATHERING" selects durability, and only the soundness test measures it.**

**Why the three distractors are the well-made ones:**

> **All three are genuine, important tests that a candidate will have met — and none of them concerns weathering at all.**

| Test | What a road engineer uses it for |
|---|---|
| **ABRASION** | **Will the surface aggregate polish and wear under traffic?** Los Angeles abrasion value limit typically 30-50 % by layer |
| **CRUSHING** | **Will the aggregate break under wheel loads?** Crushing value limit 30-45 % |
| **IMPACT** | **Will it shatter under the sudden blow of a wheel striking it?** Impact value limit 30-45 % |

> **The IMPACT test is worth a note because its existence is easy to question: why not just use the crushing test?**

> **Because a sudden blow gives the stress no time to redistribute through the particle, so a BRITTLE aggregate can pass a crushing test and fail an impact test.**

> **And a wheel striking a pothole edge delivers impact, not gradual compression** — so the impact test represents a real loading the crushing test misses.

> **That is a good example of why apparently redundant tests exist: they represent different loadings that fail materials differently.**

**Why soundness matters particularly in Nepal:**

> **The country has severe weathering conditions over much of its area:**

| Condition | Effect |
|---|---|
| **FREEZE-THAW at altitude** | **Water in pores expands 9 % on freezing and splits the particle** |
| **Intense monsoon wetting and drying** | Repeated saturation cycles |
| **Weak SIWALIK sandstone widely available** | **Locally convenient and often unsound** ← |
| Thermal cycling on exposed slopes | Large diurnal ranges |

> **The Siwalik point is the practical one.** Siwalik sandstone is close at hand along much of the Terai-hill margin and is therefore tempting as a source — **but it is geologically young, poorly cemented and often fails the soundness test.**

> **An aggregate that passes crushing and abrasion and fails soundness will build a road that looks perfect and disintegrates in its second or third monsoon** — which is precisely the failure the soundness test exists to prevent, and precisely the failure that a contractor testing only strength will not foresee.

**The related durability indicator, since it is cheaper and quicker:**

> **WATER ABSORPTION is the most diagnostic single indicator of durability, and it should be below about 2 per cent for road aggregate (and below 0.6 per cent for high-quality concrete aggregate).**

> **The reason it works as a proxy: almost every mechanism that destroys an aggregate — freezing, salt crystallisation, chemical attack — needs WATER TO GET INSIDE IT FIRST.**

> **So a low-absorption aggregate is largely immune to all of them at once**, and a high-absorption one should be viewed with suspicion whatever its strength.

> **That is why absorption is measured routinely and soundness only where there is reason for concern** — the cheap test screens, and the expensive test confirms.

examTip.trick: **Four tests, four distinct properties: abrasion = hardness, crushing = strength, impact = toughness, SOUNDNESS = durability.** The word "weathering" selects durability.
examTip.trap: **All three distractors are genuine, important tests** — none concerns weathering. And note why the impact test is not redundant: a sudden blow gives stress no time to redistribute, so a brittle aggregate can pass crushing and fail impact.
examTip.mnemonic: **Water absorption below ~2 % is the cheap proxy for durability**, because nearly every destructive mechanism needs water inside the particle first. Screen with absorption, confirm with soundness — and be wary of Siwalik sandstone.

questions.stem: Find the delta for a crop if the duty for a base period of 120 days is 1500 hectares/cumec.
questions.solution:
**691 mm (computed 691.2 mm).**

**The relation:**

> **Δ = 8.64 B / D**

| Symbol | Meaning | Value |
|---|---|---|
| **Δ** | **DELTA — total depth of water required, in METRES** | ? |
| **B** | **BASE PERIOD, in days** | **120** |
| **D** | **DUTY, in hectares per cumec** | **1500** |

**The computation:**

> **Δ = 8.64 × 120 / 1500**

> **= 1036.8 / 1500**

> **= 0.6912 m**

> **= 691.2 mm ≈ 691 mm** ✓

> **The four options differ by ONE MILLIMETRE each**, so the arithmetic must be carried to three significant figures — **there is no room for rounding at an intermediate step.**

> **The clean way is 8.64 × 120 = 1036.8 exactly, then divide by 1500. Dividing 8.64 by 1500 first (= 0.00576) and then multiplying invites a rounding error that lands on the wrong option.**

**Where the 8.64 comes from — deriving it removes the need to remember it:**

> **One cumec flowing for one day delivers 1 × 86,400 = 86,400 m³ of water.**

> **Over B days: 86,400 B m³.**

> **That volume irrigates D hectares = 10,000 D m².**

> **So the depth applied is  Δ = 86,400 B / (10,000 D) = 8.64 B / D** metres ✓

> **The constant is simply 86,400 seconds in a day divided by 10,000 square metres in a hectare.** Rebuilt in ten seconds, and — more usefully — **the units can then never be muddled: the answer comes out in METRES.**

> **A candidate who forgets the metre/millimetre step reports 0.691 and finds no matching option**, which is at least a warning rather than a wrong answer.

**The check on the direction, which catches gross errors:**

> **Duty and delta are INVERSELY related.** A thirsty crop (large delta) means a given flow can serve less land (small duty).

> **A duty of 1500 ha/cumec is fairly LOW, so the delta should be fairly HIGH** — and 691 mm (about 69 cm) is indeed a substantial depth, in the region of rice or sugarcane rather than wheat.

| Crop | Base period (days) | Delta (cm) | Duty (ha/cumec) |
|---|---|---|---|
| **RICE** | **120** | **125** | **~830 — the LOWEST duty, the thirstiest crop** |
| **Sugarcane** | **320** | **90** | ~3070 (long base period) |
| **Wheat** | **120** | **40** | **~2590** |
| Cotton | 200 | 50 | ~3456 |
| Maize | 100 | 25 | ~3456 |

> **Note the trap the table reveals: DUTY depends on BOTH the delta AND the base period.** Sugarcane has a large delta AND a high duty, because it grows over a long season. **The duty is a rate; the delta is a total.**

> **So a low duty does not by itself mean a thirsty crop — it means a lot of water in a short time.**

**The definitions, since these terms are used together and confused:**

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **DELTA (Δ)** | **TOTAL DEPTH of water required over the whole base period** |
| **DUTY (D)** | **AREA a unit discharge, run continuously, can irrigate — ha/cumec** |
| **BASE PERIOD (B)** | **From the FIRST to the LAST watering** |
| **CROP PERIOD** | **From sowing to harvest — slightly LONGER than the base period** |
| **KOR depth and KOR period** | **The single most critical watering, soon after sowing, and its duration** |
| **INTENSITY of irrigation** | Percentage of the culturable area actually cropped in a season |

> **The base-period/crop-period distinction is small and examined: the crop period is longer, because the crop keeps ripening after the last watering.**

> **And the KOR watering is what determines the CANAL'S CAPACITY**, not the average demand: the whole command needs its first critical watering within a short window, **so the canal must be sized for that peak and stands under-used for much of the rest of the season.**

**And the efficiency chain, which is why the field delta is not the delta at the head:**

| Efficiency | Typical | Loss to |
|---|---|---|
| **Conveyance** | **60-80 %** | **SEEPAGE and evaporation in the canals — the largest loss** |
| **Field application** | **60-80 %** | Deep percolation and runoff at the field |
| **OVERALL project** | **~40-60 %** | The product of the two |

> **So the discharge required at the canal HEAD is roughly TWICE what the crops actually consume**, and the duty at the head is about half the duty at the field.

> **Lining the canals attacks the largest single loss in the chain**, which is why it is the standard first improvement to an existing scheme — and why an unlined canal in permeable ground can lose more water than it delivers.

examTip.trick: **Δ = 8.64B/D = 8.64 × 120/1500 = 0.6912 m = 691.2 mm.** The 8.64 is just 86,400 s/day ÷ 10,000 m²/ha, and it delivers the answer in METRES.
examTip.trap: **The options differ by ONE millimetre**, so compute 8.64 × 120 = 1036.8 exactly and then divide. Dividing 8.64 by 1500 first invites a rounding error onto the wrong option.
examTip.mnemonic: **Duty depends on BOTH the delta AND the base period** — sugarcane has a large delta and a HIGH duty, because its season is long. Duty is a rate; delta is a total. And the **KOR watering sets the canal capacity**, not the average demand.

questions.stem: A sewerage system is designed with:
options: return factor × population × rate of water supply × peak factor
questions.solution:
**DWF + WWF — dry weather flow plus wet weather flow.**

**Why the total must include both:**

> **A COMBINED sewerage system carries two quite different flows, and it must be sized for their sum:**

| Component | What it is |
|---|---|
| **DRY WEATHER FLOW (DWF)** | **The sanitary sewage — from domestic, commercial and industrial sources, plus infiltration** |
| **WET WEATHER FLOW (WWF)** | **The STORM runoff entering the same sewers during rain** |

> **The storm component is far the larger.** A rainfall event can produce a flow many times the sanitary flow — **commonly four to six times DWF in design, and much more in an intense storm.**

> **So a combined sewer sized on sanitary flow alone would surcharge and flood every time it rained**, which is why the total is the design basis.

**Why option (c) is the substantive near-miss and deserves care:**

> **Option (c) — return factor × population × rate of water supply × peak factor — is the correct expression for the DRY WEATHER FLOW alone.**

> **It is not wrong; it is INCOMPLETE.** It computes one of the two components:

> **DWF = population × per capita water supply × RETURN FACTOR (about 0.8) × PEAK FACTOR**

| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Return factor ≈ 0.8** | **About 80 per cent of the water supplied returns as sewage; the rest is consumed, evaporated, or used in gardens** |
| **Peak factor** | **Converts average to peak flow — 2.5 to 3.0 for small systems** |

> **So the question is testing whether the candidate knows that the sanitary flow is only PART of a sewerage system's design flow.** A candidate who has learned the DWF formula thoroughly will pick (c) and be caught by exactly that thoroughness.

> **Options (a) and (b) are cruder versions of the same partial answer**: (a) applies a peak factor to a flow that is already peaked, and (b) omits the return factor entirely.

**The three types of sewerage system, since the design basis depends on which is built:**

| System | Carries | Design flow |
|---|---|---|
| **SEPARATE** | **Sewage and stormwater in TWO separate pipe networks** | **Sanitary sewer: DWF only. Storm sewer: WWF only** |
| **COMBINED** | **BOTH in ONE network** | **DWF + WWF** ← this question |
| **PARTIALLY separate** | **Sewage plus roof and yard drainage in one; road drainage separate** | DWF + part of WWF |

> **The separate system is the modern preference and the reason is the TREATMENT WORKS:**

| | **SEPARATE** | **COMBINED** |
|---|---|---|
| **Pipe sizes** | **Two networks, both smaller** | **One network, much larger** |
| **Cost of pipework** | Higher (two systems) | **Lower (one system)** |
| **Flow to treatment** | **STEADY — only sewage** | **Hugely variable** |
| **Treatment plant size** | **Sized for sewage only** | **Must handle storm flow, or overflow untreated** |
| **Self-cleansing at dry weather** | **Achieved by design** | **Difficult — a storm-sized sewer runs nearly empty in dry weather and SILTS** |
| **Pollution risk** | Low | **COMBINED SEWER OVERFLOWS discharge dilute sewage to watercourses during storms** ← |

> **The overflow problem is the decisive argument against combined systems.** No treatment works can economically be sized for storm flow, **so a combined system must have overflows — and every overflow discharges dilute raw sewage into a river.**

> **And the self-cleansing problem is the second: a sewer large enough for storm flow carries dry-weather flow at a trickle**, far below the 0.6 m/s scouring velocity, so it silts up between storms.

> **Which is why a combined sewer needs the same devices as a depressed sewer — a smaller channel within the larger section to concentrate the low flow.**

**The design flows in full, for a separate sanitary sewer:**

| Flow | Value |
|---|---|
| **Average DWF** | **Population × per capita supply × return factor (0.8)** |
| **Maximum (peak) DWF** | **2.5 to 3.0 × average** |
| **Minimum DWF** | **1/2 to 1/3 × average** |
| **INFILTRATION** | **An allowance for groundwater entering through joints — 5,000 to 50,000 l/ha/day** |
| **Design capacity** | **Peak DWF + infiltration** |

> **The sewer is sized for the PEAK and checked at the MINIMUM** — and the minimum matters as much, because it determines whether the sewer is self-cleansing at night. **Both ends of the range are design conditions.**

> **And the INFILTRATION allowance is regularly omitted and regularly significant**, especially in old systems below the water table: **it can exceed the sanitary flow itself, and it arrives whether it rains or not.**

examTip.trick: **Total sewage = DWF + WWF.** The storm component is far the larger — commonly 4-6 times the sanitary flow — so a system sized on sanitary flow alone floods whenever it rains.
examTip.trap: **Option (c) is the correct expression for DWF ALONE** — not wrong, just incomplete. A candidate who has learned the DWF formula thoroughly is caught by exactly that thoroughness.
examTip.mnemonic: **Return factor ≈ 0.8** (80 % of water supplied returns as sewage). And the decisive argument against COMBINED systems: no plant can be sized for storm flow, so overflows discharge dilute raw sewage — plus the sewer silts between storms.

questions.stem: Find the CBR value at 2.5 mm penetration. The load sustained by the specimen at 2.5 mm penetration is 64.6 kg and the load sustained by standard aggregates at the 2.5 mm penetration level is 1370 kg.
questions.solution:
**4.7 per cent.**

**The definition and the arithmetic:**

> **CBR = (load carried by the test specimen ÷ load carried by the standard crushed aggregate) × 100**

> **CBR = (64.6 / 1370) × 100**

> **= 0.04716 × 100**

> **= 4.716 ≈ 4.7 %** ✓

> **A quick check: 1370 × 0.05 = 68.5, and 64.6 is a little less than that — so the answer is a little under 5 per cent.** That estimate picks 4.7 from the four options immediately, without dividing.

**Why each distractor is wrong:**

| Option | Where it comes from |
|---|---|
| **4.7 %** | ✓ |
| **10.3 %** | **Roughly TWICE the answer — a doubling slip, or dividing by half the standard load** |
| **8.4 %** | Roughly twice 4.2; no clean derivation |
| **2.1 %** | **HALF the answer — 64.6/2740, or dividing by twice the standard load** |

> **Options (b) and (d) are the answer doubled and halved**, which is the commonest pair of arithmetic slips. **The 5 per cent estimate above rules out all three at once**, which is why the estimate is worth making before dividing.

**The standard loads, since the question supplies one and may not next time:**

| Penetration | Standard load | Standard pressure |
|---|---|---|
| **2.5 mm** | **1370 kg** | **70 kg/cm²** |
| **5.0 mm** | **2055 kg** | **105 kg/cm²** |
| 7.5 mm | 2630 kg | 134 kg/cm² |
| 10.0 mm | 3180 kg | 162 kg/cm² |
| 12.5 mm | 3600 kg | 183 kg/cm² |

> **1370 and 2055 are the two to memorise**, and note their ratio: **2055/1370 = 1.50 exactly.** That clean ratio is a useful check when the two figures must be recalled.

> **The plunger is 50 mm in diameter, giving an area of 19.635 cm² — which is where the pressures come from.**

**The rule that this question sets up, and which the source states:**

> **Compute the CBR at BOTH 2.5 mm and 5.0 mm.**

> **If CBR(2.5) > CBR(5.0) — the normal case — the 2.5 mm value is REPORTED.**

> **If CBR(2.5) < CBR(5.0), the test must be REPEATED.** If the repeat confirms it, the 5.0 mm value is reported.

> **The reason is diagnostic rather than arbitrary: a higher 5 mm value usually indicates a defective TOP SURFACE** — unevenness, a loose layer, or poor preparation — which depresses the early readings.

> **So the anomaly is treated first as a sign of a bad test and only accepted as real on confirmation.** That is a sound principle generally: **an unexpected result should prompt a check of the method before a revision of the conclusion.**

**What a CBR of 4.7 per cent means in practice:**

| Material | CBR (%) |
|---|---|
| **Very poor clay subgrade** | **2-3** |
| **Poor to fair subgrade** | **3-7** ← 4.7 sits here |
| **Fair to good subgrade** | 7-20 |
| **Good gravelly subgrade** | **20-30** |
| **Sub-base material** | **> 20-30** |
| **Base course (WBM/WMM)** | **> 80** |
| **Standard crushed stone (the reference)** | **100 by definition** |
