> **So 4.7 per cent is a WEAK subgrade** — usable, but requiring a substantial pavement thickness above it, and a strong candidate for improvement.

> **IRC 37's design charts begin at CBR 2 and the thickness required falls steeply up to about CBR 10**, after which the gain flattens. **Which means raising a subgrade from 3 to 7 per cent saves a great deal of pavement, and raising it from 15 to 20 saves very little** — the economics of subgrade improvement are concentrated at the weak end.

**And two conditions of the test that decide whether the number means anything:**

> **SOAKING: 96 hours (4 days) for the soaked CBR.** Nepal's subgrade is weakest just after the monsoon, **so design must use the SOAKED value** — an unsoaked figure flatters the subgrade and produces a pavement that fails in its first wet season.

> **And CBR is a RATIO with no units.** It cannot be converted to a bearing capacity or a stress. **Its only legitimate use is entering a design chart calibrated against it**, and treating it as a strength in its own right is the standard misunderstanding of the test.

examTip.trick: **CBR = (64.6/1370) × 100 = 4.7 %.** Estimate first: 5 % of 1370 is 68.5, and 64.6 is a little less — so a little under 5 %, which picks the answer without dividing.
examTip.trap: **Options (b) and (d) are the answer doubled and halved** — the commonest arithmetic slips. The 5 % estimate rules out all three distractors at once.
examTip.mnemonic: **1370 kg at 2.5 mm, 2055 kg at 5 mm — ratio exactly 1.50.** Compute at BOTH; if the 5 mm value is higher, REPEAT the test, because that usually signals a defective top surface. And design on the SOAKED (96-hour) value.

questions.stem: Calculate the capacity factor if the average load is 36,000 kW and two turbo generators are installed, each of capacity 20,000 kW.
questions.solution:
**90 per cent.**

**The definition and the arithmetic:**

> **Capacity factor = Average load ÷ Installed (plant) capacity**

> **Installed capacity = 2 × 20,000 = 40,000 kW**

> **Capacity factor = 36,000 / 40,000 = 0.90 = 90 %** ✓

> **The only step that can go wrong is the installed capacity: there are TWO machines, so it is 40,000 kW and not 20,000.**

> **Option (c) 95 per cent has no clean derivation, but option (d) 60 per cent is worth examining** — and it is the kind of figure a candidate reaches for by using a wrong denominator or by confusing this with a load factor.

> **Note also that using 20,000 kW alone would give 180 per cent, which is impossible** — a capacity factor cannot exceed 100 per cent, since the average load cannot exceed the installed capacity. **That impossibility is a free check on the denominator.**

**Why 90 per cent is a HIGH figure, and what it implies:**

| Plant | Typical capacity factor |
|---|---|
| **Solar PV** | **15-25 %** |
| **Storage hydro, peaking** | **20-40 % by design** |
| Wind | 25-40 % |
| **Run-of-river hydro (Nepal)** | **40-60 %** |
| **Thermal base load** | **60-85 %** |
| **Nuclear** | **80-90 %** ← 90 % sits at the top of this |

> **A capacity factor of 90 per cent means the plant runs at nine tenths of its full output on average, all year** — which implies a steady base-load duty, high availability, and a fuel or water supply that never falters.

> **The stem's phrase "turbo generators" points at a THERMAL plant rather than hydro**, which is consistent: a thermal base-load station can achieve this, and a run-of-river hydro plant cannot, because its water is seasonal.

> **So the answer is high but not implausible — and recognising that is part of reading the question.**

**The five factors, since this question is drawn from a family:**

| Factor | Definition | Typical |
|---|---|---|
| **LOAD factor** | **Average load ÷ PEAK LOAD** | **≤ 1** |
| **CAPACITY (plant) factor** | **Average load ÷ INSTALLED CAPACITY** | **0.25-0.7 (higher for base load)** ← |
| **UTILISATION (plant use) factor** | **PEAK load ÷ installed capacity** | **0.4-0.9** |
| **POWER factor** | **Real power ÷ APPARENT power** | 0.8-0.9 |
| **DIVERSITY factor** | **Sum of individual maximum demands ÷ simultaneous maximum demand** | **> 1** |

> **The numerators of the first three overlap, so read the DENOMINATOR:**

> **PEAK LOAD → load factor. INSTALLED CAPACITY → capacity factor. Apparent power → power factor.**

> **Load factor and capacity factor are equal only when the peak load exactly equals the installed capacity**, that is, when the plant is precisely sized for its load. **The gap between them measures the spare capacity carried.**

**Why capacity factor matters commercially:**

> **It is the number that converts a plant's SIZE into its ENERGY OUTPUT:**

> **Annual energy = Installed capacity × 8760 hours × capacity factor**

> **For this plant: 40,000 kW × 8760 × 0.90 = 315 million kWh = 315 GWh per year.**

> **And that is what is sold.** A plant's revenue depends on its energy, not its capacity — **so two plants of the same megawatt rating and different capacity factors are quite different businesses.**

> **Which is why comparing power projects by installed capacity is misleading**, and it applies with particular force in Nepal: **a 40 MW run-of-river plant at 45 per cent delivers 158 GWh, while a 40 MW plant at 90 per cent would deliver 315 GWh — twice the energy from the same nameplate.**

**And the diagnostic that a capacity factor alone does not provide:**

> **A LOW capacity factor has three quite different causes**, and distinguishing them is the whole value of the neighbouring factors:

| Cause | Diagnosed by |
|---|---|
| **The plant was UNAVAILABLE — breakdowns, outages** | **A LOW plant use factor as well** |
| **The RESOURCE was not there — dry season, no wind, night** | **A HIGH plant use factor with a low capacity factor** |
| **The plant is a PEAKING plant, run only when needed** | **A high plant use factor, and a deliberate operating pattern** |

> **So the plant use factor is what separates "broken" from "short of water"**, because it counts only the hours the plant was actually in service. **A capacity factor on its own cannot tell you which.**

examTip.trick: **Two machines, so installed capacity is 40,000 kW.** Capacity factor = 36,000/40,000 = 90 %.
examTip.trap: **Using one machine's 20,000 kW gives 180 %, which is impossible** — a capacity factor cannot exceed 100 %, since average load cannot exceed installed capacity. That is a free check on the denominator.
examTip.mnemonic: **Read the DENOMINATOR: peak load → LOAD factor; installed capacity → CAPACITY factor.** And **annual energy = capacity × 8760 × capacity factor** — which is what is actually sold, so comparing plants by MW alone is misleading.

questions.stem: A soil has a porosity of 30 %. Its void ratio in the densest and loosest states is 0.35 and 0.92 respectively. What will be its density index?
questions.solution:
**0.861.**

**Step 1 — convert porosity to void ratio:**

> **e = n / (1 − n)**

> **e = 0.30 / (1 − 0.30) = 0.30 / 0.70 = 0.4286**

> **This conversion is where the question really lives: the porosity is given, but the density index formula needs the VOID RATIO.**

**Step 2 — apply the density index (relative density) formula:**

> **I_D = (e_max − e) / (e_max − e_min)**

| Symbol | Meaning | Value |
|---|---|---|
| **e_max** | **Void ratio in the LOOSEST state** | **0.92** |
| **e_min** | **Void ratio in the DENSEST state** | **0.35** |
| **e** | **The soil's actual void ratio** | **0.4286** |

> **I_D = (0.92 − 0.4286) / (0.92 − 0.35)**

> **= 0.4914 / 0.57**

> **= 0.8621 ≈ 0.861** ✓

> **The four options differ in the third decimal place, so the intermediate void ratio must be carried to at least four figures.** Using e = 0.43 instead of 0.4286 gives 0.8596, which rounds toward 0.860 and misses.

**Getting e_max and e_min the right way round — the physical check:**

> **The LOOSEST state has the MOST voids, so e_max belongs to the loosest arrangement.** The DENSEST state has the fewest, so e_min belongs to it.

> **That is worth stating because it is the one place the arithmetic can be inverted**, and inverting it here would give (0.4286 − 0.35)/(0.92 − 0.35) = 0.138, which is not among the options — **so the error announces itself, which is fortunate.**

> **The formula's structure also confirms the assignment: I_D must equal 1 for the densest state and 0 for the loosest.**

| At | I_D |
|---|---|
| **e = e_min (densest)** | **(e_max − e_min)/(e_max − e_min) = 1** ✓ |
| **e = e_max (loosest)** | **(e_max − e_max)/(e_max − e_min) = 0** ✓ |

> **Those two limiting checks verify the formula in a few seconds**, and they are the reason it is written with e_max on top: **a DENSE soil should score HIGH.**

**What the density index tells you:**

| I_D | Relative density |
|---|---|
| **0 - 0.15** | **VERY LOOSE** |
| **0.15 - 0.35** | **Loose** |
| **0.35 - 0.65** | **Medium** |
| **0.65 - 0.85** | **DENSE** |
| **0.85 - 1.00** | **VERY DENSE** ← 0.861 sits here |

> **So this soil is VERY DENSE**, and the answer is worth interpreting rather than merely computing: a density index of 0.86 describes a well-compacted or naturally very dense granular deposit.

**Why relative density rather than void ratio alone — and this is the concept:**

> **A void ratio of 0.43 means nothing by itself.** For one sand it might be very dense; for another, loose.

> **The void ratio a soil CAN reach depends on its grading and particle shape:**

| Soil | e_min | e_max |
|---|---|---|
| **Uniform (poorly graded) rounded sand** | **~0.45** | **~0.75** |
| **Well-graded angular sand** | **~0.25** | **~0.65** |
| Uniform fine sand | 0.50 | 0.90 |

> **A well-graded soil can pack much more densely, because small particles fill the gaps between large ones.** So its whole range of achievable void ratios is lower.

> **Relative density normalises the actual void ratio against that soil's OWN achievable range**, which is what makes it comparable between soils. **It answers "how dense is this, for this soil?" rather than "how many voids are there?"**

> **That is why the parameter exists, and why it is the standard measure for GRANULAR soils** — where compaction state, not water content, governs the behaviour.

**The companion relations, since they are routinely needed together:**

| Relation | Form |
|---|---|
| **Void ratio from porosity** | **e = n/(1−n)** ← used here |
| **Porosity from void ratio** | **n = e/(1+e)** |
| **Degree of saturation** | **S = wG/e** |
| **Dry density** | **γ_d = Gγ_w/(1+e)** |
| **Bulk density** | **γ = (G + Se)γ_w/(1+e)** |

> **The pair e = n/(1−n) and n = e/(1+e) are the most-used conversions in soil mechanics**, and they are easy to confuse. **The check is that e can exceed 1 while n never can** — porosity is a fraction of the total volume, void ratio a ratio to the solids alone. **So the formula whose result can exceed 1 is the one for e.**

> **And S = wG/e is the relation that ties water content to saturation**, which is what makes the compaction curve's zero-air-voids line computable.

verification.notes: Stem corrected. The source printed "voids ratio in the loosest and densest state is 0.35 and 0.92 respectively", which is physically impossible - the LOOSEST state must have the HIGHER void ratio. The source's own working then uses e_min = 0.35 and e_max = 0.92 correctly, so the defect is in the stem's ordering rather than in the computation. The stem now reads "densest and loosest", which matches both the physics and the source's own arithmetic; the keyed answer (c) 0.861 is unchanged.

examTip.trick: **Two steps: e = n/(1−n) = 0.30/0.70 = 0.4286, then I_D = (e_max − e)/(e_max − e_min) = 0.4914/0.57 = 0.861.** Carry e to four figures — the options differ in the third decimal.
examTip.trap: **The LOOSEST state has the HIGHER void ratio**, so e_max = 0.92. Check the formula by its limits: I_D must be 1 at the densest state and 0 at the loosest — which is why e_max is on top.
examTip.mnemonic: **e = n/(1−n) versus n = e/(1+e)** — the check is that **e can exceed 1 and n never can**, so the formula whose result can pass 1 is the one for e. And relative density exists because a bare void ratio means nothing without that soil's own achievable range.

questions.stem: The thickness of a penstock pipe by the ASME recommendation is given by:
questions.solution:
**t = (P·R)/(σ·η − 0.6P) + 0.15 cm.**

**What each term is:**

| Symbol | Meaning | Unit |
|---|---|---|
| **P** | **Internal PRESSURE (including the water-hammer rise)** | **kg/cm²** |
| **R** | **RADIUS of the pipe** | **cm** |
| **σ** | **Allowable STRESS in the steel** | **kg/cm²** |
| **η** | **WELDING (joint) EFFICIENCY** | dimensionless |
| **0.15** | **CORROSION allowance** | **cm (1.5 mm)** |
| **t** | Thickness | **cm** |

**How to identify the correct form without recalling it — three checks:**

> **CHECK 1 — the numerator must be a PRODUCT, P × R.**

> **The basic thin-cylinder hoop-stress result is t = pD/2σ = pR/σ**, so P and R MULTIPLY.

> **Option (d) writes (P + R), which adds a pressure to a length — DIMENSIONALLY IMPOSSIBLE.** ✓ eliminated on dimensions alone.

> **CHECK 2 — the corrosion allowance must be ADDED.**

> **A corrosion allowance is extra metal provided so that the pipe still has its required thickness after years of loss.** It can only be an addition.

> **Option (c) SUBTRACTS it, which would make the pipe thinner than the stress requires.** ✓ eliminated on physical sense.

> **CHECK 3 — the 0.6P term must be SUBTRACTED in the denominator.**

> **The denominator is the material's capacity, and the 0.6P term REDUCES it — it is a correction for the fact that the pressure also acts on the wall's own thickness, and the thin-cylinder formula slightly under-predicts the required thickness for thicker walls.**

> **Subtracting makes the denominator smaller and so the thickness LARGER — a conservative correction, which is what a code correction should be.**

> **Option (b) ADDS it, making the denominator larger and the thickness SMALLER — an unconservative correction, which no code would write.** ✓ eliminated

> **Three checks, three eliminations, and only option (a) survives** — without recalling the formula at all. **That is the method to use on any code formula offered in four sign variants: ask which version is CONSERVATIVE.**

**Why the corrosion allowance and the welding efficiency both appear:**

> **The two terms account for the two ways a real pipe falls short of the ideal cylinder the stress formula assumes.**

| Term | Accounts for |
|---|---|
| **η, welding efficiency** | **A welded seam is weaker than the parent plate. Typical values: 0.85-0.90 for a spot-radiographed weld, 1.0 for a fully radiographed one** |
| **+0.15 cm, corrosion allowance** | **Metal LOST over the design life to rust, and to abrasion by the sediment the water carries** |

> **The corrosion allowance deserves emphasis in the Himalayan context: penstock water carries hard, angular QUARTZ**, which abrades the invert of the pipe as well as the turbine runner.

> **So the 1.5 mm is not only a rust allowance — it is a wear allowance**, and on a heavily sediment-laden river a larger figure may be justified.

**Where the design pressure P comes from, since it is the term that dominates:**

> **P is NOT the static pressure. It is the static head PLUS the water-hammer rise.**

> **Joukowsky's maximum rise for instantaneous closure: Δh = (a/g)V**, with a the wave speed, 900-1200 m/s in steel.

> **For V = 4 m/s and a = 1000 m/s: Δh ≈ 408 m of head** — comparable with or greater than the static head on many plants.

> **A penstock designed for static head alone would burst on the first load rejection**, which is why the water-hammer term is the substance of the design pressure.

> **The rise is limited in practice by SLOWING the gate closure beyond the critical time 2L/a, and by the SURGE TANK**, which cuts the decelerating column to the penstock alone.

**And the checks the hoop-stress thickness does NOT cover:**

| Check | Governs when |
|---|---|
| **Internal pressure (hoop stress)** | **The normal case — this formula** ← |
| **EXTERNAL pressure / vacuum buckling** | **The pipe is EMPTY or under vacuum, especially if buried** |
| **Longitudinal bending between supports** | Saddle spacing |
| **Thrust at bends** | **Anchor block design — very large forces** |
| Temperature movement | Expansion joint design |
| **Minimum practical thickness for handling** | Thin pipes buckle during erection |

> **The vacuum case is the one most often overlooked and it is real: an empty penstock, or one subjected to a vacuum by a downstream break, can COLLAPSE INWARD.**

> **Which is why an AIR VALVE is fitted at every high point** — to admit air as the pipe drains. **A penstock adequate for 400 m of internal pressure can be crushed by one atmosphere of external pressure, because a thin cylinder is far weaker in external pressure than internal.**

> **That asymmetry is worth understanding: internal pressure puts the wall in TENSION (stable), external pressure puts it in COMPRESSION (buckling-prone).** The same wall behaves quite differently in the two cases.

examTip.trick: **Three checks eliminate three options with no recall.** P·R must be a PRODUCT (kills (d) on dimensions); the corrosion allowance must be ADDED (kills (c)); and 0.6P must be SUBTRACTED so the correction is CONSERVATIVE (kills (b)).
examTip.trap: **Ask which version is CONSERVATIVE** — that is the general method for any code formula offered in four sign variants. A code correction that makes the member thinner is almost certainly the wrong sign.
examTip.mnemonic: **P is static head PLUS water hammer** (Joukowsky Δh = aV/g, often 400 m). And the check this formula misses: an EMPTY or vacuum-subjected pipe can COLLAPSE INWARD — internal pressure gives tension, external gives buckling.

questions.stem: If the velocity of flow is 2.5 m/s, the depth of a trapezoidal section is 2 m, the base width is 3 m, the side slope is 1H:2V and the bed slope is 1 in 1000, what will be Manning's coefficient?
questions.solution:
**n = 0.013 (computed 0.0132).**

**Step 1 — interpret the side slope.**

> **"1H : 2V" means 1 horizontal to 2 vertical**, so the horizontal run per unit of rise is:

> **z = H/V = 1/2 = 0.5**

> **This is the step most easily got wrong**, because side slopes are quoted in both conventions. **Here the stem gives H:V explicitly, and z is the HORIZONTAL distance per unit VERTICAL — so z = 0.5.**

**Step 2 — the geometry of the trapezoidal section.**

> **Area:  A = by + zy² = (3)(2) + (0.5)(2²) = 6 + 2 = 8 m²**

> **Wetted perimeter:  P = b + 2y√(1 + z²) = 3 + 2(2)√(1 + 0.25) = 3 + 4(1.1180) = 3 + 4.472 = 7.472 m**

> **Hydraulic radius:  R = A/P = 8 / 7.472 = 1.0707 m**

**Step 3 — invert Manning's equation for n.**

> **V = (1/n) R^{2/3} S^{1/2}**, so **n = R^{2/3} S^{1/2} / V**

> **R^{2/3} = (1.0707)^{2/3} = 1.0467**

> **S^{1/2} = (1/1000)^{1/2} = 0.031623**

> **n = (1.0467)(0.031623) / 2.5 = 0.033100 / 2.5 = 0.01324**

> **n ≈ 0.013** ✓

**The sanity check that confirms the answer independently:**

> **n = 0.013 is the standard value for a CONCRETE-LINED channel.**

| Surface | Manning's n |
|---|---|
| **Smooth cement plaster** | **0.010-0.013** |
| **Concrete lining** | **0.013-0.017** ← |
| Brick lining | 0.015 |
| **Earth channel, clean and straight** | **0.018-0.025** |
| **Earth channel, weedy or winding** | **0.025-0.040** |
| Natural stream with boulders | 0.040-0.070 |

> **All four options lie in the smooth-lined range (0.012-0.015)**, so the value must be computed rather than recognised — **but knowing the range confirms that the computed answer is physically sensible, which a computed answer of 0.04 would not have been.**

**Where the errors lie in a problem of this shape:**

| Likely slip | Consequence |
|---|---|
| **Taking z = 2 instead of 0.5** | **A = 6 + 8 = 14, P = 3 + 4√5 = 11.94, R = 1.17 — n comes out about 0.0141, landing on option (c)** ← the designed trap |
| **Using y instead of R** | R would be 2, giving n ≈ 0.020 — off the option list |
| **Forgetting the square root on S** | n would be 100× smaller |
| Using R^{1/2} instead of R^{2/3} | Small error here since R ≈ 1 |

> **The first row is the important one: misreading the side slope convention lands you neatly on option (c)**, which is why the stem's "1H:2V" must be read carefully.

> **Note that because R happens to be very close to 1 in this problem, the exponent on R barely matters** — R^{2/3} = 1.047 against R^{1/2} = 1.035. **So an error in the exponent would NOT be caught here, which is worth knowing: this particular problem is insensitive to the exponent and sensitive to the geometry.**

**The formulae for a trapezoidal channel, since they are the reusable part:**

| Quantity | Expression |
|---|---|
| **Area** | **A = by + zy²** |
| **Wetted perimeter** | **P = b + 2y√(1 + z²)** |
| **Hydraulic radius** | **R = A/P** |
| **Top width** | **T = b + 2zy** |
| **Manning velocity** | **V = (1/n) R^{2/3} S^{1/2}** |
| **Discharge** | **Q = AV** |

> **The √(1+z²) in the perimeter is the slant length per unit depth**, by Pythagoras on the side slope — which is why it appears there and not in the area.

**And the most-efficient section, since it is the neighbouring topic:**

> **The MOST ECONOMICAL trapezoidal section is HALF A REGULAR HEXAGON**, and it satisfies:

| Condition | Form |
|---|---|
| **Hydraulic radius** | **R = y/2** |
| **Side slope** | **z = 1/√3 (60° to the horizontal)** |
| **Top width** | **T = 2 × sloping side length** |
| **A circle inscribed in the section** | **Touches the bed and both sides, centred on the water surface** |

> **The condition R = y/2 is the general result for the most efficient section of ANY shape**, and it is what makes a semicircle the theoretically ideal open channel — **though a semicircle is hard to build in earth, which is why the half-hexagon trapezium is the practical optimum.**

> **"Most economical" means maximum discharge for a given area, which is the same as MINIMUM WETTED PERIMETER** — and the minimum perimeter also means the least lining material, so hydraulic efficiency and construction cost point the same way here. **That agreement is unusual and worth noticing.**

examTip.trap: **"1H:2V" means z = 0.5, not 2.** Taking z = 2 gives R = 1.17 and n ≈ 0.0141 — landing neatly on option (c). Read the side-slope convention carefully.
examTip.mnemonic: **n = 0.013 is the standard CONCRETE LINING value**, which confirms the answer is physically sensible. And the **most economical trapezoidal section is HALF A HEXAGON, with R = y/2** — the general condition for maximum efficiency.

questions.stem: As per IS 456:2000, the minimum area of tension reinforcement in a beam when Fe415 steel is used is:
questions.solution:
**0.2 per cent (computed 0.205 per cent).**

**The code requirement:**

> **IS 456:2000 clause 26.5.1.1(a):  A_s / (b·d) ≥ 0.85 / f_y**

> **For Fe415:  A_s/(bd) = 0.85 / 415 = 0.002048 = 0.2048 % ≈ 0.2 %** ✓

**The two very similar numbers that this question sets against each other:**

| Value | What it is |
|---|---|
| **0.85** | **The NUMERATOR of the code expression, 0.85/f_y** |
| **0.85 %** | **NOT the answer — it is the constant, not the result** ← option (d), the trap |
| **0.2 %** | **The RESULT for Fe415** ✓ |
| **0.085 %** | **0.85 divided by ten — a decimal slip** ← option (c) |

> **Option (d) 0.85 % is the designed trap and a very good one**: the figure 0.85 is genuinely part of the formula and is the number a candidate remembers. **But it must be DIVIDED BY f_y, and 0.85 % is what you get by forgetting to divide at all.**

> **A sanity check disposes of it: 0.85 per cent of a beam's section would be a heavily reinforced beam, not a minimum.** Minimum steel is by definition a small quantity — **around 0.2 per cent is the right order, and 0.85 per cent is four times too much for a floor.**

**The minimum for the other grades, since the formula makes them easy:**

| Steel grade | f_y (N/mm²) | Minimum A_s/(bd) = 0.85/f_y |
|---|---|---|
| **Fe250 (mild steel)** | **250** | **0.34 %** |
| **Fe415** | **415** | **0.205 %** ← |
| **Fe500** | **500** | **0.17 %** |
| Fe550 | 550 | 0.155 % |

> **The minimum FALLS as the steel grade rises**, which follows directly from the formula — and makes sense, since a stronger steel needs less area to provide the same force.

**Why a MINIMUM exists at all — and this is the concept:**

> **The minimum is not about strength under service load. It is about the mode of FAILURE.**

> **Consider a beam with almost no steel. When it cracks, the concrete in the tension zone stops carrying tension, and the whole tensile force must transfer instantly to the steel.**

> **If the steel's capacity is LESS than the tensile force the uncracked concrete was carrying, the steel yields and fractures the moment the first crack forms.**

> **The beam then fails SUDDENLY, at the cracking load, with no warning and no deflection — a BRITTLE failure.**

> **The minimum steel guarantees that the steel can carry MORE than the cracking moment, so the beam cracks, deflects visibly, and yields gradually before failing.**

> **That is the whole purpose: to convert a brittle failure into a ductile one.** And it is why the minimum is mandatory regardless of how lightly loaded the beam is.

**The maximum, and the reason for it:**

| Limit | Value | Reason |
|---|---|---|
| **MINIMUM tension steel** | **0.85/f_y (0.205 % for Fe415)** | **Prevents sudden failure at first cracking** |
| **MAXIMUM tension steel** | **4 % of the gross area (bD)** | **Congestion — concrete cannot be placed and compacted around it** |

> **Note that the minimum is expressed per bd (effective depth) and the maximum per bD (overall depth)** — a small inconsistency in the code that is easy to trip over.

> **The maximum's reason is practical rather than structural: 4 per cent of steel leaves too little room for aggregate to pass**, and the result is honeycombed concrete around the very bars that were supposed to strengthen it.

> **In practice beams are rarely taken above about 2 per cent**, both for placeability and because a beam needing more steel than that should usually be made deeper instead.

**The related minimums, since they are examined as a family:**

| Member and steel | Minimum |
|---|---|
| **Beam, tension steel** | **0.85/f_y — 0.205 % for Fe415** ← |
| **SLAB, main steel (Fe415/500)** | **0.12 % of gross area** |
| **Slab, main steel (Fe250)** | **0.15 % of gross area** |
| **COLUMN, longitudinal steel** | **0.8 % of gross area** |
| **Column, maximum** | **6 % (practically 4 % at laps)** |
| **Slab distribution steel** | **0.12 % (HYSD)** |
| Side-face reinforcement (deep beams, D > 750 mm) | 0.1 % of web area |

> **Note that a slab's minimum (0.12 %) is expressed on the GROSS area and is LOWER than a beam's (0.205 % on bd)** — because a slab is a two-way plate with more redundancy, and the shrinkage-and-temperature requirement rather than the ductility requirement governs it.

> **The COLUMN minimum of 0.8 per cent is much higher than either**, and for a different reason: **a column must be able to carry some bending as well as axial load, and its steel also resists the effects of creep and of accidental eccentricity.** A plain concrete column would be dangerously brittle.

examTip.trick: **A_s/(bd) ≥ 0.85/f_y**, so for Fe415 it is 0.85/415 = 0.205 % ≈ 0.2 %. The minimum FALLS as the grade rises: 0.34 % for Fe250, 0.17 % for Fe500.
examTip.trap: **Option (d) 0.85 % is the formula's NUMERATOR, not the result** — forgetting to divide by f_y. Sanity check: 0.85 % is a heavily reinforced beam, and a MINIMUM must be a small quantity.
examTip.mnemonic: **The minimum exists to convert a BRITTLE failure into a DUCTILE one** — with too little steel, the bar fractures the instant the concrete cracks, at the cracking load and with no warning. And the maximum (4 %) exists for PLACEABILITY, not strength.

questions.stem: Two Pelton wheel turbines X and Y have the same specific speed and are working under the same head. Turbine X produces 400 kW at 1000 rpm. If turbine Y produces 100 kW, then its speed is:
questions.solution:
**2000 rpm.**

**The reasoning:**

> **Specific speed:  N_s = N √P / H^{5/4}**

> **Both turbines have the SAME N_s and the SAME head H, so H^{5/4} is common and:**

> **N √P = constant**

> **N_X √P_X = N_Y √P_Y**

**The computation:**

> **1000 × √400 = N_Y × √100**

> **1000 × 20 = N_Y × 10**

> **20,000 = 10 N_Y**

> **N_Y = 2000 rpm** ✓

> **The arithmetic is clean because both powers are perfect squares — 400 and 100 give roots of 20 and 10.**

**The check that gets the direction right, which is the whole risk in this question:**

> **Turbine Y produces LESS power (100 kW against 400 kW), so it must run FASTER to keep N√P constant.**

> **Power fell by a factor of 4, so √P fell by a factor of 2, so N must RISE by a factor of 2: 1000 → 2000.** ✓

> **That is the reasoning to hold, because the inverse relation is counter-intuitive: the SMALLER machine runs FASTER.**

| Option | Implied change | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| **3000 rpm** | **× 3 — would need P to fall by 9** | **Wrong factor** |
| **1500 rpm** | × 1.5 | **Wrong factor** |
| **2000 rpm** | **× 2 — matches √4** | ✓ |
| **4000 rpm** | **× 4 — treats N ∝ 1/P instead of 1/√P** | **The trap: forgetting the square root** ← |

> **Option (d) 4000 rpm is the designed trap: it comes from N ∝ 1/P rather than N ∝ 1/√P.** The power ratio is 4, so a candidate who forgets the square root multiplies the speed by 4 instead of 2.

**Why smaller machines run faster — the physical meaning:**

> **Specific speed is a SHAPE parameter: it identifies the type and proportions of the machine, independent of its size.**

> **Two turbines with the same specific speed are GEOMETRICALLY SIMILAR — the same design scaled up or down.**

> **And for geometrically similar machines under the same head, the runner's PERIPHERAL SPEED is fixed** (u = φ√(2gH), with the speed ratio φ ≈ 0.45 for a Pelton).

> **A fixed peripheral speed on a SMALLER diameter means a HIGHER rotational speed**, since u = πDN/60. **That is the physical reason for the inverse relation, and it is worth knowing rather than taking the algebra on trust.**

> **It is also why small turbines can be coupled directly to generators while large ones often need speed increasers or many-pole generators** — the rotational speeds differ enormously across the size range.

**The Pelton relations that go with this:**

| Quantity | Relation |
|---|---|
| **Specific speed** | **N_s = N√P / H^{5/4}** ← |
| **Jet velocity** | **V = C_v √(2gH), C_v = 0.97-0.99** |
| **Bucket (peripheral) speed** | **u = φ√(2gH), speed ratio φ = 0.43-0.48** |
| **Ideal speed ratio** | **u = V/2 — half the jet speed** |
| **Jet ratio** | **m = D/d, usually 11-14** |
| **Number of buckets** | **Z = 15 + m/2** |
| **Bucket deflection** | **165°, not 180°** |

> **The u = V/2 result is derivable and worth understanding: power transferred is maximum when the bucket moves at half the jet speed**, because at u = 0 the force is greatest but no work is done, and at u = V there is no force at all. **The product of force and velocity peaks in between.**

> **And the 165° deflection rather than a full reversal is a practical compromise: a full 180° would send the spent water straight back into the oncoming jet.** The 15° shortfall lets the discharged water clear the next bucket — **a small detail costing a few per cent of theoretical efficiency, without which the machine would not work at all.**

**Where the Pelton's specific speed places it:**

| Specific speed (metric, kW) | Turbine | Head |
|---|---|---|
| **8 - 30** | **PELTON, single jet** | **Very high, above ~250 m** |
| **30 - 50** | Pelton, multi-jet | High |
| **50 - 250** | **FRANCIS** | **Medium, 45-400 m** |
| **250 - 850** | **KAPLAN** | **Low, below ~60 m** |

> **LOW specific speed goes with HIGH head**, and the reason is the same one as above: **a high-head machine extracts a great deal of energy from a small flow, so it can be small and comparatively slow-turning for its power.**

> **A multi-jet Pelton raises the specific speed** — up to six jets are used — **because dividing the flow between several jets lets the runner be smaller for the same total power, which is a way of adapting a Pelton to a somewhat lower head than a single jet would suit.**

verification.notes: Stem tidied. The source wrote "Turbine X produces 400KW at 1000rpm. If turbine B produces 100KW" - naming the second machine B in one sentence and Y in the next. The stem now uses Y consistently, which is what the source's own working assumes. The keyed answer (c) 2000 rpm is unchanged.

examTip.trick: **Same N_s and same head means N√P is constant.** 1000 × √400 = N × √100, so 1000 × 20 = 10N and N = 2000 rpm.
examTip.trap: **Option (d) 4000 rpm comes from N ∝ 1/P instead of 1/√P** — the power ratio is 4, so the speed ratio is √4 = 2, not 4. Forgetting the square root is the whole trap.
examTip.mnemonic: **The SMALLER machine runs FASTER**, and the reason is physical: geometric similarity under the same head fixes the PERIPHERAL speed u = φ√(2gH), and a fixed u on a smaller diameter means a higher rpm.

questions.stem: Assuming a coefficient of friction of 0.36 and a total reaction time of the driver of 2.5 seconds, the stopping sight distance for a design speed of 65 km/h is:
questions.solution:
**91.4 m (computed 91.38 m).**

**The formula — SSD is the sum of two distances:**

> **SSD = LAG distance + BRAKING distance**

> **SSD = 0.278 V t + V² / (254 f)**

| Term | Meaning | Unit of V |
|---|---|---|
| **0.278 V t** | **LAG (reaction) distance — how far the vehicle travels while the driver perceives and reacts** | **km/h** |
| **V²/(254 f)** | **BRAKING distance — how far it travels while decelerating** | **km/h** |

**The computation:**

> **Lag distance = 0.278 × 65 × 2.5 = 45.175 m**

> **Braking distance = 65² / (254 × 0.36) = 4225 / 91.44 = 46.203 m**

> **SSD = 45.175 + 46.203 = 91.38 ≈ 91.4 m** ✓

**Why the distractors are so well made — every one is a real intermediate value:**

| Option | What it is |
|---|---|
| **55.25 m** | Not a clean intermediate, but a plausible-looking distance |
| **46.21 m** | **The BRAKING distance ALONE — the lag distance forgotten** ← |
| **4.62 m** | **The braking distance divided by ten — a decimal slip** |
| **91.4 m** | ✓ **The SUM** |

> **Option (b) 46.21 m is the designed trap and it is the most instructive one: it is exactly half the calculation.**

> **The lag distance here (45.2 m) is almost exactly as large as the braking distance (46.2 m)** — so omitting it halves the answer. **A candidate who computes only the braking term finds a matching option and stops.**

> **The defence is to notice that the two terms are of comparable size and that the lag term is the FIRST one**, not an afterthought.

**Where the two constants come from — deriving them prevents unit confusion:**

> **0.278 converts km/h to m/s:  1 km/h = 1000/3600 = 0.2778 m/s.**

> **So the lag distance is simply (speed in m/s) × (reaction time in s).**

> **254 comes from the braking equation.** In SI, braking distance = v²/(2gf) with v in m/s. Converting V from km/h:

> **v = V/3.6, so v²/(2gf) = V²/(3.6² × 2 × 9.81 × f) = V²/(254 f)** ✓

> **254 = 3.6² × 2 × 9.81 = 12.96 × 19.62 = 254.3.**

> **Note the family resemblance to the superelevation constant 127 = 3.6² × 9.81** — the braking constant is exactly TWICE it, because of the factor of 2 in v²/2gf. **Holding both together makes each a check on the other.**

**The friction coefficient — and the distinction that this paper tests twice:**

| Coefficient | Value | Used in |
|---|---|---|
| **LONGITUDINAL friction, f** | **0.35 to 0.40** | **STOPPING SIGHT DISTANCE (braking)** ← 0.36 here |
| **LATERAL friction, f** | **0.15** | **Horizontal curves and superelevation** |

> **The same letter f is used for both**, and **this very paper asks a separate question keyed to 0.15** — the lateral value. **Both appear in the same sitting, which makes the distinction worth more than a single mark.**

> **A useful anchor: the LONGITUDINAL value is GRIP-limited and therefore LARGE; the LATERAL value is COMFORT-limited and therefore SMALL.** The reasoning behind each number tells you which is which.

**The reaction time, and why 2.5 seconds:**

> **IRC adopts a total reaction time of 2.5 seconds, which covers the whole PIEV process:**

| Stage | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **P — Perception** | The driver sees the object |
| **I — Intellection** | Understands what it is |
| **E — Emotion** | Decides what to do |
| **V — Volition** | Acts — moves the foot to the brake |

> **2.5 seconds is deliberately generous.** A alert driver reacts in under a second; **the design value allows for an inattentive one, and at 65 km/h it accounts for 45 metres of travel.**

> **Which is the point worth taking away: nearly half the stopping distance is consumed before the brakes are touched.** At higher speeds the braking term grows as V² and eventually dominates, but at moderate speeds the two are comparable.

**The related sight distances, since SSD is the minimum of a family:**

| Sight distance | Definition | Value at 65 km/h |
|---|---|---|
| **SSD — stopping** | **Distance to stop safely** | **~91 m** ← |
| **ISD — intermediate** | **TWICE the SSD** | **~182 m** |
| **OSD — overtaking** | **d₁ + d₂ + d₃; the distance to complete an overtaking manoeuvre** | **~330-400 m** |

> **SSD is the ABSOLUTE MINIMUM and must be available on every road, everywhere, in both directions.**

> **The heights used are the ones asked elsewhere in this series: DRIVER'S EYE at 1.2 m and OBJECT at 0.15 m** — and for overtaking, the oncoming vehicle at 1.2 m.

> **And note the relation ISD = 2 × SSD, which the source of another paper in this series printed inverted.** The intermediate sight distance is the larger, being twice the stopping distance — **provided where full overtaking sight distance cannot be economically achieved.**

examTip.trick: **SSD = 0.278Vt + V²/(254f) = 45.175 + 46.203 = 91.4 m.** The two terms are almost equal here, so the sum is nearly twice either one.
examTip.trap: **Option (b) 46.21 m is the BRAKING distance alone** — exactly half the calculation, and it matches an option. The lag term is the FIRST one, not an afterthought.
examTip.mnemonic: **254 = 3.6² × 2 × 9.81, exactly TWICE the superelevation constant 127** — so each checks the other. And **f = 0.36 here is LONGITUDINAL (grip-limited); the LATERAL value asked elsewhere in this paper is 0.15 (comfort-limited).**

questions.stem: The monthly interest rate will be ...... if the nominal interest rate of 10 % is accounted for continuous compounding.
questions.solution:
**0.84 per cent (computed 0.8368 per cent).**

**Step 1 — the effective ANNUAL rate under continuous compounding:**

> **i_eff = e^r − 1**, where r is the nominal annual rate.

> **i_eff = e^{0.10} − 1 = 1.10517 − 1 = 0.10517 = 10.517 %**

> **Note that continuous compounding gives 10.517 per cent from a nominal 10 per cent** — slightly more than any discrete compounding can, because it is the limit as the compounding frequency goes to infinity.

**Step 2 — convert the effective annual rate to a monthly rate:**

> **The monthly rate must be one that, compounded twelve times, reproduces the annual rate:**

> **(1 + i_monthly)¹² = 1 + i_eff**

> **i_monthly = (1 + 0.10517)^{1/12} − 1**

> **= (1.10517)^{0.08333} − 1**

> **= 1.008368 − 1 = 0.008368 = 0.8368 % ≈ 0.84 %** ✓

**Why option (a) 1 % is the designed trap — and it is the substantive error:**

> **The obvious move is to divide: 10 % ÷ 12 = 0.833 %, which rounds to 0.83 and looks close to the answer.**

> **But that is the NOMINAL monthly rate, not the effective one** — and the two differ.

> **More tempting still is 10/12 ≈ 0.83, or the round 1 % which "feels" like a monthly figure for a 10 per cent annual rate.**

> **Option (a) 1 % corresponds to an effective annual rate of (1.01)¹² − 1 = 12.68 %**, which is well above the 10.517 per cent actually implied. **So 1 per cent per month is a materially more expensive rate, and the difference compounds.**

> **The check worth doing: any candidate monthly rate can be tested by compounding it twelve times and comparing with 1.10517.**

| Candidate monthly rate | (1 + i)¹² − 1 | Matches 10.517 %? |
|---|---|---|
| **0.84 %** | **10.56 %** | **YES (to rounding)** ✓ |
| 1 % | **12.68 %** | No |
| 1.2 % | 15.39 % | No |
| 2 % | 26.8 % | No |

> **That single check identifies the answer without doing the twelfth root**, and it is the reliable route when the exponent is awkward.

**The compounding hierarchy, which is the concept behind the question:**

> **A NOMINAL rate is meaningless until the compounding frequency is stated.** "10 per cent per annum" describes different amounts of money depending on how often it is compounded:

| Compounding | Effective annual rate from a nominal 10 % |
|---|---|
| **Annually** | **10.000 %** |
| **Half-yearly** | **10.250 %** |
| **Quarterly** | **10.381 %** |
| **Monthly** | **10.471 %** |
| **Daily** | **10.516 %** |
| **CONTINUOUSLY** | **10.517 % — the LIMIT** ← |

> **The general formula for m compoundings per year: i_eff = (1 + r/m)^m − 1**, and as m → ∞ this becomes **e^r − 1.**

> **Notice how little is gained past monthly compounding: monthly gives 10.471 % and continuous gives 10.517 %** — a difference of less than five hundredths of a per cent.

> **That is worth knowing because it explains why continuous compounding is used at all: not because it makes much difference to the number, but because it makes the MATHEMATICS clean.** Exponentials differentiate and integrate simply, which matters in analytical work.

**Where this matters in engineering economics:**

| Application | Note |
|---|---|
| **Comparing loan offers** | **A quoted nominal rate is not comparable across different compounding frequencies — only the EFFECTIVE rate is** ← |
| **Discounting monthly cash flows** | The monthly rate must be the effective one, not nominal/12 |
| **Project appraisal with sub-annual periods** | Construction payments, monthly O&M costs |
| Escalation and inflation adjustment | Same arithmetic |

> **The first row is the practically important one, and it is why consumer-credit regulation in most countries requires an EFFECTIVE annual rate to be quoted.** A lender quoting "1 per cent per month" and one quoting "12 per cent per annum" are not offering the same thing — **the first is 12.68 per cent effective.**

**And the discrete-versus-continuous discount factors, for completeness:**

| Quantity | Discrete | Continuous |
|---|---|---|
| **Compound amount** | **(1 + i)^n** | **e^{rn}** |
| **Present worth** | **1/(1 + i)^n** | **e^{−rn}** |
| **Effective from nominal** | **(1 + r/m)^m − 1** | **e^r − 1** |

> **The continuous forms are simpler to manipulate, and the numerical difference from monthly compounding is negligible in practice** — so the choice between them is a matter of convenience, not accuracy.

examTip.trick: **Two steps: i_eff = e^{0.10} − 1 = 10.517 %, then i_monthly = (1.10517)^{1/12} − 1 = 0.8368 %.** The annual rate must be found first — you cannot go straight to a monthly figure.
examTip.trap: **Option (a) 1 % implies an effective annual rate of (1.01)¹² − 1 = 12.68 %**, well above the 10.517 % given. Test each candidate by compounding it twelve times — that identifies the answer without the twelfth root.
examTip.mnemonic: **A NOMINAL rate is meaningless without its compounding frequency** — 10 % gives 10.00 % annually and 10.517 % continuously. And note how little is gained past monthly (10.471 %): continuous compounding is used for clean MATHEMATICS, not for the number.

questions.stem: The velocity distribution for flow over a flat plate is given by u = 2y − y², where u is the velocity in m/s at a distance y metres above the plate. Determine the shear stress at y = 0.15 m. Take the dynamic viscosity of the fluid as 8.5 poise.
questions.solution:
**1.445 N/m².**

**Step 1 — differentiate the velocity profile to get the velocity gradient:**

> **u = 2y − y²**

> **du/dy = 2 − 2y**

> **At y = 0.15 m:  du/dy = 2 − 2(0.15) = 2 − 0.30 = 1.70 s⁻¹**

**Step 2 — convert the viscosity to SI:**

> **1 poise = 0.1 N·s/m² (that is, 1 Pa·s = 10 poise)**

> **μ = 8.5 poise = 0.85 N·s/m²**

> **This conversion is the step the question is really testing, and getting it wrong by a factor of ten is the standard error.**

**Step 3 — apply Newton's law of viscosity:**

> **τ = μ (du/dy)**

> **τ = 0.85 × 1.70 = 1.445 N/m²** ✓

**Why the four options are so close — and how to be sure:**

> **The options are 1.455, 1.545, 1.445 and 1.554** — the same digits rearranged. **They cannot be distinguished by estimation, so the arithmetic must be exact.**

> **0.85 × 1.70 = 1.445 exactly**, with no rounding anywhere in the calculation. **That exactness is the confirmation: if your answer needs rounding to reach an option, a step has gone wrong.**

> **The digit-shuffled option set is a deliberate device to defeat estimation**, and the defence is to carry the two clean numbers 0.85 and 1.70 and multiply them once.

**The definitions the question rests on:**

> **NEWTON'S LAW OF VISCOSITY:  τ = μ (du/dy)**

| Quantity | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **τ** | **Shear stress on a plane parallel to the flow** |
| **μ** | **DYNAMIC (absolute) viscosity** |
| **du/dy** | **VELOCITY GRADIENT — the rate of shear strain, with units of s⁻¹** |

> **The statement worth holding: a SOLID's shear stress is proportional to the shear STRAIN; a FLUID's is proportional to the RATE of shear strain.**

> **That is what distinguishes a fluid from a solid — and it is why a fluid at rest can sustain no shear stress at all, which is the starting point of hydrostatics.**

**The unit conversions, gathered, since they are where this class of problem fails:**

| Quantity | SI | CGS | Conversion |
|---|---|---|---|
| **DYNAMIC viscosity μ** | **N·s/m² = Pa·s** | **POISE** | **1 Pa·s = 10 poise** |
| **KINEMATIC viscosity ν** | **m²/s** | **STOKE** | **1 m²/s = 10⁴ stokes** |

> **The poise is named after Poiseuille and the stoke after Stokes**, and both are CGS units that survive in the literature because the SI values for common fluids are awkwardly small.

> **Water at 20 °C: μ = 1 × 10⁻³ Pa·s = 0.01 poise = 1 CENTIPOISE.** The centipoise is convenient precisely because water is 1 of them — **which is why viscosities are so often quoted in cP.**

> **So 8.5 poise = 850 centipoise, which is a fairly viscous oil** — about 850 times water. **That sanity check confirms the conversion: a fluid at 8.5 poise should be oil-like, and it is.**

**A note on where the shear stress is greatest, since it is the natural next question:**

> **du/dy = 2 − 2y is LARGEST at y = 0** (the plate surface), where it equals 2 s⁻¹.

> **So the maximum shear stress is at the PLATE: τ₀ = 0.85 × 2 = 1.70 N/m².**

> **And du/dy = 0 at y = 1 m**, where the profile reaches its maximum velocity of u = 1 m/s and the shear stress vanishes.

> **That is the general pattern of a boundary layer: shear is maximum AT THE WALL and falls to zero at the edge of the layer**, because the velocity gradient does the same.

> **Which is why the WALL SHEAR STRESS τ₀ is the quantity of engineering interest** — it is what produces skin friction drag on a plate, head loss in a pipe, and the tractive force that scours a channel bed.

**And the boundary-layer context, since the problem is a boundary-layer profile:**

| Concept | Note |
|---|---|
| **NO-SLIP condition** | **u = 0 at the wall — which this profile satisfies, since u = 0 at y = 0** ✓ |
| **Boundary layer thickness δ** | Where u reaches 99 % of the free-stream value |
| **Laminar sublayer** | Exists even in turbulent flow, immediately at the wall |
| **Skin friction drag** | **= ∫τ₀ dA over the surface** |

> **The profile given satisfies the no-slip condition and has zero gradient at y = 1**, so it is a plausible boundary-layer profile with δ = 1 m — **a check worth making, because a profile that violated no-slip would not describe a real flow at all.**

examTip.trap: **1 Pa·s = 10 poise**, so 8.5 poise is 0.85 not 8.5 — a factor of ten. And the four options are the same digits rearranged, deliberately defeating estimation, so the arithmetic must be exact.
examTip.mnemonic: **Shear is MAXIMUM AT THE WALL and zero at the layer's edge**, because du/dy does the same — here 2.0 s⁻¹ at y = 0 giving τ₀ = 1.70 N/m². The wall value is the one that produces drag, head loss and bed scour.

questions.stem: A launching apron is to be designed downstream of a weir for a discharge intensity of 6.5 m³/s/m. For the design of launching aprons the scour depth is taken as two times Lacey's scour depth. The silt factor of the bed material is unity. If the tailwater depth is 4.4 m, the length of the launching apron in the launched position is:
questions.solution:
**5 m (computed 5.004 m).**

**Step 1 — Lacey's normal scour depth from the discharge intensity:**

> **R = 1.35 (q² / f)^{1/3}**

| Symbol | Meaning | Value |
|---|---|---|
| **q** | **Discharge intensity, m³/s per metre width** | **6.5** |
| **f** | **Lacey's silt factor** | **1** |

> **R = 1.35 (6.5² / 1)^{1/3} = 1.35 (42.25)^{1/3}**

> **(42.25)^{1/3} = 3.4823**

> **R = 1.35 × 3.4823 = 4.701 m**

**Step 2 — the design scour depth for a launching apron:**

> **The stem states it: TWO TIMES Lacey's scour depth.**

> **Design scour depth D = 2R = 2 × 4.701 = 9.404 m**

**Step 3 — the depth of scour BELOW the existing bed:**

> **The tailwater depth is 4.4 m, so the scour hole extends below the bed by:**

> **9.404 − 4.4 = 5.004 m**

> **Length of the launching apron in the launched position ≈ 5 m** ✓

> **The source's own working gives exactly this: 9.404 − 4.4 = 5.004 m, rounded to 5 m.**

**What "in the launched position" means, because it is the concept the question rests on:**

> **A launching apron is stone laid FLAT on the bed beyond the toe of the pitching.**

> **When a flood scours the bed, the apron stone SLIDES — "launches" — down into the developing scour hole, armouring the new slope as it forms.**

> **The apron is therefore DESIGNED TO BE DESTROYED in an orderly way**, and the design question is simply: **is there enough stone to cover the slope that will form?**

| Design element | Value |
|---|---|
| **Launched slope assumed** | **2:1 (H:V)** |
| **Apron thickness** | **1.5 to 2.25 × the pitching thickness** |
| **Length in the launched position** | **The DEPTH of scour below the bed, as computed here** |
| **Length of the apron as LAID** | **Longer, because the flat apron must supply the stone for the slanting launched slope** |

> **The distinction between the LAUNCHED length and the LAID length is worth understanding: the stone must travel to reach its final position, so the apron laid on the bed is longer than the vertical depth it will armour.**

> **On a 2:1 slope the slant length is √5 ≈ 2.24 times the depth**, so the volume of stone needed is correspondingly greater — and the laid apron's length is computed from that volume divided by its thickness.

> **The question asks for the launched-position length, which is the scour depth below the bed — the simpler of the two figures, and the one the source computes.**

**Why a launching apron rather than a rigid protection:**

> **The alternative would be to build a rigid structure down to the maximum scour depth — a deep cut-off wall or a sheet pile line to 9.4 m.**

| | **LAUNCHING APRON** | **RIGID cut-off to full scour depth** |
|---|---|---|
| **Cost** | **LOW — loose stone on the bed** | **Very high — deep excavation under water** |
| **Adapts to actual scour** | **YES — launches only as far as the scour goes** | Fixed, whatever happens |
| **Constructible in a live river** | **YES — dumped from the bank or a boat** | **Very difficult** |
| **Maintenance** | **Requires topping up after floods** | Little |
| Failure mode | Gradual, observable | Sudden if undermined beyond it |

> **The apron's decisive advantage is CONSTRUCTABILITY in a live alluvial river.** Excavating 9 m below the bed of a Himalayan river to build a cut-off is a major undertaking; **dumping stone on the bed is not.**

> **And the apron self-adjusts: in a mild flood it launches a little, in a severe one further.** A rigid structure has to be built for the worst case whether it comes or not.

> **The price is maintenance — the apron must be inspected and replenished after major floods**, and a scheme without that maintenance regime will eventually find its protection has launched away.

**The scour multipliers, since the stem supplies one and may not next time:**

| Location | Design scour depth |
|---|---|
| **Straight reach of a guide bank / apron** | **1.25 to 1.75 R** |
| **Upstream CURVED HEAD of a guide bank** | **2.0 to 2.5 R — the DEEPEST on the whole work** |
| **Downstream of a weir or barrage** | **~2 R** ← as the stem states |
| **Nose of a bridge pier** | **2 R** |
| Abutment | 1.27 to 2 R |

> **The multipliers reflect how concentrated the flow is at each location**, and the curved head of a guide bank is the worst because the flow turns there and the secondary currents dig deepest.

> **Which is why the heaviest apron on a river training work is always at the nose**, and why a uniform apron thickness along the whole structure is a waste at one end and a risk at the other.

**And Lacey's scour formulae, both forms:**

| Given | Formula |
|---|---|
| **Discharge intensity q (per metre)** | **R = 1.35 (q²/f)^{1/3}** ← used here |
| **Total discharge Q** | **R = 0.47 (Q/f)^{1/3}** |

> **The two are consistent** (the second follows from the first with Lacey's regime width) **and the choice depends on which datum the problem supplies** — a point worth noticing, because using the Q formula with a q value is wrong by a large factor.

examTip.trap: **Two Lacey formulae exist: R = 1.35(q²/f)^{1/3} for discharge INTENSITY and R = 0.47(Q/f)^{1/3} for TOTAL discharge.** Using the wrong one with the given datum is wrong by a large factor.
examTip.mnemonic: **The apron is DESIGNED TO BE DESTROYED in an orderly way** — stone slides into the scour hole and armours the new 2:1 slope. Its advantage is constructability in a live river; its price is replenishment after floods.

questions.stem: The basic wind speed is 55 m/s and k1, k2 and k3 are all 1. The wind pressure considered is:
questions.solution:
**1815 N/m².**

**The formula and the arithmetic:**

> **p_z = 0.6 V_z²**, where **V_z = V_b × k₁ × k₂ × k₃**

> **With all three factors equal to 1:  V_z = 55 m/s**

> **p_z = 0.6 × 55² = 0.6 × 3025 = 1815 N/m²** ✓

> **Note that the four options are the same digits with the decimal point moved**, so the question is entirely about the ORDER OF MAGNITUDE — and the arithmetic itself is trivial.

**Two independent ways to fix the magnitude, since that is the whole difficulty:**

> **METHOD 1 — do the arithmetic carefully.** 55² = 3025, and 0.6 × 3025 = 1815. **There is no decimal point to lose: both numbers are exact.**

> **METHOD 2 — sanity-check against a familiar pressure.** 

| Pressure | Value |
|---|---|
| **Atmospheric pressure** | **101,325 N/m²** |
| **A typical floor imposed load (residential)** | **2000 N/m² (2 kN/m²)** |
| **This wind pressure** | **1815 N/m²** ← |

> **A severe wind pressure should be of the same order as a floor live load — around 1 to 2 kN/m² — and about 2 per cent of atmospheric pressure.**

> **1815 N/m² fits both comparisons.** 18.15 N/m² would be a barely perceptible breeze; **18,150 N/m² would be nine times a residential floor load, which no wind produces.**

> **That check is worth making because the option set is built entirely to punish a misplaced decimal**, and an order-of-magnitude sense is the defence.

**Where the coefficient 0.6 comes from:**

> **The dynamic pressure of a moving fluid is ½ρV².**

> **For air, ρ ≈ 1.2 kg/m³, so ½ρ = 0.6.**

> **p = 0.6V² is therefore not an empirical constant but the dynamic pressure of the airstream**, with V in m/s and p in N/m².

> **Knowing that removes any need to remember the number, and it also explains why the formula would change at high altitude**, where air is less dense — **though codes generally ignore that, being conservative at sea level.**

**What the three k factors do:**

| Factor | Accounts for | Typical range |
|---|---|---|
| **k₁ — risk coefficient** | **The structure's IMPORTANCE and design life** | **0.82 to 1.08** |
| **k₂ — terrain, height and size** | **Roughness of the surroundings, height above ground, and the size of the structure** | **0.67 to 1.17** |
| **k₃ — topography** | **Hills, ridges, escarpments — local speed-up** | **1.0 to 1.36** |

> **The stem sets all three to 1, which is a simplification for the arithmetic — a real design almost never has all three at unity.**

> **The k₂ factor is the one that varies most and matters most: wind speed increases with height above ground**, because the ground's friction slows the lower air. **So the pressure on the top of a tall building is substantially higher than at its base.**

> **And k₃ is the factor that matters most in Nepal.** A structure on a RIDGE CREST can attract a factor of 1.36, because the terrain compresses and accelerates the airflow over the crest.

> **1.36 on the speed becomes 1.36² = 1.85 on the pressure** — nearly double. **And ridge tops are exactly where communication towers, viewing platforms and hilltop temples get built.**

**Nepal's two wind zones, since they set V_b:**

| Zone | Region | Basic wind velocity |
|---|---|---|
| **Lower plains and hills** | **Terai, Kathmandu Valley, generally below 3000 m** | **47 m/s** |
| **Mountains** | **Above 3000 m** | **55 m/s** ← the value used here |

> **So this question is set in the mountain zone**, and the resulting 1815 N/m² is the highest basic pressure the Nepali code produces before the k factors are applied.

> **Compare the lower zone: 0.6 × 47² = 1325 N/m².** A 17 per cent difference in speed gives a 37 per cent difference in pressure — **because pressure goes as the SQUARE.**

**And what wind pressure actually governs:**

| Structure | Wind's role |
|---|---|
| **Low-rise buildings** | **Usually NOT critical — seismic and gravity govern** |
| **ROOFS, especially light ones** | **CRITICAL — wind UPLIFT is the classic failure** ← |
| **Tall or slender structures** | Critical, and dynamic effects appear |
| **Towers, chimneys, poles, hoardings** | **Wind usually GOVERNS** |

> **Roof uplift is what causes most actual wind damage, and it is routinely under-appreciated.** Wind flowing over a roof produces SUCTION on the upper surface, and for a light roof — CGI sheeting on a light frame — **the net uplift can exceed the roof's self-weight and the roof leaves the building.**

> **The remedy is not a stronger roof but better ANCHORAGE**: sheets to purlins, purlins to trusses, trusses to walls, walls to foundation — **a continuous load path in TENSION, which is the opposite of what a gravity-designed structure provides.**

> **Which is why roof failures in high winds are almost always CONNECTION failures rather than member failures**, and why the detailing matters more than the member sizes.

examTip.trick: **p = 0.6V² = 0.6 × 3025 = 1815 N/m².** The 0.6 is ½ρ for air (ρ ≈ 1.2 kg/m³), so it is the dynamic pressure of the airstream, not an empirical constant.
examTip.trap: **The four options are the same digits with the decimal moved** — the question is purely about magnitude. Sanity-check: a severe wind pressure should be of the same order as a floor live load (~2 kN/m²) and about 2 % of atmospheric.
examTip.mnemonic: **Nepal's two zones: 47 m/s below 3000 m, 55 m/s above** — giving 1325 and 1815 N/m². A 17 % speed difference is a 37 % pressure difference, because pressure goes as the SQUARE. And k₃ on a ridge crest (1.36) nearly doubles it.

questions.stem: The sequent depth ratio of a hydraulic jump in a rectangular channel is 16.48. What is the approximate Froude number at the beginning of the jump?
questions.solution:
**12.**

**The Belanger (sequent depth) equation:**

> **y₂/y₁ = ½ [√(1 + 8 Fr₁²) − 1]**

| Symbol | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **y₁** | **PRE-jump (supercritical) depth** |
| **y₂** | **POST-jump (subcritical) depth** |
| **Fr₁** | **Froude number BEFORE the jump** |

**Solving for Fr₁:**

> **16.48 = ½ [√(1 + 8Fr₁²) − 1]**

> **32.96 = √(1 + 8Fr₁²) − 1**

> **33.96 = √(1 + 8Fr₁²)**

> **1153.3 = 1 + 8Fr₁²**

> **8Fr₁² = 1152.3**

> **Fr₁² = 144.04**

> **Fr₁ = 12.0** ✓

> **The numbers are chosen so that Fr₁² comes out at almost exactly 144 = 12²**, which is the confirmation that the algebra has been done correctly.

**The approximation worth knowing for large Froude numbers:**

> **When Fr₁ is large, the 1 under the root and the −1 outside it both become negligible:**

> **y₂/y₁ ≈ ½ √(8Fr₁²) = ½ × 2√2 × Fr₁ = √2 × Fr₁ ≈ 1.414 Fr₁**

> **Check it: 1.414 × 12 = 16.97, against the exact 16.48.** Close enough to identify the answer.

> **So the rough rule is Fr₁ ≈ (y₂/y₁) / 1.414 = 16.48/1.414 = 11.65 ≈ 12** ✓

> **That approximation identifies the answer in one division and is well worth carrying**, because it also gives a feel for the relation: **the depth ratio is roughly 1.4 times the Froude number for a strong jump.**

**Why the jump exists at all:**

> **A HYDRAULIC JUMP is the abrupt transition from SUPERCRITICAL to SUBCRITICAL flow.**

> **Supercritical flow cannot become subcritical smoothly**, because a smooth transition would require passing through critical depth, and the energy grade line will not permit it in that direction.

> **So the transition happens abruptly, with a large and irreversible ENERGY LOSS in the turbulence and air entrainment of the roller.**

> **That energy loss is not a nuisance — it is the reason jumps are deliberately created.** A stilling basin downstream of a spillway exists to force a jump and destroy the flow's energy before it reaches the river bed.

**The classification of jumps by Froude number:**

| Fr₁ | Type | Energy loss |
|---|---|---|
| **1.0 - 1.7** | **UNDULAR — a train of standing waves, no roller** | **< 5 %** |
| **1.7 - 2.5** | **WEAK** | **5-15 %** |
| **2.5 - 4.5** | **OSCILLATING — the jet oscillates, generating waves that travel downstream** | **15-45 %** |
| **4.5 - 9.0** | **STEADY — well-defined, stable roller; the DESIGN RANGE** | **45-70 %** |
| **> 9.0** | **STRONG (choppy) — very rough, large energy loss** | **70-85 %** ← Fr = 12 here |

> **The OSCILLATING range (2.5 to 4.5) is the one to AVOID in design**, and the reason is specific: **the oscillating jet generates surface waves that travel a long way downstream**, eroding banks and interfering with navigation. **A stilling basin operating in this range is a nuisance rather than a solution.**

> **The STEADY range (4.5 to 9) is the design target**: stable position, good energy dissipation, no wave train.

> **A Froude number of 12 gives a STRONG jump — excellent energy dissipation (70-85 per cent) but very rough**, with high velocities and severe demands on the basin's floor and side walls.

**The other jump relations, since they are asked together:**

| Quantity | Expression |
|---|---|
| **Sequent depth ratio** | **y₂/y₁ = ½[√(1 + 8Fr₁²) − 1]** ← |
| **Energy loss** | **ΔE = (y₂ − y₁)³ / (4 y₁ y₂)** |
| **Height of the jump** | **y₂ − y₁** |
| **Length of the jump** | **≈ 5 to 7 y₂ (empirical)** |
| **Efficiency** | E₂/E₁ |

> **The energy loss formula's CUBE on (y₂ − y₁) is the striking feature**: the loss grows very rapidly with the height of the jump, **which is why a strong jump dissipates so much more than a weak one.**

> **And the length ≈ 5 to 7 times the post-jump depth is what sizes a stilling basin** — a basin shorter than that lets the jump sweep out downstream, and the energy arrives at the river bed undissipated.

**The practical warning that goes with it:**

> **A jump must be CONTAINED within the basin at all discharges, and its position depends on the TAILWATER LEVEL.**

| Tailwater | Consequence |
|---|---|
| **Exactly at the sequent depth y₂** | **The jump forms at the design point — ideal** |
| **HIGHER than y₂** | **The jump is DROWNED — submerged, less effective, but safe** |
| **LOWER than y₂** | **The jump SWEEPS OUT downstream, beyond the basin — the DANGEROUS case** ← |

> **The swept-out jump is the failure mode to design against**, because the energy is then dissipated on the erodible river bed rather than on the concrete floor. **Many spillway failures are of exactly this kind, and the remedy is a depressed basin floor, an end sill, or baffle blocks — all devices to hold the jump in place at low tailwater.**

examTip.trick: **y₂/y₁ = ½[√(1+8Fr₁²) − 1].** Working back: 33.96² = 1153.3, so 8Fr² = 1152.3 and Fr² = 144.04 — exactly 12².
examTip.trap: **For large Fr the relation approximates to y₂/y₁ ≈ √2 · Fr₁**, so Fr ≈ 16.48/1.414 = 11.65 ≈ 12 in one division. Worth carrying: the depth ratio is about 1.4 times the Froude number.
examTip.mnemonic: **AVOID the oscillating range Fr 2.5-4.5** — it sends wave trains far downstream. Design for the STEADY range 4.5-9. And the dangerous case is a **SWEPT-OUT jump at low tailwater**, dissipating energy on the river bed instead of the concrete.

questions.stem: The wetted perimeter of a trapezoidal channel section, where z is the side slope, y the depth and B the bed width, is:
questions.solution:
**P = B + 2y√(1 + z²).**

**Where each term comes from — the perimeter is simply the sum of three wetted sides:**

| Part of the boundary | Length |
|---|---|
| **The BED** | **B** |
| **Each SLOPING SIDE** | **y√(1 + z²)** |
| **Both sides** | **2y√(1 + z²)** |
| **TOTAL wetted perimeter** | **B + 2y√(1 + z²)** ✓ |

> **The √(1 + z²) is Pythagoras on the side slope:** for a depth y the horizontal run is zy, so the slant length is **√(y² + (zy)²) = y√(1 + z²).** ✓

> **So the factor is the SLANT LENGTH PER UNIT DEPTH**, and it is the only non-obvious term in the expression.

**Three checks that identify the answer without recall:**

> **CHECK 1 — the sign must be PLUS.** A perimeter is a sum of lengths; **it cannot be reduced by adding sides.**

> **Option (a) SUBTRACTS the sides, which would make a wide shallow channel have a NEGATIVE perimeter.** ✓ eliminated

> **CHECK 2 — the factor must be 2.** There are **TWO** sloping sides.

> **Option (c) counts only one.** ✓ eliminated

> **CHECK 3 — the limiting case z = 0 (a rectangle).** Then P should be B + 2y.

| Option | At z = 0 | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| B − 2y√1 = **B − 2y** | Wrong | Fails |
| **B + 2y√1 = B + 2y** ✓ | **Correct** | **Passes** |
| B + y√1 = B + y | Only one side | Fails |

> **The rectangle check is decisive and takes five seconds**, and it is the right instinct for any channel-geometry formula: **set the side slope to zero and see whether the rectangle's answer emerges.**

**The companion formulae for a trapezoidal section:**

| Quantity | Expression |
|---|---|
| **AREA** | **A = By + zy²** |
| **WETTED PERIMETER** | **P = B + 2y√(1 + z²)** ← |
| **HYDRAULIC RADIUS** | **R = A/P** |
| **TOP WIDTH** | **T = B + 2zy** |

> **Note that the AREA uses z directly (zy²) while the PERIMETER uses √(1+z²)**, and the reason is geometric: **the area of each triangular side element is ½(zy)(y), needing only the horizontal run; the perimeter needs the slant length.**

> **Confusing the two — putting √(1+z²) in the area or z in the perimeter — is the standard error**, and the check is that the area's side term must reduce to zero at z = 0 (a rectangle has no triangular parts) while the perimeter's must reduce to 2y.

**Why the wetted perimeter matters so much:**

> **It appears in the HYDRAULIC RADIUS R = A/P, which is the single geometric parameter in both Manning's and Chezy's equations.**

> **A LARGE perimeter for a given area means a SMALL R, which means a LOW velocity and a LOW discharge** — because more of the flow is in contact with the rough boundary and slowed by it.

> **So minimising the wetted perimeter for a given area is the same thing as maximising the discharge, which is the definition of the MOST ECONOMICAL SECTION.**

**The most economical trapezoidal section, since it follows directly:**

> **Minimise P for a given A, and the result is HALF A REGULAR HEXAGON:**

| Condition | Form |
|---|---|
| **Side slope** | **z = 1/√3 (the sides at 60° to the horizontal)** |
| **Hydraulic radius** | **R = y/2** |
| **Top width** | **T = 2 × (length of a sloping side)** |
| **A circle inscribed in the section** | **Touches the bed and BOTH sides, centred on the water surface** |

> **The condition R = y/2 is the general result for the most efficient section of ANY shape**, which is why a SEMICIRCLE is the theoretical ideal open channel — it has the least perimeter for its area of any shape.

> **A semicircle is hard to build and to maintain in earth**, which is why the half-hexagon trapezium is the practical optimum. **But the reason semicircular channels are used in precast concrete and in sewers is exactly this efficiency.**

> **And note the agreement that makes the optimisation unusually attractive: minimum wetted perimeter also means MINIMUM LINING MATERIAL.**

> **So hydraulic efficiency and construction cost point the SAME WAY here**, which is rarely the case in engineering and worth noticing when it happens.

**A practical caution, since the most economical section is not always adopted:**

| Reason to depart from the optimum | Note |
|---|---|
| **Soil stability** | **The side slope must be flatter than the soil allows, whatever the hydraulics wants** ← |
| **Constructability and maintenance access** | A deep narrow section is hard to build and to desilt |
| **Freeboard and safety** | — |
| **Depth limited by the command level** | The canal must be able to deliver water where it is needed |
| Available land width | — |

> **The soil-stability constraint usually governs in practice.** The hexagonal optimum needs z = 1/√3 = 0.577, a side slope of about 1.73 horizontal to 1 vertical — **steeper than most earth will stand, which typically requires 1.5:1 to 2:1 or flatter.**

> **So the most economical section is a benchmark rather than a specification**, and a real canal is the closest practicable approach to it.

verification.notes: Duplicate option removed. The source paper printed options (a) and (d) IDENTICALLY as B - 2y root(1+Z^2), leaving the question with only three distinct choices. Option (d) has been replaced with "None of the above". The keyed answer is unchanged - (b) B + 2y root(1+Z^2), which the source's own worked answer to a later question in the same paper confirms (P = b + 2y(1+Z^2)^0.5 = 7.47 m).

examTip.trick: **P = bed + two slant sides = B + 2y√(1+z²)**, the √(1+z²) being Pythagoras on the side slope — the slant length per unit depth.
examTip.trap: **Three checks with no recall: the sign must be PLUS (a perimeter is a sum), the factor must be 2 (two sides), and at z = 0 it must reduce to B + 2y (a rectangle).** The rectangle check is decisive in five seconds.
examTip.mnemonic: **AREA uses z directly (By + zy²); PERIMETER uses √(1+z²)** — area needs the horizontal run, perimeter the slant length. And minimising P for a given A gives the **HALF-HEXAGON with R = y/2**, where hydraulic efficiency and lining cost agree.

questions.stem: If the total hydroelectric potential of a plant is 84 GW, convert the potential into energy considering a load factor of 60 %.
questions.solution:
**441 TWh (computed 441.5 TWh).**

**The conversion — capacity to energy:**

> **Energy = Power × Load factor × Hours in the period**

> **E = 84 × 10⁹ W × 0.60 × 8760 h**

> **= 84 × 0.60 × 8760 × 10⁹ Wh**

> **= 50.4 × 8760 × 10⁹ Wh**

> **= 441,504 × 10⁹ Wh**

> **= 441.5 × 10¹² Wh = 441.5 TWh ≈ 441 TWh** ✓

> **The clean route is 84 × 0.6 = 50.4 GW average, then 50.4 × 8760 = 441,504 GWh = 441.5 TWh.**

> **Reducing the capacity to an AVERAGE POWER first, and only then multiplying by the hours, keeps the arithmetic in one line and the units obvious.**

**The unit ladder, since this question is really about magnitude:**

| Prefix | Factor | In this problem |
|---|---|---|
| **k (kilo)** | 10³ | — |
| **M (mega)** | 10⁶ | — |
| **G (giga)** | **10⁹** | **84 GW capacity** |
| **T (tera)** | **10¹²** | **441 TWh energy** |

> **Note that GW × hours gives GWh, and 1 TWh = 1000 GWh** — so 441,504 GWh becomes 441.5 TWh. **A candidate who stops at GWh will find no matching option, which is at least a warning.**

> **And 8760 = 365 × 24 is the number to have automatically.** It appears in every capacity-to-energy conversion.

**Why each distractor is wrong:**

| Option | Where it comes from |
|---|---|
| **441 TWh** | ✓ |
| **735 TWh** | **84 × 8760 = 735,840 GWh = 735.8 TWh — the LOAD FACTOR OMITTED** ← the trap |
| **1226 TWh** | 84 × 8760 / 0.6 — dividing by the load factor instead of multiplying |
| **504 TWh** | Roughly 84 × 0.6 × 10,000 — a rounded hours figure |

> **Option (b) 735 TWh is the designed trap, and it is exactly the answer with the load factor left out.** It is what you get by treating the 84 GW as though the plant ran flat out all year.

> **Option (c) inverts the factor**, which is worth guarding against: **the load factor must REDUCE the energy, since it is a fraction less than one.** A result LARGER than the flat-out figure is impossible, and 1226 > 735 fails that test at a glance.

> **That impossibility check disposes of (c) instantly.**

**Nepal's hydropower potential figures, which is what the 84 GW refers to:**

| Figure | Value |
|---|---|
| **THEORETICAL potential** | **~83,000 MW = 83 GW** ← the stem's 84 GW |
| **TECHNICALLY feasible** | **~45,000 MW** |
| **ECONOMICALLY feasible** | **~42,000 MW** |
| Currently installed | A small fraction of the last figure |

> **The 83,000 MW figure comes from Dr Hari Man Shrestha's 1966 doctoral study** and has been quoted in almost every Nepali policy document since.

> **The three figures descend for good reasons, and the descent matters more than the headline:**

> **THEORETICAL potential counts every drop of water falling through every metre of head** — it is a physical accounting, not an engineering estimate.

> **TECHNICALLY feasible removes the sites that cannot be built** — inaccessible, geologically impossible, or too small to be worth a scheme.

> **ECONOMICALLY feasible removes those that could be built but would not pay.**

> **So the 83 GW headline is a physics number and the 42 GW is the engineering one** — and quoting the first as though it were developable is a common and misleading practice.

**Why the LOAD FACTOR is the essential term:**

> **A plant's CAPACITY is what it can produce at an instant; its ENERGY is what it actually produces over time.** The load factor is the bridge.

> **And it is where Nepal's hydropower situation is most often misrepresented.** Installed capacity in megawatts is quoted; **energy in gigawatt-hours, and especially DRY-SEASON energy, is what matters.**

| Plant type | Typical annual factor |
|---|---|
| **Run-of-river hydro (Nepal)** | **40-60 %** |
| **Storage hydro, peaking** | **20-40 % by design** |
| **Thermal base load** | 60-85 % |

> **A 60 per cent factor, as the stem assumes, is at the optimistic end for Nepali run-of-river hydro** — achievable on a well-sited scheme, and not achievable on many.

> **The reason is the monsoon: roughly 80 per cent of the annual runoff arrives in four months.** A run-of-river plant generates at capacity through the monsoon and at a fraction of it through the winter.

> **Which is why STORAGE matters so much and why Nepal having essentially one storage plant (Kulekhani) is a structural rather than an incidental problem** — storage is what converts a high monsoon flow into dry-season energy, and dry-season energy is what the system is short of.

examTip.trick: **Reduce to average power first: 84 × 0.6 = 50.4 GW, then × 8760 h = 441,504 GWh = 441.5 TWh.** Have 8760 = 365 × 24 automatically.
examTip.trap: **Option (b) 735 TWh is the answer with the LOAD FACTOR OMITTED** — the plant treated as running flat out all year. And option (c) DIVIDES by the factor, giving more than the flat-out figure, which is impossible.
examTip.mnemonic: **Nepal: 83 GW theoretical, 45 GW technically feasible, 42 GW economically feasible.** The first is a physics number, the last an engineering one — and quoting the theoretical figure as developable is common and misleading.

questions.stem: The horizontal thrust in a two-hinged semicircular arch subjected to a udl of w kN/m over the left half span will be:
questions.solution:
**2wR/3π.**

**The two standard results for a two-hinged semicircular arch of radius R:**

| Loading | Horizontal thrust |
|---|---|
| **udl w over the ENTIRE span** | **H = (4/3) × wR/π = 4wR/3π** |
| **udl w over HALF the span** | **H = ½ × 4wR/3π = 2wR/3π** ← |

> **The half-span result is exactly HALF the full-span result**, and the source's own working states it that way: **H = ½ × (4/3) × wR/π = 2wR/3π.**

> **So option (a) 4wR/3π is the FULL-SPAN value, and it is the designed trap** — the stem's phrase "over the left half span" is the whole discrimination.

**Why halving the load halves the thrust — and why that is not obvious:**

> **The horizontal thrust in a two-hinged arch is a LINEAR functional of the applied loading:**

> **H = (∫Myds/EI) / (∫y²ds/EI)**

> **The DENOMINATOR depends only on the arch's own geometry and stiffness — it does not involve the load at all.**

> **The NUMERATOR contains M, the free bending moment, which is LINEAR in the load.**

> **So H is proportional to the load, and superposition applies: half the load gives half the thrust.**

> **That is worth spelling out because it is easy to assume that a HALF-SPAN load is a different KIND of problem** — an unsymmetrical loading on a symmetrical arch. **It is unsymmetrical, and it still superposes: a full-span udl is the sum of two half-span udls, so each contributes half the thrust.**

> **Which also gives a useful check: two half-span loads, left and right, must add to the full-span result. 2wR/3π + 2wR/3π = 4wR/3π** ✓

**Two dimensional and limiting checks on the form:**

> **CHECK 1 — dimensions.** w is a force per length and R a length, so **wR is a FORCE.** ✓ All four options pass, so dimensions do not discriminate here.

> **CHECK 2 — the rise appears where?** For a semicircular arch the rise IS the radius R, so R plays the role of both span-related and rise-related dimension. **That is why no separate h appears, and it is a feature peculiar to the semicircular case.**

> **For a PARABOLIC arch of span L and rise h, the full-span result is H = wL²/(8h)** — with the rise in the DENOMINATOR, as it must be. **In the semicircular case the geometry collapses both into R, so the rise-dependence is hidden.**

> **Recognising that prevents a false alarm: a candidate checking for "h in the denominator" will not find one, and should not conclude the formula is wrong.**

**Why the unsymmetrical case is the one that governs design:**

> **For a FUNICULAR shape under its design udl, the bending moment is zero everywhere and the arch is in pure compression** — which is the whole point of an arch.

> **But a HALF-SPAN load is not the design udl.** The thrust falls to half while the free moment diagram is unchanged in shape over the loaded half, **so the two no longer cancel and BENDING MOMENTS appear.**

| Loading | Bending in the arch |
|---|---|
| **Full-span udl on a funicular arch** | **ZERO — pure compression** |
