| **HALF-span udl** | **Substantial bending — and this case usually GOVERNS the rib section** ← |
| Point load | Substantial bending |
| Temperature change | Bending in a two- or three-hinged arch |

> **So the arch SHAPE is chosen from the full-span case and the arch SECTION is designed from the partial-load cases.** Those are two different calculations answering two different questions, and confusing them is a real error.

> **In bridge terms: dead load is full-span and roughly uniform, so the arch is shaped for it; LIVE LOAD can occupy half the span, and that is what sizes the rib.**

**And the standard results worth having, gathered:**

| Arch and loading | Horizontal thrust |
|---|---|
| **Two-hinged PARABOLIC, udl over full span** | **wL²/(8h)** |
| **Two-hinged parabolic, udl over half span** | **wL²/(16h)** |
| **Two-hinged parabolic, central point load W** | **25WL/(128h)** |
| **Two-hinged SEMICIRCULAR, udl over full span** | **4wR/3π** |
| **Two-hinged semicircular, udl over half span** | **2wR/3π** ← |
| **Three-hinged, any loading** | **H = M_beam(crown)/h — from statics alone** |

> **Note the last row: for a THREE-hinged arch no integration is needed at all**, because the crown hinge supplies the condition M = 0 there and the thrust follows from statics.

> **Which is another argument for the three-hinged arch beyond its insensitivity to movement: it is far simpler to analyse**, and the analysis does not depend on assumptions about EI or on the accuracy of an integration.

examTip.trick: **Full-span udl on a two-hinged semicircular arch gives 4wR/3π; HALF-span gives exactly half, 2wR/3π.** H is linear in the load, so superposition applies.
examTip.trap: **Option (a) 4wR/3π is the FULL-span value** — the stem's "left half span" is the whole discrimination. Check by superposition: two half-span loads must add to the full-span result, and they do.
examTip.mnemonic: **The arch SHAPE comes from the full-span case; the arch SECTION comes from the PARTIAL-load cases**, which produce the bending the funicular shape eliminates. Dead load is full-span; live load can occupy half.

questions.stem: The bearing stress is 180 kN/m², the unit weight of soil is 20 kN/m³ and the internal angle of friction is 30°. According to Rankine's theory, what is the minimum depth of foundation?
questions.solution:
**1 m.**

**Rankine's formula for the minimum depth of a foundation:**

> **D_min = (q / γ) × [(1 − sin φ) / (1 + sin φ)]²**

| Symbol | Meaning | Value |
|---|---|---|
| **q** | **Bearing pressure (intensity of loading)** | **180 kN/m²** |
| **γ** | **Unit weight of the soil** | **20 kN/m³** |
| **φ** | **Angle of internal friction** | **30°** |

**The computation:**

> **sin 30° = 0.5**

> **(1 − 0.5)/(1 + 0.5) = 0.5/1.5 = 1/3**

> **(1/3)² = 1/9**

> **q/γ = 180/20 = 9 m**

> **D_min = 9 × (1/9) = 1 m** ✓

> **The numbers are chosen so that the two factors cancel exactly** — 9 metres times one ninth — which is the confirmation that the formula has been applied correctly.

**What the bracketed term is, because recognising it makes the formula intelligible:**

> **(1 − sin φ)/(1 + sin φ) is RANKINE'S COEFFICIENT OF ACTIVE EARTH PRESSURE, K_a.**

> **For φ = 30°, K_a = 1/3** — a value worth committing to memory, since φ = 30° is the standard textbook sand.

> **So the formula is D_min = (q/γ) × K_a².**

> **And the reasoning behind it: the soil immediately beside the footing must be able to resist being pushed sideways and upward by the footing's pressure.**

> **The minimum depth is the depth at which the soil's own ACTIVE resistance balances the applied pressure**, and the squared K_a arises because the pressure is transferred through the soil in two stages of the active-passive relation.

> **The corresponding PASSIVE coefficient is its reciprocal: K_p = (1 + sin φ)/(1 − sin φ) = 3 for φ = 30°.**

> **Note K_p = 1/K_a, so K_p/K_a = 9 for φ = 30°** — the factor of nine between active and passive pressure, which is why passive resistance is such a large and such a dangerous term to rely on.

**Why the depth increases as φ DECREASES — the direction check:**

| φ | K_a | K_a² | D_min for q/γ = 9 m |
|---|---|---|---|
| **20°** | **0.49** | **0.240** | **2.16 m** |
| **30°** | **0.333** | **0.111** | **1.00 m** ← |
| **40°** | **0.217** | **0.047** | **0.42 m** |

> **A WEAKER soil (lower φ) needs a DEEPER foundation**, which is physically obvious and a good check that the formula has not been inverted.

> **If a computed depth FELL as the soil got weaker, the bracket has been used upside down** — and that is the commonest error, since K_a and K_p are so easily exchanged.

**What this formula is and is NOT for — the honest limitation:**

> **Rankine's minimum depth is a rough preliminary figure, and it is NOT the depth at which a footing should be founded.**

> **The actual founding depth is governed by considerations the formula knows nothing about:**

| Governing consideration | Note |
|---|---|
| **Reaching a stratum of adequate BEARING CAPACITY** | The primary criterion |
| **SETTLEMENT — often more restrictive than capacity** | **Especially on clay** |
| **Below the ZONE OF SEASONAL VOLUME CHANGE** | **Shrinkage and swelling of expansive clay — 1.5 m or more** ← |
| **Below the frost line** | Where relevant |
| **Below the maximum SCOUR depth** | **Bridge and river foundations — often several metres** |
| **Below topsoil, fill and organic matter** | Always |
| Below adjacent excavations and services | — |
| **Minimum of 0.5 m in any case (IS 1904)** | A floor on all of the above |

> **In practice the seasonal-volume-change and scour criteria usually govern**, and both can demand depths several times the Rankine figure.

> **So a candidate should be able to compute the Rankine depth and should also know that it is rarely the answer to "how deep should this footing go?"** — which is the distinction between doing the arithmetic and understanding the design.

**The other bearing-capacity relations, for context:**

| Theory | Form |
|---|---|
| **RANKINE minimum depth** | **D = (q/γ)K_a²** ← |
| **TERZAGHI ultimate bearing capacity (strip footing)** | **q_u = cN_c + γDN_q + ½γBN_γ** |
| **Net ultimate** | q_nu = q_u − γD |
| **Net safe** | **q_ns = q_nu / FOS, with FOS commonly 2.5-3** |
| Allowable | The lesser of the safe capacity and the settlement-limited pressure |

> **The three terms of Terzaghi's equation are worth naming, because each dominates for a different soil: cN_c is the COHESION term (governs in clay), γDN_q the SURCHARGE term (grows with depth), and ½γBN_γ the FRICTION/WIDTH term (governs in sand).**

> **Which is why bearing capacity in SAND increases with footing WIDTH and in CLAY does not** — the third term contains B and the first does not. **That is the same size effect that appears in the plate load test correction.**

verification.notes: Unit corrected in the stem. The source printed "Bearing stress is 180kN/m3" - a volumetric unit for a pressure. Bearing stress is a pressure and its unit is kN/m2, which is also what the source's own working requires for q/gamma to come out in metres (180/20 = 9 m). The unit weight, correctly given as 20 kN/m3, is unchanged, as is the keyed answer (a) 1 m.

examTip.trick: **D = (q/γ)K_a² with K_a = (1−sinφ)/(1+sinφ).** For φ = 30°, K_a = 1/3 exactly, so D = 9 × 1/9 = 1 m — the two factors cancel.
examTip.trap: **K_a and K_p are easily exchanged.** Check the direction: a WEAKER soil (lower φ) must need a DEEPER foundation. If your computed depth falls as φ falls, the bracket is upside down.
examTip.mnemonic: **For φ = 30°: K_a = 1/3, K_p = 3, so K_p/K_a = 9.** And know that the Rankine depth is a PRELIMINARY figure — real founding depth is usually governed by seasonal volume change, scour, or settlement instead.

questions.stem: If the initial population of a country is 1,000,000 and the birth rate and death rate are 10 % and 4 % respectively, what is the population of the country after 2 years?
questions.solution:
**1,123,600.**

**Step 1 — the net growth rate:**

> **Net growth rate = birth rate − death rate = 10 % − 4 % = 6 % = 0.06**

**Step 2 — apply GEOMETRIC (compound) growth for two years:**

> **P_n = P₀ (1 + r)^n**

> **P₂ = 1,000,000 × (1.06)²**

> **= 1,000,000 × 1.1236**

> **= 1,123,600** ✓

> **The arithmetic is exact: 1.06² = 1.1236, with no rounding.** That exactness is the confirmation — **an answer that needs rounding to reach an option has gone wrong.**

**Why the options are so close, and how to discriminate:**

| Option | Where it comes from |
|---|---|
| **1,126,000** | Not a clean derivation — a near-miss to defeat pattern recognition |
| **1,023,600** | **A digit-transposed version of the answer** — 1,0**2**3,600 against 1,1**2**3,600 ← |
| **1,123,000** | **The answer with the last significant figure dropped** ← |
| **1,123,600** | ✓ |

> **Options (b), (c) and (d) share most of their digits**, so this is a question about carrying the arithmetic exactly rather than about method.

> **The defence is to compute 1.06² = 1.1236 and read off all four decimal places**, which gives 1,123,600 unambiguously.

> **Note that ARITHMETIC growth would give a different and simpler answer: 1,000,000 + 2 × 60,000 = 1,120,000** — which is not among the options. **So the question requires the geometric method, and the absence of 1,120,000 from the options is itself a hint.**

**The population forecasting methods, since the choice of method is the real content:**

| Method | Assumption | Formula | Suits |
|---|---|---|---|
| **ARITHMETIC increase** | **Constant NUMBER added per decade** | **P_n = P₀ + n·x̄** | **LARGE, OLD, SATURATED cities** |
| **GEOMETRIC increase** | **Constant PERCENTAGE growth — compound** | **P_n = P₀(1 + r)^n** | **YOUNG, RAPIDLY GROWING towns** ← used here |
| **INCREMENTAL increase** | Arithmetic plus the average change in the increment | P_n = P₀ + nx̄ + [n(n+1)/2]ȳ | Intermediate cases |
| **Decrease-in-rate-of-growth** | The percentage rate itself declines | — | Towns approaching saturation |
| **Graphical / comparative** | Compare with a similar city's history | — | Where data are poor |
| **LOGISTIC (S-curve)** | **Growth is limited by a SATURATION population** | **P = P_sat/(1 + m·e^{nt})** | **The most realistic over a long period** |

> **The geometric method gives the HIGHEST forecast and the arithmetic the LOWEST**, so the choice materially changes the answer — and therefore the size of the works designed.

> **Which is why the choice must be justified rather than assumed: a young growing town forecast arithmetically will have works too small, and a saturated city forecast geometrically will have works too large and a tariff that cannot pay for them.**

**Why the logistic curve is the most realistic, and worth understanding:**

> **No population grows geometrically for ever.** Growth is eventually limited by land, employment, water, or the simple fact that people leave.

> **The logistic curve has three phases:**

| Phase | Character |
|---|---|
| **Early** | **Growth accelerating — geometric in behaviour** |
| **Middle** | **Growth roughly constant in number — arithmetic in behaviour** |
| **Late** | **Growth decelerating toward a SATURATION population** |

> **So the arithmetic and geometric methods are each approximations to a DIFFERENT PART of the same curve** — which is exactly why one suits young towns and the other old ones.

> **Recognising that unifies the methods instead of leaving them as a list to memorise.**

**Why any of this matters for a civil engineer:**

> **Every water supply, sewerage and solid-waste scheme is sized for a FUTURE population, and the DESIGN PERIOD is long:**

| Component | Design period |
|---|---|
| **Storage reservoirs and dams** | **50 years** |
| **Water treatment plant** | **15-20 years** |
| **Pipe mains and trunk sewers** | **30-50 years** |
| **Distribution network** | **30 years** |
| **Pumps and mechanical plant** | **10-15 years — replaced within the works' life** |

> **The components have DIFFERENT design periods, and that is deliberate: what is expensive to enlarge later is built large now, and what is cheap to replace is not.**

> **A trunk sewer laid under a city cannot be enlarged at any reasonable cost, so it is sized for fifty years. A pump can be swapped in a week, so it is sized for ten.**

> **That principle — match the design period to the cost of future enlargement — is the practical reason population forecasting matters**, and it is a better answer than "because the code says 30 years".

> **And the honest limitation: a fifty-year population forecast is a guess.** Which is why staged construction, and leaving room for a second pipe or a second module, is generally wiser than a single confident forecast.

examTip.trick: **Net rate = 10 % − 4 % = 6 %, then P = 1,000,000 × 1.06² = 1,123,600 exactly.** 1.06² = 1.1236, so read all four decimals.
examTip.trap: **Three options share most of their digits** — this is a question about exact arithmetic, not method. Note that ARITHMETIC growth would give 1,120,000, which is absent from the options: a hint that the geometric method is wanted.
examTip.mnemonic: **Arithmetic suits OLD saturated cities, geometric suits YOUNG growing ones** — and both are approximations to different parts of the LOGISTIC curve, which unifies them. Design periods differ by component: sewers 50 years, pumps 10-15.

questions.stem: Seasoning of timber is carried out principally to:
options: increase its density so that it carries more load
reduce its moisture content to the level at which it will be used in service
remove the sapwood, which is weaker than the heartwood
close the pores so that the timber becomes impermeable
questions.solution:
**To reduce its moisture content to the level at which it will be used in service.**

**Why seasoning matters — and the reason is DIMENSIONAL STABILITY, not strength:**

> **Freshly felled (green) timber contains 50 to 200 per cent moisture by dry weight.** Timber in a heated building settles at 10 to 14 per cent; in unheated shelter, 15 to 18 per cent.

> **Timber SHRINKS as it dries and SWELLS as it takes up moisture**, and it does so unequally in three directions.

> **So if unseasoned timber is built in, it dries in place — and shrinks in place.** Joints open, boards cup and split, doors jam and then rattle, and fixings loosen.

> **Seasoning brings the timber to its service moisture content BEFORE it is fixed**, so the movement happens in the yard rather than in the building.

> **That is the whole purpose, and it explains a rule that otherwise looks fussy: timber should be seasoned to roughly the moisture content it will LIVE at, not simply "dried".** Over-drying is as bad as under-drying, because the timber will then swell after installation.

**The FIBRE SATURATION POINT, which is the key concept:**

> **At 25 to 30 per cent moisture content, all the free water in the cell cavities has gone and only the water bound within the cell walls remains.** That is the **FIBRE SATURATION POINT (FSP).**

| Moisture range | Behaviour |
|---|---|
| **ABOVE the FSP** | **NO shrinkage and NO strength change — only free water is being lost** |
| **BELOW the FSP** | **Shrinkage begins AND strength rises steadily as drying continues** ← |

> **So nothing useful happens until the FSP is passed**, and everything happens after it. **That single fact explains why partial drying achieves nothing and why the 25-30 per cent figure is worth knowing.**

> **Strength does increase on seasoning — roughly doubling between green and 12 per cent** — so option (a) is not entirely unrelated. **But density does NOT increase; it FALLS, because water is being removed.** Option (a) has the mechanism backwards.

**The anisotropic shrinkage, which is why timber distorts rather than merely shrinking:**

| Direction | Shrinkage from green to oven-dry |
|---|---|
| **LONGITUDINAL (along the grain)** | **0.1-0.3 % — negligible** |
| **RADIAL (across the rings)** | **2-6 %** |
| **TANGENTIAL (along the rings)** | **4-12 % — the LARGEST, roughly TWICE the radial** ← |

> **Tangential shrinkage being about double radial is what causes CUPPING**: a flat-sawn board's outer face shrinks more along the rings than across them, so the board curls away from the heart.

> **And it is why QUARTER-SAWN timber is more stable than flat-sawn**: in a quarter-sawn board the rings run across the thickness, so the width shrinks radially (the smaller figure) and the board stays flat.

> **That is a genuine reason to pay more for quarter-sawn boards for flooring and joinery**, and it follows entirely from the table above.

**The methods of seasoning:**

| Method | Note |
|---|---|
| **NATURAL (air) seasoning** | **Stacked with spacers under cover; SLOW — months to years; cheap; less risk of degrade** |
| **KILN seasoning** | **Controlled temperature and humidity; DAYS to weeks; more expensive; can reach lower moisture contents** |
| **Water seasoning** | Immersion to leach sap, then air drying |
| **Boiling / steaming** | Rapid but reduces strength somewhat |
| Chemical (salt) seasoning | Impregnation to slow the surface drying |
| Electrical | Rarely used |

> **KILN seasoning is the only method that can reliably reach 10-12 per cent**, which is what interior joinery needs — air seasoning in a humid climate settles at 15-18 per cent and no lower.

> **And the reason kilning is controlled rather than merely hot: drying the SURFACE much faster than the core causes the classic seasoning defects.**

| Defect | Cause |
|---|---|
| **CHECKS and splits** | **Surface shrinks while the core is still wet — surface tension exceeds strength** |
| **CASE HARDENING** | **Surface dries and sets while the core is wet; internal stresses lock in** |
| **HONEYCOMBING** | **Internal splits from case hardening — invisible from outside** ← |
| **Cupping, bowing, twisting** | Anisotropic shrinkage, aggravated by uneven drying |
| Collapse (washboarding) | Cell walls crush in very rapid drying |

> **HONEYCOMBING is the one to fear, because it cannot be seen.** A board that looks perfect may be split internally, and the defect only appears when the timber is cut or loaded.

**Why each remaining distractor is wrong:**

> **Option (c) — removing sapwood — is not seasoning at all.** Sapwood is separated by CONVERSION (sawing) and by selection, not by drying. **And while sapwood is indeed less durable, it is not much weaker; the durability difference is about decay resistance, not strength.**

> **Option (d) — closing the pores to make timber impermeable — is not achievable by drying.** Timber remains permeable and HYGROSCOPIC for its whole life: **it continues to take up and give off moisture with the surrounding humidity, for ever.**

> **That permanence is the point.** Seasoning does not stop timber moving; **it brings it to equilibrium so that the remaining movement is small and seasonal rather than large and once-and-for-all.** Impermeability, where it is wanted, comes from a coating or a preservative treatment.

examTip.trick: **Nothing happens until the FIBRE SATURATION POINT (25-30 %) is passed** — above it, no shrinkage and no strength change; below it, both. So partial drying achieves nothing.
examTip.trap: **Option (a) has the mechanism backwards** — strength does rise on seasoning, but DENSITY FALLS, since water is being removed. And option (d) is impossible: timber stays HYGROSCOPIC for life.
examTip.mnemonic: **Tangential shrinkage is about TWICE radial**, which is what causes cupping — and why QUARTER-SAWN timber stays flatter. Season to the moisture content the timber will LIVE at, since over-drying makes it swell later.

questions.stem: In the slump test on fresh concrete, a TRUE slump is one in which:
options: the concrete collapses completely and spreads on the base plate
the concrete subsides evenly, keeping its shape roughly symmetrical
one half of the cone slides down an inclined plane
questions.solution:
**The concrete subsides evenly, keeping its shape roughly symmetrical.**

**The three kinds of slump, which is what the question is testing:**

| Slump | Appearance | What it means |
|---|---|---|
| **TRUE slump** | **The cone subsides evenly and stays roughly symmetrical** | **A VALID measurement — the mix is cohesive** ← |
| **SHEAR slump** | **ONE HALF of the cone slides down an inclined plane** | **The mix is NOT cohesive — the result is UNRELIABLE** |
| **COLLAPSE slump** | **The concrete collapses completely and spreads out** | **The mix is far too wet — the slump test is INAPPLICABLE** |

> **Only a TRUE slump gives a measurement that means anything**, which is why the distinction matters rather than being a piece of vocabulary.

> **The three options (a), (b) and (c) are precisely the three kinds** — so the question is a clean match, and option (d) is a red herring about magnitude rather than form.

**What to do when the slump is not true — the procedure, which is the practical content:**

> **SHEAR slump: REPEAT the test.** If a shear slump occurs on a second attempt with a fresh sample, **the concrete lacks the cohesion required and the mix should be rejected or redesigned.**

> **The remedy for a shear slump is usually more FINES — more sand, more cement, or a better-graded aggregate.** A harsh mix short of fine material shears rather than subsiding.

> **COLLAPSE slump: the test is unsuitable.** For very wet or flowing concrete, use the **COMPACTING FACTOR test or the FLOW TABLE test** instead.

> **So the response to a bad slump is not to record the number anyway — it is to recognise that the instrument is telling you something about the mix rather than about its workability.**

**The test itself, since its details are examined:**

| Parameter | Value |
|---|---|
| **Mould** | **A frustum of a cone: 200 mm bottom, 100 mm top, 300 mm high** |
| **Filling** | **FOUR layers, each about a quarter of the height** |
| **Tamping** | **25 strokes per layer with a 16 mm diameter, 600 mm long rod** |
| **Lifting** | **Slowly and vertically, in 5-10 seconds** |
| **Measurement** | **The DIFFERENCE in height between the mould and the highest point of the subsided concrete** |

> **The 300 mm mould height is the reference from which the slump is measured**, so a slump of 75 mm means the concrete subsided to 225 mm.

> **And the 25 strokes in four layers is the detail most often got wrong — it is per LAYER, so 100 strokes in total.**

**The recommended slump values, since the number is the test's purpose:**

| Placing condition | Slump (mm) |
|---|---|
| **Road pavements, heavily vibrated** | **20-40** |
| **Mass concrete, lightly reinforced sections** | **25-50** |
| **Beams, slabs, columns — normal reinforcement** | **50-100** |
| **Heavily reinforced sections; thin walls** | **100-150** |
| **Concrete pumped, or placed by tremie** | **100-150 or more** |

> **The pattern: the more difficult the placing and the more congested the reinforcement, the higher the slump required.**

> **But higher slump is bought with water, and water is bought with strength** — which is the trade-off behind the whole subject.

**Why the slump test survives, given how crude it is:**

| Argument | Note |
|---|---|
| **It needs no power and almost no equipment** | A cone, a rod and a rule |
| **It takes two minutes** | Testable on every load |
| **It detects a CHANGE in the mix immediately** | **Its real value — a sudden slump change means the batching or the aggregate moisture has changed** ← |
| It is universally understood | Every site knows what a slump number means |

> **The third row is the honest case for the test.** As an absolute measure of workability the slump is poor — **it does not measure cohesion, or segregation resistance, or the effort needed to compact.**

> **But as a CONSISTENCY CONTROL on repeated batches of a known mix, it is excellent**, because any change in water content, aggregate moisture or batching shows up at once.

> **So the slump test is a process-control instrument rather than a property measurement**, and using it as the latter is the standard misunderstanding.

**And the reason a wet mix is dangerous, since option (a) describes one:**

> **Excess water does three things at once, all bad:**

| Effect | Consequence |
|---|---|
| **Raises the water/cement ratio** | **Lower strength — the single strongest determinant of concrete strength (ABRAMS' LAW)** |
| **Increases permeability** | **Poorer durability; faster reinforcement corrosion** |
| **Promotes SEGREGATION and BLEEDING** | **Aggregate settles, water rises, and a weak laitance layer forms at the top** |

> **A collapse slump therefore signals a mix that will be weak, permeable and segregated** — and the correct response on site is to reject the load, not to place it and record a large number.

> **The right way to get workability without water is a PLASTICISER or superplasticiser**, which disperses the cement particles and increases the slump at constant water content. **That is the whole reason those admixtures exist.**

examTip.trick: **Options (a), (b) and (c) ARE the three kinds of slump** — collapse, true and shear. Only a TRUE slump (even, symmetrical subsidence) gives a valid measurement.
examTip.trap: **A shear slump means REPEAT the test; if it recurs, the mix lacks cohesion and needs more FINES.** A collapse slump means the slump test is inapplicable — use the compacting factor or flow table instead.
examTip.mnemonic: **The slump test's real value is detecting CHANGE between batches**, not measuring workability absolutely. And get workability from a PLASTICISER, not from water — water costs strength (Abrams' law), durability and cohesion at once.

questions.stem: In brick masonry, the primary purpose of providing a BOND (such as English or Flemish bond) is to:
options: reduce the quantity of mortar required in the wall
make the wall face look attractive and regular
prevent continuous vertical joints, so that a load is distributed across several bricks
allow the wall to be built faster with fewer cut bricks
questions.solution:
**To prevent continuous vertical joints, so that a load is distributed across several bricks.**

**Why a continuous vertical joint is the thing to avoid:**

> **A vertical joint running unbroken through several courses divides the wall into independent, slender columns.**

> **Each such column is only one brick wide, so it is very slender — and a slender masonry column buckles or overturns at a load far below the wall's capacity as a monolith.**

> **Worse, a load applied at the top of one column travels straight down it, with no way of spreading sideways into the neighbouring brickwork.** The wall cannot share the load.

> **A BOND breaks those joints by overlapping the bricks course by course**, so that a load applied at one point spreads through the thickness and along the length of the wall as it descends.

> **That is the structural purpose, and it is why bonding is a requirement rather than a matter of appearance.**

**The overlap that achieves it:**

| Requirement | Value |
|---|---|
| **Minimum LAP** | **One quarter of a brick length** |
| **Achieved by** | **A QUEEN CLOSER (a brick cut lengthwise in half, giving a half-width brick) placed next to the quoin header** |
| **Vertical joints must be broken** | **In EVERY successive course** |

> **The queen closer is the small cut brick whose whole function is to displace the course by a quarter brick and so break the joint** — which is why a bricklayer's first act at a corner is to cut one.

**The two principal bonds:**

| | **ENGLISH bond** | **FLEMISH bond** |
|---|---|---|
| **Arrangement** | **ALTERNATE courses of headers and stretchers** | **Headers and stretchers ALTERNATING in the SAME course** |
| **STRENGTH** | **STRONGER — the best bond for load-bearing work** ← | Slightly weaker |
| **APPEARANCE** | Plainer | **Better looking — a more attractive face** |
| **Cut bricks required** | **Fewer** | **MORE — half bats in every course** |
| **Skill required** | Less | More |
| **Use** | **Structural walls** | **Facing work where appearance matters** |

> **The trade-off is clean: English bond is stronger and cheaper to build; Flemish bond looks better.** So the choice is made on which matters for that wall.

> **Note that Flemish bond needs more cut bricks and more skill, which is why it costs more** — and that fact disposes of option (d), which claims bonding reduces cut bricks. **Bonding REQUIRES cut bricks; it does not save them.**

**Why each distractor is wrong:**

| Option | Note |
|---|---|
| **Reduce mortar** | **Bonding does not change the mortar quantity materially.** The joints are the same thickness and roughly the same total area whatever the pattern ← |
| **Look attractive** | **A real CONSEQUENCE, and the reason Flemish bond is chosen over English for facing work — but not the primary purpose** ← the closest distractor |
| **Prevent continuous vertical joints** | ✓ |
| **Faster with fewer cut bricks** | **Backwards — bonding REQUIRES cut bricks (closers and bats) and takes MORE skill and time than stacking** |

> **Option (b) deserves a careful answer because appearance genuinely matters and genuinely influences the choice of bond.** But the question asks for the PRIMARY purpose: **an unbonded stack-bonded wall is both ugly and structurally unsound, and it is the second that makes bonding compulsory.**

> **Stack bond — bricks stacked directly above one another with continuous vertical joints — does exist**, and it is used only as a non-structural facing over a backing wall, or with reinforcement in the joints. **Its existence proves the point: remove the structural requirement and the bond can be dispensed with.**

**The other bonds worth naming:**

| Bond | Note |
|---|---|
| **Header bond** | **All headers; used for CURVED walls and for half-brick-thick footings** |
| **Stretcher bond** | **All stretchers; used for HALF-BRICK partition walls and for the outer skin of a cavity wall** |
| **Rat-trap bond** | **Bricks laid on edge, forming cavities — saves about 25 % of bricks and improves insulation** |
| **Garden wall bond** | Three stretchers to one header; economical for boundary walls |
| **Raking, herringbone, zigzag** | Decorative and for thick walls |
| **Stack bond** | **NO overlap — non-structural facing only** |

> **RAT-TRAP bond is worth knowing in the Nepali and Indian context** because it is a genuine economy: **laying bricks on edge produces a 230 mm wall using about a quarter fewer bricks, with an internal cavity that improves thermal performance.**

> **Its limitation is that the cavities must be closed at openings, at lintel bearings and at the top of the wall**, and that it needs careful workmanship — but where bricks are the dominant cost, it repays that care.

**And the rules that accompany bonding:**

| Rule | Reason |
|---|---|
| **Bricks must be SOAKED before laying** | **A dry brick sucks water out of the mortar, which then does not hydrate and never gains strength** ← |
| **Joint thickness 10 mm nominal** | Thicker joints reduce wall strength |
| **Raise no more than 1 m of height per day** | Green mortar cannot carry the weight above it |
| **Cure for 7-10 days** | Mortar is cement and needs curing like any other |
| **Vertical joints must be fully filled** | An unfilled perpend is a hole in the wall |

> **The soaking rule is the one most often ignored and most consequential.** A wall laid with dry bricks has mortar that was dewatered before it could hydrate — **and no amount of subsequent curing recovers it, because the cement never had the water when it needed it.**

examTip.trick: **A continuous vertical joint divides the wall into independent slender columns that cannot share load.** A bond breaks those joints so a point load spreads through the wall as it descends.
examTip.trap: **Option (d) is backwards — bonding REQUIRES cut bricks (closers and bats) and more skill.** Flemish bond needs MORE cut bricks than English, which is why it costs more.
examTip.mnemonic: **English bond is STRONGER and cheaper; Flemish LOOKS BETTER and needs more cut bricks.** Minimum lap is a QUARTER brick, achieved with a queen closer. And **soak bricks before laying**, or the mortar is dewatered before it can hydrate.

questions.stem: In levelling, the height of instrument (HI) is:
options: the height of the telescope above the ground at the instrument station
the reduced level of the line of collimation
the difference between a backsight and a foresight
the reduced level of the point on which the staff is held
questions.solution:
**The reduced level of the line of collimation.**

**The definition and why it is not what the name suggests:**

> **HEIGHT OF INSTRUMENT (also called the height of collimation, or the plane of collimation) is the REDUCED LEVEL OF THE LINE OF SIGHT of the levelled telescope.**

> **It is an ELEVATION above the datum — not a height above the ground.**

> **HI = RL of the point + Staff reading on that point**

> **And then: RL of any other point = HI − staff reading there.**

> **So HI is a working elevation: add a staff reading to get up to the line of sight, subtract one to come back down to the ground.**

**Why option (a) is the designed trap:**

> **"Height of instrument" sounds exactly like the height of the telescope above the ground at the tripod** — which is about 1.4 m and has nothing to do with the calculation.

> **That quantity has a use in other surveying work (in tacheometry and in total-station work it is the instrument height above the station mark), but in LEVELLING the term means the collimation elevation.**

> **So the trap is a genuine ambiguity in the terminology rather than a manufactured one**, and the safe practice is to call it the **HEIGHT OF COLLIMATION** — which is unambiguous and is why many texts prefer it.

**The two methods of reducing levels, since HI belongs to one of them:**

| | **HEIGHT OF COLLIMATION method** | **RISE AND FALL method** |
|---|---|---|
| **Computes** | **HI, then RL = HI − staff reading** | **The RISE or FALL between consecutive points** |
| **Speed** | **FASTER — fewer computations** | Slower |
| **Checks available** | **ΣBS − ΣFS = last RL − first RL** | **ΣBS − ΣFS = ΣRise − ΣFall = last RL − first RL** |
| **Checks the INTERMEDIATE sights?** | **NO — an error in an intermediate sight is UNDETECTED** ← | **YES — every reading enters the check** |
| **Suits** | Long sections with many intermediate sights | **Work requiring accuracy and full checking** |

> **That difference in checking is the decisive one and is the reason the rise-and-fall method survives despite being slower.**

> **In the collimation method, an intermediate sight enters only the RL of its own point** — so if it is misread, that one RL is wrong and NOTHING in the arithmetic reveals it.

> **In the rise-and-fall method every reading is differenced against its neighbour, so every reading appears in the ΣRise − ΣFall check.**

> **So: use the collimation method for speed where intermediate sights are numerous and individually unimportant (a profile), and the rise-and-fall method where each point matters.** That is a real engineering choice, not a preference.

**The terminology of levelling, gathered, since the options are drawn from it:**

| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **BENCH MARK (BM)** | **A point of KNOWN reduced level** |
| **BACKSIGHT (BS)** | **The FIRST reading after setting up — always on a point of known RL** |
| **FORESIGHT (FS)** | **The LAST reading before moving the instrument** |
| **INTERMEDIATE SIGHT (IS)** | **Any reading between the BS and the FS from the same setup** |
| **CHANGE POINT (CP)** | **A point on which both an FS and the next BS are taken — where the instrument moves** |
| **HEIGHT OF INSTRUMENT / COLLIMATION (HI)** | **RL of the line of sight** ← |
| **REDUCED LEVEL (RL)** | **Elevation of a point above the datum** |

> **Option (c) — the difference between a backsight and a foresight — is the RISE or FALL**, which belongs to the other method. **And option (d) is the REDUCED LEVEL of the staff point, which is what HI is used to compute rather than what it is.**

> **So all three distractors are real quantities in the same calculation**, which makes this a definition question rather than a recall one.

**The arithmetic checks, since they are what make levelling reliable:**

> **ΣBS − ΣFS = last RL − first RL**

> **And in the rise-and-fall method additionally: ΣBS − ΣFS = ΣRise − ΣFall**

> **These checks verify the ARITHMETIC only.** They do not detect a misread staff, a wrongly booked reading, or an instrument out of adjustment — **a point regularly misunderstood.**

> **To detect those, the levelling must CLOSE: run back to the starting bench mark, or forward to another bench mark of known level.**

| Closure | Permissible error |
|---|---|
| **Ordinary levelling** | **±24√K mm, K in kilometres** |
| **Precise levelling** | **±12√K mm** |
| Rough levelling | ±100√K mm |

> **The √K form is the signature of RANDOM error accumulation** — errors partly cancel, so the total grows as the square root of the distance rather than in proportion to it.

**And the field practice that removes the largest systematic error:**

> **BALANCE the backsight and foresight distances at every setup.**

> **If BS and FS distances are equal, a COLLIMATION ERROR (the line of sight not truly horizontal) affects both readings equally and CANCELS in the difference.**

> **So does the effect of the earth's CURVATURE and of atmospheric REFRACTION.**

> **Three systematic errors eliminated by one simple field discipline**, which is why balancing sight distances is the first rule of good levelling — and why it is worth more than any amount of careful arithmetic afterwards.

examTip.trick: **HI is an ELEVATION — the RL of the line of sight — not a height above the ground.** HI = RL + staff reading; then RL elsewhere = HI − staff reading.
examTip.trap: **Option (a) is a genuine terminological ambiguity**, since "height of instrument" does mean the tripod height in other survey work. Call it the HEIGHT OF COLLIMATION and the ambiguity disappears.
examTip.mnemonic: **The collimation method does NOT check intermediate sights; rise-and-fall does** — which is why the slower method survives. And **balance BS and FS distances**: one discipline cancels collimation error, curvature and refraction together.

questions.stem: In the preparation of a detailed estimate, the PLINTH AREA of a building is measured:
options: as the carpet area plus the area of the walls only
excluding the thickness of the external walls
as the sum of the floor areas of all habitable rooms only
as the built-up area at floor level, including the thickness of the external walls
questions.solution:
**The built-up area at floor level, including the thickness of the external walls.**

**The three areas, which must be kept apart:**

| Area | Definition | Relative size |
|---|---|---|
| **PLINTH area (built-up area)** | **The built-up area measured at floor level, INCLUDING the external wall thickness** | **LARGEST** ← |
| **CARPET area (usable / lettable area)** | **The NET usable floor area — plinth area LESS walls, columns, stairs, lifts, verandahs, porches, corridors** | **SMALLEST** |
| **FLOOR area** | **Plinth area less the area of the walls** | Intermediate |

> **The relation: PLINTH > FLOOR > CARPET**, and the differences are the wall areas and the non-usable spaces respectively.

> **Carpet area is typically 50 to 70 per cent of plinth area**, and the gap is large enough to matter commercially — **which is why property is sold on one basis and valued on another, and why the two are often deliberately confused in marketing.**

**What is and is not included in plinth area:**

| Included | Excluded |
|---|---|
| **All floor area at floor level** | **Open courtyards and open areas** |
| **THICKNESS of external walls** | **Cornices, cantilevered chajjas** |
| **Internal walls, columns, pillars** | **Open balconies (or counted at 50 %)** |
| **Staircase, lift well, shafts** | **Areas of walls common with an adjoining building (half counted)** |
| **Verandahs, porches (as specified)** | Loft, mumty (counted separately or at a fraction) |

> **The wall-thickness inclusion is the whole point of the question, and it is what makes plinth area the largest of the three.**

> **Option (b) — excluding external wall thickness — is the exact negation of the definition, and it is the designed trap** because it sounds like a reasonable convention. **It is not the convention.**

**Why plinth area is the basis for the PLINTH AREA RATE method of estimating:**

> **A preliminary (approximate) estimate is often made as:**

> **Cost = PLINTH AREA × RATE PER UNIT AREA**

> **The rate is derived from recently completed comparable buildings, and it must correspond to the same specification, the same locality and the same period.**

| Use | Note |
|---|---|
| **Preliminary / approximate estimate** | **At the concept stage, before drawings exist** |
| **Administrative approval** | A figure to seek sanction against |
| **Comparing design options quickly** | Two schemes of different area |
| Checking a detailed estimate | A sanity check on the total |

> **The method's value is speed: an area and a rate give a cost in minutes**, long before there is anything to measure in detail.

> **Its limitation is that the RATE carries every assumption**: a building with more storeys, deeper foundations, better finishes, a difficult site or a different structural system will not match the comparable. **So the rate must be chosen with judgement, and adjusted — which is where the skill lies.**

**The types of estimate, since plinth area belongs to one of them:**

| Estimate | Basis | Accuracy |
|---|---|---|
| **PLINTH AREA estimate** | **Area × rate** | **±15-25 %** ← |
| **CUBE RATE estimate** | **Volume (plinth area × height) × rate — better where storey heights vary** | ±15-20 % |
| **Approximate quantity method** | Running metres of walls, etc. × composite rates | ±10 % |
| **DETAILED estimate** | **Every item measured from drawings, priced by RATE ANALYSIS** | **±5 %** |
| **Revised estimate** | When the detailed estimate is exceeded by more than 5 % | — |
| **Supplementary estimate** | For additional work not originally covered | — |
| Annual repair / maintenance estimate | For upkeep | — |

> **The CUBE RATE method is worth noting as the refinement of the plinth-area method**: it multiplies by height as well as area, **so it distinguishes a building with 4 m storeys from one with 2.8 m storeys — which the plinth area rate cannot.**

> **And the REVISED estimate has a precise trigger — a 5 per cent excess** — which is a procedural fact rather than a technical one but appears in examinations.

**How measurement is standardised, since estimating depends on it:**

> **IS 1200 — the Method of Measurement of Building and Civil Engineering Works** — specifies exactly how each item is measured, in many parts.

| Item | Measured as |
|---|---|
| **Earthwork, concrete, masonry** | **CUBIC metres (volume)** |
| **Plastering, painting, flooring, formwork** | **SQUARE metres (area)** |
| **Reinforcement, structural steel** | **Kilograms or QUINTALS (weight)** |
| **Skirting, cornice, kerb, pipe** | **RUNNING metres (length)** |
| **Doors, windows, fittings** | **NUMBER** |

> **The reason a standard method exists at all is that a bill of quantities is a CONTRACT DOCUMENT.** Two parties must be able to measure the same work and arrive at the same quantity — **otherwise every payment is a dispute.**

> **Which is also why deductions are specified precisely: whether an opening under a stated size is deducted from plasterwork, for instance, is not a matter of judgement but of the code** — and it is where a great many small estimating errors arise.

examTip.trick: **PLINTH > FLOOR > CARPET.** Plinth area INCLUDES external wall thickness; floor area excludes walls; carpet area excludes walls, stairs, lifts and corridors too — typically only 50-70 % of plinth.
examTip.trap: **Option (b) is the exact negation of the definition** and sounds like a reasonable convention. It is not — the wall thickness is precisely what plinth area includes.
examTip.mnemonic: **Cost = plinth area × rate** gives a ±15-25 % preliminary estimate in minutes, but the RATE carries every assumption. The **CUBE RATE method** refines it by including height, distinguishing tall storeys from short ones.

questions.stem: The total stress at a depth of 6 m in a saturated soil of unit weight 19 kN/m³ is 114 kN/m². If the water table is at the ground surface, the effective vertical stress at that depth is:
questions.solution:
**55.1 kN/m².**

**The principle of effective stress:**

> **σ′ = σ − u**

**Step 1 — the total stress (given, and confirmed):**

> **σ = γ_sat × z = 19 × 6 = 114 kN/m²** ✓ as stated.

**Step 2 — the pore water pressure.**

> **With the water table AT THE GROUND SURFACE, the pore pressure is hydrostatic from the surface down:**

> **u = γ_w × z = 9.81 × 6 = 58.86 kN/m²**

**Step 3 — the effective stress:**

> **σ′ = 114 − 58.86 = 55.14 ≈ 55.1 kN/m²** ✓

> **Equivalently and more directly: σ′ = γ′ z, with the SUBMERGED (buoyant) unit weight γ′ = γ_sat − γ_w = 19 − 9.81 = 9.19 kN/m³.**

> **σ′ = 9.19 × 6 = 55.14 kN/m²** ✓ — the same answer in one step.

> **The submerged-unit-weight route is quicker and less error-prone**, and it is the one to prefer when the water table is at the surface.

**Why each distractor is wrong — and every one is a real quantity in the problem:**

| Option | What it actually is |
|---|---|
| **114.0** | **The TOTAL stress — the pore pressure not subtracted at all** ← |
| **55.1** | ✓ **The effective stress** |
| **58.9** | **The PORE WATER PRESSURE, 9.81 × 6 — reported instead of the effective stress** ← the interesting trap |
| **78.6** | Roughly 13.1 × 6; no clean derivation |

> **Options (a) and (c) are the two terms of the subtraction, offered as answers.** A candidate who computes one of them and stops finds a matching option — **which is why the question is a test of reading as much as of method.**

> **Option (c) 58.9 is the better-made trap, because computing the pore pressure feels like the "hard" step** and it is tempting to treat it as the answer once found.

**Why effective stress matters — it is the single most important idea in soil mechanics:**

> **Terzaghi's principle: the STRENGTH and the DEFORMATION of a soil are governed by the EFFECTIVE stress, not the total stress.**

> **The reason is physical: shear is resisted at the CONTACTS BETWEEN GRAINS, and only the effective stress presses the grains together.**

> **Water in the pores carries part of the total load, and water cannot resist shear at all.** So the water's share does nothing for the soil's strength.

> **Mohr-Coulomb, correctly written, is therefore in effective stress: τ = c′ + σ′ tan φ′.**

**The consequences, which are why the principle is so central:**

| Change | Effect on σ′ | Effect on strength |
|---|---|---|
| **Water table RISES** | **σ′ FALLS** | **Strength FALLS** ← |
| **Water table falls (dewatering)** | **σ′ RISES** | Strength rises; but SETTLEMENT occurs |
| **Surcharge added** | σ′ rises (after consolidation) | Strength rises |
| **Excavation (unloading)** | σ′ falls | Strength falls with time |
| **Rapid loading of clay** | **u rises, so σ′ barely changes at first** | **No immediate strength gain** |

> **The first row explains a great deal of what goes wrong in geotechnical engineering.** A slope stable through the dry season fails after prolonged rain — **not because the rain added weight, but because it raised the water table and cut the effective stress.**

> **In this problem, if the water table were LOWERED to 6 m depth, the effective stress at 6 m would rise from 55.1 to about 114 kN/m² (using the bulk unit weight above the water table)** — roughly DOUBLE. **The soil's strength would roughly double with it.**

> **That is the magnitude of the water table's influence, and it is why drainage is the most powerful and cheapest stabilisation measure available.**

**And the counter-intuitive consequence for settlement:**

> **Dewatering to raise effective stress also causes CONSOLIDATION SETTLEMENT of the whole soil profile** — which is why pumping groundwater under a city subsides it, and why dewatering an excavation can damage neighbouring buildings.

> **So lowering the water table strengthens the soil and settles it at the same time**, and both effects must be considered. **The strength gain is often wanted and the settlement almost never is.**

**The unit weights to keep apart, since choosing the wrong one is the other error in this class of problem:**

| Unit weight | Symbol | Use |
|---|---|---|
| **BULK (moist)** | **γ** | **Total stress ABOVE the water table** |
| **SATURATED** | **γ_sat** | **Total stress BELOW the water table** |
| **SUBMERGED (buoyant)** | **γ′ = γ_sat − γ_w** | **EFFECTIVE stress below the water table, directly** ← |
| **DRY** | **γ_d** | Compaction control; γ_d = γ/(1+w) |

> **γ′ = γ_sat − γ_w is the relation that makes this problem a one-liner**, and it is worth having as a reflex: **below the water table, effective stress accumulates at the submerged unit weight.**

> **For most soils γ′ is around 9 to 11 kN/m³ — roughly HALF the saturated value** — which is a useful order-of-magnitude check on any effective-stress calculation.

examTip.trick: **Use the submerged unit weight and it is one step: γ′ = 19 − 9.81 = 9.19 kN/m³, so σ′ = 9.19 × 6 = 55.1 kN/m².**
examTip.trap: **Options (a) and (c) are the two TERMS of the subtraction** — 114 is the total stress and 58.9 the pore pressure. Computing the pore pressure feels like the hard step, which makes it tempting to report.
examTip.mnemonic: **Only effective stress presses grains together, and water cannot resist shear** — so strength depends on σ′ alone. A slope fails after rain because the WATER TABLE ROSE and cut σ′, not because the rain added weight.

questions.stem: In the stability analysis of a slope, the factor of safety is defined as the ratio of:
options: the height of the slope to the critical height
the driving moment to the resisting moment
the available shear strength to the shear stress required for equilibrium
the cohesion of the soil to the total normal stress on the failure surface
questions.solution:
**The available shear strength to the shear stress required for equilibrium.**

**The definition:**

> **FOS = (shear strength AVAILABLE along the failure surface) ÷ (shear stress REQUIRED to maintain equilibrium)**

> **Equivalently, in moment terms for a circular failure: FOS = (RESISTING moment) ÷ (DRIVING moment).**

> **The essential structure is CAPACITY over DEMAND — what the soil can supply, divided by what equilibrium asks of it.**

| FOS | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **> 1** | **Stable — the soil can supply more than is needed** |
| **= 1** | **On the point of failure — the limiting equilibrium condition** |
| **< 1** | **Unstable — it has already failed, or will** |

**Why option (b) is the designed trap, and it is a very good one:**

> **Option (b) says DRIVING over RESISTING — the ratio the RIGHT WAY UP but INVERTED.**

> **That would make a factor of safety of 0.5 mean a safe slope and 2.0 an unstable one**, which is backwards.

> **The check is immediate and needs no recall: a factor of SAFETY must be GREATER than 1 for a safe structure.** So the numerator must be the CAPACITY (resistance, strength) and the denominator the DEMAND.

> **Any candidate expression can be tested that way, and it is the reliable defence against inverted-ratio distractors generally.**

**Why options (a) and (d) are wrong:**

> **Option (a) — height to critical height — is INVERTED and misconceived.** The **CRITICAL HEIGHT H_c** is the maximum height at which a slope of given soil and angle is just stable, so **a safety measure would be H_c/H, not H/H_c.**

> **And even inverted it is a stability NUMBER rather than a factor of safety on strength** — a different and less general concept, since it applies only to particular idealised geometries.

> **Option (d) — cohesion to total normal stress — mixes incompatible quantities.** Cohesion is only PART of the shear strength (the other part is frictional), and TOTAL normal stress is the wrong stress: **strength depends on EFFECTIVE normal stress.** The ratio has no standing.

**How the FOS is actually computed — the methods:**

| Method | Suits | Note |
|---|---|---|
| **INFINITE SLOPE analysis** | **A long uniform slope with failure parallel to the surface** | **FOS = tan φ′/tan β for a cohesionless soil, dry** |
| **φ = 0 (Swedish circle) analysis** | **SATURATED CLAY, undrained** | **Total stress; a circular arc; moments about the centre** |
| **METHOD OF SLICES (Fellenius / Swedish)** | **Any soil; c-φ soils** | **Simple, and CONSERVATIVE — it ignores inter-slice forces** |
| **BISHOP'S simplified method** | Any soil | **More accurate; includes inter-slice normal forces; needs iteration** |
| **Friction circle method** | Homogeneous c-φ soil | Graphical |
| **Taylor's stability number** | Homogeneous soil, simple geometry | **A chart solution — quick preliminary answer** |

> **The METHOD OF SLICES is the workhorse**, and its logic is worth knowing: **the failure mass is divided into vertical slices, and for each slice the weight, the normal force and the mobilised shear are resolved.**

> **Fellenius' version ignores the forces between slices, which makes it simple and CONSERVATIVE — it typically underestimates the FOS by 5 to 20 per cent.**

> **Bishop's method includes the inter-slice normal forces and is substantially more accurate, at the cost of requiring iteration** — which is why it became standard once computers were available.

**The values required in practice:**

| Situation | Minimum FOS |
|---|---|
| **Permanent slope, well-investigated soil** | **1.5** |
| **Permanent slope, uncertain soil data** | **2.0 or more** |
| **Temporary works (short-term excavation)** | **1.2-1.3** |
| **Earth dam, steady seepage** | **1.5** |
| **Earth dam, SUDDEN DRAWDOWN** | **1.2-1.3** |
| **Seismic loading** | **1.1-1.2** |

> **The lower values for temporary and seismic cases are deliberate: the exposure is brief, and the consequences of the assumed event are already extreme.** A factor of 1.5 against an earthquake would give an uneconomically massive structure.

**And the case that dominates practice, since it is where slopes actually fail:**

> **A slope's FOS is not a fixed number — it changes with the WATER TABLE.**

> **Raising the water table cuts the EFFECTIVE stress on the failure surface, which cuts the frictional part of the strength, which cuts the FOS.**

> **For a typical slope, full saturation can HALVE the factor of safety.**

> **Which is why:**

| Fact | Consequence |
|---|---|
| **Most slope failures occur DURING or just after heavy rain** | Not from added weight but from raised pore pressure |
| **DRAINAGE is the most cost-effective stabilisation measure** | **Surface drains, sub-surface drains, horizontal drains into the slope** ← |
| A slope stable for years can fail in one monsoon | Because the water table reached a level it had not before |

> **So the honest summary is that a slope-stability calculation is largely a calculation about WATER**, and the soil parameters matter less than the pore pressure assumption. **Which is why a slope-stability report without a stated groundwater condition is not a report at all.**

examTip.trick: **FOS is CAPACITY over DEMAND** — available shear strength divided by the shear stress equilibrium requires. Equivalently resisting moment over driving moment.
examTip.trap: **Option (b) is the ratio INVERTED.** Test any candidate expression: a factor of SAFETY must EXCEED 1 for a safe slope, so the capacity must be on top. That check needs no recall and defeats every inverted-ratio distractor.
examTip.mnemonic: **Full saturation can HALVE a slope's FOS**, because raised pore pressure cuts the effective stress and so the frictional strength. Which is why failures happen in the monsoon and why DRAINAGE is the cheapest stabilisation.

questions.stem: A cantilever retaining wall retains dry sand of unit weight 18 kN/m³ and angle of internal friction 30° to a height of 5 m. The total active thrust per metre run of wall is:
questions.solution:
**75 kN per metre run.**

**Step 1 — Rankine's coefficient of active earth pressure:**

> **K_a = (1 − sin φ)/(1 + sin φ)**

> **For φ = 30°:  K_a = (1 − 0.5)/(1 + 0.5) = 0.5/1.5 = 1/3**

> **K_a = 1/3 for φ = 30° is worth committing to memory** — it is the standard textbook sand and it recurs constantly.

**Step 2 — the total active thrust:**

> **P_a = ½ K_a γ H²**

> **= ½ × (1/3) × 18 × 5²**

> **= ½ × (1/3) × 18 × 25**

> **= ½ × 6 × 25**

> **= 75 kN per metre run** ✓

> **The arithmetic is clean because (1/3) × 18 = 6 exactly.**

**Where the formula comes from — and it is worth seeing, because it explains the ½:**

> **The active pressure at any depth z is  p_a = K_a γ z** — LINEAR in depth, so the pressure diagram is a TRIANGLE.

> **The total thrust is the AREA of that triangle: ½ × (base) × (height) = ½ × (K_a γ H) × H = ½ K_a γ H².** ✓

> **And the resultant acts at the triangle's CENTROID, which is H/3 ABOVE THE BASE** — that is the second fact the calculation always needs.

**Why each distractor is wrong — every one is a real intermediate:**

| Option | What it is |
|---|---|
| **225 kN** | **½γH² = ½ × 18 × 25 — K_a OMITTED entirely** ← |
| **112.5 kN** | Half of 225 — a doubled or halved slip |
| **45 kN** | **0.6 × the answer — no clean derivation, but a plausible-looking near value** |
| **75 kN** | ✓ |

> **Option (a) 225 kN is the designed trap: it is the answer with the earth pressure coefficient left out**, which is the single commonest error in retaining wall problems.

> **A magnitude check catches it: the active thrust must be a FRACTION of the soil's own weight pressure, because K_a < 1.** With K_a = 1/3, the answer must be one third of 225 — **and noticing that 225 is exactly three times an option present in the list is itself a warning.**

**The three earth pressure states, since choosing the wrong K is the other error:**

| State | Coefficient | For φ = 30° | When it applies |
|---|---|---|---|
| **ACTIVE** | **K_a = (1−sinφ)/(1+sinφ)** | **0.333** | **The wall MOVES AWAY from the soil — the soil pushes it** ← |
| **AT REST** | **K₀ ≈ 1 − sin φ** | **0.500** | **NO movement — a rigid, restrained wall (a basement wall)** |
| **PASSIVE** | **K_p = (1+sinφ)/(1−sinφ)** | **3.000** | **The wall PUSHES INTO the soil — the soil resists** |

> **Note K_p = 1/K_a, so the ratio K_p/K_a = 9 for φ = 30°** — a NINEFOLD difference between the active and passive pressures on the same soil.

> **That factor of nine is the most consequential number in retaining wall design**, and the reason is the movement required:

| State | Wall movement needed to develop it |
|---|---|
| **ACTIVE** | **Very small — about 0.1-0.5 % of the wall height** |
| **PASSIVE** | **LARGE — 2-5 % of the height, sometimes more** ← |

> **So active pressure develops almost immediately and can be relied on; PASSIVE resistance requires movement that a real structure may not be permitted to make.**

> **Which is why passive resistance is usually taken with a large factor of safety or discounted altogether** — a wall that must not move cannot mobilise it, and a wall that has moved enough to mobilise it has probably already failed in service terms.

> **And the at-rest case is the one most often overlooked: a basement wall braced by the floors CANNOT move, so it sees K₀ ≈ 0.5, not K_a = 0.33 — fifty per cent more pressure than an active design would give.** Designing a restrained wall for active pressure is a real and serious error.

**The additions to the basic triangle that a real wall must consider:**

| Effect | Treatment |
|---|---|
| **SURCHARGE q on the backfill** | **Adds a RECTANGULAR block of K_a·q over the full height, resultant at H/2** ← |
| **WATER in the backfill** | **Adds a hydrostatic triangle of FULL γ_w — and uses γ′ for the soil. Very large increase** |
| **Cohesive backfill** | Reduces active pressure by 2c√K_a, but tension cracks and long-term softening make this unreliable |
| **Sloping backfill** | Modified K_a (Coulomb or Rankine with slope) |
| **Seismic** | Mononobe-Okabe increase |

> **The WATER row is the one that destroys walls.** A drained granular backfill gives the 75 kN computed here; **the same wall with a saturated backfill sees roughly 2 to 3 times that thrust**, because the water contributes its full hydrostatic pressure with no K_a reduction at all.

> **Which is why WEEP HOLES and a granular drainage layer behind the wall are not optional details but the principal structural measure** — and why a blocked weep hole is a structural defect rather than a maintenance nuisance.

> **The corresponding site error is placing an impermeable clay backfill against a wall designed for drained sand**, which produces both the water pressure and, in an expansive clay, swelling pressure on top of it.

examTip.trick: **K_a = (1−sinφ)/(1+sinφ) = 1/3 for φ = 30°, then P_a = ½K_aγH² = ½ × (1/3) × 18 × 25 = 75 kN/m.** Resultant acts at H/3 above the base.
examTip.trap: **Option (a) 225 kN is the answer with K_a OMITTED** — the commonest error in retaining wall problems. Check the magnitude: since K_a < 1, the thrust must be a FRACTION of ½γH².
examTip.mnemonic: **K_p/K_a = 9 for φ = 30°**, but passive needs 2-5 % wall movement against active's 0.1-0.5 % — so passive is discounted. And a RESTRAINED basement wall sees K₀ ≈ 0.5, not K_a: designing it for active pressure is a serious error.

questions.stem: A pile driven into soft clay and deriving most of its capacity from the resistance along its shaft is called:
questions.solution:
**A friction pile.**

**The two ways a pile carries load:**

> **Total capacity  Q_u = Q_s + Q_p** — skin friction plus end bearing.

| Pile type | Carries its load by | Suits |
|---|---|---|
| **FRICTION (floating) pile** | **SKIN FRICTION (adhesion) along the SHAFT** | **A deep deposit of soft or medium soil with NO firm stratum within reach** ← |
| **END-BEARING (point) pile** | **BEARING at the TIP, on rock or a dense stratum** | **A firm layer at a practicable depth** |

> **The classification is by which mechanism DOMINATES, not by which is present — every pile has both.**

> **A friction pile is sometimes called a FLOATING pile**, which is a helpful name: **it does not reach anything firm; it hangs in the soil, supported along its length.**

**Why soft clay produces friction piles specifically:**

> **Soft clay deposits are often very deep** — a filled lake basin or a deltaic deposit may be tens or hundreds of metres thick.

> **There is no firm stratum to reach**, so end bearing is not available at any practicable depth.

> **But clay provides ADHESION along the shaft**, and a long pile has a great deal of shaft area.

> **So the capacity is accumulated along the length rather than concentrated at the point** — which is the definition of a friction pile.

> **The Kathmandu Valley, with its deep soft lacustrine deposits, is exactly such a setting.**

**The capacity formulae, since they show where each term comes from:**

| Component | For CLAY | For SAND |
|---|---|---|
| **SKIN FRICTION Q_s** | **α · c_u · A_s**, α the adhesion factor (0.4-1.0) | **K · σ′_v · tan δ · A_s** |
| **END BEARING Q_p** | **N_c · c_u · A_p, with N_c ≈ 9** | **σ′_v · N_q · A_p** |

> **In soft clay, A_s (the shaft area) is large and A_p (the tip area) is small — often by a factor of a hundred or more for a slender pile.** So even a modest unit friction, applied over a large area, dominates a high unit end bearing applied over a small one.

> **That area ratio is the arithmetic reason friction dominates in a long pile**, and it is worth seeing explicitly: **a 20 m long, 400 mm diameter pile has a shaft area of 25 m² and a tip area of 0.126 m² — a ratio of 200.**

**Why the distractors are wrong — and each names a real pile:**

| Option | What it actually is |
|---|---|
| **END-BEARING pile** | **Carries load at the TIP on a firm stratum — the opposite mechanism** ← |
| **FRICTION pile** | ✓ |
| **BATTER (raker) pile** | **A pile driven at an INCLINE, to resist LATERAL loads and thrusts — classified by ORIENTATION, not by load transfer** ← |
| **SHEET pile** | **A thin interlocking section forming a continuous WALL to retain soil or exclude water — not a load-bearing pile at all** |

> **Options (c) and (d) are the instructive ones, because they are classified on entirely different bases.**

> **A BATTER pile is described by its inclination**; it may itself be a friction or an end-bearing pile. **The categories are independent.**

> **A SHEET pile serves a different function altogether — retention, not support** — and is a wall rather than a column.

> **So the four options are drawn from three different classification schemes**, which is what makes the question test understanding rather than vocabulary.

**The full classification of piles, for orientation:**

| By LOAD TRANSFER | By MATERIAL | By INSTALLATION | By FUNCTION |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Friction (floating)** | Timber | **DRIVEN (displacement)** | **Bearing** |
| **End-bearing** | **Concrete (precast or cast-in-situ)** | **BORED (replacement)** | **Tension / anchor** |
| Combined | Steel | Driven cast-in-situ | **Batter — lateral load** |
| **Tension (uplift)** | Composite | Jacked, screwed | **Sheet — retention** |
| Compaction | | | Fender, dolphin |

> **The DRIVEN versus BORED distinction has a large practical consequence:**

| | **DRIVEN (displacement)** | **BORED (replacement)** |
|---|---|---|
| **Effect on surrounding soil** | **DISPLACES and DENSIFIES it — often increasing capacity** | **REMOVES it — may LOOSEN or relax the surrounding soil** |
| **In loose sand** | **Beneficial — compacts the sand** | Less effective |
| **Noise and vibration** | **SEVERE — often prohibited in urban areas** ← | Low |
| **Suits soft clay?** | **Yes, but causes remoulding and heave** | Yes |
| Length verification | By driving records | By inspection of the bore |

> **The noise and vibration objection is why bored piles dominate urban work despite driven piles' advantages in sand**, and it is a constraint imposed from outside engineering.

**And the phenomenon particular to friction piles in clay, worth knowing:**

> **Driving a pile into soft clay REMOULDS the clay around it, destroying its structure and temporarily reducing its strength.**

> **The clay then RECOVERS — partly by thixotropy (regaining strength at constant water content) and partly by reconsolidation as the driving-induced pore pressures dissipate.**

> **So a driven friction pile in clay GAINS CAPACITY over weeks or months after driving** — the phenomenon called **SET-UP** or **freeze**, and the gain can be a factor of two or more.

> **Which is why a pile load test performed the day after driving understates the capacity badly**, and why codes require a waiting period before testing. **Testing too early is a real and expensive error: it can condemn a perfectly adequate pile.**

examTip.trick: **Q_u = Q_s + Q_p, and the classification names whichever DOMINATES.** A deep soft clay offers no firm stratum, so capacity accumulates along the shaft — a friction (floating) pile.
examTip.trap: **Options (c) and (d) come from DIFFERENT classification schemes** — batter describes ORIENTATION (and may itself be a friction pile), sheet pile describes a retaining WALL. Three schemes in four options.
examTip.mnemonic: **A 20 m × 400 mm pile has 25 m² of shaft against 0.126 m² of tip — a ratio of 200**, which is the arithmetic reason friction dominates. And driven piles in clay **GAIN capacity for weeks (set-up)**, so testing too early condemns a good pile.

questions.stem: Bernoulli's equation, in the form p/γ + V²/2g + z = constant, is valid for:
options: any real fluid, whether or not it is viscous
unsteady, compressible flow along any path
steady, incompressible, non-viscous flow along a streamline
flow in which energy is added by a pump between the two sections
questions.solution:
**Steady, incompressible, non-viscous flow along a streamline.**

**The assumptions the equation rests on:**

| Assumption | Why it is needed |
|---|---|
| **STEADY flow** | **The derivation integrates along a streamline at one instant; unsteady flow adds a local acceleration term** |
| **INCOMPRESSIBLE** | **ρ must be constant to integrate dp/ρ to p/ρ** |
| **NON-VISCOUS (inviscid)** | **Viscosity dissipates energy, so the total head would not be constant** ← |
| **ALONG A STREAMLINE** | **The derivation follows a fluid particle; two points on different streamlines need irrotational flow as well** |
| No energy added or removed | No pump or turbine between the sections |

> **All five must hold for the equation in that form, and each of the wrong options violates one of them** — which makes this a clean test of whether the assumptions are known rather than the formula.

**The three terms and what they are:**

> **p/γ + V²/2g + z = constant** — every term has the dimension of LENGTH, which is why they are called heads.

| Term | Name | Physical meaning |
|---|---|---|
| **p/γ** | **PRESSURE head** | Energy per unit weight from pressure |
| **V²/2g** | **VELOCITY (kinetic) head** | Energy per unit weight from motion |
| **z** | **DATUM (potential) head** | Energy per unit weight from elevation |
| **Sum** | **TOTAL head** | **Constant along a streamline, for the ideal case** |

> **Bernoulli's equation is CONSERVATION OF ENERGY per unit weight**, and reading it that way makes the assumptions intelligible: **anything that adds, removes or dissipates energy breaks it.**

**Why each distractor fails, and each names a real extension:**

> **Option (a) — any real fluid, viscous or not — fails on the viscosity assumption.** A real fluid loses energy to friction, so:

> **p₁/γ + V₁²/2g + z₁ = p₂/γ + V₂²/2g + z₂ + h_L**

> **The h_L term is the head LOST between the sections**, and it is what turns Bernoulli's equation into the practical energy equation. **Every pipe-flow calculation uses that extended form.**

> **Option (b) — unsteady, compressible flow — fails on two assumptions at once.** Both have their own extensions: **an unsteady term ∂V/∂t appears for unsteady flow, and for compressible flow the pressure term becomes ∫dp/ρ, which requires a stated relation between p and ρ.**

> **Option (d) — energy added by a pump — fails on the last assumption, and its extension is the one used in every pumping calculation:**

> **p₁/γ + V₁²/2g + z₁ + h_pump = p₂/γ + V₂²/2g + z₂ + h_turbine + h_L**

> **So all three distractors describe situations that Bernoulli's equation CAN be extended to cover** — but not in the form the question quotes. **Recognising that the question is about the FORM given, not about the principle, is the discrimination.**

**Where Bernoulli's equation is used, since the ideal assumptions are never quite met:**

| Application | Note |
|---|---|
| **VENTURI meter, orifice meter, nozzle** | **A discharge COEFFICIENT absorbs the small real-fluid deviation** ← |
| **Pitot tube** | Stagnation minus static gives the velocity head directly |
| **Flow over a weir or through a sluice** | With a coefficient |
| **Pipe flow** | **With the h_L term added — the practical energy equation** |
| Aerofoil lift (qualitatively) | Often over-simplified in popular accounts |

> **The role of the discharge coefficient is the point worth understanding: it is precisely the factor that reconciles the ideal Bernoulli prediction with the real measured flow.**

> **A venturi's C_d of 0.97-0.98 says the ideal equation is 97-98 per cent right for that geometry; an orifice's 0.60-0.65 says it is much further off, because the jet contracts and the losses are large.**

> **So the coefficient is not a fudge but a measure of how well the assumptions hold in that device**, which is why a well-shaped venturi has a coefficient near unity and a sharp-edged orifice does not.

**And the assumption most often forgotten — "along a streamline":**

> **Bernoulli's constant is generally DIFFERENT ON DIFFERENT STREAMLINES.**

> **Applying the equation between two points on separate streamlines is valid only if the flow is also IRROTATIONAL**, in which case the constant is the same throughout the field.

> **Most engineering applications quietly assume irrotational flow and get away with it**, because the flow is nearly so away from boundaries. **But it is the assumption that fails inside a boundary layer, in a wake, or downstream of a bend — which is exactly where naive applications of Bernoulli's equation give wrong answers.**

> **The practical version of that warning: do not apply Bernoulli's equation across a region of strong mixing or separation.** A hydraulic jump, a sudden expansion and the wake behind an obstruction all destroy energy in ways the equation cannot represent — **which is why the momentum equation, not the energy equation, is used to analyse a hydraulic jump.**

> **Knowing WHICH conservation law to apply to a given problem is a large part of the subject: use ENERGY where losses are small or known, and MOMENTUM where losses are large and unknown.**

examTip.trick: **Steady, incompressible, non-viscous, along a streamline, no energy added.** Each wrong option violates exactly one of those — so the question tests the assumptions, not the formula.
examTip.trap: **All three distractors name situations Bernoulli CAN be extended to** — add h_L for a real fluid, h_pump for a pump, ∂V/∂t for unsteady flow. The question is about the FORM quoted, not the principle.
examTip.mnemonic: **A discharge coefficient measures how well the assumptions hold** — venturi 0.97 (nearly ideal), orifice 0.62 (far from it). And use **MOMENTUM, not energy, where losses are large and unknown** — as in a hydraulic jump.

questions.stem: In the Darcy-Weisbach equation h_f = fLV²/(2gD), for fully developed turbulent flow in a rough pipe at high Reynolds number, the friction factor f depends on:
options: both the Reynolds number and the relative roughness equally
neither — it is a universal constant
questions.solution:
**The relative roughness only.**

**Why — the three flow regimes and what governs f in each:**

| Regime | f depends on | Reason |
|---|---|---|
| **LAMINAR (Re < 2000)** | **Re ONLY:  f = 64/Re** | **Roughness is irrelevant — the flow slides in layers and never reaches the wall projections** |
| **TRANSITIONAL / partly rough turbulent** | **BOTH Re and ε/D** | **The laminar sublayer partly covers the projections** |
| **FULLY ROUGH TURBULENT (high Re)** | **RELATIVE ROUGHNESS ε/D ONLY** | **The laminar sublayer is thinner than the projections, which stand fully exposed in the turbulent flow** ← |

> **The mechanism is the LAMINAR SUBLAYER, and it explains all three rows.**

> **A very thin layer of laminar flow clings to the pipe wall even in turbulent flow, and its thickness DECREASES as the Reynolds number rises.**

| Comparison | Pipe behaves as |
|---|---|
| **Sublayer THICKER than the roughness projections** | **SMOOTH — the projections are submerged and the flow does not feel them** |
| **Sublayer comparable to the projections** | **Transitional — both effects matter** |
| **Sublayer THINNER than the projections** | **FULLY ROUGH — the projections generate form drag, and Re no longer matters** ← |

> **So at high Reynolds number the sublayer has effectively vanished, the roughness is fully exposed, and f becomes INDEPENDENT OF Re.**

> **That is why the curves on the MOODY DIAGRAM become HORIZONTAL at high Re** — a flat line means f no longer changes with Re, only with ε/D. **Recognising that flat region is the whole answer to this question.**

**The Moody diagram, since it is the map of all this:**

| Feature | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **A single straight line at low Re** | **The laminar relation f = 64/Re** |
| **A gap around Re = 2000-4000** | **The transition zone — unpredictable** |
| **A family of curves, one per ε/D** | Turbulent flow |
| **The curves FLATTEN at high Re** | **The FULLY ROUGH regime — f depends on ε/D alone** ← |
| **The lowest curve (ε/D = 0)** | The smooth-pipe limit |

> **Note that laminar flow's f = 64/Re contains NO roughness term at all**, which is the cleanest illustration of the principle: **in laminar flow the wall's texture is genuinely irrelevant, and a rough pipe and a smooth one of the same diameter have exactly the same friction factor.**

> **That is counter-intuitive and is worth holding, because it is the strongest evidence that roughness matters only through its interaction with turbulence.**

**The correlations, for completeness:**

| Regime | Relation |
|---|---|
| **Laminar** | **f = 64/Re** |
| **Turbulent, smooth** | **Blasius: f = 0.316/Re^{0.25} (Re up to ~10⁵)** |
| **Turbulent, general** | **COLEBROOK-WHITE — implicit in f, needs iteration** |
| **Fully rough** | **f = [2 log(3.7 D/ε)]^{−2} — Re absent** ← |
| Explicit approximation | Swamee-Jain, Haaland |

> **The fully rough relation contains no Re, which is the algebraic statement of the answer.**

> **And the Colebrook-White equation being IMPLICIT is why the Moody diagram existed at all**: before computers, iterating an implicit equation by hand for every pipe was impractical, so a chart was read instead.

**A caution on the definition of f, because two conventions exist:**

| Convention | Form | Laminar relation |
|---|---|---|
| **DARCY-WEISBACH friction factor f** | **h_f = fLV²/(2gD)** | **f = 64/Re** ← used here |
| **FANNING friction factor f′** | h_f = 4f′LV²/(2gD) | **f′ = 16/Re** |

> **The Darcy factor is FOUR TIMES the Fanning factor**, and both are written f in different literatures — chemical engineering tends to use Fanning, civil engineering Darcy.

> **A reported friction factor of 0.005 is almost certainly Fanning; 0.02 is almost certainly Darcy.** Confusing them is a factor-of-four error in the head loss, and it is a real hazard when reading across disciplines.

**Typical roughness values, since ε/D is what the answer depends on:**

| Pipe material | ε (mm) |
|---|---|
| **Drawn tubing, PVC, plastic** | **0.0015-0.003** |
| **Commercial steel, wrought iron** | **0.045** |
| **Galvanised iron** | **0.15** |
| **Cast iron, new** | **0.26** |
| **Concrete** | **0.3-3.0** |
| **Riveted steel** | 0.9-9.0 |
| **Old, encrusted cast iron** | **1-3 or more** ← |

> **The last row is the one that matters in practice: pipes get ROUGHER WITH AGE.** Tuberculation, corrosion products and biofilm can raise ε by an order of magnitude over decades.

> **So a distribution main designed for f = 0.02 may be running at 0.035 after forty years**, which nearly doubles its friction loss and correspondingly reduces its capacity at the available head.

> **Which is why an ageing allowance is built into design — commonly by using a higher roughness or a lower Hazen-Williams C than the new-pipe value** — and why a network that has lost capacity may need cleaning and relining rather than replacement.

> **The Hazen-Williams C value falls from about 130-140 for new pipe to 60-80 for old encrusted pipe**, and that fall is often the real explanation of a network's declining performance.

examTip.trick: **The LAMINAR SUBLAYER explains all three regimes.** At high Re it is thinner than the roughness projections, which stand fully exposed — so f depends on ε/D alone and the Moody curves go HORIZONTAL.
