examTip.trap: **In LAMINAR flow, roughness is genuinely irrelevant: f = 64/Re contains no roughness term at all.** A rough and a smooth pipe of the same diameter have identical f. That is the strongest evidence for the mechanism.
examTip.mnemonic: **Darcy f is FOUR TIMES Fanning f′** (64/Re against 16/Re), and both are written f in different literatures — a factor-of-four hazard. And **pipes get rougher with age**: Hazen-Williams C falls from 130 to 60-80.

questions.stem: A UNIT HYDROGRAPH is defined as the hydrograph of direct runoff resulting from:
options: one unit depth (1 cm) of effective rainfall occurring uniformly over the catchment in a specified duration
one cubic metre per second of runoff sustained for one hour
a rainfall of one hour's duration, whatever its depth
the total rainfall of a storm, including the base flow
questions.solution:
**One unit depth (1 cm) of effective rainfall, occurring uniformly over the catchment in a specified duration.**

**The definition, phrase by phrase — because every phrase is doing work:**

| Phrase | Why it matters |
|---|---|
| **ONE UNIT DEPTH (1 cm)** | **The "unit" refers to the RAINFALL DEPTH, not to the discharge or the duration** ← |
| **EFFECTIVE rainfall (rainfall EXCESS)** | **Only the part that becomes DIRECT RUNOFF — losses to infiltration, interception and depression storage are excluded** |
| **UNIFORMLY over the catchment** | Spatially uniform |
| **In a SPECIFIED duration** | **A unit hydrograph is always "of a stated duration" — a 2-hour UH differs from a 6-hour UH** |
| **DIRECT runoff** | **BASE FLOW is separated out and is NOT part of the unit hydrograph** |

> **The commonest misunderstanding is thinking the "unit" is one hour.** It is not — **the unit is the 1 cm depth, and the duration is a separate label attached to the hydrograph.**

> **Option (c) contains exactly that error, and it is the designed trap.**

**Why each distractor is wrong:**

| Option | Note |
|---|---|
| **1 cm effective rainfall in a specified duration** | ✓ |
| **1 m³/s sustained for an hour** | **Confuses the unit of RAINFALL with a unit of DISCHARGE.** The UH's ordinates are discharges, but the "unit" is the input depth |
| **A rainfall of one hour, whatever its depth** | **The "unit" is the DEPTH, not the duration** ← the main trap |
| **Total storm rainfall including base flow** | **Wrong on two counts: it must be EFFECTIVE rainfall (not total), and base flow must be SEPARATED (not included)** |

> **Option (d) is worth noting because it violates two of the definition's phrases at once**, and either violation alone would be fatal.

**The assumptions the method rests on:**

| Assumption | Statement |
|---|---|
| **LINEARITY (proportionality)** | **2 cm of effective rainfall in the same duration produces ordinates exactly TWICE the unit hydrograph's** |
| **SUPERPOSITION** | **The runoff from successive rainfall blocks can be ADDED, with appropriate time offsets** |
| **TIME INVARIANCE** | **The same rainfall produces the same hydrograph whenever it occurs** |
| Uniform spatial distribution | The storm covers the catchment evenly |
| Constant base duration | The direct-runoff duration is independent of the rainfall intensity |

> **LINEARITY and SUPERPOSITION are what make the unit hydrograph USEFUL**, because together they let any storm be handled: **break the storm into blocks of the unit duration, scale the UH by each block's depth, offset each by its time, and add.**

> **That procedure — scale, shift, add — is the whole practical method**, and it is exactly a discrete convolution.

**Why the assumptions are known to be imperfect, stated honestly:**

> **A real catchment is NOT linear.** A large storm produces a proportionally LARGER and FASTER peak than a small one, because:

| Non-linearity | Cause |
|---|---|
| **Higher intensity gives higher runoff coefficient** | **Infiltration capacity is exceeded more completely** |
| **Higher flows travel FASTER** | Greater depth means higher velocity, so the time to peak shortens |
| **Channel and floodplain storage behave differently at high stage** | The routing changes |

> **So a unit hydrograph derived from a moderate storm UNDERESTIMATES the peak of a very large one**, and that is a systematic bias rather than random scatter.

> **The practical response is to derive the UH from storms of similar magnitude to the design event where possible**, and to treat a UH derived from small storms as a lower bound for a flood estimate.

**The derived hydrographs, since they extend the method:**

| Hydrograph | What it is |
|---|---|
| **Unit hydrograph of duration D** | **The basic tool, for 1 cm in D hours** |
| **S-CURVE (S-hydrograph)** | **The response to a CONTINUOUS effective rainfall of 1 cm/hour — obtained by superposing UHs at intervals of D** |
| **UH of a DIFFERENT duration** | **Derived from the S-curve, by offsetting it and scaling — the S-curve method** |
| **INSTANTANEOUS unit hydrograph (IUH)** | **The limit as D → 0 — a catchment property independent of any duration** |
| **SYNTHETIC unit hydrograph** | **Derived from CATCHMENT CHARACTERISTICS where no rainfall-runoff records exist — Snyder's or SCS methods** ← |

> **The SYNTHETIC unit hydrograph is the one with the most practical importance in Nepal**, because it is the tool for an UNGAUGED catchment — which describes most of them.

> **It estimates the peak, the time to peak and the base width from measurable catchment properties (area, length, slope, centroid distance) rather than from streamflow records.** The result is far less reliable than a derived UH, and it is often the only option available.

**And the base flow separation, since the definition excludes it:**

> **Total streamflow = DIRECT RUNOFF + BASE FLOW**, and the unit hydrograph concerns only the first.

> **Base flow is the groundwater contribution — the flow that sustains a river between storms** — and it must be subtracted from the observed hydrograph before a UH can be derived.

| Separation method | Note |
|---|---|
| **Straight line** | **From the start of the rise to the point where the recession returns to the pre-storm slope** |
| **Fixed base length** | Uses an empirical N = 0.83A^{0.2} days |
| **Variable slope** | Extends the pre-storm recession forward and the post-storm recession back |

> **All three are approximations, and the choice affects the derived UH's ordinates** — which is one reason two engineers deriving a UH from the same storm can reach slightly different answers. **The separation is a judgement, not a measurement.**

examTip.trick: **The "unit" is the 1 cm RAINFALL DEPTH, not the duration.** A unit hydrograph is always labelled with its duration separately — a 2-hour UH differs from a 6-hour UH.
examTip.trap: **Option (c) makes the classic error of treating the duration as the unit.** And option (d) violates two phrases at once: it must be EFFECTIVE rainfall, and base flow must be SEPARATED.
examTip.mnemonic: **Scale, shift, add** — that is the whole method, and it works because of LINEARITY and SUPERPOSITION. But a real catchment is non-linear, so a UH from moderate storms UNDERESTIMATES a large flood's peak.

questions.stem: A simply supported beam of span L carries a uniformly distributed load w over its whole span. The shear force diagram is:
options: a rectangle of constant value wL/2
a parabola with its maximum at mid-span
a triangle with its apex at mid-span
a straight line varying from +wL/2 at one support to −wL/2 at the other
questions.solution:
**A straight line from +wL/2 at one support to −wL/2 at the other, passing through zero at mid-span.**

**The derivation, which is two lines:**

> **Reactions: each support carries half the total load, so R_A = R_B = wL/2.**

> **Shear at a distance x from A:**

> **V(x) = R_A − wx = wL/2 − wx**

> **This is LINEAR in x:**

| At | V |
|---|---|
| **x = 0 (support A)** | **+wL/2** |
| **x = L/2 (mid-span)** | **0** |
| **x = L (support B)** | **−wL/2** |

> **So the diagram is a single straight sloping line crossing zero at the centre.** ✓

**The rule that generates this and every related answer:**

> **dV/dx = −w**  — the SLOPE of the shear diagram equals minus the load intensity.

> **For a UNIFORM load, w is constant, so the slope is constant — hence a STRAIGHT LINE.**

> **And dM/dx = V — the slope of the moment diagram is the shear.**

| Loading | Shear force diagram | Bending moment diagram |
|---|---|---|
| **Point load** | **Constant, with a STEP at the load** | **LINEAR → triangle** |
| **UNIFORM load (udl)** | **LINEAR → sloping straight line** ← | **PARABOLIC** |
| **Triangular load** | **Parabolic** | **Cubic** |
| **Applied couple** | No change | **STEP jump** |

> **Each integration raises the degree by one**, and reading down that table answers any question of this kind without recall.

**Why each distractor is wrong — and each is a real diagram for a different case:**

| Option | What it actually describes |
|---|---|
| **Rectangle of constant wL/2** | **The shear diagram of a CANTILEVER carrying a point load at its tip — constant shear** ← |
| **Parabola with maximum at mid-span** | **The BENDING MOMENT diagram of this very beam** ← the substantive trap |
| **Triangle with apex at mid-span** | **The bending moment diagram for a CENTRAL POINT LOAD** |
| **Straight line ±wL/2 through zero at mid-span** | ✓ |

> **Option (b) is the designed trap and is the most instructive: it correctly describes the BENDING MOMENT diagram of the same beam.** A candidate who visualises "udl on a simply supported beam" and recalls the parabola has recalled the wrong diagram.

> **The pairing to hold is: udl gives a LINEAR shear diagram and a PARABOLIC moment diagram.** One degree apart, always.

**Why the zero crossing at mid-span matters:**

> **Since dM/dx = V, the bending moment is MAXIMUM where the shear crosses zero.**

> **Here V = 0 at x = L/2, so the maximum moment is at mid-span:**

> **M_max = R_A(L/2) − w(L/2)(L/4) = wL²/4 − wL²/8 = wL²/8** ✓

> **So the shear diagram LOCATES the maximum moment, which is its principal use** — and that is why the two diagrams are always drawn together.

> **The general procedure follows: draw the shear diagram, find where it crosses zero, and evaluate the moment there.** For an unsymmetrical loading that is far quicker than differentiating a moment expression.

**The standard results for this beam, gathered:**

| Quantity | Value |
|---|---|
| **Reactions** | **wL/2 each** |
| **Maximum SHEAR** | **wL/2, AT THE SUPPORTS** |
| **Maximum MOMENT** | **wL²/8, at MID-SPAN** |
| **Maximum DEFLECTION** | **5wL⁴/384EI, at mid-span** |
| **Shear at mid-span** | **ZERO** |
| **Moment at the supports** | **ZERO** |

> **Note the complementary pattern: shear is maximum where moment is zero, and moment is maximum where shear is zero.**

> **That is not a coincidence but a direct consequence of dM/dx = V**, and it has a design consequence worth stating: **shear governs the design near the SUPPORTS and bending governs it near MID-SPAN.**

> **Which is why shear reinforcement (stirrups) is closely spaced near the supports of an RCC beam and widely spaced in the middle**, while the main tension bars are fullest at mid-span and may be curtailed toward the supports.

> **A candidate who understands that pairing understands why a beam is detailed the way it is**, rather than merely remembering the detail.

**And the reason shear governs SHORT beams:**

> **Maximum moment goes as wL² and maximum shear as wL.**

> **So halving the span quarters the moment but only halves the shear** — the shear becomes relatively more important as the span shortens.

> **Hence a short, deep, heavily loaded beam is a SHEAR problem, and a long slender one is a BENDING (or deflection) problem.** Checking only the bending stress on a short deep beam is a real and dangerous omission.

examTip.trick: **dV/dx = −w, so a constant load gives a constant slope — a straight line.** V(x) = wL/2 − wx, running from +wL/2 to −wL/2 through zero at mid-span.
examTip.trap: **Option (b) correctly describes the BENDING MOMENT diagram of the same beam.** Hold the pairing: udl gives a LINEAR shear diagram and a PARABOLIC moment diagram — always one degree apart.
examTip.mnemonic: **Shear is maximum where moment is zero and vice versa**, since dM/dx = V. So **shear governs near the SUPPORTS and bending near MID-SPAN** — which is exactly why stirrups are closely spaced at the ends of an RCC beam.

questions.stem: The Euler buckling load for a column of length L, both ends hinged, is P_cr = π²EI/L². For the same column with BOTH ENDS FIXED, the buckling load becomes:
questions.solution:
**4π²EI/L² — four times the hinged-end value.**

**The effective length concept, which generates every case:**

> **P_cr = π²EI / L_e²**, where **L_e is the EFFECTIVE LENGTH** — the length of an equivalent both-ends-hinged column.

| End conditions | Effective length L_e | P_cr relative to hinged-hinged |
|---|---|---|
| **BOTH ENDS FIXED** | **L/2** | **4 ×** ← |
| **Both ends hinged (pinned)** | **L** | **1 ×** (the reference) |
| **One fixed, one hinged** | **L/√2 ≈ 0.7L** | **2 ×** |
| **One fixed, one FREE (cantilever)** | **2L** | **1/4 ×** |

> **Since L_e appears SQUARED, halving it multiplies the load by FOUR.**

> **L_e = L/2 for fixed-fixed, so P_cr = π²EI/(L/2)² = 4π²EI/L².** ✓

> **The whole family follows from the effective length table, and the squaring is what makes the differences so large: from a cantilever (L_e = 2L) to a fixed-fixed column (L_e = L/2) is a factor of SIXTEEN.**

**Why the effective length is L/2 — the physical picture:**

> **The effective length is the distance between successive POINTS OF INFLECTION (points of zero moment) in the buckled shape.**

> **A hinged-hinged column buckles into a single half sine wave, with zero moment at each end** — so the inflection points are the ends themselves and L_e = L.

> **A fixed-fixed column cannot rotate at its ends, so its buckled shape has inflection points at the QUARTER POINTS** — a distance L/2 apart.

> **Between those two inflection points the column behaves exactly like a hinged-hinged column of length L/2**, which is why the substitution works.

> **That is worth visualising rather than memorising, because it also explains the 0.7L for the fixed-pinned case: one inflection point at the pinned end and the other about 0.3L from the fixed end.**

**Why each distractor is wrong:**

| Option | What it corresponds to |
|---|---|
| **π²EI/(4L²)** | **L_e = 2L — a CANTILEVER (one end fixed, one FREE). The load is a QUARTER, not four times** ← the inverted trap |
| **2π²EI/L²** | **L_e = L/√2 — one end FIXED, one HINGED** |
| **4π²EI/L²** | ✓ **Both ends fixed** |
| **π²EI/(2L²)** | Not a standard case |

> **Option (a) is the designed trap and it is the exact inversion: it is the CANTILEVER value.** A candidate who knows the factor is 4 but not which way round will choose between (a) and (c).

> **The check is physical and needs no recall: FIXING the ends RESTRAINS the column, so it must carry MORE load.** Any answer smaller than the hinged value is wrong for fixed ends.

> **That single test disposes of (a) and (d) immediately, leaving a choice between factors of 2 and 4 — settled by L_e = L/2 and the squaring.**

**The assumptions behind Euler's formula, since they bound its use:**

| Assumption | Note |
|---|---|
| **The column is PERFECTLY STRAIGHT** | No initial curvature |
| **The load is PERFECTLY AXIAL** | No eccentricity |
| **The material is HOMOGENEOUS and remains ELASTIC** | **The critical limitation** ← |
| **The column is LONG and SLENDER** | Failure is by buckling, not crushing |
| Self-weight neglected | — |

> **The elastic assumption is the one that fails first, and it fails for SHORT columns.**

> **Euler's formula predicts an infinite load as L → 0**, which is obviously wrong: a very short column CRUSHES at its yield stress rather than buckling.

> **So Euler's formula applies only above a certain slenderness ratio:**

> **Critical stress  σ_cr = π²E/(L_e/k)²**, where **L_e/k is the SLENDERNESS RATIO** and k the radius of gyration.

> **Euler is valid only while σ_cr < the yield (or crushing) stress.** For mild steel that means a slenderness ratio above roughly 80 to 100.

| Slenderness ratio L_e/k | Failure mode | Formula |
|---|---|---|
| **< ~30** | **CRUSHING** | **σ = f_y** |
| **30 - 100** | **Combined — the practical range** | **RANKINE, or a code curve** |
| **> ~100** | **Elastic BUCKLING** | **EULER** ← |

> **Most real columns lie in the INTERMEDIATE range**, where neither pure crushing nor pure Euler buckling applies — **which is why codes use empirical or semi-empirical curves rather than Euler's formula directly.**

> **RANKINE'S formula covers the whole range: 1/P = 1/P_crushing + 1/P_Euler**, which tends to each limit at the appropriate end. **Its elegance is that it needs no decision about which regime applies.**

**And the practical caution about "fixed" ends:**

> **A truly fixed end is very difficult to achieve.** A real connection has some rotational flexibility, so the actual effective length lies between the theoretical values.

> **Codes therefore give CONSERVATIVE effective length factors that are worse than the theoretical ones** — for example 0.65L rather than 0.5L for a nominally fixed-fixed column.

> **Claiming full fixity for a connection that cannot deliver it is an unconservative assumption**, and since L_e enters squared, a 30 per cent error in L_e is a 70 per cent error in the buckling load. **Which is why the effective length is the assumption a column design most depends on.**

examTip.trick: **L_e = L/2 for fixed-fixed, and L_e appears SQUARED — so the load is 4×.** The family: fixed-fixed L/2, hinged L, fixed-hinged 0.7L, cantilever 2L.
examTip.trap: **Option (a) is the CANTILEVER value — the exact inversion.** Check physically: FIXING the ends restrains the column, so it must carry MORE. Any answer below the hinged value is wrong for fixed ends.
examTip.mnemonic: **Effective length is the distance between POINTS OF INFLECTION** in the buckled shape — at the quarter points for fixed-fixed, hence L/2. And Euler applies only above slenderness ~100; below ~30 the column CRUSHES.

questions.stem: In limit state design to IS 456, the partial safety factor for the load combination of dead load plus imposed load, at the ultimate limit state of collapse, is:
questions.solution:
**1.5 DL + 1.5 LL.**

**The load combinations of IS 456:2000, Table 18:**

| Combination | ULTIMATE limit state (collapse) | SERVICEABILITY limit state |
|---|---|---|
| **DL + LL** | **1.5 DL + 1.5 LL** ← | **1.0 DL + 1.0 LL** |
| **DL + WL (or EL)** | **1.5 DL + 1.5 WL**, or **0.9 DL + 1.5 WL** | 1.0 DL + 1.0 WL |
| **DL + LL + WL** | **1.2 (DL + LL + WL)** | 1.0 DL + 0.8 LL + 0.8 WL |

> **Every option in this question is a real entry from that table**, which is what makes it a matching question rather than a recall one.

| Option | Where it belongs |
|---|---|
| **1.0 DL + 1.0 LL** | **The SERVICEABILITY combination for the same loads** ← |
| **1.5 DL + 1.5 LL** | ✓ **Ultimate, DL + LL** |
| **1.2 DL + 1.2 LL** | **Part of the THREE-load ultimate combination 1.2(DL+LL+WL)** ← |
| **1.5 DL + 1.0 LL** | Not a standard combination |

> **So the question tests whether the candidate can place a factor in the right combination AND the right limit state**, and two of the distractors are correct factors from the wrong row.

**Why the factors are what they are — the logic is worth knowing:**

> **1.5 on both dead and imposed load** for the basic combination, at collapse.

> **1.0 on both** at serviceability, because **deflection and cracking are checked under the loads the structure will actually experience**, not under factored loads. **Serviceability is about behaviour in use, so the loads must be service loads.**

> **1.2 on all three when wind or earthquake is included**, because it is very unlikely that the full imposed load and the full design wind occur simultaneously. **The lower factor reflects that reduced probability.**

> **That is the principle behind every load combination: the factor falls as the number of independent variable loads rises**, because their simultaneous maxima become less likely.

**Why 0.9 DL appears in the wind combination — a subtle and important case:**

> **For DL + WL, IS 456 gives 1.5 DL + 1.5 WL and also 0.9 DL + 1.5 WL.**

> **The second exists because dead load can be STABILISING.** For an overturning check, or for uplift on a light roof, **the dead load RESISTS the wind.**

> **Applying a factor of 1.5 to a stabilising load would be UNCONSERVATIVE — it would overstate the resistance.** So the factor is reduced to 0.9, understating the dead load deliberately.

> **The rule generalises: a load factor is greater than 1 when the load is ADVERSE and less than 1 when it is BENEFICIAL.** Which is why the same dead load appears with two different factors in the same code.

> **Forgetting the 0.9 case is a real design error, and it appears exactly where it matters most: light roofs in high wind, and the overturning of slender structures.**

**The partial safety factors for MATERIALS, since they are the other half of the method:**

| Material | γ_m | Design strength |
|---|---|---|
| **CONCRETE** | **1.5** | **0.67 f_ck / 1.5 = 0.446 f_ck** |
| **STEEL** | **1.15** | **f_y / 1.15 = 0.87 f_y** |

> **Two facts to note.**

> **First, concrete's factor (1.5) is larger than steel's (1.15)** — because concrete is a site-made material with far more variability than factory-rolled steel. **The factor reflects the confidence in the material, which is exactly what a partial factor is for.**

> **Second, the 0.67 in the concrete expression is an additional reduction** — from the cube strength to the strength of concrete in a flexural member, accounting for the difference between a cube's confined loading and a beam's sustained loading.

> **So the concrete design strength is 0.446 f_ck, not f_ck/1.5**, and the 0.446 (often written 0.45) is the number that actually appears in design calculations.

> **And 0.87 f_y is the steel figure to have automatically** — it appears in every reinforcement calculation.

**Why the method is called PARTIAL safety factors:**

> **The older WORKING STRESS method applied a single global factor of safety to the material strength, and used unfactored loads.**

> **The LIMIT STATE method splits the safety into two parts: a factor on the LOADS (γ_f) for the uncertainty in what will be applied, and a factor on the MATERIALS (γ_m) for the uncertainty in what they will supply.**

| | **Working stress** | **LIMIT STATE** |
|---|---|---|
| **Safety applied to** | **Material strength only** | **BOTH loads and materials, separately** |
| **Loads used** | Service | **FACTORED for collapse; service for serviceability** |
| **Basis** | Elastic behaviour throughout | **Actual behaviour at each limit state** |
| **Economy** | Conservative and uneven | **More uniform reliability, generally more economical** |

> **The advantage of splitting the factors is that each uncertainty is treated where it arises**, so a well-controlled material or a well-known load can be given a smaller factor without weakening the whole design.

> **That is the conceptual step that makes limit state design better than working stress design** — not the arithmetic, which is merely different, but the recognition that load uncertainty and material uncertainty are separate things.

examTip.trick: **1.5 DL + 1.5 LL at collapse; 1.0 DL + 1.0 LL at serviceability; 1.2(DL+LL+WL) when wind is included.** Every option here is a real entry from Table 18 — placed in the wrong row.
examTip.trap: **The factor FALLS as more independent variable loads are combined** (1.5 → 1.2), because their simultaneous maxima are less likely. And note **0.9 DL + 1.5 WL**: a factor below 1 where the dead load is STABILISING.
examTip.mnemonic: **Concrete γ_m = 1.5, steel 1.15** — concrete is site-made and more variable. Design strengths: **0.446 f_ck (the 0.67 is an extra flexural reduction) and 0.87 f_y.** The whole point of PARTIAL factors is treating each uncertainty where it arises.

questions.stem: In a reinforced concrete beam, the shear reinforcement (stirrups) is provided principally to:
options: hold the main bars in position during concreting
reduce the deflection of the beam under service load
resist the diagonal tension caused by shear, which the concrete alone cannot carry
questions.solution:
**To resist the diagonal tension caused by shear, which the concrete alone cannot carry.**

**Why shear produces DIAGONAL TENSION — this is the mechanism the whole subject rests on:**

> **A beam under load carries both bending stress (σ) and shear stress (τ) at any section.**

> **Those two combine into PRINCIPAL STRESSES acting on INCLINED planes**, and one of the principal stresses is TENSILE.

> **Near the neutral axis, where the bending stress is zero and the shear stress is greatest, the principal tension acts at 45° to the axis of the beam.**

> **Concrete is weak in tension — about a tenth of its compressive strength — so it cracks on the plane perpendicular to that tension, producing the characteristic DIAGONAL crack rising from the support toward mid-span.**

> **Stirrups cross that crack and carry the tension across it.** That is their function, and it is why they are placed perpendicular to the beam axis (or occasionally inclined at 45° to lie along the tension direction).

> **So "shear reinforcement" is a slight misnomer: the steel resists TENSION, as steel always does.** It is called shear reinforcement because shear is what causes that tension.

**Why the failure it prevents is so dangerous — the case for the requirement:**

| | **FLEXURAL failure** | **SHEAR (diagonal tension) failure** |
|---|---|---|
| **Warning** | **Cracks widen, deflection grows, steel yields visibly** | **Sudden — little or no warning** ← |
| **Ductility** | **DUCTILE — large deformation before collapse** | **BRITTLE** |
| **Load redistribution** | Possible | **None** |
| **Design philosophy** | May be allowed to govern | **Must NEVER govern — design so that flexure fails first** |

> **The design principle that follows is fundamental and worth stating explicitly: a beam is deliberately designed so that its SHEAR capacity EXCEEDS the shear corresponding to its flexural capacity.**

> **That way, if the beam is ever overloaded, it fails in bending — visibly, slowly, and with warning — rather than in shear.**

> **This is CAPACITY DESIGN, and it is the same idea that underlies the strong-column/weak-beam rule in seismic design and the requirement that a connection be stronger than the members it joins.**

> **The general form: choose which member and which mode will fail, and make everything else stronger.**

**Why the distractors are wrong:**

| Option | Note |
|---|---|
| **Increase flexural capacity** | **Flexure is resisted by the LONGITUDINAL bars.** Stirrups contribute negligibly to it |
| **Hold the main bars in position** | **A REAL and useful secondary function — the stirrup cage does locate the bars during concreting.** But it is incidental, not the purpose ← the closest distractor |
| **Reduce deflection** | **Deflection depends on EI and the span, not on stirrups.** Shear deflection is negligible in a normal beam |
| **Resist diagonal tension** | ✓ |

> **Option (b) deserves care because it is genuinely true as a description of what stirrups also do.** The cage does hold the bars, and in a beam requiring no shear reinforcement by calculation, **nominal stirrups are still provided partly for that reason.**

> **But it is a construction convenience, not a structural purpose**, and the question asks for the principal function.

**The design provisions, since they follow from the mechanism:**

| Provision | Value |
|---|---|
| **Nominal shear stress** | **τ_v = V_u/(bd)** |
| **Concrete's own shear capacity** | **τ_c, from IS 456 Table 19 — depends on the grade AND the percentage of tension steel** |
| **If τ_v < τ_c/2** | **No stirrups needed by calculation (but provide nominal)** |
| **If τ_c/2 < τ_v < τ_c** | **MINIMUM shear reinforcement** |
| **If τ_v > τ_c** | **Design stirrups for the EXCESS shear (V_u − τ_c bd)** |
| **If τ_v > τ_c,max** | **REDESIGN THE SECTION — no amount of stirrups is permitted** ← |
| **Minimum stirrups** | **A_sv/(b·s_v) ≥ 0.4/(0.87 f_y)** |
| **Maximum spacing** | **The LEAST of 0.75d, 300 mm, or the calculated spacing** |

> **The τ_c,max row is the one with a lesson: beyond a certain shear stress the code FORBIDS the use of more stirrups and requires a larger section.**

> **The reason is that the failure mode changes: at very high shear the concrete between the diagonal cracks CRUSHES, and no reinforcement crossing the cracks can prevent that.** Adding stirrups to a section failing by web crushing achieves nothing.

> **That is a genuinely important limit, because it is the one case where "add more steel" is not the answer.**

> **And the fact that τ_c depends on the PERCENTAGE OF TENSION STEEL is worth noticing: more longitudinal steel raises the concrete's shear capacity**, because it controls the crack widths and so preserves aggregate interlock across the crack.

**And the seismic detailing requirement, since it changes the stirrup itself:**

> **IS 13920 requires stirrups in ductile detailing to have **135° HOOKS with a 10φ tail**, not 90° hooks.**

> **The reason is specific and instructive: when the concrete cover SPALLS in an earthquake, a 90° hook OPENS OUT and the stirrup loses its anchorage — exactly when the confinement is most needed.**

> **A 135° hook, bent back into the core of the section, cannot open out.**

> **So a detail that looks like a drafting preference is the difference between a stirrup that works after the cover has gone and one that does not** — and it is a common site error to bend seismic stirrups at 90° because that is what the fabricator is used to.

examTip.trick: **Shear produces PRINCIPAL TENSION at 45°, and concrete is weak in tension** — so it cracks diagonally and stirrups carry the tension across the crack. The steel resists TENSION, as always.
examTip.trap: **Option (b) is genuinely true as a secondary function** — the cage does locate the bars, which is partly why nominal stirrups are provided even where none are needed by calculation. But it is a convenience, not the purpose.
examTip.mnemonic: **Shear failure is BRITTLE and sudden, so a beam is designed so FLEXURE fails first** — capacity design, the same idea as strong-column/weak-beam. And beyond τ_c,max the code FORBIDS more stirrups: the web crushes, and steel cannot stop it.

questions.stem: In the design of a steel beam, LATERAL TORSIONAL BUCKLING is a mode of failure that:
options: occurs only in short, deep beams carrying high shear
is prevented if the compression flange is restrained laterally at sufficiently close intervals
depends only on the beam's bending capacity and not on its span
cannot occur in a beam bent about its major axis
questions.solution:
**It is prevented if the compression flange is restrained laterally at sufficiently close intervals.**

**What lateral torsional buckling is:**

> **A beam bent about its MAJOR axis has one flange in COMPRESSION.**

> **That compression flange behaves like a long, slender COLUMN — and like any column it wants to buckle sideways, out of the plane of bending.**

> **But it cannot move sideways on its own, because it is attached to the web and to the tension flange.** So the section BUCKLES SIDEWAYS AND TWISTS at the same time — a combined lateral displacement and rotation.

> **Hence the name: LATERAL (sideways) TORSIONAL (twisting) buckling.**

> **It happens at a moment BELOW the beam's full plastic or elastic bending capacity**, which is why it must be designed against rather than ignored.

**Why lateral restraint of the compression flange is the answer:**

> **The compression flange is behaving as a column, and a column's buckling load depends on its EFFECTIVE LENGTH squared.**

> **Restraining the flange laterally at intervals reduces that effective length.**

> **Halve the unrestrained length and the buckling resistance rises by a factor approaching four** — the same squared relation as in ordinary column buckling.

> **So the design variable is the SPACING OF LATERAL RESTRAINTS, and with restraints close enough the beam reaches its full bending capacity and lateral torsional buckling ceases to govern.**

> **A beam so restrained is called LATERALLY RESTRAINED, and it may be designed for its full moment capacity.**

**Where lateral restraint comes from in practice:**

| Source of restraint | Note |
|---|---|
| **A concrete slab CAST ON or composite with the top flange** | **Continuous restraint — the beam is fully restrained** ← the commonest case |
| **Secondary beams framing into the beam** | Restraint at each connection point |
| **Purlins on a roof beam** | Restraint at purlin spacing |
| **Explicit bracing or ties to the compression flange** | Where nothing else restrains it |
| **The tension flange only** | **NOT effective — it is the COMPRESSION flange that must be held** ← |

> **The last row is the point most often got wrong on site.** Restraining the tension flange does little: **the compression flange is the one trying to buckle, and it must be the one held.**

> **Which has a consequence worth stating for continuous beams: near a support, the moment is HOGGING, so the BOTTOM flange is in compression.** A slab on the top flange gives no restraint there at all.

> **So the region of a continuous beam most vulnerable to lateral torsional buckling is exactly the region where the slab appears to be helping and is not** — and that is why bottom-flange bracing near supports is a standard detail in continuous steel construction.

**Why each distractor is wrong:**

| Option | Note |
|---|---|
| **Only in short, deep beams with high shear** | **Backwards — it afflicts LONG, UNRESTRAINED beams. Short beams have little unrestrained length and are governed by shear instead** ← |
| **Prevented by lateral restraint of the compression flange** | ✓ |
| **Depends only on bending capacity, not span** | **Directly false — the UNRESTRAINED LENGTH is the primary variable** |
| **Cannot occur when bent about the major axis** | **Exactly inverted — major-axis bending is precisely when it DOES occur.** Minor-axis bending is not susceptible |

> **Option (d) is worth reasoning about, because the inversion is instructive: a beam bent about its MINOR axis is not susceptible**, since the section is already being bent in its weak direction and there is no weaker direction to buckle into.

> **It is major-axis bending — the efficient way to use an I-section — that creates the vulnerability.** So the mode is a penalty attached to using the section efficiently, which is why it cannot simply be avoided by choice of orientation.

**The factors that govern the resistance:**

| Factor | Effect |
|---|---|
| **UNRESTRAINED LENGTH L_LT** | **The dominant variable — resistance falls steeply as it grows** |
| **Section's TORSIONAL stiffness (GJ) and warping stiffness** | **An I-section is torsionally weak, which is why it is susceptible; a hollow section is torsionally stiff and largely immune** ← |
| **Shape of the bending moment diagram** | **A uniform moment is the worst case; a moment varying along the span is less severe** |
| **Position of the applied load** | **Load applied at the TOP flange is DESTABILISING; at the bottom flange it is stabilising** |
| End restraint conditions | Affect the effective length |

> **The hollow-section point is a real design option: a rectangular hollow section is so torsionally stiff that lateral torsional buckling essentially does not govern it**, which is why RHS beams are used for long unrestrained spans despite costing more per kilogram.

> **And the load-position effect is worth knowing because it is counter-intuitive: a load hanging from the BOTTOM flange is safer than the same load sitting on the TOP flange**, because as the beam twists, a top load moves further off-centre and drives the twist further, while a bottom load swings back and resists it.

> **That is why a crane runway beam with an underslung hoist is treated differently from one with a load on top.**

**And the design route in IS 800:2007:**

> **M_d = β_b Z_p f_bd**, where **f_bd = χ_LT f_y/γ_m₀** and **χ_LT** is the bending stress reduction factor — a function of the non-dimensional slenderness **λ_LT**, which depends on the unrestrained length.

> **For a fully restrained beam, χ_LT = 1 and the full plastic moment is available.** The whole apparatus exists to quantify how much capacity is lost when it is not.

examTip.trick: **The compression flange behaves as a slender COLUMN wanting to buckle sideways, but the web and tension flange make it TWIST as well.** Restrain the compression flange at close intervals and the effective length falls — resistance rises with the square.
examTip.trap: **It must be the COMPRESSION flange that is restrained.** In a continuous beam near a support the moment HOGS, so the BOTTOM flange is in compression — and the slab on top gives no restraint at all there.
examTip.mnemonic: **An I-section is torsionally WEAK, which is why it is susceptible; a hollow section is torsionally stiff and largely immune.** And a load on the TOP flange is DESTABILISING — it moves further off-centre as the beam twists.

questions.stem: In an unreinforced masonry wall, the SLENDERNESS RATIO is defined as the ratio of:
options: the height of the wall to its length
the length of the wall to its thickness
the effective height (or effective length, whichever is less) to the effective thickness
the wall's self-weight to the applied vertical load
questions.solution:
**The effective height or effective length, WHICHEVER IS LESS, divided by the effective thickness.**

**The definition, and why "whichever is less" is essential:**

> **SR = (the LESSER of the effective height and the effective length) ÷ effective thickness**

> **A wall can buckle in two ways: about a horizontal axis (over its height) or about a vertical axis (over its length between cross walls or piers).**

> **It will buckle in whichever direction is EASIER — that is, whichever span is SHORTER relative to the thickness.**

> **So the governing slenderness is the SMALLER of the two ratios**, and taking the lesser of the two effective dimensions is how that is expressed.

> **Options (a) and (b) each take one dimension and ignore the other**, which is precisely the error the definition guards against.

**The effective dimensions, since each is a modified value rather than the actual one:**

| Dimension | How it is modified |
|---|---|
| **EFFECTIVE HEIGHT** | **Depends on the RESTRAINT at top and bottom: 0.75H for a wall laterally supported and restrained against rotation at both ends; 1.0H for simple lateral support; up to 1.5H for a free-standing wall** |
| **EFFECTIVE LENGTH** | **Depends on the support at the vertical edges — cross walls, piers, or returns** |
| **EFFECTIVE THICKNESS** | **The actual thickness for a solid wall; for a wall with PIERS or a CAVITY wall, a modified value that credits the stiffening** |

> **The 0.75H for a properly restrained wall is the value most often used**, and it reflects the same physics as a column's effective length: **restraint against rotation at the ends reduces the effective span.**

> **And the effective thickness of a CAVITY WALL is worth noting: it is taken as two thirds of the sum of the two leaves' thicknesses**, which credits the pair for acting partly together while acknowledging that the wall ties cannot make them fully composite.

**Why slenderness matters — it controls the permissible stress:**

> **A slender wall carries LESS load than a stocky one of the same material, because it can BUCKLE.**

> **IS 1905 applies a STRESS REDUCTION FACTOR that falls with slenderness:**

| Slenderness ratio | Stress reduction factor (roughly, for axial load) |
|---|---|
| **6** | **1.0 — no reduction** |
| **12** | **~0.84** |
| **18** | **~0.63** |
| **24** | **~0.45** |
| **27 (the limit)** | **~0.33** |

> **So a wall at the slenderness limit carries only about a third of what a stocky wall of the same masonry would.** The penalty is severe, and it is the reason load-bearing masonry walls are thick.

**The maximum permitted slenderness ratios:**

| Situation | Maximum SR |
|---|---|
| **Load-bearing wall, cement or lime mortar, up to 2 storeys** | **27** |
| **Load-bearing wall, more than 2 storeys** | **24** |
| **Wall in MUD mortar** | **12** |
| Non-load-bearing partition | Higher limits apply |

> **The MUD MORTAR limit of 12 is less than half the cement-mortar value**, and the reason is worth stating: **mud mortar has negligible tensile and flexural strength, so a wall built in it has almost no capacity to resist the bending that accompanies buckling.**

> **That is directly relevant in Nepal, where a great deal of existing masonry is stone or brick in mud mortar** — and it is why NBC 203 treats low-strength masonry as a separate category with construction guidelines rather than design rules.

**Why an ECCENTRICITY interacts with slenderness, since the two are always considered together:**

> **A vertical load applied off the wall's centre line produces bending as well as compression.**

> **And a slender wall is far more sensitive to that eccentricity**, because the initial bending deflection increases the eccentricity, which increases the bending — the P-δ effect.

> **So the stress reduction factor in IS 1905 is tabulated against BOTH slenderness AND eccentricity**, and the two together can reduce the permissible stress to a small fraction of the masonry's strength.

> **The practical consequence: a floor slab bearing on only part of a wall's thickness creates an eccentricity, and on a slender wall that is a serious matter rather than a detail.** Centring the bearing, or providing a bearing pad that spreads the load, is worth real effort.

**And why option (d) can be dismissed immediately:**

> **Slenderness is a GEOMETRIC property — a ratio of two lengths, and therefore dimensionless in a specific way.**

> **A ratio of two forces (self-weight to applied load) is also dimensionless, but it says nothing about the wall's proportions** and could not predict buckling, which depends on shape.

> **Recognising that a slenderness ratio must be a ratio of LENGTHS eliminates option (d) with no knowledge of masonry at all.**

> **The same test applies to every slenderness ratio in engineering: a column's L_e/k, a beam's unrestrained length to depth, a plate's width to thickness — all are geometric.**

examTip.trick: **Take the LESSER of the effective height and effective length, over the effective thickness** — because a wall buckles in whichever direction is easier. Options (a) and (b) each ignore one of the two possibilities.
examTip.trap: **Option (d) is a ratio of FORCES.** A slenderness ratio must be a ratio of LENGTHS — a geometric property — which eliminates it without any knowledge of masonry.
examTip.mnemonic: **Maximum SR is 27 (two storeys), 24 (more), but only 12 in MUD MORTAR** — because mud has no flexural strength to resist the bending that accompanies buckling. Directly relevant to Nepal's existing masonry stock.

questions.stem: In a diversion headworks, the principal function of the DIVIDE WALL is to:
options: separate the undersluice section from the weir section, so that a still pond forms in front of the canal head regulator
raise the upstream water level so that the canal can be fed by gravity
dissipate the energy of the water passing over the weir crest
prevent the river from outflanking the structure
questions.solution:
**To separate the undersluice section from the weir section, so that a still pond forms in front of the canal head regulator.**

**What the divide wall does:**

> **A DIVIDE WALL is a masonry or concrete wall built at right angles to the weir axis**, separating the **UNDERSLUICE** portion (adjacent to the canal head regulator) from the main **WEIR** portion.

| Function | Note |
|---|---|
| **Creates a STILL POND in front of the head regulator** | **Water slows in the pocket, so SEDIMENT SETTLES there rather than entering the canal** ← the primary purpose |
| **Separates the two flow regimes** | The weir passes flood flow; the undersluices pass the low flow and the sediment |
| **Provides a straight approach to the regulator** | Reduces cross-currents and oblique flow at the intake |
| **Isolates the sluice section for scouring** | The gates can be opened to flush the pocket without disturbing the weir flow |
| Houses a road or a walkway | Incidental |

> **The STILL POND is the concept the question rests on, and the idea is elegant: the sediment problem is solved not by removing sediment but by ARRANGING FOR IT TO SETTLE SOMEWHERE ELSE and then flushing it away.**

> **Water entering the canal is drawn from the upper layers of a slow-moving pocket**, and the upper layers of slow water carry the least sediment — **because coarse sediment travels near the bed.**

**Why sediment exclusion matters so much here:**

> **A canal that admits the river's bed load will silt up**, and a silted canal has lost its capacity and must be desilted at continuing cost.

> **The whole sediment-exclusion apparatus of a headworks exists for that reason:**

| Device | What it does |
|---|---|
| **DIVIDE WALL** | **Creates the still pond; separates weir and undersluice flows** ← |
| **UNDERSLUICES** | **Low-level gated openings that pass the low flow and FLUSH the accumulated sediment downstream** |
| **SILT EXCLUDER (silt tunnels)** | **Tunnels along the bed in front of the regulator; the BOTTOM, sediment-laden layer is drawn into them and passed downstream, while the top layer enters the canal** |
| **SILT EJECTOR (extractor)** | **Placed IN the canal, downstream of the regulator — removes sediment that got in anyway** |
| Canal head regulator | Controls the discharge entering the canal |

> **The EXCLUDER/EJECTOR distinction is a favourite examination point and the naming is logical:**

> **An EXCLUDER keeps sediment OUT, and sits at the head, upstream of the regulator.**

> **An EJECTOR throws sediment OUT after it has entered, and sits in the canal downstream.**

> **Exclusion is better than ejection, because the sediment never has to be handled in the canal** — but exclusion is never complete, so many schemes have both.

**Why each distractor is wrong — and each names a real component's function:**

| Option | The component that does it |
|---|---|
| **Separate sluices from weir; create a still pond** | ✓ **DIVIDE WALL** |
| **Raise the upstream level for gravity feed** | **The WEIR itself — that is the weir's whole purpose** ← |
| **Dissipate energy below the crest** | **The CISTERN / STILLING BASIN, with baffle blocks and an end sill** |
| **Prevent outflanking** | **GUIDE BANKS (Bell's bunds) — and the marginal embankments** ← |

> **Option (d) is the most substantive distractor and the one worth separating carefully**, because guide banks and divide walls are both walls associated with a headworks:

| | **DIVIDE WALL** | **GUIDE BANK** |
|---|---|---|
| **Orientation** | **PERPENDICULAR to the weir axis, projecting upstream and downstream** | **Roughly PARALLEL to the flow, upstream and downstream of the abutments** |
| **Purpose** | **Separate flow regimes; create a still pond for SEDIMENT control** | **Guide the river into the waterway and prevent OUTFLANKING** |
| **Length** | A few tens of metres | **1.25 L upstream, 0.25 L downstream** |
| **Located** | **Between the undersluice bay and the weir bay** | **At the ends of the structure** |

> **So one is INSIDE the structure managing sediment, and the other is OUTSIDE it managing the river's course.** Both are walls, and their functions do not overlap.

**The components of a diversion headworks, gathered, since the question is drawn from the list:**

| Component | Function |
|---|---|
| **WEIR or BARRAGE** | **RAISE the water level to command the canal** |
| **UNDERSLUICES** | Pass low flow; flush sediment |
| **DIVIDE WALL** | **Separate the two; create the still pond** ← |
| **CANAL HEAD REGULATOR** | **Control the discharge entering the canal** |
| **SILT EXCLUDER** | Keep bed load out of the canal |
| **FISH LADDER** | **Allow fish to migrate past the barrier** |
| **GUIDE BANKS** | Guide the river; prevent outflanking |
| **MARGINAL EMBANKMENTS** | Confine the pond; protect adjoining land |
| **CISTERN / stilling basin, launching apron** | **Dissipate energy; resist scour** |
| Impervious floor, cut-offs | Resist uplift and piping |

> **The FISH LADDER is worth naming because it is the one component with a purely environmental purpose**, and it is the one most often omitted or built badly.

> **A weir is a complete barrier to migratory fish**, and in rivers where migration matters the ladder is not a decoration. **Its design — a series of pools with small drops between them, sized so that fish can ascend each in one movement — is a genuine hydraulic problem, and a ladder with drops too large is an expensive ornament.**

> **Which is a fair example of a wider point: a headworks is a system of components each solving one problem the others create**, and understanding the list means understanding what each was added to fix.

examTip.trick: **The divide wall creates a STILL POND in front of the head regulator**, so sediment settles there and the canal draws from the cleaner upper layers. The sediment is then flushed by the undersluices.
examTip.trap: **Option (d) belongs to GUIDE BANKS.** A divide wall runs PERPENDICULAR to the weir, inside the structure, managing sediment; guide banks run parallel to the flow, outside it, managing the river's course.
examTip.mnemonic: **EXCLUDER keeps sediment OUT (at the head, upstream of the regulator); EJECTOR throws it OUT after entry (in the canal).** Exclusion beats ejection, but is never complete — so many schemes have both.

questions.stem: In hydropower planning, the FIRM (primary) power of a plant is:
options: the maximum power the plant can generate at any instant
the average power generated over a year
the power corresponding to the installed capacity of the machines
the power that can be guaranteed to be available at all times, corresponding to the minimum dependable flow
questions.solution:
**The power that can be guaranteed at all times, corresponding to the minimum dependable flow.**

**The definitions, which the four options are drawn from:**

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **FIRM (primary) power** | **The power available at ALL times, based on the MINIMUM DEPENDABLE FLOW — what can be promised** ← |
| **SECONDARY power** | **The power available IN EXCESS of firm power, when the flow is greater than the minimum — available only part of the time** |
| **INSTALLED capacity** | **The nameplate rating of the machines — what the equipment could produce if the water were there** |
| **AVERAGE power** | Total annual energy divided by the hours in the year |
| **PEAK power** | The maximum output at any instant |

> **Firm power is the quantity that can be SOLD UNDER A FIRM CONTRACT**, and that is why it exists as a separate concept: **a buyer paying for guaranteed supply is buying firm power, and everything above it is sold, if at all, on an interruptible basis at a lower price.**

**Why firm power is small in Nepal, and why that is the central fact of the topic:**

> **Firm power depends on the MINIMUM flow, not the average.**

> **Roughly 80 per cent of Nepal's annual runoff arrives in the four monsoon months.** A river's dry-season flow can be a small fraction of its monsoon flow.

| Plant type | Firm power relative to installed capacity |
|---|---|
| **RUN-OF-RIVER, no pondage** | **LOW — set by the driest period's flow, sometimes 20-30 % of installed capacity** ← |
| **Run-of-river with pondage** | Somewhat higher — daily peaking possible |
| **STORAGE plant** | **HIGH — the reservoir converts monsoon flow into dry-season energy** |

> **So a run-of-river plant may have a large installed capacity and a small firm power**, and the two numbers describe quite different things.

> **That mismatch is why comparing Nepali hydropower projects by MEGAWATTS is misleading**, and it is worth stating plainly: **a 40 MW run-of-river plant and a 40 MW storage plant are not comparable assets.** The first delivers most of its energy when the system already has a surplus; the second delivers when the system is short.

> **And it is why STORAGE is the strategic gap in Nepal's system**: storage is precisely the mechanism that converts secondary power into firm power. **With essentially one storage plant (Kulekhani), the country's firm capacity is far below its installed capacity.**

**How the dependable flow is defined, since firm power rests on it:**

> **The design flow is taken from a FLOW DURATION CURVE — a plot of discharge against the percentage of time that discharge is equalled or exceeded.**

| Exceedance | Meaning | Use |
|---|---|---|
| **Q₁₀₀ (minimum recorded)** | Available 100 % of the time | Absolute firm power |
| **Q₉₅** | **Available 95 % of the time** | **A common basis for FIRM power** ← |
| **Q₅₀ (median)** | Available half the time | — |
| **Q₄₀ or Q₃₀** | **Available 30-40 % of the time** | **A common basis for the DESIGN (installed) capacity** |

> **The choice of design exceedance is the central economic decision in planning a run-of-river plant.**

> **A plant sized on Q₉₅ runs at full output almost always and wastes the monsoon flow.** A plant sized on Q₃₀ captures far more monsoon energy but sits part-loaded for much of the year.

> **The optimum maximises the value of the energy generated less the cost of the capacity installed**, and since monsoon energy is worth less than dry-season energy, the answer is not simply "capture as much as possible".

> **So the flow duration curve is not a piece of hydrology attached to the design — it IS the design decision**, and reading it correctly is the planner's principal skill.

**Why the other options are wrong, and each names a real quantity:**

| Option | What it is |
|---|---|
| **Maximum power at any instant** | **PEAK power** — limited by the machines, not by the dependable flow |
| **Average power over a year** | **AVERAGE power** — total energy ÷ 8760 h; larger than firm power |
| **Power corresponding to installed capacity** | **INSTALLED (nameplate) capacity — what the plant COULD do, not what it can guarantee** ← the closest distractor |
| **Guaranteed at all times, at minimum dependable flow** | ✓ **FIRM power** |

> **Option (c) is the well-made distractor because installed capacity is the number always quoted publicly.** It is a statement about the MACHINES; firm power is a statement about the WATER. **A plant can have any installed capacity the owner chooses to buy; its firm power is set by the river.**

> **The relation between them: installed capacity ≥ peak power ≥ average power ≥ firm power**, and the gaps between those four numbers describe the plant's character completely.

**And the terms that complete the vocabulary:**

| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **PONDAGE** | **Small storage, for DAILY or weekly regulation — lets a run-of-river plant meet the evening peak** |
| **STORAGE** | **Large reservoir, for SEASONAL regulation — moves monsoon water into the dry season** |
| **Load factor** | Average load ÷ peak load |
| **Capacity factor** | Average load ÷ installed capacity |
| **Utilisation factor** | Peak load ÷ installed capacity |

> **The PONDAGE/STORAGE distinction is the one with the most practical weight: pondage shifts water by HOURS, storage by MONTHS.**

> **Pondage is cheap and often available — a small forebay or a widened headrace can provide it — and it converts a plant that generates flat output into one that can meet the evening peak**, which is worth a great deal because peak energy commands the highest price.

> **So pondage is frequently the cheapest available improvement to a run-of-river scheme's revenue**, and it is worth considering even where seasonal storage is impossible.

examTip.trick: **Firm power depends on the MINIMUM dependable flow, not the average** — it is what can be promised under a firm contract. Everything above it is SECONDARY power, saleable only on an interruptible basis.
examTip.trap: **Option (c) installed capacity is the number always quoted publicly** — but that is a statement about the MACHINES, while firm power is a statement about the WATER. Installed ≥ peak ≥ average ≥ firm.
examTip.mnemonic: **Read firm power from the FLOW DURATION CURVE — commonly Q₉₅ — while installed capacity is often sized on Q₃₀-Q₄₀.** Choosing that exceedance IS the design decision. And **pondage shifts water by HOURS, storage by MONTHS.**
